## Dīgha Nikāya ## Sīlakkhandhavagga Abhinavaṭīkā ## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. ## Introduction to the Text

The Buddha, having preached the profound, hard-to-see, and noble True Dhamma, and seeing the long future, established the Sāsana to endure for a long time. (1)

I pay homage to that Buddha—who is skilled in the inclinations of those to be disciplined (veneyya), who possesses great wisdom and great compassion, and who is the object of reverence—together with the True Dhamma and the multitude of the Saṅgha. (2)

There is a commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) on the noble Dīgha Nikāya which was included in the three councils; the explanation of that commentary is well-praised by the wise. (3)

It was well-composed by the teacher Dhammapāla Thera, clarifying the subtle, profound, and hard-to-see meanings. (4)

Although that old sub-commentary (ṭīkā) is correct in its nature, because it has been handed down through succession, there are many errors in writing, both in terms of the text (Pāḷi) and the meaning. (5)

Because of its brevity, it is also very difficult for listeners to understand well; therefore, recollecting the request of my fellow practitioners, (6)

there is a Great King (King Bodawpaya), the lord of many white elephants, the ruler of various countries, whose mind is always striving to purify the Sāsana. (7)

Relying on that King, and thinking, "May this work of mine also be a support in illuminating the Sāsana of the Teacher," (8)
2:
9. I shall begin this explanation (sub-commentary), based on the meaning of that [old sub-commentary] and also other methods as appropriate, with definitive judgment and without diminishing the sense.

10. Listen with a concentrated mind to this work named "Sādhuvilāsinī," which delights the minds of the wise who desire the growth of the Wheel of the Sāsana and pleases the hearts of the virtuous.

## Explanation of the Introductory Verses

Desiring to compose this Commentary (named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī) which clarifies the profound and difficult-to-understand meanings of the noble Dīgha Nikāya (Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi)—which is a collection of the three trainings that are subtle, profound, and diverse through various methods; which is explained by the Buddha and the Arahats who understood the Buddha's teaching; and which is endowed with qualities that inspire faith—this teacher (Buddhaghosa), who is a great grammarian capable of penetrating the thicket of his own and other doctrines, first uttered the verse beginning with "Karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ" in order to pay homage to the Triple Gem at the start of the commentary and to state the purpose of that homage.

Regarding this, the teachers of the commentaries and sub-commentaries have extensively explained the purpose of paying homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of a work in various places. Thus they explain:

"Paying homage to the Teacher at the beginning of a commentary is for the purpose of generating faith in the Teacher because the Dhamma is well-expounded, and for generating faith in the Dhamma by demonstrating that the Teacher's teaching is unerring. Through faith in both [the Teacher and the Dhamma], the accomplishment of great benefit (both mundane and supramundane) occurs." (Thus it is stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Mūlaṭīkā).

Alternatively: "The utterance of homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of making known one's own devotion to the Triple Gem; that making known is to please the minds of the wise; that pleasing is to encourage the study of the commentary; and that study is for the accomplishment of all success and prosperity."

Alternatively: "Homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of a commentary is for the purpose of making known the purity of the source (the Buddha) of the Dhamma to be explained; that making known is to generate great respect among the wise for the explanation of the Dhamma; and that respect is for the accomplishment of all welfare and happiness through the right practice obtained in the sequence of proper learning, memorizing, and so forth by those wise ones."

Alternatively: "The act of paying homage to the Triple Gem in a commentary is performed because it is auspicious, because it is the preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it is well-practiced by the wise, and for the purpose of setting an example for future generations to follow."

Alternatively: "For one who wishes to explain the Dhamma-Vinaya endowed with the fourfold profundity, great fear may arise even if one possesses swift and sharp wisdom, like one entering the great ocean. And this [homage to the Triple Gem] is a means of removing that fear..."
3: The arrangement of paying homage and worship, which arises from the repeated recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem, and the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the commentary because of such worship, [is performed]. Alternatively, it is the act of paying homage in the commentary for the purpose of establishing the recognition of the Teacher in the Truly and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha as He really is, for the sake of the world which attributes the status of Teacher even to those who are not teachers; for the purpose of making them abandon the recognition of teacherhood in those who are not teachers; and for the purpose of avoiding the fault stated as: 'Having learned the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he holds it as his own.' Alternatively, it is the act of paying homage in the commentary for the purpose of inspiring effort in those practicing the Buddha-vehicle to attain the state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha through the arrangement of paying homage to the Buddha, the Blessed One; for the purpose of inspiring effort in those practicing the Paccekabuddha-vehicle to attain the state of a Paccekabuddha through the arrangement of paying homage to the True Dhamma; and for the purpose of inspiring effort in those practicing the Disciple-vehicle to attain the state of the ultimate Saṅgha through the arrangement of paying homage to the Saṅgha. Alternatively, it is the act of paying homage in the commentary for the purpose of satisfying the minds of those who hold the view that treatises beginning with auspiciousness are free from obstacles, long-lasting, and highly esteemed. Alternatively, it is the act of paying homage in the commentary for the purpose of enabling the listeners to accomplish the learning and retention [of the teaching] without obstacles through the aforementioned homage. Indeed, making the benefit of the listeners the primary concern, teachers place sentences illustrating praise and homage at the beginning of a commentary. Otherwise, even without placing them, since the desired purpose can be achieved merely through the homage of body and mind, why write these sentences that make the text heavy? Such things are said. We, however, shall show only the purpose intended here. Therefore, it should be understood that the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the commentary is for the purpose of completing the promised commentary without obstacles. This very purpose is what the Teacher intends here. For he will say later: 'Thus, I, with a clear mind... through the power of that [Triple Gem]...' and so on. In fact, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the promised commentary without obstacles because the worship of the Triple Gem results in the sharpening of wisdom, and that sharpening of wisdom comes from the dispelling of impurities such as lust. For it has been said: 'Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is simply upright,' and so on.
4: Therefore, through the worship of the Triple Gem, or through the meritorious intention of homage which is the worship of the collective Triple Gem, the sharpening of wisdom, which has been cleansed of the impurities of defilements, is accomplished. Alternatively, because the worship of the Triple Gem is the cause of concentration, which is the proximate cause of wisdom, the sharpening of wisdom arises. This statement is true; the Blessed One taught this in the Mahānāma Sutta: 'Mahānāma, a noble disciple whose meritorious mind is thus upright gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.' That concentration is the proximate cause of wisdom has also been stated by the Blessed One: 'One who is concentrated knows things as they really are.' With wisdom that has thus clearly arisen, overcoming the weariness of body and mind, he will bring the promised commentary to completion. Therefore, I said: 'The act of paying homage to the Triple Gem... because of the state of sharpened wisdom.' Alternatively, it should be understood that through the worship of the Triple Gem, because of the increase in life, beauty, happiness, and strength, the work is completed without obstacles. Through the homage to the Triple Gem, life, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. This statement is true; the Blessed One has said: 'For one who is habitually respectful, who always honors the elders, four qualities increase: life, beauty, happiness, and strength.' Intending that 'through the increase of life, beauty, happiness, and strength, may the completion of the work be achieved,' it is said: 'Through the worship of the Triple Gem, life... and so on, should be understood.' Alternatively, it should be understood that the worship of the Triple Gem brings about the non-decline of wisdom, and thus completion without obstacles. The worship of the Triple Gem brings about non-decline. This statement is true; the Blessed One has said: 'Monks, these seven are the conditions that lead to non-decline. What seven? Respect for the Teacher, respect for the Dhamma, respect for the Saṅgha, respect for the Training, respect for Concentration, having good friends, and being easy to admonish.' Intending that 'through the non-decline of wisdom, may the completion be achieved as promised,' it is said: 'Ratanattaya... and so on, should be understood.' Alternatively, it should be understood that worship of the objects of faith, namely the Triple Gem, leads to completion without obstacles because of the excellence of merit. Worship of the objects of faith is the excellence of merit. This statement is true; the Blessed One has said in the Apadāna Pali:
5:
For one who honors those worthy of honor—the Buddhas or their noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) who have transcended the conceptual proliferations (papañca) of craving, conceit, and wrong view, and who have crossed over sorrow and lamentation—for one who honors such ones who have extinguished the defilements and are fearless for any reason, no one is able to calculate the momentum of merit arising from such worship, even by means of great power, saying 'it is this much.'

Such an abundance of merit is also the cause for the fulfillment of desired aims. Regarding this, it was said: 'This treasure-store of merit provides all desires to devas and humans; whatever worldly or transcendental prosperity they long for, all that is obtained by this treasure-store of merit.'

It has been stated that for one who practices the worship of the Triple Gem, which is the cause of fulfilling benefits, the completion of the work undertaken will surely occur: 'In the objects of devotion... it should be understood.' Thus, because the worship of the Triple Gem arises from the peerless field of merit, the Enlightened One, it results in an abundance of merit with inconceivable power. Therefore, it is capable of destroying all defilements that bind one to dangers in this world of many hazards, and it wards off calamities such as fear. Thus, it is well said: 'It should be understood that performing the salutation to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the commentary is for the purpose of completing the promised commentary without obstacles.'

The commentator, wishing to perform this beneficial salutation to the Triple Gem, first offers salutation to the Buddha Gem with the verses beginning 'Whose heart is cooled by compassion... who is liberated from the realms of rebirth,' because the Buddha Gem is the root of the remaining Gems. Indeed, the Dhamma Gem and the Sangha Gem have the Buddha Gem as their root. This fact should be clarified by the analogies found in the commentaries, such as: 'The Blessed One is like the full moon; the Dhamma taught by him is like the mass of moonlight; the Sangha is like the world delighted and nourished by the moonlight.'

Alternatively, the Buddha is mentioned first because he is supreme among all beings. The Dhamma is mentioned immediately after him because it originates from and was taught by that Buddha. The Sangha is mentioned immediately after the Dhamma because they are the repository of that Dhamma and they frequent and practice it. According to the method in the commentaries: 'The Buddha is mentioned first because he directs all beings toward their welfare; the Dhamma is mentioned next because it is the welfare of all beings; the Sangha is mentioned next because they practice to attain that welfare and have attained it.' Thus, the sequence should be understood.
6:
The commentator, in performing the salutation to the Buddha Gem, considers that a salutation preceded by praise is far superior to a mere salutation. Thus, he demonstrates the nature of a salutation preceded by praise with the words beginning 'Karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.' Indeed, through a salutation preceded by praise, the connection with the Exalted One's extraordinary qualities is shown; from that, his state of being matchlessly worthy of worship; because of that worthiness, the fact that one's own salutation has reached the 'good field' (khetta) of the Buddha Gem; and because of reaching that good field, the fact that the salutation is the cause for the fulfillment of the desired aim is demonstrated.

The teacher, demonstrating the nature of being preceded by praise, intends to comment on this Suttanta teaching, which is characterized by both compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā). It is not primarily characterized by compassion alone like the Vinaya teaching, nor primarily by wisdom alone like the Abhidhamma teaching. Thus, he undertakes the praise characterized by both. It is the nature of the teacher to offer praise in accordance with the work he is about to undertake. Therefore, at the start of the commentary on the Vinaya teaching, he undertook praise primarily characterized by compassion: 'He who, even through billions of aeons... to that Great Compassionate One.' At the start of the commentary on the Abhidhamma teaching, he undertook praise primarily characterized by wisdom: 'Like compassion... as desired.'

The reason is that in the Vinaya teaching, out of pure Great Compassion and without regard for the inclinations (āsaya) of those to be disciplined, the Buddha established training rules (sikkhāpada) while listening to words that ordinary beings should not listen to, asking questions that should not be asked, and speaking words that should not be spoken; thus, it is primarily characterized by compassion. This is indeed true: even the Blessed One, who possessed the highest moral shame and dread (hiri-ottappa), spoke in the midst of the great assembly words such as 'sikharani' and 'sambhinna'—which are avoided even by worldly virtuous people—as well as words of reproach according to the offense, because his mind was urged by Great Compassion. Out of regard for the reason for prescribing those various training rules, he also experienced physical exhaustion in places like Verañjā.

Therefore, although wisdom is extremely active in establishing Vinaya rules because of its unique nature—just as wisdom is extremely active in teaching the specific planes (bhūmi), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and various doctrines—the function of Great Compassion is even more prominent than that of wisdom. Thus, the Vinaya teaching is said to be primarily characterized by compassion. Because the activity of Great Compassion is predominant, the teaching is called compassion-led. The Abhidhamma teaching, however, is primarily characterized by wisdom alone, because wisdom functions preeminently there in its capacity to penetrate the true nature of ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma). The Suttanta teaching is characterized by both compassion and wisdom, because both wisdom—capable of discerning the various differences in beings' inclinations (āsaya), latent tendencies (anusaya), dispositions (adhimutti), and temperaments (carita)—and Great Compassion toward beings function preeminently in that teaching. For in the Suttanta teaching, the Blessed One, frequently entering the attainment of Great Compassion, [discerns] in the continuities of those to be disciplined...
7: The Blessed One established deep meanings in accordance with the dispositions of those to be led. Therefore, it should be understood that he offered praise primarily based on compassion and wisdom, consistent with the initial teaching. This is the collective meaning (samudāyattha) here. As for the analytical meaning (avayavattha): it is called compassion (karuṇā) because it dispels the suffering of others, or because it removes it by making the cause of suffering deficient. Alternatively, it is called compassion because it is extended toward those who are suffering. Or, according to the root 'kiṇāti', it is called compassion because it afflicts the compassionate person when others suffer, or because it destroys the suffering of others. Or, it is called compassion because it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble when others suffer. Alternatively, 'kaṃ' means happiness; it is called compassion because it obstructs that happiness. This compassion has the characteristic of desiring to remove the suffering of others, and because it disregards one's own happiness, it obstructs the happiness of the compassionate. In all instances, the derivation of the word should be understood according to the science of grammar. It is called 'sīta' (cool) because it is sought by those oppressed by heat, or because it quenches heat. Because it takes up that coolness, it is called 'sītala'. In the passage, 'I will throw down your mind, or I will split your heart,' 'hadaya' refers to the chest. In 'the kidney, the heart,' it refers to the heart-base (hadayavatthu). In 'knowing another's mind with one's own mind,' it refers to the mind. Here too, 'hadaya' refers to the mind in the sense of the internal state. Alternatively, it is called 'hadaya' because it carries its own nature; etymologists say the letter 'ra' is changed to 'da'. One who has a heart cooled by compassion is 'karuṇāsītalahadaya'. Although it is true that loving-kindness (mettā) and appreciative joy (muditā) also cause coolness of mind—since they have the nature of bringing welfare and not falling away from the happiness of others, directly oppose ill-will, and function by cutting off the fever within the continuity of beings—nevertheless, because it functions by removing the suffering of others, has the function of not enduring the affliction of others, and is of the nature of non-cruelty, compassion alone is specifically the cause for the coolness of the Buddha's mind, like the tranquility of the mind. Therefore, compassion alone is stated as the cause of the mind's coolness. Alternatively, by mentioning compassion as the primary factor, the coolness of mind due to loving-kindness and appreciative joy is also understood to be stated. This is because, although the absolute meaning is not indicated in every instance, one takes what is available through methods such as the primary method (padhāna-naya), the method of association (sahacaraṇa-naya), and the method of inseparability (avinābhāva-naya). Furthermore, because the knowledge associated with that compassion is included within the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), it is superlative and exhaustive, being the basis for the distinction of uncommon knowledge...
8: Just as omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) pervades its own object, Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) also pervades its own object. Thus, having reached the state of Great Compassion and attained a superlative state unshared by others, compassion alone is stated as the cause for the coolness of the heart. Alternatively, although loving-kindness and appreciative joy—having the nature of bringing welfare to others and not falling away from their happiness—are connected to the superlative coolness of the heart, compassion is the cause of even those qualities, as it is the cause of all the Buddha's special virtues. Therefore, compassion alone is stated as the cause of the heart's coolness. Indeed, all the Buddha's virtues have compassion as their source. For the Blessed One, whose fever of the suffering of saṃsāra was quenched by the power of compassion, and who desired to remove the suffering of others, spent many incalculable aeons without weariness, devoted to fulfilling the requisites for Buddhahood without remainder. Having attained the sovereignty of the Dhamma, even when the causes of heart-affliction brought about by the masses of beings were present, his mental coolness did not undergo even the slightest change. Among the three interpretations presented here, in the first interpretation, compassion in the stage of Buddhahood without distinction should be taken. In the second, compassion that has reached the state of Great Compassion. In the third, the Buddha's compassion occurring in all three stages, starting from the initial aspiration for Buddhahood, should be understood as included. It is called wisdom (paññā) because it knows in various ways. The meaning is that it penetrates the true nature of things in various ways. Alternatively, it is called wisdom because it makes others know; it means it makes the respective meaning clear. That wisdom itself is called the 'light of wisdom' (paññāpajjota) because it can abandon the hindrance of the ignorable and because it illuminates the nature of things in various ways. For a wise person, even while sitting on a single seat, the ten-thousandfold world system is illuminated at once. For it was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. Which four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the four lights. The best of these four lights, bhikkhus, is the light of wisdom.' Because it is specifically destroyed by that light of wisdom, it is called 'paññāpajjotavihata' (destroyed by the light of wisdom); the specific nature of this will be made clear later. It is called delusion (moha) or ignorance (avijjā) because one is confused by it, or it is confused itself, or it is just the state of being confused. That delusion is called 'mohatama' (the darkness of delusion) because it is like darkness in concealing the true nature of objects. Although the word 'tama' (darkness) can directly signify ignorance without the need for a metaphor, since it is used in conjunction with the word 'moha', it is appropriate here to treat it as a metaphor to specify it. Destroyed by the light of wisdom.
9:
The darkness of delusion exists for that Blessed One; therefore, that Blessed One is called 'paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo'. That Blessed One is so called because the darkness of delusion has been specifically dispelled by the light of the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship.

Do not all Arahants also have the darkness of ignorance dispelled by the light of the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship? If so, why is the Blessed One praised with a quality that is shared with others (not unique)? It is because His abandonment of ignorance along with the latent tendencies (vāsanā) is a unique quality not shared with others. For although all Arahants have the darkness of ignorance dispelled by the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship, just as there is a difference in the abandonment of defilements between those liberated by wisdom (paññā-vimutta) and those liberated by faith (saddhā-vimutta), so too the abandonment of defilements along with latent tendencies by the Fully Enlightened Buddhas is particularly superior to that of the Disciples (sāvakas) and Paccekabuddhas.

Alternatively, He is to be praised specifically as 'paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo' because He achieved the ultimate removal of the darkness of ignorance within His own continuity by Himself without the instruction of others; because He attained mastery (vasībhāva) over omniscience and the Powers (balas) therein; and because He can perfectly cause the removal of the darkness of ignorance in the continuities of others through the supreme power of His Dhamma teaching. In this second interpretation, by the term 'paññāpajjota' (lamp of wisdom), both 'penetrative wisdom' (paṭivedha-paññā) which destroys delusion in one's own continuity, and 'teaching wisdom' (desanā-paññā) which destroys delusion in the continuities of others, are included either by way of general designation (sāmañña-niddesa) or by the method of 'ekasesa'. It should be understood that it is not only penetrative wisdom that is to be taken, as in the first interpretation.

Another method: Because the Blessed One's knowledge reaches the limit of all knowable things (ñeyya), and because the darkness of delusion which covers the nature of all knowable things has been dispelled by the light of wisdom called 'unobstructed knowledge' (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), which is capable of realizing the nature of all knowable things, the Blessed One is praised for the quality of having dispelled the darkness of delusion by the light of wisdom that is unobstructed knowledge, which is not shared with others. In this interpretation, however, because it leads to the destruction of the darkness of delusion, unobstructed knowledge is to be understood as the 'destruction of the darkness of delusion' in one's own continuity by way of 'metonymy of the cause' (kāraṇūpacāra). Indeed, the abandonment of defilements along with latent tendencies due to the perfection of the initial resolve (abhinīhāra) is itself the abandonment of the 'obstruction to the knowable' (ñeyyāvaraṇa). Furthermore, because it is the cause of destroying the darkness of delusion in the continuities of others, unobstructed knowledge itself is called the 'destruction of the darkness of delusion' by way of 'metonymy of the effect' (phalūpacāra). Unobstructed knowledge is indeed omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) itself, by which He performs the teaching of Dhamma and reflection. These two knowledges are one in essence. Because of having as their object the conditioned (saṅkhata), the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and conventional designations (sammuti-paññatti) without remainder—
11:
The word 'garu' occurs in the sense of parents and teachers; in things difficult to endure (or difficult to do); in objects that are not light (heavy); in great matters; in fame and renown; in the exercise of subtle skill and so forth; and also in special characters (long vowels).

In this context, however, [the word 'garu' occurs] in reference to the Buddha, who is the teacher of the entire world. Some teachers, taking 'garu' and 'guru' as two forms, say that the word 'garu' expresses the meaning of heaviness (bhāriya), while the word 'guru' expresses the meaning of teacher. That [view] should not be accepted. In the sphere of the Pali language, the word 'garu' alone should be desired to express all the aforementioned meanings. This is because the derivative (taddhita) term 'gārava' is seen with the strengthening (vuddhi) of the letter 'a' to 'ā'. In the sphere of the Sanskrit language, however, the word 'guru' alone should be desired, as other derivative terms [such as gaurava] are seen through the strengthening of the letter 'u' [to 'o'].

That world which exists together with humans and gods is called 'sanaramaraloka'. Because he is the teacher of that world, he is called 'sanaramaralokagaru'. Some also recite it as 'sanaramarūlokagaru'. Such a recitation is also appropriate, both according to the metrical requirements (vuttilakkhaṇa) of the Ariyā verse and according to the meaning. In terms of meaning, although gods are long-lived, they are called 'marū' (those who die) because they are subject to death according to their allotted lifespan. By this, it is shown that the Buddha is a benefactor to other beings as well, just as he is to gods and humans, by bringing about special qualities as appropriate.

Here, one might ask: "Since gods and humans are the primary [beings], why are they indicated as if they were secondary?" [The answer is:] Because they should be taken as primary in terms of meaning. Since the order of words is one thing and the order of meaning is another, one should not object to the status of being primary or secondary based solely on the word order. In such compound words (samāsa), even the primary [element] is indicated as if it were secondary, as in the phrase "with the assembly including the king" (sarājikāya parisāya) [where the king is primary but appears subordinate]. Therefore, in all places, one should seek the intended meaning through the sense (attha) and not merely through the phrasing (byañjana). The ancient teachers said this:

"The Great Sage, the Protector who seeks the welfare of the world, declared the meaning as the refuge, not the phrasing. Therefore, a wise person, not taking delight in the letters, should apply his intellect to the meaning alone."

In this context, although there are three types of worlds—the world of beings (sattaloka), the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka)—the meaning should be taken only by way of the world of beings, as it is capable of being revered, which is the intended sense of "teacher." It is called 'loka' (world) because in that world of beings, wholesome and unwholesome [actions] and their results (vipāka) are seen.
12:
Those skilled in linguistics (sadda-vidū) maintain that it is called 'loka' because merit, demerit, and their results are seen (lokīyanti) therein. And here, by the mention of 'amara' (immortals), the devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva) are intended. Another way: here the word 'loka' expresses the sense of a group (samūha), because it is perceived and designated as a collective. Because they exist together with humans (nara), they are called 'sanara'; those very ones are 'amara' because they are free from death; their group is the 'sanarāmaraloka'. It should be construed in the same way as the previous method. Here, by the word 'amara', the devas of purity (visuddhi-deva) are also included along with the devas by rebirth. This is because those devas of purity are also called 'amara' because, in the ultimate sense, they have no death. However, in these various interpretations, only humans and devas are taken by way of an eminent designation (ukkaṭṭha-niddesa), as in the teaching 'teacher of devas and humans' (satthā devamanussānaṃ).

Indeed, because he is preceded by the abandonment of all harm, because he is dedicated to providing complete welfare and happiness, because he is endowed with unsurpassed success in effort (payoga-sampatti), because he is extremely helpful to the generation of beings including devas and humans, and because he is endowed with immeasurable and incomparable power and attributes, the Blessed One is the most excellent of all beings and is the peerless, unique object of reverence (teacher) for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems. Although the Blessed One is indeed a teacher to be honored by women as well because he is a benefactor to them in the same way, it should be understood that he is spoken of in the masculine gender to show the world in its primary aspect. Teachers of linguistics desire such a designation in a general context where no distinction is made, just as it is taught: 'Humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas, having paid homage, departed.' So it has been said: 'It should be known that a word is indicated by the neuter gender or the masculine gender when a general sense is determined without distinction.'

Regarding the word 'vande' (I worship): although the word 'vand' can occur in the three tenses/moods of present (vattamānā), imperative (pañcamī), and optative (sattamī), here it is only the present tense because others are not possible. And in that present tense, the meaning should be taken in the first person (uttama-purisa) as 'I worship'. Teachers desire the word 'vand' in the senses of paying homage (namana) and praising (thuti); therefore, it should be construed by supplying the word 'Sugata' or 'Nātha'. He is called 'Sugata' because he has a beautiful going (gata). Here, 'going' is of two kinds: physical going and intellectual going. Physical going is also of two kinds: approaching those to be guided (vineyya-jana) and natural walking. The Blessed One's approaching those to be guided is truly beautiful because it definitely brings about their welfare and happiness. Likewise, his natural walking is also faultless because his physical body is adorned with the major and minor marks, and although it is associated with the special qualities of extensive compassion, mindfulness, and energy...
13:
Because He brings about welfare and happiness, His going is beautiful; therefore, that Blessed One is called 'Sugata'. In this context, 'going' is of two kinds: the going of the body and the going of knowledge. Among these, the going of the body is again of two kinds: approaching those to be guided (veneyya) and natural gait. The Blessed One's approaching of the veneyya is truly beautiful because it definitely brings about their welfare and happiness. Furthermore, because He possesses a physical body (rūpakāya) adorned with the eighty minor marks and the major marks, His natural gait is free from defects such as the gait of a messenger, dragging the feet, stumbling, limping, shuffling, treading on heels, crookedness, or agitation; it is a natural gait that puts to shame the gait of a royal swan, a noble bull, a lordly elephant, or a lion king. Also, the going of knowledge, which is endowed with special qualities such as pure and vast compassion, mindfulness, and energy, is beautiful because it has been faultless from the time of the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) until reaching the Great Bodhi; thus He is called 'Sugata'.

Alternatively, He is called 'Sugata' because He has known well (avagata) the entire world through the power of penetration by full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) with His self-evolved knowledge (sayam-bhū ñāṇa). Indeed, the word with the sense of 'going' (gati) also has the sense of 'knowing' (buddhi). Likewise, He is called 'Sugata' because He has well transcended (atīta) the world by abandoning the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), the cause of the world, through the power of penetration by abandoning (pahānābhisamaya), bringing it to the state of non-arising. He is called 'Sugata' because He has well attained (adhigata) Nibbāna, the cessation of the world, through the power of penetration by realization (sacchikiriyābhisamaya). He is called 'Sugata' because He has well practiced (paṭipanna) the path leading to the cessation of the world through the power of penetration by development (bhāvanābhisamaya). This meaning should be clarified by the method of the Mahāniddesa: 'He does not return, does not go back, does not come again to those defilements which have been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry,' and so on.

Another way: He is called 'Sugata' because He has reached (adhigata) the excellent Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or Nibbāna itself. Or, He is called 'Sugata' because He speaks (gadati) well—truthful, beneficial, and timely words—to the veneyya who are to be tamed (by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta', 'Sugada' becomes 'Sugata'). The specific states of existence to be reached due to wholesome and unwholesome kamma are called 'gati' (destinations). These destinations are fivefold, beginning with hell. Because the Blessed One has averted all kamma leading to existence by making it incapable of yielding results through the attainment of the Ariyan Path, He is disconnected from those five destinations and is liberated; thus He is called 'Gativimutta' (Released from Destinations). Indeed, the devas who reach higher and higher existences are liberated from those respective existences only when the time for the result of that particular kamma ends, but they are liberated only momentarily; they are not liberated by way of disconnection (visaññoga), and they are still included within the destinations (gati) because the kamma leading to those respective existences has not been averted by the Ariyan Path. The Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One is liberated by being disconnected in the manner aforementioned. Therefore, this term shows that the Blessed One is not included in any destination whatsoever. For this reason, the Blessed One is called 'Devātideva' (God of gods). That is why He said to the brahmin Doṇa in the Aṅguttara Nikāya:

'Those taints (āsavas) by which I might become a deva, or become a gandhabba flying in the sky, those taints by which I might reach the state of a yakkha or arrive at the state of a human—those taints are destroyed by me, demolished, and rendered like uprooted stalks.'

This statement is perfectly consistent with the fact that He abandoned the kamma and defilements that cause birth in various destinations at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree.
14:
“Those taints (āsavas) by which rebirth as a deva might occur for me, or the state of a gandhabba deity flying in the sky might occur, those taints by which I might reach the state of a yakkha or arrive at the state of a human—those taints have been entirely destroyed by me, demolished, and rendered like uprooted stalks” (as taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya). Because the kamma and defilements leading to those respective destinations (gati) were abandoned by the Path of Arahatship at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, there is no longer any inclusion in those destinations for the Blessed One. Therefore, the Blessed One is absolutely liberated from all existences (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), and groups of beings (sattanikāya). Alternatively, He is certainly liberated from those destinations by the Nibbāna element with remainder (saupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). However, since that meaning is already included in the phrase 'paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ' (who has destroyed the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom), it should be understood that with this term 'gativimuttaṃ', He is praised specifically by way of the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

In this context, the praise of the Blessed One is made through two aspects: the attainment of His own welfare (attahita-sampatti) and the practice for the welfare of others (parahita-paṭipatti). Among these, the attainment of Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), the absolute abandonment of defilements along with their habitual traces (vāsanā), and the attainment of Nibbāna without remainder are called 'attahita-sampatti'. The practice for the welfare of others (parahita-paṭipatti) by way of intention (āsaya) consists of: teaching the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering with a mind regardless of gain, honor, and offerings; having a constant intention for the welfare even of hostile beings such as Devadatta; and waiting for the time when the knowledge of beings to be guided becomes mature. That practice for the welfare of others is twofold by way of intention (āsaya) and application (payoga), and the attainment of one's own welfare is threefold; these are revealed appropriately by this verse. By the phrase 'karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ' (whose heart is cooled by compassion), the practice for the welfare of others by way of intention is shown. By the word 'Sugata' in the sense of 'speaking well', the practice for the welfare of others by way of application is shown. By the phrases 'paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ' and 'gativimuttaṃ', and by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of penetrating the Four Truths, the threefold attainment of one's own welfare is shown. By the word 'Sugata' in its remaining senses and by the phrase 'sanarāmaralokagaruṃ' (the teacher of the world of men and gods), all attainments of one's own welfare and practices for the welfare of others are revealed.

Alternatively, the praise is made through three aspects: cause (hetu), result (phala), and benefit to beings (sattūpakarā). Therein, 'cause' refers to being endowed with Great Compassion and the accumulation of the requisites for Enlightenment (bodhisambhāra); both of these are revealed by the first phrase, both by direct meaning and by implication. The 'result' (phala), by way of knowledge, abandonment, power, and the perfection of the physical body (rūpakāya-sampadā)...
15:
The fulfillment of the fruit (phala-sampadā) is of four kinds. Among these four, the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa), which is the proximate cause of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and the knowledges such as the Ten Powers (dasabala) which have that Path-knowledge as their root, are called the fulfillment of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā). The bringing of all defilements (kilesa) along with their residual tendencies (vāsanā) to the state of absolute non-arising is called the fulfillment of abandoning (pahāna-sampadā). Mastery in accomplishing desired benefits is called the fulfillment of power (ānubhāva-sampadā). The fulfillment of the individual form, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, which is like an anointment for the eyes of the entire world of beings, is called the fulfillment of the physical body (rūpakāya-sampadā).

Among these four, the fulfillment of knowledge and the fulfillment of abandoning are shown by the second word and by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. The fulfillment of power is shown by the third word. The fulfillment of the physical body is shown by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of the beautiful gait of the body; for without the perfection of the major and minor marks, that fulfillment of the physical body cannot exist. The practice for the welfare of others, which is of the two kinds mentioned above, is called the fulfillment of benefiting beings (sattūpakāra-sampadā). It should be understood that this fulfillment of benefiting beings is shown by the word 'Sugata' in the sense of speaking well.

In another way, by this verse, the Teacher shows Supreme Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), the practice that is its root, and many other Buddha-qualities. It is the nature of teachers to make known a particular meaning through any available means. How is it shown? By the phrase 'karuṇā-sītala-hadayaṃ' (heart cooled by compassion), the root of Supreme Enlightenment is shown. For the Blessed One, whose heart was urged by Great Compassion, made the resolution to rescue beings from the mire of saṃsāra, fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) in due order, and attained the peerless Supreme Enlightenment; thus, compassion is the root of Supreme Enlightenment. By the phrase 'paññā-pajjota-vihata-moha-tamaṃ' (darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom), Supreme Enlightenment is shown. The Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, which is the proximate cause of Omniscience, and Omniscience, which is the proximate cause of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, are called 'Supreme Enlightenment' (sammāsambodhi).

By the word 'Sugata' in the sense of going well, the practice that leads to Supreme Enlightenment is shown. This is because it reveals the Noble Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā), which is embraced by compassion and wisdom and is free from the two extremes: the extremes of sloth, distraction, stagnation, and over-exertion; the extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification; and the two extremes of the eternalist view and the annihilationist view. By the remaining words, the distinction between the primary and secondary benefits of Supreme Enlightenment is shown. Here, the rescuing of beings from the great flood of saṃsāra is the primary benefit, while others are secondary. Among these two, the practice for the welfare of others (parahita-paṭipatti) is shown by the primary benefit, and the fulfillment of one's own welfare (attahita-sampatti) is shown by the secondary benefit. By both of these, the Blessed One's status as the 'fourth kind of person' among the four types of persons (such as those practicing for their own benefit) is revealed. By that, His peerless status as one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), His supreme status as one worthy of veneration, and the fact that veneration towards Him is like a fertile field are made clear.

In another way, by mentioning compassion, the fulfillment of all mundane qualities is shown, as it illustrates qualities that are superior to mundane excellences and are not shared with Paccekabuddhas and disciples. By mentioning wisdom, the fulfillment of all supramundane qualities is shown, as it illustrates the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, which is the proximate cause of Omniscience. This is because the meaning completed by taking both compassion and wisdom is expanded and shown by words such as 'sanarāmara-loka-garu' (teacher of the world of gods and men). Alternatively, by mentioning compassion, the approaching of beings without the defilement of attachment is shown, and by mentioning wisdom, the withdrawal from defilements is shown. Likewise, by mentioning compassion, the Buddha's existence in accordance with worldly convention (sammuti) is shown, because compassion takes worldly designation as its object. By mentioning wisdom, the fact that He does not overstep worldly conventions is shown. Because...
16:
By showing the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa), which is the proximate cause of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), it amounts to showing the fulfillment of all supramundane qualities. The meaning achieved by taking both Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) and Wisdom (Paññā) is explained in detail with words such as "Teacher of gods and humans" and so forth.

By taking Compassion, He shows the approach free from defilements; by taking Wisdom, He shows the departure from defilements. Likewise, by taking Compassion, He shows the Buddha’s conduct in accordance with worldly conventions, as Compassion has worldly designations as its object. By taking Wisdom, He shows non-attachment to worldly conventions. Indeed, due to not penetrating the ultimate reality (paramattha), one tends to transcend the true nature of things and wrongly grasp them as 'beings', 'persons', and so on.

Similarly, by taking Compassion, He shows the Buddha’s abiding in the attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti). By taking Wisdom, He shows the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three periods of time, the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, the fourfold Analytical Knowledge (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), and the fourfold Knowledge of Fearlessness (Vesārajja-ñāṇa). Since the Knowledge of the Attainment of Great Compassion is already included by taking Compassion, by taking Wisdom, He shows the range of His knowledge through various divisions of wisdom such as: the remaining Uncommon Knowledges (Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the six Higher Powers (Abhiññā), the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies, the ten Powers (Dasa-bala), the fourteen Buddha-qualities, the sixteen types of Knowledge-conduct (Ñāṇa-cariyā), the eighteen Buddha-qualities (Buddha-dhamma), the forty-four bases of knowledge (Ñāṇa-vatthu), the seventy-seven bases of knowledge, and so forth.

Likewise, by taking Compassion, He shows the perfection of conduct (Caraṇa-sampatti), and by taking Wisdom, the perfection of true knowledge (Vijjā-sampatti). By taking Compassion, He shows self-governance (Attādhipati); by taking Wisdom, governance by the Dhamma (Dhammādhipati). By taking Compassion, He shows being the refuge of the world; by taking Wisdom, being His own refuge. Similarly, by taking Compassion, He shows being a prior benefactor (Pubbakārī); by taking Wisdom, gratitude (Kataññutā). By taking Compassion, He shows not causing distress to others; by taking Wisdom, not causing distress to Himself. Or, by taking Compassion, He shows the fulfillment of the Perfections (Pāramī) that make one a Buddha; by taking Wisdom, the fulfillment of Buddhahood itself. Likewise, by taking Compassion, He shows the saving of others; by taking Wisdom, the saving of Himself. Similarly, by taking Compassion, He shows the mind that desires to benefit all beings; by taking Wisdom, the mind that is detached from all phenomena. Among all Buddha-qualities, Compassion is the beginning because it is the root cause, and Wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all Buddha-qualities are shown.

Likewise, by taking Compassion, He shows the aggregate of concentration (Samādhikkhandha) preceded by the aggregate of virtue (Sīlakkhandha). Indeed, virtue has Compassion as its root. Because of that Compassion, there is the practice of abstaining from killing and so forth. That Compassion also occurs in association with the three jhānas. By the word 'Wisdom', He shows the aggregate of wisdom (Paññākkhandha). Virtue is the beginning of all Buddha-qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end. In this way, all Buddha-qualities, which are beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, are shown by way of method. Indeed, this taking by way of method is the only way to show the Buddha-qualities without remainder. Otherwise, who would be able to show the qualities of the Blessed One word by word without remainder? No one is able.
17:
Who indeed is able to show the qualities of the Blessed One in succession without remainder? Therefore, it was said:

“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of a Buddha, and were to speak of nothing else for an entire aeon (kappa), the aeon would come to an end in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

It is for this very reason that when the Venerable Sāriputta Thera was questioned by the Blessed One regarding the limit of the Buddha’s qualities, he declined, saying, “No indeed, Bhante (it is not possible to know the qualities of all past Buddhas),” and stated in the Sampasādanīya Sutta, “But, Bhante, the lineage of the Dhamma (Dhammanvaya) is known to me.”

Having thus performed the salutation preceded by the praise of the Blessed One with all His omniscient qualities in brief, now, desiring to perform the salutation preceded by the praise of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma), he spoke the verse beginning with “Buddho pi”. Therein, the summary meaning along with the connection of words is as follows: The Buddha, endowed with the various groups of qualities mentioned above, having developed the Dhamma known as the Noble Path (Ariya-magga), or the Dhamma of the Noble Path together with the practice of the preliminary stage, and having realized the Dhamma known as Fruition and Nibbāna (Phala-Nibbāna), or the Dhamma of Fruition and Nibbāna together with the Dhamma of study (Pariyatti) and the Dhamma of practice (Paṭipatti), has attained the state of Buddhahood known as Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). I also salute that Dhamma, which is stainless and unsurpassed.

In that verse, the meaning of the word “Buddha” should first be understood. According to the method of the Niddesa: “He is the Buddha because He has known the Truths. He is the Buddha because He awakens the generation (of beings) to the Truths,” and so forth. Alternatively, He is the Buddha because He has truly awakened from the deep sleep of delusion along with its latent tendencies (vāsanā) by attaining the supreme Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, and because He has blossomed through the attainment of Omniscience adorned with infinite groups of qualities; thus He is the Buddha in the sense of awakening and blossoming. Or else, because there is no knowable phenomenon (ñeyya-dhamma) that He has not understood, and because He does not grasp any specific knowable object as a grammatical object (kamma), and because there is no desire to express the object, but only the sense of penetration, only the description as an agent (kattu-niddesa) is obtained. Therefore, it should be said: “He is the Buddha because He has known.” When a part is not specifically taken, the remainderless nature of the meaning to be taken is understood. For example, when it is said, “The initiate does not give,” without specifying any object, it is understood as not giving anything at all, thus taking the meaning without remainder. In this way, without regarding a specific object, the establishment of the word “Buddha” should be understood only in the sense of the agent.
18:
In terms of meaning, the continuum of aggregates (khandha-santāna) is called 'Buddha' because it is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) and Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), having completely destroyed all defilements along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā) through Self-Enlightened Knowledge (Sayambhū-ñāṇa) nurtured by the Perfections (Pāramitā). With reference to this meaning, it is said: "The Buddha is that Blessed One who, being self-enlightened without a teacher, personally realized the Truths among teachings not heard before, attained omniscience therein, and achieved mastery over the Powers (Bala)."

The word 'api' is used in the sense of commendation (sambhāvana). By that word 'api', it is shown that if even the Blessed One, endowed with such special qualities, attained Buddhahood by developing and realizing such a Dhamma, what need is there to speak of others attaining the state of a disciple (sāvaka) and so forth? Thus, it expresses commendation for the Dhamma. 'Buddhabhāva' refers to Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). For, the name 'Buddha' and the knowledge that takes that name as its object arise in the Blessed One through the Path Knowledge of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa), which is the proximate cause for Omniscience, and through Omniscience, which is the proximate cause for the Path Knowledge of Arahatship. This very thing is called 'bhāva' (state) here. Indeed, it is because of this cause that the knowledge (buddhi) and the word (Buddha) arise. Thus the teachers say:

"By whatever cause knowledge and the word arise, that cause is expressed by suffixes having the sense of state (bhāva)."

'Bhāvetvā' means having produced or having developed. 'Sacchikatvā' means having realized or having experienced directly. The words 'ceva' and 'ca' are used in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). By these two words, it is shown that the Blessed One attained Buddhahood not merely by developing the Dhamma, nor merely by realizing it, but by both. 'Upagato' means attained or reached. This word is connected with the term 'Buddhabhāvaṃ'.

In the term 'vītamalaṃ', it is called 'vīta' because it occurs by way of departure; it is 'vītamala' because it is free from stains (mala). Alternatively, that Dhamma whose stains have departed is 'vītamala'. The variant reading 'gatamalaṃ' is also seen. In that case, since roots have multiple meanings, the word 'gata' without a prefix should be understood to express the sense of departure, just like 'vigata' with a prefix. It is 'gata' because it goes away or departs. Or, the Dhamma whose stains have gone, according to the previous method of compound. 'Anuttaraṃ' means having nothing superior to it. It is called 'Dhamma' because it upholds those who practice according to the instruction, preventing them from falling into the lower realms (apāya) and saṃsāra. This refers to the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma (nava-vidha-lokuttara-dhamma). Because it makes that Dhamma clear and because it is the means for realization and reflection, the Scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti-dhamma) is also taken as 'Dhamma' here.
19:
(The Dhamma of learning is also) included in this term 'Dhamma'. For this reason, it is stated in the Commentary: "He penetrated the ocean of the Abhidhamma method; he contemplated the three Piṭakas." Furthermore, because it is said, "having developed and realized which Dhamma," it should be understood that the perfections (pāramīs), which are the factors that bring about Buddhahood as they are suitable for the development of the Path and the realization of the Fruit and Nibbāna, as well as the training in higher morality (adhisīla-sikkhā) and so forth occurring prior to the Path, are also included here. These perfections, higher morality, and so forth are stainless (vītamala) because they are free from opposing factors, and they are unrivaled (anuttara) because they are not shared with others.

How, then, did the Blessed One attain Buddhahood by developing and realizing those Dhammas? It is said in reply: Having made the great aspiration (mahābhinīhāra) at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara for the sake of delivering beings from the suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), being possessed of great compassion, supreme patience, and a disposition that loves virtue, the Blessed One—through the special quality of wisdom—developed and realized the noble perfections such as giving (dāna), self-control (dama), and restraint (saṃyama), which are pure and stainless, respectfully, continuously, and without remainder for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. Having attained mastery (vasībhāva) in acts such as giving, and possessing wonderful and inconceivable great power, having reached the ultimate pinnacle of the perfections of higher morality and higher mind (adhicitta), the Blessed One sent forth the Great Vajira Insight Knowledge (mahāvajira-vipassanā-ñāṇa), which is like a thunderbolt, through two trillion four hundred billion (2,400,000,000,000) modes in the context of Dependent Origination, and thus attained Buddhahood, known as the unsurpassed Right Self-Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi).

With this verse, he praises the True Dhamma through many qualities such as the accomplishment of knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti), as appropriate. How? Here, with the word "having developed," he praises the accomplishment of knowledge; with the word "having realized," he praises the accomplishment of liberation. Similarly, with the first term, he praises the accomplishment of meditative absorption (jhāna), and with the second term, the accomplishment of liberation (vimokkha). Or, with the first term, the accomplishment of concentration (samādhi), and with the second, the accomplishment of attainment (samāpatti). Again, with the first term, the state of the knowledge of destruction (khaya-ñāṇa), and with the second, the state of the knowledge of non-arising (anuppāda-ñāṇa). With the first term, the state of being like lightning, and with the second, the state of being like a thunderbolt (vajira). With the first term, the achievement of dispassion (virāga-sampatti), and with the second, the achievement of cessation (nirodha-sampatti). Similarly, with the first term, the state of leading out from saṃsāra (niyyāna), and with the second, the state of deliverance from saṃsāra (nissaraṇa). Or, with the first term, the state of being the cause (hetu), and with the second, the state of being the unconditioned (asankhata). With the first term, the state of seeing (dassana), and with the second, the state of seclusion (viveka). With the first term, the state of predominance (adhipati), and with the second, the state of the deathless (amata).

Alternatively, with the phrase "having developed which Dhamma, he attained Buddhahood," he praises the Dhamma for its quality of being well-expounded (svākkhāta); with the word "having realized," he praises it for its quality of being visible here and now (sandiṭṭhika). Similarly, with the first term, for its quality of being timeless (akālika), and with the second, for its quality of "come and see" (ehipassika). Or, with the first term, for its quality of leading inward (opanayika), and with the second, for its quality of being realized by the wise individually (paccattaṃ veditabbo). Or, with the first term, he praises it through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the trainees (sekha) along with the virtue and so forth occurring prior to the Path. With the second term, he praises it through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the adepts (asekha) along with the unconditioned element, Nibbāna. With the term "stainless," he praises the Dhamma for its quality of purity by showing the absence of defilements. With the term "unrivaled," he praises the Dhamma for its quality of perfection by showing that there is no other Dhamma superior to it. Or, with the first term, he praises it through the perfection of the abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna); with the second term, through the perfection of its non-perverted nature. Or, with the first term, he praises it by its suitability as the fruit of developing the Path. This is because, due to the quality of developing the Path, that Dhamma cleanses and destroys the stains of defilements.
20:
He praises the Dhamma through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom (of those in training), and by the second verse, through the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu, Nibbāna) along with the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of those beyond training (asekkha).

By the word 'vītamalaṃ' (free from stain), he praises the Dhamma for its purity, showing the absence of the stains of defilements. By the word 'anuttaraṃ' (unsurpassed), he praises it for its perfection, showing that there is no other Dhamma superior to it. Alternatively, he praises it by the first word for its accomplishment in abandoning (pahānasampadā), and by the second word for its accomplishment in nature (sabhāvasampadā). Or, he praises it by the first word because it is suitable as the fruit of mental development (bhāvanā). This is because that Path (magga), through the quality of bhāvanā, is capable of uprooting the stains of defilements; therefore, by that word, he speaks of the fruit of the act of bhāvanā. By the second word, he praises it because it is suitable as the fruit of realization (sacchikiriyā). Because there is no further duty to be done beyond realizing that Nibbāna, and because it is not shared with other mundane states, its unsurpassed nature is accomplished through realization; therefore, by that word, he speaks of the fruit of realization.

Having thus performed the salutation preceded by the praise of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) through all its qualities in brief, he now speaks the words beginning with 'sugatassa orasānaṃ' (the breast-born sons of the Sugata), wishing to perform the salutation preceded by the praise of the Noble Saṅgha (Ariyasaṅgha). In that phrase, 'sugatassa' is a term indicating a connection and should be linked with the word 'puttānaṃ' (sons). Those who are born in the breast or who have grown up in the breast are called 'orasa' (breast-born). Among the four types of sons—namely, the self-born son (attaja), the son born of the field (khettaja), the resident pupil son (antevāsika), and the adopted son (dinnaka)—the Noble persons are called 'orasa' because they resemble the self-born son. Just as the breast-born sons of humans, being self-born, are special heirs to their father's property, so too these Noble disciples, having been born into the Noble birth at the end of hearing the True Dhamma, are special heirs to the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha) and the Dhamma-treasure (dhammaratana) which belong to the Blessed One.

Alternatively, the Noble disciples who are entering or have entered the Noble ground (ariyabhūmi) by the power of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching are worthy of being called 'orasa' in the primary sense (nippariyāyena), without metaphor, because they are born from the exertion produced in the Blessed One's breast. This is because the Blessed One, having taken them into His heart by observing their inclinations (āsaya), latent tendencies (anusaya), temperaments (carita), and dispositions (adhimutti), etc., and by reflecting on their faults, restrained them from faults and established them in faultless states, causing them to grow by nourishing their Dhamma-body consisting of virtue and so forth. As the Blessed One said in the Itivuttaka: 'O monks, I am a Brahmin... you are my breast-born sons, born from my mouth,' and so on. One might ask: 'Does not the teaching given by the disciples also lead to the state of a Noble one?' True, but because that teaching is rooted in the Blessed One and lacks distinct characteristics of its own, it is counted only as the 'Blessed One's Dhamma teaching.' Therefore, those Noble ones are called only the 'breast-born sons' of the Blessed One.
21:
They are counted only as 'Dhamma teachings' (of the Buddha); therefore, only the status of being the Blessed One's breast-born sons (orasaputta) should be stated for those Noble ones. By this, among the four types of sons, he shows the Noble Saṅgha's status as self-born sons (attajaputta). They are called 'putta' (sons), such as the self-born and others, because they purify their own lineage or because they fulfill the hearts of their parents. The Noble ones are called the Blessed One's sons because they resemble Him through purifying the lineage of the Dhamma, through practicing the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti), and through pleasing the Blessed One's mind. Their status as sons should be linked with the word 'samūha' (assembly).

He is called 'Māra' (the Killer), specifically Devaputta Māra, because he becomes the cause of defilement and kills or obstructs virtues such as virtue (sīla). It is called 'senā' (army) because he binds others with it; the army of Māra is 'mārasenā'. Likewise, they are called 'mārasenamathana' (crushers of Māra's army) because they harass and destroy Māra and Māra's army. Although it should be said as 'māramārasenamathanānaṃ', it is stated this way (as mārasenamathanānaṃ) by the method of elision (ekasesa) where one part represents the whole. Or, by the word 'senā' placed near the word 'māra', Māra's army is to be understood. Due to the requirements of the verse, the vowel is shortened here. In some versions, there is the reading 'mārasenamaddanānaṃ', but that is inappropriate because this verse is of the Noble (ariya) class.

One might ask: 'At the time of attaining the Path, do Devaputta Māra or Māra's army not threaten the Noble disciples to create obstacles, as they did to the Blessed One? If so, why is this said?' It is said because the defilements, which are the cause of being threatened, have been destroyed. When the defilements (saṅkilesa), which are the cause for those Noble ones to be threatened, are destroyed, those armies of Māra are also said to be destroyed.

Alternatively, just as with the Māra of the aggregates (khandhamāra) and the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāramāra), because Devaputta Māra also becomes a companion in killing virtues, the host of defilements is called 'mārasenā' here. As the Blessed One said:

'Sensual pleasures are your first army,
The second is called discontent.
Your third army is hunger and thirst,
The fourth is called craving.
Your fifth army is sloth and torpor,
The sixth is called fear.
Your seventh army is doubt,
Hypocrisy and obstinacy are your eighth army.
Gain, fame, honor,
And whatever renown is wrongly obtained,
And whoever exalts oneself
And disparages others.'
22:
O Evil Māra, these ten (sloth and torpor, fear, doubt, contempt, stubbornness, false gain, fame, honor, retinue, and praising oneself while disparaging others) are your armies; they are the oppressive weapons of the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra). One who lacks courage cannot conquer this army; only the victorious one (having conquered) attains happiness.

Those Noble Disciples (Ariya-sāvaka) have crushed, destroyed, and annihilated the army of defilements, which consists of fifteen hundred or infinite varieties, using the weapons of virtue such as mindfulness (sati), investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (viriya), and tranquility (samatha), according to their respective limits. Therefore, those Noble Disciples are called "Mārasenamathana" (Crushers of Māra's army). In this context, "vilothana" means destruction or annihilation and oppression. Alternatively, the meaning of "Mārasenamathana" should be taken as the destruction of the Māra of defilements, which is called an army because it has entered into a state of companionship with the Māra of the aggregates (Khandha-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (Abhisaṅkhāra-māra), the Māra of death (Maccu-māra), and the Māra as a deity (Devaputta-māra). In this way, the meaning is complete as the crushing of the five Māras.

Indeed, the Noble Disciples crush the Māra of the aggregates (Khandha-māra) by means of abandoning the origin (samudaya) and fully understanding suffering (dukkha); they crush the Māra of volitional formations (Abhisaṅkhāra-māra) by depriving it of companions in every way and by making it cease to arise; they crush the Māra of death (Maccu-māra) and the Māra as a deity (Devaputta-māra) by the power of overcoming the sphere of destruction of the powerful; and they crush the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) by making it cease to arise in every way through the power of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). By this, the reason for their being the breast-born sons (orasa-putta) and their being the "born-after" (anujāta) sons among the three types of sons is shown. Because they crush the army of Māra, they are the breast-born sons of the Blessed One and also the "born-after" sons.

"Aṭṭhannaṃ" (of the eight) is a numerical delimitation. By this term, it is shown that although those Noble Persons may be of many hundreds of thousands of varieties in different ways, they do not exceed this numerical delimitation because they do not exceed the status of those standing on the four Paths and those standing in the four Fruitions, according to the divisions of the Path and Fruition states that make one a Noble One. The word "pi" or "api" is used in an inappropriate place for reasons such as poetic embellishment; it should be connected with the term "Ariya-saṅghaṃ." By that word "api," it is collectively shown that (I pay homage) not only to the Buddha and the Dhamma but also to the Noble Saṅgha. Although there is no such thing as a whole (samudāya) independent of its parts, and a whole is spoken of only in dependence on its parts, the term "aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ" (the group of even the eight) is used because an unknown whole deserves to be distinguished by a known whole. By this, it is specified that in the term "Ariya-saṅghaṃ," the state of being a group is not by any shape or physical assembly, but only by the state of being those standing on the Paths and Fruitions. It is called "samūha" (group) because the parts are gathered and should be considered, reflected upon, or joined together. That same "samūha" is also called "samoha" for the sake of euphony. Both readings are appropriate. They are called "Ariya" (Noble) because they are far from defilements, because they do not move towards misfortune, and because they move towards welfare and happiness.
23:
According to the etymological method (Nirutti) or grammatical method; alternatively, they are called "Ariya" because they are to be approached (araṇīya) as a refuge by the world including the devas, and because they fulfill the welfare of those who have approached them. They are called "Saṅgha" because they are united (saṃhata) by the equality of virtue (sīla) and view (diṭṭhi), or alternatively, because they are well-formed by the collection of major and minor acts performed in harmony. They are called "Ariya-saṅgha" because they are a group of those Noble Ones, or because they are both Noble and a Saṅgha according to the method already mentioned. (I pay homage to) that Noble Saṅgha. Since the attainment of the Buddha-gem and the Dhamma-gem after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna is dependent on the Saṅgha-gem, the phrase "I pay homage with my head" (sirasā vande) is stated here to show the great gratitude owed to the Noble Saṅgha. This meaning must certainly be accepted because it is stated likewise in the Vinaya Commentary and other texts. Some teachers, however, bring that word "with the head" from the previous verses and connect it here. This is not very appropriate because this is the place for manifesting the unique (unshared) qualities of the Three Jewels, and because the aforementioned reason is the intended manner of all commentators.

By this verse, many qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are shown, such as the perfection of origin (pabhava-sampadā) and the perfection of abandonment (pahāna-sampadā). How? By the phrase "sugatassa orasānaṃ puttānaṃ" (the breast-born sons of the Sugata), the perfection of origin of the Noble Saṅgha is shown, as it illustrates their arising from the Fully Enlightened Buddha. By the phrase "mārasenamathanānaṃ" (the crushers of Māra's army), the perfection of abandonment is shown, as it illustrates the abandonment of all defilements. By the phrase "aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ" (the group of even the eight), the perfection of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā) is shown, as it illustrates the status of those standing on the Paths and Fruitions. By the phrase "ariya-saṅghaṃ" (the Noble Saṅgha), the perfection of nature (sabhāva-sampadā) is shown, as it illustrates their supremacy over all other groups.

Alternatively, the phrase "sugatassa orasānaṃ puttānaṃ" illustrates the Noble Saṅgha's state of having a pure basis (āsayavisuddhi). The phrase "mārasenamathanānaṃ" illustrates their state of having proper practice (sāmīcipaṭipatti) practiced with right and upright knowledge. The phrase "aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ" illustrates their state of being worthy of offerings (āhuneyya) and other qualities. The phrase "ariya-saṅghaṃ" illustrates their state of being the unsurpassed field of merit (puññakkhetta).

Likewise, by the phrase "sugatassa orasānaṃ puttānaṃ," the existence of the supramundane refuge-going (lokuttara-saraṇagamana) of the Noble Saṅgha is shown. Indeed, it is through the supramundane refuge-going that those persons become the true breast-born sons of the Blessed One. By the phrase "mārasenamathanānaṃ," the good practice of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-sammapaṭipatti) accomplished through the perfection of aspiration (abhinīhāra) is shown. For those who have made aspirations and practice well conquer Māra or the army of Māra. By the phrase "aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ," the states of the Trainee (sekha) and the Beyond-training (asekha) who have destroyed opposing states are shown, as the Path and Fruition states are illustrated through the designation of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). By the phrase "ariya-saṅghaṃ," their state of being the supreme recipient of offerings (agga-dakkhiṇeyya) is shown, as their state of being the unsurpassed field of merit is illustrated. Refuge-going is the beginning of all qualities of the disciples; the virtue-aggregate and others of the Trainee together with the preliminary practice are the middle; the virtue-aggregate and others of the Beyond-training are...
24:
The aggregates of virtue of those in training (sekha-sīlakkhandha) and so forth are at the end. In this way, all the virtues of the Noble Saṅgha, which are good in the beginning, middle, and end, have been shown in brief.

Having thus performed the salutation to the Triple Gem by means of praising the virtues of all the Jewels in brief through these three verses, he now says "Iti me" and so forth, intending to direct that humble act of respectful salutation towards the desired purpose. In that text, the word "iti" is used in the sense of pointing out. By that word "iti", he points out the method already mentioned in the three verses. By the word "me", he indicates himself as the agent. That word "me" should be connected with the remaining text as "the merit that has been obtained by me". Or, it should be understood in the dative sense as "the merit that exists for me". Or, it should be understood in the possessive sense as "the merit of mine consisting of salutation".

Clarity is called "pasāda"; one who has such clear wisdom or mind is called "pasannamati". Since this compound word takes the gender of another word, it is stated as "pasannamatino". It is called "ratana" (jewel) because it causes delight (rati) to arise in the mind or because it carries it. Grammarians say it is called "ratana" because it is similar to the seven or ten kinds of worldly jewels. Setting aside other mere figurative comparisons, the state of being a jewel is appropriate for the Buddha and others only according to the aforementioned etymological meaning. For one who contemplates the virtues of the Jewels such as the Buddha as they truly are, saying "Itipi so Bhagavā" and so forth, there arises immense rapture and joy (pīti-pāmojja), which is the cause for attaining the Deathless Nibbāna.

The Buddha taught how this occurs as follows:
"Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the virtues of the Buddha, at that time his mind is not obsessed by greed, not obsessed by hatred, not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight, having the Buddha as its object. Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains an understanding of the meaning (atthaveda), gains an understanding of the Dhamma (dhammaveda), and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture (pīti) arises," and so forth.

Alternatively, the state of being honored is the meaning of "ratana". It is stated thus in the Commentaries:
"Because it is honored, of great value, incomparable, rare to see, and fit to be used only by noble beings, it is called a jewel (ratana)."

Such virtues as being honored and so forth are found pre-eminently only in the Buddha and others, and are not shared with other jewels. The details should be taken from the Commentary on the Ratana Sutta.
25:
This meaning is not stated by the power of etymological derivation (nibbacana), but rather, the masters of grammar say it is stated by the power of the meaning such as being highly esteemed, which belongs to objects regarded as jewels in the world. It is called "ratana" by the power of a compound with similar meaning because it delights the minds of the virtuous, because it enables one to cross the ocean of Saṃsāra, and because it leads to a good destination (sugati) and Nibbāna; there is no need for further elaboration. By the method of "ekasesa" (retention of one) or by the etymology of the plural form, it becomes "ratanāni" (jewels). A group of three, or three things combined, or that which has three parts is called "taya". Since it is a group only of jewels and not of other things, it is called "ratanattaya" (the Triple Gem). Since there is no whole apart from its parts, the three jewels themselves are so called; it does not mean the group alone, but the singular form is used in consideration of the group.
