Because it is to be saluted, it is called "vandanā" (salutation); that vandanā itself is "vandanāmaya", just as one says "dānamaya" or "sīlamaya". Here, "vandanā" is the inclining towards or praising the virtues of the Triple Gem by way of body, speech, and mind. Alternatively, the associated mental states such as faith (saddhā), wisdom (paññā), mindfulness (sati), and energy (vīriya) that assist and arise together with that volition of salutation are called "vandanā". Because it is performed by that vandanā, it is called "vandanāmaya", just as one says "made of gold" (sovaṇṇamaya) or "made of silver" (rūpiyamaya). In terms of meaning, however, it is the aforementioned volition (cetanā) itself. That which is accomplished in the Triple Gem or for the Triple Gem by way of salutation is called "ratanattayavandanāmaya". It is called "puñña" (merit) by the method of nirutti (etymology) because it produces the fruit of being worthy of worship, and it is called "puñña" because it purifies one's own continuity (santāna). According to the grammarians, although the word "puñña" has a transitive meaning and its explanation is obtained through the causative power, its grammatical formation is through the pure agent (suddha-kattā) alone.

It is called "antarāya" (obstacle/danger) because it comes (eti) into the midst (antara) of the continuity of beings by way of obstructing various successes; it refers to misfortunes in the present life and so forth. One whose obstacles are well-destroyed by the aforementioned method as a result of performing the salutation is called "suvihatantarāya". Here, "destroying" should be understood as making those obstacles not arise by avoiding the causes that produce them. The preceding verb "hutvā" (having been/become) is connected with the statement "I shall manifest the meaning". "Tassa" refers to the power of the merit consisting of salutation indicated by the word "yaṃ". "Ānubhāေvena" means by the power or influence.

"Majesty (teja), effort (ussāha), counsel (manta), mastery (pabhu-satti), and energy (āṇā-satti)—these five are called ānubhāva, and they are also called pabhāva."

Among the meanings stated, here it applies to "energy" (satti). It is called "anubhāva" because it repeatedly develops or increases (bhāveti) the one who possesses it; that itself is "ānubhāva".
26:
In the Udāna Commentary, these five—power (satti), glory (teja), effort (viriya), mastery (issariya), and energy (balānupaddāna)—are called influence (ānubhāva). These five are also called 'vikkama' and 'pabhāva'. Among these meanings, in this context, it refers to 'power' (satti). Influence is called 'ānubhāva' because it repeatedly develops that fulfillment. This very influence is called 'ānubhāva' in the Udāna Commentary. In terms of its essence, it is the power of merit accomplished through the volition of salutation (paṇāma-cetanā), which provides strength to past kamma that is the cause of attained prosperity. This power of merit from salutation is either the instrument (karaṇa) or the cause (hetu) for the thorough removal of obstacles.

In this verse, by the word 'having a confident mind' (pasannamatino), he shows the fulfillment of his own faith and confidence (saddhā-pasāda). By the word 'made of salutation to the Triple Gem' (ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ), he shows the fulfillment of the Triple Gem as a supreme field [of merit] for salutation. By showing this, he demonstrates that in the exposition of the meaning, the merit of saluting the Triple Gem is capable of destroying oppressive dangers through two factors: the fulfillment of one's own faith and the fulfillment of the Triple Gem as a supreme field. Just as the volition of giving (dāna-cetanā) endowed with four factors yields results in the present life, the volition of salutation (paṇāma-cetanā) endowed with two factors also brings benefits in the present life by removing obstacles.

Having thus shown the benefit of paying respect to the Triple Gem, and now wishing to explain the meaning of the Dhamma teaching, he spoke the words beginning with 'Dīghassa' to show that teaching as the Dhamma to be explained and to praise it with a special eulogy of its qualities. It is the nature of the Teacher to praise the special qualities of the Dhamma to be explained at the beginning of various commentaries. Thus, in the Papañcasūdanī, Sāratthappakāsinī, Manorathapūraṇī, Atthasālinī, and others, praises are made respectively: 'of the crusher of opposing doctrines, of the generator of various types of knowledge, of the generator of diverse intuition for the preeminent Dhamma-preachers, of that Abhidhamma which is deeply entered into by profound knowledges and is diverse in various methods at the beginning,' and so on.

In those words, 'Dīghassa' means of the collection named Dīgha (Dīgha Nikāya). 'Dīghasuttaṅkitassa' means marked (named) by discourses that have very long sequences of words. By this, he shows that the name 'Dīgha' is a designation that follows the meaning of this collection (āgama). If it is asked, 'Are not the suttas themselves the Āgama? How can the Āgama be marked by those suttas?', the answer is: this is true in the ultimate sense (paramattha), but in terms of conventional designation (paññatti), the status of Āgama is designated based on the suttas. Therefore, the Āgama, which is the whole, is marked by the suttas, which are the parts. Just as the term 'Sutta' is used for a collection of meanings and sounds, so the term 'Āgama' is used for a collection of suttas. It is called 'Nipuṇa' (subtle) because it contains subtle meanings such as Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). It is called 'Āgama' because one's own welfare, others' welfare, and so on, come (āgacchanti) in it, by it, or from it. That Āgama is called 'Vara' (excellent) because it has a noble meaning and because it is a desirable meaning.
27:
It is called 'Āgamavara' because it is excellent. Alternatively, it is called 'Āgamavara' because it is superior to external texts known as traditions, such as the Bhārata-purāṇa-kathā and Narasīha-purāṇa-kathā. It is called 'Buddhānubuddhasamvaṇṇita' because it is explained by the noble ones (ariyas) such as the chief disciples who realized the truths following the Buddhas' penetration of the truths, through the exposition of meaning and the praise of qualities.

Alternatively, it was explained by the Buddha and the noble disciples in the manner already stated. The teachers say that the Supreme Buddha himself taught the sequence of the exposition of the meaning of the three Pitakas, and thereafter, the disciples explained them through the councils and so on. In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, in the explanation of the Upāli Sutta, it is stated in the detailed explanation of 'to the one who explains the meaning (veyyākaraṇassa)': 'There is no sequence of words (tantipada) that was not taught by the Blessed One; he taught the meaning of all words.'

'Saddhāvahaguṇa' means having the quality of bringing confidence (pasāda) in the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha. If it is asked, 'Does not the entire word of the Buddha in the three Pitakas have the quality of bringing faith? Why then is the Dīgha Nikāya praised with this quality that is not common to others?', the answer is: because this Dīgha Nikāya is preeminently endowed with that quality. The reason is that this Dīgha Nikāya brings supreme confidence in the Triple Gem through the complete description of virtue (sīla) and views (diṭṭhi) in the Brahmajāla Sutta and others; through the description of the qualities of former Buddhas in the Mahāpadāna Sutta and others; through the lion's roar that cannot be countered, crushing the doctrines of heretics in the Pāthika Sutta and others; and through making the qualities of the Buddha particularly clear in the Anuttariya Sutta and others.

Having thus highly praised the Dhamma to be explained, he now spoke the verse beginning with 'Atthappakāsanatthaṃ' to show the purity of the lineage of the commentary now to be spoken. By this verse, he shows the purity of the lineage of his commentary by stating that this commentary to be spoken has descended from the old Dīgha Nikāya Commentary established at the three councils, merely removing the Sinhalese language, and not from any other source.

Alternatively, because others are unable to say they will explain this excellent Āgama, which is the domain of the Buddha and is extremely subtle and profound, by their own power alone, he spoke the words beginning with 'Atthappakāsanatthaṃ' to show the support for the explanation. By this verse, he shows the support for his commentary, stating that he will explain the meaning of that Dīgha Nikāya only by relying on the influence of the former teachers (pubbācariya). In that verse, 'Atthappakāsanatthaṃ' refers to the meaning of the Pali text, the natural meaning, the meaning to be known, the meaning consistent with the Pali text, the meaning consistent with that [commentary], the meaning with a remainder, the meaning without remainder, and the meaning to be taken directly,
28:
It is for the purpose of showing or explaining various meanings, such as *neyyattha* (the meaning to be inferred). The word-definition is made twofold to complete the metrical structure of the verse. It is called '*Atthakathā*' because the meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathīyati*) by this speech. That very '*Atthakathā*' becomes '*Aṭṭhakathā*' by changing the letter '*ttha*' to '*ṭṭha*'. This is similar to the term '*dukkha-pīḷanaṭṭho*' (the sense of oppression in suffering). This phonetic change occurs because it is of the *Ariya* (noble) class of verse. Grammarians, too, citing the rule '*tathānaṃ lahu gaṃ*', provide this very word '*Aṭṭhakathā*' as an example.

That by which the meaning is described, following the syllables, meanings, and words,
And which is connected to the origin stories—that is known by the wise as '*Aṭṭhakathā*'.

'*Ādito*' (from the beginning) refers to the First Council. By the five hundred great elders, such as the Venerable Mahākassapa, who are called '*Vasī*' (masters) because they were endowed with the six supernormal powers, supreme mastery of the mind, and the five kinds of mastery in meditation. '*Yā saṅgītā*' (which was rehearsed) refers to the commentary that was compiled and spoken at appropriate places to clarify the meaning, saying, 'This is the meaning of this word; this is the meaning of that word.' '*Anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi*' means it was not only rehearsed at the First Council but also subsequently at the Second and Third Councils. It should be understood that it was not only rehearsed from the beginning by the five hundred masters but also subsequently rehearsed by the Venerable Yasa and others. This is because both the conjunctive particles (*ca* and *api*) combine the respective actions and times.

Now, considering the potential fault of redundancy and uselessness—asking what the benefit is of this commentary being made again now when the old ancient commentary already exists—he said '*Sīhaḷadīpaṃ*' etc., to dispel that fault. By dispelling that fault, he shows the reason for the emergence of this [new] commentary. In that context, it is called '*Sīhaḷa*' because it 'takes' (*lāti*) or 'conquers' a lion (*sīha*), with the letter '*la*' being changed to '*ḷa*' as in the word '*garuḷa*'. The first person in that lineage was Prince Sīha [Sīhabāhu]. The royal families and all the people born of that lineage in the island of Tambapaṇṇi are called '*Sīhaḷa*' by virtue of that lineage or by common usage. The island where they reside should also be known as '*Sīhaḷa*' [Sīhaḷadīpa] by virtue of those Sīhaḷa people or by the figurative name of the place. It is called '*dipa*' because it shines (*dippati*) in the middle of the water, or because the water flows (*sandati*) in two directions (*dvidhā*) here. That very '*dipa*' is '*dīpa*' (island). It is called so [Sīhaḷadīpa] as the island of those people, without considering the distinctions. The word '*pana*' is used to indicate dissatisfaction. By that word '*pana*', he indicates a sense of dissatisfaction that although that commentary was indeed rehearsed in the three Councils, it has again become like this [translated into the Sinhalese language]. Being connected to that meaning, in the previous verse, 'Indeed...'
29:
The connection of the words with '*kāmañca*' (indeed), which has the sense of commendation, as in '*saṅgītā anusaṅgītā ca*', is possible. Such a manner is seen in other commentaries as well. '*Ābhatā*' means brought from Jambudīpa. '*Atha*' (then) refers to the time after the Council; in this case, it connects with the word '*ābhatā*'. Or, '*atha*' refers to the time after it was brought by the Elder Mahā-Mahinda; in this case, it connects with the word '*ṭhapitā*' (placed/established). Indeed, that Great Commentary was already rehearsed in the three Councils because the Elders who rehearsed the Dhamma first rehearsed the three Piṭakas and then established the sequence of the text in accordance with the explanation of the meaning of those three Piṭakas. After those three Councils, it was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahā-Mahinda. Subsequently, the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi established it in the Sīhaḷa language to avoid the confusion of the views of other sects. However, the teacher, Elder Dhammapāla, clarifies only the latter connection because it is difficult to see. Similarly, this phrase '*dīpavāsīnamatthāya*' (for the benefit of the island dwellers) should be connected with the words '*ṭhapitā*', '*apanetvāna*', and '*āropento*'. Indeed, even a single word can be connected to many meanings through methods such as repetition (*āvutti*). In this text, by the former connection, he shows the purpose of the establishment by the Elders of Tambapaṇṇi: 'It was established in the Sīhaḷa language for the benefit of the dwellers of the island of Sīhaḷa by avoiding the confusion of the views of other sects.' By the latter connection, he shows the purpose of removing the Sīhaḷa language and translating it into a language suitable for the method of the sacred texts (*tanti-naya*) for the benefit of the dwellers of Jambudīpa and other islands. He was named '*Mahinda*' during his time as a prince because of his great power (*mahā-issariya*); later, he was called '*Mahā-Mahinda*' because of the greatness of his virtues. The Sīhaḷa language is the language habitually used by the people of Sīhaḷa, which is very difficult for others to use, like a casing, because it uses many syllables to express even a single meaning.

Let the ancient commentary be as it is; but if there is an inquiry as to how the commentary being made now is being produced, he said '*apanetvāna*' etc., to show the manner of making this commentary. In that context, the connection is: 'removing the Sīhaḷa language from that original commentary (*mūla-aṭṭhakathā*) and discarding it by not placing it on the [new] palm leaves.' By this, he shows that this commentary to be spoken of matches and agrees in meaning with the original commentary rehearsed in the three Councils—except for the mere removal of the Sīhaḷa language—just as the water of the Ganges [matches] the water of the Yamuna. The words such as '*manoramaṃ*' (pleasing) are adjectives that clarify the nature of this language as a natural linguistics (*sabhāva-nirutti*). Indeed, it is called '*manoramā*' because it pleases the minds of the wise by being a natural linguistics. By this [Pali], the meaning is expanded; or it is expanded and opened by the power of the meaning; or [it leads] beings from the round of rebirths...
30:
Pali is called 'Tanti' because it saves beings from the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) and because through this Pali, one can cross over doubts regarding various meanings. It is called 'Tantinayānucchavika' because it follows the shadow of the method of that Tanti (Pali). It is called 'Vigatadosa' because it is free from the fault of being mixed with other non-natural languages. Such a natural language (sabhāva-nirutti) is described as follows:

'That Māgadhī is the root language; the first humans of the aeon, the Brahmas, children who have never heard the speech of others, and the fully Enlightened Buddhas speak it.'

By presenting the language that follows the course of Pali through writing in books, it implies the absence of faults in phonology (sadda-dosa).

'Samayaṃ avilomento' means not contradicting the established doctrine (siddhānta), and by this, it implies the absence of faults in meaning (attha-dosa). Because they are consistent and non-contradictory, the doctrines of those Elders (Theras) will also be presented here. To the question 'Whose doctrine?', it is said 'Therānaṃ' (of the Elders), etc. By this, the doctrines of the sects such as the followers of Teacher Rāhula, the Jetavanavāsī, and the Abhayagirivāsī are excluded. They are called 'Theras' because they are endowed with firm qualities such as virtue (sīla), learning (suta), absorption (jhāna), and liberation (vimutti). As the Blessed One said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 'Monks, there are these four qualities that make one an Elder. What four? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous,' and so forth. Alternatively, they are called Elders because they are endowed with firming qualities such as truth (sacca) and righteousness (dhamma). As the King of Dhamma, the Buddha, said in the Dhammapada:

'In whom there is truth and righteousness, non-violence, restraint, and self-control;
That wise one who has cast out impurities is indeed called an "Elder".'

The lineage of teachers descending from the Elder Mahākassapa and others is called the 'Theravaṃsa' (Lineage of the Elders). Because they illuminate that lineage with the light of wisdom, being part of that lineage and endowed with scriptural learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama), or because they are like lamps in that lineage, they are called 'Theravaṃsapradīpa' (Lamps of the Elder Lineage). It is called 'Vinicchaya' (Decision) because it is decided through various modes; it is a discourse that cuts off doubt by crushing obstacles in difficult places. Because those Elders possess very subtle and skillful decisions, they are called 'Sunipuṇavinicchaya'. Alternatively, the knowledge that decides is called 'Vinicchaya'; because they possess a very skillful deciding knowledge regarding the aforementioned meanings, they are called 'Sunipuṇavinicchaya'. The monastery situated in the Mahāmeghavana is called the 'Mahāvihāra'. That monastery shines with the Great Bodhi tree of the Teacher. Those who habitually dwell in that Mahāvihāra...
31:
...dwelling in the Mahāvihāra, it means without contradicting the doctrine of such successive Great Elders. By this, he shows through the authority of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) that the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins—which has descended through the lineage of Elders starting with Mahākassapa and is therefore unerring and extremely subtle in its decisions—is the standard.

'Hitvā punappunabhatamatthaṃ' means that although a meaning has been stated in one place, it is brought up again in another; because of such repetition and to avoid the text becoming too bulky, such repetitions are abandoned, and the meaning of that noble scripture (āgama) will be illustrated.

Having thus shown the manner of composing the text, in order to show another purpose of the commentary besides the purpose stated as 'for the benefit of the island-dwellers' (dīpavāsīnamatthāya), he said 'Sujanassa ca' (and for the good people), etc. Therein, the word 'ca' (and) in the phrase 'Sujanassa ca' has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya). By that word 'ca', it includes not only the benefit of the dwellers of Jambudīpa but also the purpose of gladdening virtuous people (sādhujana). Consequently, the meaning 'for the benefit of the dwellers of the island of Tambapaṇṇi' is also established, as it is of great benefit to them due to the ease of learning and so forth. In the phrase 'Ciraṭṭhitatthañca' (and for the sake of long endurance), the word 'ca' also shows the sense of inclusion, meaning not only for those two benefits but also for the long endurance of the three-fold Sāsana or the Pariyatti Dhamma for a period of five thousand years. Indeed, through the endurance of the Pariyatti Dhamma, the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti) and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha) also endure, because Pariyatti is the root of those two. 

The Pariyatti Dhamma endures well for a long time through well-placed words and syllables (pada-byañjana) and through their meanings. Through the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), the words and syllables are well-placed without distortion, and their meanings are also well-placed without distortion. Therefore, based on the commentary being the means for the well-placed, undistorted words, syllables, and meanings, it is said: 'Ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassa' (and for the long endurance of the Dhamma). For this was said by the Blessed One:

'Monks, these two things lead to the stability, the non-confusion, and the non-disappearance of the True Dhamma. Which two? Well-placed words and syllables, and a meaning that is well-conveyed. These two, monks... lead to [stability],' and so forth.

Having thus shown the purpose, in order to avoid the bulkiness of the text by abandoning excessive elaborations in the forthcoming commentary, he said 'Sīlakathā' (Discourse on Virtue), etc. For that reason, it is said: 'I shall not analyze all of that.' Alternatively—if one wishes to compose a commentary, the Visuddhimagga should be taken as a part of that commentary; thus, the teacher, wishing to provide guidance to those who have doubts, said 'Sīlakathā', etc., to show in brief the doctrines already analyzed in that Visuddhimagga. Therein, 'Sīlakathā' refers to the detailed discourse on virtue by way of virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla) and virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla), etc. 'Dhutadhammā' refers to the thirteen ascetic practices, such as the alms-food eater's practice, which shake off defilements.
32:
In order to show the dhammas investigated in that Visuddhimagga by way of a brief summary, he said the words beginning with "Sīlakathā". In that context, "Sīlakathā" refers to the detailed talk on virtue (sīla) by way of virtue of performance (cāritta), virtue of avoidance (vāritta), and so on. "Dhutadhamma" refers to the thirteen practices that shake off the defilements, such as the practice of the alms-food eater (piṇḍapātikanga). "Kammaṭṭhāna" (meditation subjects) refers to the collection of dhammas named as such because they are the places of occurrence for the work of yoga known as meditation (bhāvanā). To indicate that one should not only take the thirty-eight subjects mentioned in the Pāḷi but also the two mentioned in the Commentaries, he said "sabbānipi" (all of them too).

"Cariyāvidhānasahito" means being together with the classification of the nature of temperaments such as the greedy temperament (rāgacarita), and this term is an adjective (visesana) for the term "jhānasamāpattivitthāro" (the detailed exposition of jhānas and attainments). Here, the fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna) are called "jhāna", and the immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara-jhāna) are called "samāpatti" (attainment). Alternatively, both are called "jhāna" when they are merely obtained, and "samāpatti" when mastery in attainment (samāpajjanavasībhāva) is reached. Furthermore, both are simply "jhāna", while only the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are called "samāpatti"; the meaning is the detailed exposition of those jhānas and attainments.

He said "sabbā ca abhiññāyo" (and all supernormal knowledges) in order to include the six supernormal knowledges categorized as mundane and supramundane. "Paññāsaṅkalanavinicchaya" (investigation by the grouping of wisdom) refers to the investigation by grouping, counting, or summarizing wisdom by way of the one-fold classification and so on, according to the method found in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts. "Ariyāni" is so called because they are to be penetrated by the Noble Ones (ariya) such as the Buddha, or because they accomplish the state of being a Noble One; it is called "ariya" by the elision of the subsequent word (uttarapada-lopa). Alternatively, they are called "ariya" because they are to be known as unerring (avitatha); it is an adjective for the word "saccāni" (truths).

"Paccayākāra" (the mode of conditions) is the state of the conditional dhammas such as root-cause (hetu) being of service to the conditionally arisen dhammas (paccayuppanna) by way of being a root-cause condition and so on. The teaching of that is the teaching of the mode of conditions; the meaning is the talk on Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). That teaching is said to be "investigated in that Visuddhimagga" because it is extremely pure (suparisuddha) due to being free from the confusion of the views of other sects, subtle (nipuṇa) because it is very difficult to analyze the compact mass (ghana-vinibbhoga), and accompanied by methods such as the method of unity (ekattanaya); thus he said "suparisuddhanipuṇanayā". All these three words are adjectives for the teaching of the mode of conditions. "Avimuttatantimaggā" refers to the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) which has a lineage of Pāḷi that does not deviate from the method of the Buddha's word, because it is composed without abandoning the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and other texts. Here, "magga" (path) is the means (upāya) known as Pāḷi, because it is the means for understanding various meanings or for the penetration of the Truths. Alternatively, it is called "magga" because it is a continuous sequence (pabandha) which, by its length, is like a natural path. This term is an adjective for the two words "vipassanā" and "bhāvanā".
33:
In the phrase "iti pana sabbaṃ", the word "iti" is a particle used in the sense of conclusion, because the summary as pointed out has been completed; the meaning is "all this is just so much". The word "pana" is a mere ornament of speech (vacanālaṅkāra) since it has no separate meaning. It is "extremely pure" (suparisuddhaṃ) in the sense of being easy to understand, because there is no confusion of word-meanings, no meaning yet to be spoken, no meaning not yet spoken, and no meaning remaining after being spoken. This word "suparisuddhaṃ" connects with "sabbaṃ". Alternatively, it is an adverbial neuter (bhāvanā-napuṃsaka) because it connects with "vuttaṃ". "Bhiyyo" means excessively or in great detail; by this, he shows: "I shall investigate only the word-meanings." The intention is: "I shall not investigate all this in this commentary because of repetition and because the book would become too bulky." In the word "vicarayissāmi", it should be noted that the letter "i" is not lengthened (dīgha) due to the metrical requirements of the verse.

Even if the Visuddhimagga does not show the meaning of the four great Nikāyas in this way, if there is an objection that the entire Visuddhimagga should still be investigated in this commentary, he said "majjhe Visuddhimaggo" and so on, determining the primary reason for not doing so and wishing to dismiss that objection. In that context, "majjhe" (in the middle) means within the four great Nikāyas other than the Khuddaka Nikāya. The word "hi" is used in the sense of reason and illuminates the reason already stated. "Tattha" means in those four great Nikāyas. "Yathābhāsitaṃ" means as spoken by the Blessed One, or in accordance with what was taught. Alternatively, it also means as explained by the commentators by way of explanation, or in accordance with what was explained. In the term "icceva", the word "iti" points to the reason already stated; the meaning is "for this reason only" or "having this very reason in mind". In the word "kato", the phrase "Visuddhimaggo esa" connects as the object (kamma).

"Tampi" means having taken that Visuddhimagga also with knowledge. "Etāya" means by this commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. Here, by showing the state of standing in the middle with the phrase "majjhe ṭhatvā", he shows that the Visuddhimagga is a general (sādhāraṇa) commentary for all four Nikāyas, and is not a specific (asādhāraṇa) commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. Specifically, it is indeed a general commentary for the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as well, as is appropriate. Although it is also specifically general to the remaining Khuddaka Nikāya because of its mixture with those Vinaya and Abhidhamma texts, it is said to be a general commentary for only the four Nikāyas, excluding that Khuddaka Nikāya.

## Thus ends the explanation of the sixteen verses.
## Thus ends the explanation of the introduction to the book.
34:
## Explanation of the Introductory Discourse (Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā)

Having thus performed the preliminary procedures for composing the treatise, such as the salutation (paṇāma) and so forth, through the various methods already mentioned, and because the nature of the things to be analyzed is now well-clarified and well-understood only by demonstrating their divisions, the author says "Tattha dīghāgamo nāma" and so forth, in order to first show the division by way of groups (vagga) and discourses (sutta).

In that context, regarding the word "Tattha," the statement was made: "I shall explain the meaning of the noble Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghāgama)." In that statement, that which is known as the Dīgha Nikāya, the meaning of which was promised to be explained, should be understood by way of groups and discourses in the following manner; or it means this is the division. Alternatively, "Tattha" refers to the Dīgha Nikāya mentioned in the phrase "Dīghāgamanissitaṃ." That Dīgha Nikāya is to be divided by way of groups and discourses in this way, or it means it has such a nature. Just as a distant word like "Dīghassa" is referred back to by the word "taṃ" (that), a near word like "Dīghāgamanissitaṃ" is also referred back to by the word "taṃ" because it revolves in one's mind as if it were out of sight. In such instances, whether something is present or absent in one's mind, it is appropriate to refer back to it by expanding the term without contradicting the meaning. The etymology (nibbacana) of the groups, discourses, and so forth will be clarified later. It is called "Tivagga" (Three Groups) because it has three groups. It is called "Catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaha" (Collection of 34 Suttas) because thirty-four suttas are counted in this Dīgha Nikāya.

In order to show that in his own commentary, he proceeds according to the order established in the First Council, he says "Tassa... nidānamādi." In this regard, the fact that it is the beginning should be understood only according to the order of the Council. Why was the Dīgha Nikāya recited first among the four Nikāyas? Why was the Sīlakkhandhavagga placed first in it? Why was the Brahmajāla Sutta placed first in that group? And why was the Nidāna (Introduction) placed first in that sutta? This kind of inquiry is not such that it does not occur anywhere, because it can be asked regarding any sequence of words.

Furthermore, the Dīgha Nikāya was recited first because it possesses the quality of bringing about faith (saddhā). Faith is the seed of wholesome states. As the Blessed One said: "Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain." The faith-inspiring quality of this Dīgha Nikāya has already been shown below. Moreover, it was recited first because it is easy to learn and memorize, being a collection of only a few suttas and being small in extent. Indeed, this Dīgha Nikāya consists of a collection of thirty-four suttas and is sixty-four bhāṇavāras in length. The Sīlakkhandhavagga was placed first because it contains many discussions on virtue (sīla). Virtue is the beginning of the Dispensation, as all qualities are established on virtue.
35:
Because virtue (sīla) is the foundation of all good qualities, it is called the beginning of the Sāsana. For this very reason, the Blessed One preached: "Therefore, monk, you should first purify the beginning in wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue and straight view," and so forth (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya). Because of the abundance of talk on the aggregate of virtue, that section is called the "Sīlakkhandhavagga." It should be understood that the Brahmajāla Sutta, which analyzes all views without remainder, was placed first in the Suttanta Piṭaka as a means of untangling the web of views. In the Buddha's word of the Tipitaka, there is no sutta that analyzes and classifies wrong views, making them free from entanglement and knots, like the Brahmajāla Sutta. As for the introduction (nidāna), it was placed first by the Venerable Ānanda, when questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera at the First Council, in order to show the place, time, and so forth of the preaching. Therefore, it was said, "Brahmajālassāpi," and so on. In that statement, the speaker is specified by "āyasmatā" (by the venerable), and the time is specified by "paṭhamasaṅgītikāle" (at the time of the first council). This meaning will be made clear further on.

## Commentary on the Great First Council

Now, in connection with the phrase "paṭhamasaṅgītikāle," wishing to show that First Council, and also wishing to clarify that council because of the desire to provide a commentary according to the order established in the First Council, the author says "paṭhamasaṅgīti nāma cesā," etc., to show the reason for mentioning it here even though it was included in the Pāḷi text. Here, by the words "kiñcāpi... māruḷhā," he shows a trace of an objection: "Is that council not already included in the Saṅgītikkhandhaka of the Cullavagga Pāḷi? Why is it mentioned again here? If it is mentioned, it might be useless and make the text too heavy." By the words "nidāna... veditabbā," he resolves this by showing a special reason: that it is not a fault as mentioned because it is beneficial for mastery of the introduction.

In the phrase "paṭhamasaṅgīti nāma cesā," the particle "ca" has the meaning of conjoining (sampinḍana) what has been said with what is to be said in such a context. By that particle "ca," he conjoins these two points: that the introduction spoken at the time of the First Council is the beginning, and that this is what is called the First Council. Alternatively, the particle "ca" has the meaning of "setting forth" (upanyāsa), and "upanyāsa" means the beginning of a sentence. This is the nature of authors: when they have said something and wish to begin saying another thing, they use the particle "ca."

The statement by the Elder Vajirabuddhi that "here the particle ca has the meaning of excess (atireka), thereby indicating that there are other councils" is inappropriate. This is because that meaning cannot be understood from the particle "ca" in this context. If the particle "ca" were intended only to show that meaning, then it would not even be necessary to use it. This is because the word "paṭhama" (first) already indicates that there are other councils, such as the second. One naturally uses the word "first" in relation to the second and so on, just as one uses terms like "short" (rassa) in relation to "long" (dīgha) and so forth. Therefore, it is not very appropriate.
36:
By using the word "First," it also serves to indicate the existence of the Second and subsequent Councils. This is because, just as the word "short" (rassa) is used in relation to "long" (dīgha), the word "First" is used in relation to the Second and so on. The collection and chanting of the Dhamma and Vinaya, which were taught and prescribed in various places according to circumstances and were scattered, is called Saṅgīti (Council). By this term Saṅgīti, the words of the Great Elders who conducted the Council—placed at the beginning, end, and in between various training rules and discourses for the sake of connection—are also included. Because it has a vast scope and is honored, the great council is called the Mahā-saṅgīti. The first such great council is called the Paṭhama-mahā-saṅgīti.

The word "kiñcāpi" has the sense of concession. By this word, although that Council is already included in the Pāḷi, since mere inclusion there does not yet provide the listeners with skill in the introduction (nidāna), the word "pana" is used to show a sense of dissatisfaction [with mere inclusion]. Nidāna (Introduction) is so called because it points out the teaching by making known what was unknown regarding the place, time, and so forth. Skill in that introduction is nidāna-kosalla. For the purpose of [attaining] that skill, [these words are spoken].

Now, to show that introduction in detail, the words beginning with "dhammacakkappavattanañhi" are stated. In that context, although there are other activities of the Blessed One that are causes for beings to obtain the supreme vision (dassanānuttariya), the taking of refuge, and so forth, in accordance with his vow, "Having become a Buddha, I shall awaken [others]," only that activity which is the cause for the arising of the paths and fruits in those to be guided (vineyya) is, in the primary sense, called "Buddha-work" (buddha-kicca). To show that Buddha-work specifically, it is said: "dhammacakkappavattanañhi... pe... vinayanā."

Before the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, for those who heard what the Blessed One spoke (such as the giving of the refuges to the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika), it only became a part of their wholesome disposition (vāsana-bhāgiya); it was not yet a part of training (sekha-bhāgiya) or a part of penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya). This is indeed the natural way (dhammatā). Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta itself is stated as the boundary. The Dhamma itself, such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), is called a "Wheel" (cakka) in the sense of setting in motion; thus it is the Dhammacakka. Alternatively, "Wheel" means authority (āṇā); because it is not apart from the Dhamma, it is both Dhamma and a Wheel, thus Dhammacakka. Because it is a wheel [set in motion] by means of Dhamma and justice, it is also Dhammacakka.

As stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:
"He sets in motion the Dhamma and the Wheel, thus it is Dhammacakka. He sets in motion the Wheel and the Dhamma, thus it is Dhammacakka. He sets it in motion by means of Dhamma, thus it is Dhammacakka. He sets it in motion by means of Dhamma-practice, thus it is Dhammacakka," and so forth.

The setting in motion of that Dhamma is called Dhammacakkappavattana. In the word "pavattana," there are two meanings: "setting in motion" (present) and "having been set in motion" (past). Regarding these meanings, it is stated in the Commentaries:
37:
"The Blessed One, while teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, is said to be 'setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion'; it is said to be 'set in motion' from the moment the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña attained the paths and fruits" (stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary and Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary). Here, however, the meaning in the present sense is appropriate. The word "yāva" is an indeclinable indicating a limit; the meaning should be understood in the sense of inclusive limit (abhividhi), making the guidance of the wanderer named Subhadda the inner limit. This is because the Blessed One guided that wanderer Subhadda while lying on the couch of his Parinibbāna. The Blessed One who had finished the Buddha-work that was to be completed is called "kata-buddha-kicca." The connection is: "When the Lord of the World, the Blessed One, who had completed the Buddha-work, had attained Parinibbāna." By this, it is shown that there was not even a single task of a Buddha's duties left unfinished. For that very reason, the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna.

Is it not the case that those guided by the disciples are also considered guided by the Blessed One himself? For indeed, a discourse spoken by a disciple is called "the Word of the Buddha." One might object: "Since those to be guided by the disciples were not yet guided [at that time], it should not be said that he 'had completed the Buddha-work'." This is not a fault, because the means for guiding them had been established in the disciples. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"I shall not pass away, O Evil One, until my monks are disciples who are accomplished, disciplined, confident, learned, Dhamma-bearers... who, when a contrary doctrine has arisen, can well-refute it with the Dhamma and teach the Dhamma with its wonders," and so forth.

The mention of the specific place and time of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna with the words "at Kusinārā" and so forth is for the purpose of dispelling the false view that "the Blessed One did not attain Parinibbāna," and to show the nature of birth, growth, and so forth in the world. Indeed, to make their human nature very clear, Great Bodhisattas in their final birth even perform acts such as taking a wife. "At Kusinārā" means in the city of this name. That city is called "Kusinārā" because it was created at the place where a man holding kusa grass in his hand was seen; this locative case is used in the sense of proximity. "In the Upavattana Sal grove of the Mallas" means in the Sal garden of the Malla kings, which was near that city. That Sal grove is called "Upavattana" because those wishing to enter the city from the garden "turn towards" (upaccavattanti) it. Just as the Thūpārāma is in the south-western direction of Anuradhapura, so that garden is in the south-western direction of Kusinārā. And just as the road entering the city from the south gate of Thūpārāma goes facing east and then turns north, so the row of Sal trees from the garden goes facing east and turns north; therefore, that place is called "Upavattana." Other teachers, however...
38:
Other teachers, however, say: "It became known as Upavattana because [the Buddha] went to that Sal grove, took leave of his circle of friends, and returned (nivattana)." "Yamaka-sālānamantare" means in the middle of the twin Sal trees. It is said that there, at the head of the Parinibbāna bed prepared for the Blessed One, there was a row of Sal trees, and at the foot, another row of Sal trees. Among those rows, one young Sal tree was close to the head, and another was close to the foot. Therefore, it is called "Yamaka-sālānamantare." Alternatively, it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that "Yamaka-sālā refers to Sal trees that stand intertwined with one another by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves."

The moon is called "mā" because days are measured by its movement. At that time, the moon that is complete with all sixteen parts is called "puṇṇamā." Grammarians, however, taking the Sanskrit method which says "mo sivo candimā ceva," also desire the word "ma" ending in "o" to mean the moon. The full moon day associated with the Visākhā constellation is called Visākhā-puṇṇama; it refers to that very day. It is called "paccūsa" (dawn) because it destroys darkness. Etymologists say that the word "usa" preceded by "pati" occurs in the sense of pain. That very time refers to the specific period included in the last watch of the night. It means at such a final period of the night on the Visākhā full moon day.

The resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāma-kkhandhā) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) are called "upādi" because they are grasped as results by kamma and defilements. Although that upādi does not cease without remainder when subduing the Mara of Defilements (kilesa-māra) and the Mara of Volitional Formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), in this context, it is called "anupādisesa" because it is abandoned without remainder when subduing the Mara of the Aggregates (khandha-māra) and the Mara of Death (maccu-māra), or because of the absence of the remainder known as upādi, or because of the absence of a remainder of upādi. Here, "nibbānadhātu" is intended merely as extinction (nibbuti). It is called Nibbāna-element (nibbānadhātu) because it is Nibbāna and also an element (dhātu) as it maintains its own nature. The unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is so called by way of the cause of extinction. This is the use of the instrumental case in the sense of a characteristic (ittham-bhūta-lakkhaṇa). It means the third case [instrumental] is used in the sense of the Nibbāna-element, which is the mark of the Blessed One who has attained Parinibbāna, having reached this state called anupādisesa.

Is it not that the word "anupādisesāya" is only an adjective for the Nibbāna-element and not for the Blessed One who has attained Parinibbāna? Then why is it said that the Blessed One reached that anupādisesa? It is because of his association with the Nibbāna-element. Due to that association, the Blessed One is also said to have reached the state of anupādisesa. Alternatively, it is also proper to say that the third case is used for the act of knowing the Nibbāna-element that has reached this state called anupādisesa. "Anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā" also...
39:
It means "having become the Nibbāna-element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)." In the phrase "with a bowl having fewer than five mends," the commentators say it means "being one who has a bowl with fewer than five mends." Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say "being anupādisesa by means of the Nibbāna-element without remainder." In the commentary on the Nanda Sutta of the Udāna, it is stated: "In the phrase 'with hair partially shaved,' the instrumental case is in the sense of a characteristic (ittham-bhūta-lakkhaṇa), meaning 'one characterized by partially shaved hair.'" This same method applies in such cases.

"On the day of the distribution of the relics" refers to the fifth day of the waxing moon of the month of Jeṭṭha. That phrase is not an adjective for "those who had assembled," but rather an adjective for "aroused effort." This is because it is an adjective of different location (bhinnādhikaraṇa-visesana) by way of the time of arousing effort, meaning "he aroused the effort of the monks on the day of the distribution of the relics." For the monks had assembled even on days much earlier than the day of the distribution of the relics. Alternatively, the word "assembled" (sannipatitānaṃ) refers specifically to the gathering by way of physical unity (kāya-sāmaggī), and not merely to the act of coming together. Therefore, the phrase "on the day of the distribution of the relics" can be an adjective for "those who had assembled," and it can also be connected with the word "to the monks" in the phrase "aroused the effort of the monks."

The Great Elder of the Sangha is the "Saṅghatthera." If one asks, "What was the size of that Sangha?" it is said, "of seven hundred thousand monks." This is stated again merely to make known the size which is not known by the word "Sangha" alone. Grammarians, however, say:
"Compounds (samāsa) and secondary derivatives (taddhita) create distinction in the meaning of sentences; but when the word is formed, they reach a general state, like 'oil' or 'the Buddha's robe'."
Therefore, this is stated again only to distinguish the Saṅghatthera, which has become a mere name. Just as one says "Devadatta's teacher's family," there is a compound in such cases because of constant dependency (nicca-sāpekkhatā). Here, although the word "Sangha" depends on the words "seven hundred thousand monks," since there is no other word, it can make known the expected meaning as in a sentence. The phrase "of seven hundred thousand monks" is connected to the word "Sangha" as a part to a whole (avayava and avayavī), and that word "Sangha" is connected to the word "Thera" as a possessor (sāmi). The phrase "of seven hundred thousand monks" refers only to the monks who were leaders of groups. For at that time, the monks who had assembled were beyond counting. This is because, from the time the Buddha suppressed his illness at Veḷuvagāma and it was heard that "the Blessed One will soon attain Parinibbāna," among the monks who came from here and there, not even a single monk left. As the commentators say:
"At that time, there was only one Great Elder of the Sangha (Saṅghatthera), and the monks who were leaders of groups were seven hundred thousand." At the time of the Buddha's Parinibbāna, only the Venerable Mahā Kassapa was the Saṅghatthera. The long-lived Venerable Mahā Kassapa, reflecting and contemplating repeatedly, aroused effort for the purpose of holding the Council (Saṅgāyanā). He is called Mahā Kassapa because he was endowed with the virtues of morality and so forth, and because of his seniority in age.
40:
## 
“Among the assembly of monks who arrived at the place where the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, the leading monks numbered seven hundred thousand. At that time, the Elder Mahākassapa alone was the Saṅghatthera (Elder of the Community),” so say the commentators.

The Venerable Mahākassapa, repeatedly reflecting and contemplating on the Buddha's Parinibbāna, aroused the effort to hold a Council (Saṅgāyana). He is called 'Mahākassapa' (Great Kassapa) because he was endowed with great groups of virtues (sīlakkhandha) and so on. Alternatively, he is called 'Mahākassapa' in reference to the minor elders such as Uruvela Kassapa, Nadī Kassapa, Gayā Kassapa, and Kumāra Kassapa. If one asks why the Venerable Mahākassapa aroused this effort, the reason is explained starting with the words "Sattāhaparinibbute" and so forth.

The combination of seven days is called 'sattāha'. It means seven days have passed since the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. This is an aññapadatasmāsa (a type of compound), similar to the terms "acirapakkanto" and "māsajāto". It means the time when seven days had elapsed from the day the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. This term should be connected with the word "vuttavacanaṃ" (the spoken word) and also with "subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena" (by Subhadda, the one ordained in old age). In this context, 'Subhadda' is merely the name of that monk. Because he was ordained when he was advanced in age, he is called "vuḍḍhapabbajita" (one ordained in old age). By saying this, he is distinguished from others like Subhadda the Wanderer (Paribbājaka). The words spoken by that old monk Subhadda are shown starting with "Alaṃ āvuso" (Enough, friends) and so forth.

Seven days after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, while the Venerable Mahākassapa was traveling on the road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with about five hundred monks, those monks who were not yet free from passion (avītarāga) heard of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna from an Ājīvaka they met on the way. Seeing them throw away their bowls and robes, raise their arms, and lament in various ways, that old monk Subhadda spoke thus.

Why did that old monk Subhadda speak in such a way? It was because of a grudge he held against the Blessed One. To speak in detail, this old monk Subhadda was formerly a barber, as mentioned in the Ātumā story in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka of the Mahāvagga Pali. Having heard that the Blessed One was coming to the city of Ātumā with twelve hundred and fifty monks, he thought, "When the Blessed One arrives, I will make an offering of congee (yāgu)." While his two young sons were still novices, he said to them, "Dear sons, they say the Blessed One is coming to Ātumā with a large community of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in number. Go, dear sons, take your barber's kits and wander from house to house with a tube or a bag. Collect salt, oil, rice, and food."
41:
"Collect snacks as well; I will make an offering of congee to the Blessed One when he arrives," he said. They did as they were told. Then, when the Blessed One arrived at Ātumā and entered the threshing-floor barn, the old monk Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, called the people, and requested labor, saying, "Give me just some manual labor." When asked, "Venerable sir, what shall we do?", he had them take all the necessary materials, saying, "Take this and that." He had ovens built in the monastery, put on a dark-dyed robe, and wrapped himself in a similar one. He spent the whole night supervising, saying, "Do this, do that," and after spending a hundred thousand [coins], he had the 'bhojjayāgu' (consumable congee) and honey-balls prepared. What is called 'bhojjayāgu' is congee that is drunk after eating; it contains everything such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flower juice, fruit juice, and whatever is considered edible. It had an extremely fragrant scent, suitable for anointing the heads of those who wish to play and enjoy themselves.

Then, the Blessed One, having performed his morning bodily ablutions, set out towards the city of Ātumā for alms, surrounded by the community of monks. Then the people informed the old monk Subhadda, "The Blessed One has entered the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the congee?" That old monk Subhadda, wearing those very same dark-dyed robes, holding a ladle and a spoon in one hand, placed his right knee on the ground like a Brahma, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my congee." Then, following the method mentioned in the Khandhaka that "Tathāgatas ask even though they know," the Blessed One questioned him, and upon hearing the answer, he rebuked that old-ordained monk. He then laid down two training rules regarding that matter: the rule on accepting unallowable things (akappiya-samādāna) and the rule on carrying barber's tools (khurabhaṇḍa-pariharaṇa). He said, "Monks, you who seek food have passed through many billions of aeons. This food, which has arisen unrighteously, is not allowable for you. For you who consume this food, many thousands of future existences will arise only in the woeful states (apāya). Depart, do not take it." Having said this, he proceeded towards the alms-round. Not even a single monk took anything.

The old monk Subhadda became displeased and thought, "This Buddha wanders around saying 'I know everything.' If he did not want to take it, he should have sent word. Cooked food, at the very most, lasts only seven days. This wealth would have been enough for me to live on for the rest of my life. That Buddha has destroyed it all. This Buddha desires my harm." Thus, he harbored a grudge against the Blessed One, but while the Possessor of Ten Powers was alive, he did not dare say anything. Such a thought occurred to that old monk Subhadda: "This Blessed One is a Great Man ordained from a noble family. If I say anything to the Blessed One while he is alive, he will threaten me." Today, that old monk Subhadda, who was traveling with the monks led by Mahākassapa, having heard these words that "The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna"...
42:
He did not dare to say a single word. It is heard that this old monk Subhadda once had this thought: "This Blessed One is a Great Man who went forth from a noble family. If I were to say anything while he is still alive, he would surely rebuke me."

Today, while traveling with the Elder Mahākassapa, upon hearing that "The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna," he spoke thus, feeling as if he had gained relief and being full of joy. When the Elder heard those words, he felt as if his heart had been struck, or as if a thunderbolt had fallen upon his head, and religious urgency (dhammasaṃvega) arose in him. He thought: "The Blessed One has been attained Parinibbāna for only seven days; even today his golden-hued body still remains. In this Sasana, which the Blessed One attained with great difficulty, such a swift and grave evil, impurity, and thorn has appeared. If this wicked person grows and gains such companions, he will be able to cause the decline of the Sasana."

Then the Elder further reflected: "If I were to make this old monk wear rags, sprinkle him with ashes, and expel him right here, people would blame us, saying, 'While the body of the Ascetic Gotama still remains, his disciples are already quarreling.' Therefore, I shall endure for now. The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of unstrung flowers. Just as flowers in such a heap are scattered here and there when the wind blows, so too, as time passes under the influence of such people, one or two training rules in the Vinaya will disappear, one or two sets of questions in the Sutta will disappear, and one or two sections (bhūmantara) in the Abhidhamma will disappear. When the roots are thus gradually destroyed, we shall become like ghosts. Therefore, I will perform a rehearsal (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If I do so, this Dhamma and Vinaya will remain stable, like flowers strung together with a strong thread. It was for this purpose that the Blessed One came out to meet me for a distance of three gāvutas, granted me ordination with the three exhortations, exchanged his own robes with mine, and while teaching the moon-like practice (candūpama-paṭipadā) by waving his hand in the sky, he spoke making me his witness, and three times entrusted the treasure of the entire Sasana to me. While a monk like me exists, I must not let this wicked person gain growth in the Sasana. I shall rehearse the Dhamma and Vinaya as long as unrighteousness does not shine and the Dhamma is not obstructed, as long as non-Vinaya does not shine and the Vinaya is not obstructed, as long as those who speak unrighteousness do not become powerful and those who speak the Dhamma do not become weak, and as long as those who speak non-Vinaya do not become powerful and those who speak the Vinaya do not become weak. Only then, the monks, each according to their own..."
43:
...will learn (the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya) as much as they are able and will speak of what is allowable and what is not. When they speak thus, this wicked old monk Subhadda will naturally be subdued and will not be able to lift his head again, and the Sasana will become prosperous, flourishing, and widespread." Having thought thus, he did not inform anyone of the thought that had arisen in him, but comforted the community of monks. Later, on the day of the distribution of the relics, he inspired the monks to make an effort for the purpose of rehearsing the Dhamma and Vinaya. Therefore, it is said (by the teachers): "The Venerable Mahākassapa, on the seventh day after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna... inspired the monks to make an effort for the purpose of rehearsing the Dhamma and Vinaya."

In that passage, "Alaṃ" is a word of rejection, meaning "it is not proper." "Friends (Āvuso)" is an address to the monks who were weeping. "Do not grieve (Mā socittha)" means do not give rise to the intense grief that has arisen in the mind. "Do not lament (Mā paridevittha)" means do not make lamentations with the voice. For lamentation is called "vilāpa." He states the reason for not grieving, etc., with the words beginning with "Well-freed (Sumuttā)." In the phrase "by that Great Ascetic (tena mahāsamaṇena)," the word "tena" is in the instrumental or ablative case, or it is an indication of the "smā" suffix being like the "nā" suffix. In the word "oppressed (upaddutā)," it should be connected as the third case (instrumental) in the sense of the agent. This word (upaddutā) regards both (sumuttā and upaddutā). "We are oppressed (upaddutā ca homa)" is the present tense (vattamāna) regarding that time; the word "then (tadā)" is understood. Or, it is the present tense used in the sense of the past, meaning "we were (ahumhā)." The Elder Mahākassapa recollected this only by the power of religious urgency (dhammasaṃvega), and not by the power of anger or such. For the knowledge accompanied by moral dread (ottappa) that arises from reflecting on the nature of reality is called "dhammasaṃvega." It is also said:

"The knowledge that stands in the form of moral dread regarding all conditioned things,
For those who have laid down the burden (of the aggregates), is called religious urgency (dhammasaṃvega)."

To show another reason for inspiring effort, the words beginning with "of such (īdhisassa)" are spoken. In that context, "of such an assembly of the Saṅgha" refers to the assembly of the Saṅgha that exceeds the path of counting, headed by seven hundred thousand prominent elders (gaṇapāmokkha). By the words beginning with "This possibility indeed exists (ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati)," he shows another reason. It is called "ṭhāna" because the result stands there depending on that; it means cause (hetu). The word "kho" is for emphasis (avadhāraṇa). The word "pana" is an ornament of speech (vacanālaṅkāra). The meaning is: "This cause certainly exists, it does not not exist." What is that cause? He says, "that wicked monks (yaṃ pāpabhikkhū)," etc. "Yaṃ" is merely a particle, or it is an indication of the cause; it means "the cause by which they would make it disappear, that cause certainly exists." Wicked monks are those endowed with low and evil desires.
44:
Monks who are endowed with evil, unwholesome states are called pāpabhikkhū. In this Dispensation (or in the Dispensation of the scriptures), the Blessed One has passed away; because it has a teacher who has thus passed away, this Dispensation is called 'atītasatthuka'. This is formed in the same way as the grammatical analysis of the word 'bahukattuka'. The authoritative or sublime word is called 'pāvacana'. In this word 'pāvacana', the syllable 'pā' is a particle (nipāta), as in other instances of 'pāvacana' and so forth. Alternatively, teachers say that although this 'pā' is a prefix (upasagga), it is pronounced as 'pāvacana' by lengthening the vowel, similar to the word 'pāvadati'. 'Pakkha' refers to the faction of the shameless ones (alajjī). By the words beginning with 'yāva ca', it is shown that the holding of a Council is the cause and evidence for the long-endurance of the Dispensation. The word 'tasmā' (therefore) should be added and connected with the word 'saṅgāyeyya' (should chant/rehearse).

In that context, 'yāva ca dhammavinayo tiṭṭhati' means for as long as the Dhamma, consisting of the Suttas and Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya remain among conscientious persons (lajjī). The Blessed One, while lying on the couch of his final passing (parinibbāna), spoke the words beginning with 'vuttañhetaṃ' with reference to what was taught in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. The particle 'hi' serves to strengthen the meaning based on the traditional Pali text. 'Desito paññatto' means that the Dhamma is both expounded and prescribed. The supreme instruction and awakening regarding the Dhamma contained in the Suttas and Abhidhamma is called 'desanā' (exposition). Making that same teaching known in various ways and establishing it within the continuities of those to be led (vineyya) is called 'prajñāpana' (prescription/making known). The Vinaya is also both expounded and prescribed. The supreme instruction and awakening regarding the meaning contained in the Vinaya texts is called 'desanā'. Making that same meaning known in various ways and establishing it without confusion is called 'prajñāpana'. Therefore, it should be understood that it is appropriate to connect the two objects, Dhamma and Vinaya, with the two verbs, desita and paññatta.

'So' refers to that Dhamma and Vinaya. 'Mamaccayena' means 'at the time of my passing'. Teachers who study grammar say that the instrumental case is used here in the sense of the locative case. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (hetu); the meaning is 'by reason of my passing, [they] will be your teacher'. Indeed, in the Commentary to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, it is said: 'When I have attained parinibbāna, they will fulfill the duty of your teacher.' Here, the locative case with the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇa) accomplishes the sense of cause, just as in the sentence: 'When the lead ox goes straight (the others follow).' The intended meaning is this: While I was still alive, I taught you the Great Vinaya (Mahāvinaya)—consisting of the Khandhaka, the Parivāra, and the two Vibhaṅgas—concerning the matters that have arisen, in such a way that the seven classes of offenses should not be transgressed, saying: 'This training rule is light, this training rule is heavy; this offense is curable, this offense is incurable; this training rule is a fault by worldly standards (lokavajja), this training rule is a fault by prescription (pannaṭṭivajja); this offense is settled in the presence of an individual, this in the presence of a group, and this in the presence of the Saṅgha.' That entire Vinaya Piṭaka, when I have attained parinibbāna, will fulfill the duty of your teacher, by distinguishing what should be done and what should not be done...
45:
...because it instructs by way of distinguishing what is to be done and what is not to be done. While I was still alive, I expounded the Suttanta Piṭaka by analyzing and re-analyzing these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma)—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path—in various ways according to the inclinations (āsayas) of those to be led. That entire Suttanta Piṭaka, when I have attained parinibbāna, will fulfill the duty of your teacher, because it instructs in the right practice according to the respective temperaments (carita).

While I was still alive, I expounded the Abhidhamma Piṭaka by analyzing and re-analyzing these phenomena (dhamma)—namely, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine causes (hetu), the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, and the seven consciousnesses. Furthermore, [I distinguished them as]: 'So many phenomena belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), so many to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), so many to the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), so many are included in the cycle of existence (pariyāpanna), so many are not included (apariyāpanna), so many are mundane (lokiya), and so many are supramundane (lokuttara).' That entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, when I have attained parinibbāna, will fulfill the duty of your teacher, because it leads to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths which are known through the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.

Thus, everything spoken and uttered during the forty-five years from the Great Enlightenment until the Parinibbāna is categorized into many divisions: 'the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine factors (aṅgas), and the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandha).' These eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups will remain; I alone shall pass away. Now, I alone advise and instruct you; but when I have attained parinibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddhas will advise and instruct you, because they fulfill the task of giving advice and instruction (ovāda-anusāsana).

The term 'Sāsana' (Dispensation) is threefold: the Dispensation of learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha). In the primary sense, however, it refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. 'Addhānaṃ gamitumalaṃ' means that which is capable of reaching a long duration, that which is long-lasting. 'Ciraṭṭhitikaṃ' means having a long endurance of that Dispensation. The meaning is this: 'In whatever way this Dispensation may be long-lasting, and for that very reason, have a long endurance—in that way, if I were to hold a Council for the Dhamma and the Vinaya, it would be truly good.'

Now, wishing to show the manner of his reflection as he repeatedly recollected the special favor bestowed upon him by the Fully Enlightened One, he [Mahākassapa] spoke the words beginning with 'yañcāhaṃ bhagavatā'. In that passage, the word 'yañcāhaṃ' is connected with the words 'anuggahito' (favored) and 'pasaṃsito' (praised).
46:
The word 'yaṃ' is either the word 'yasmā' meaning 'because,' or it is the word 'kriyāparāmasana' which refers to an action. Since it is a word referring to an action, in the phrase 'anuggahito, pasaṃsito,' it refers to the actions of favoring and praising. Regarding the words 'Will you wear...' and so on, the Blessed One said this while sitting on the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) spread by the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera at the foot of a certain tree, touching that double-layered robe from its edge with his hand which had the color of a red lotus. This matter was recounted by Venerable Mahākassapa Thera himself to Venerable Ānanda in the Kassapa Saṃyutta:

'Friend Ānanda, then the Blessed One stepped off the path and approached the foot of a certain tree. Friend, I then spread my double-layered robe made of rags, folded fourfold, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One sit here; that will be for my long-term benefit and happiness." Friend, the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and said to me: "Kassapa, this double-layered robe of yours made of rags is very soft." When I said: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this double-layered robe of rags out of compassion for me," he asked: "Kassapa, will you wear my hempen refuse-heap robes that have been worn out?" I replied: "Venerable Sir, I will wear the Blessed One's hempen refuse-heap robes that have been worn out." Friend, thus I gave my rag double-layered robe to the Blessed One, and I received the Blessed One's hempen refuse-heap robes.'

In that Pali, "mudukā kho tyāyaṃ" means "mudukā kho te ayaṃ" (this robe of yours is very soft). Why did the Blessed One speak thus? Because he wished to exchange robes with the Thera. Why did he wish to exchange them? Because he wanted to place the Thera in his own position. Was it because Sāriputta and Moggallāna were not there? They were present. However, the Blessed One had this thought: "These two, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will not remain for long. But Kassapa will live to the age of 120. After my Parinibbāna, he will stay in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, conduct the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and make my Sāsana endure for a period of five thousand years." Thus, he placed him in his own position. By doing so, the monks would consider that Kassapa's words should be heeded. Therefore, he spoke thus. As for the Thera, when the qualities of a robe or a bowl are mentioned, the statement "You take this" is merely a customary practice (cāritta); therefore, he said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it."
47:
The Blessed One said, "Kassapa, will you be able to wear these refuse-heap robes of mine, worn out from use?" This was not said in reference to the physical strength of Venerable Mahākassapa (who possessed the strength of five bull elephants), but rather in reference to the fulfillment of practice (paṭipatti) such as the dhutaṅgas.

The Blessed One's intention here was: "Kassapa, I took this robe—which had been wrapped around a slave girl named Puṇṇā and discarded in the Āmaka cemetery, teeming with about a measure of maggots—after shaking off those maggots, while standing in the noble lineage of the Great Ariyas. On the day I took this robe, the great earth within the ten thousand world systems roared loudly and shook. The sky thundered. The deities and Brahmas in the world systems gave shouts of 'Sādhu!' A monk who receives this robe should naturally be a refuse-heap robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), a forest dweller (āraññika), a one-session eater (ekāsanika), and a regular alms-goer (sapadānacārika). Kassapa, will you be able to practice in a way that is worthy of this robe?"

Venerable Mahākassapa, although possessing the strength of five bull elephants, disregarded that physical strength and, with the resolve "I shall fulfill this practice," and the zeal to be worthy of the Buddha's robe, said, "Venerable Sir, I will wear it." Having thus consented, they exchanged robes; the Blessed One wore the robe previously worn by the Thera, and the Thera wore the Blessed One's robe. At the moment of this exchange, the great earth roared and shook down to the water's edge.

"Sāṇāni paṃsukūလာni" refers to refuse-heap robes made of hemp, which were taken after shaking off about a measure of maggots from a discarded corpse. "Nibbassanāni" means those for which the act of wearing is finished, meaning worn out from use. Here, although it was a single robe, the plural form is used because it is composed of many threads or parts, as stated in the Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada.

In the phrase "cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena," the word "attanā" (with oneself) is not explicitly used because the meaning "use shared with oneself" is clear, and in using words with clear meanings, one has the freedom of usage. From the statement "Kassapa, will you wear my hempen refuse-heap robes," it is understood that the use is shared with the Buddha himself and not another. This is because the meaning cannot always be determined by the word alone; it is mostly determined by the context (pakarana), etc. However, the teacher Venerable Dhammapāla Thera stated that in the phrase "cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena," the word "attanā" should be brought in from the phrase "attanā samasamaṭṭhapanena" used here, and construed as "cīvare attanā sādhāraṇaparibhogena" (shared use of the robe with oneself).
48:
Whatever word has a connection with another word, even if it stands far away, it is connected to that word. The mere proximity of words that do not match in meaning is not a reason for connection.

Alternatively, it should be construed as: 'The Blessed One was honored by the Blessed One through the shared use of the robe.' This is because even a single instrumental case ending (tatiyā-vibhatti) can express both the sense of 'together with' (sahattha) and the sense of the agent (kattā). It is called 'shared' (sādhāraṇa) because it involves wearing (dhāraṇa) similar to one's own; such use is called 'shared use' (sādhāraṇaparibhoga). The connection is that he was honored by that shared use and by being placed on an equal footing.

Now, the commentator, wishing to show in brief—by way of an ellipsis (peyyāla) and the use of the word 'ādi' (etc.)—this Pali passage from the Kassapa Saṃyutta, which was spoken by the Blessed One for the purpose of placing [Kassapa] on an equal footing with himself in terms of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) consisting of the nine successive attainments and the six higher powers, said: 'Bhikkhus, I...' and so on.

In that passage, 'yāvade' is simply 'yāvad-eva'; it means 'for as long as I wish, for that long I dwell.' For this very reason, it is written in the Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada and Cūḷa-gaṇṭhipada that 'yāvade means yāvad-eva.' In the Saṃyutta Commentary as well, the meaning is stated as: 'yāvade ākaṅkhāmi means yāvad-eva icchāmi (just as much as I wish).' Similarly, in the Līnatthappakāsanī, the sub-commentary to that work, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated: 'This word yāvade has the same meaning as yāvad-eva.' In some palm-leaf manuscripts, however, the reading 'yāvad-eva' itself is found. Furthermore, 'yāvade' should be understood in the context of attainments as 'for as long as I wish to dwell in the dwelling of attainment, for that long I dwell in the dwelling of attainment,' and in the context of the higher powers as 'as much as the exercise of higher power...'
49:
"...I wish to exercise, for that much I exercise the higher power"—thus the meaning should be understood along with the rest of the Pali text. The teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, also stated that same meaning in a comprehensive manner: 'As many dwellings of attainment or exercises of higher power as I wish, I both dwell in and exercise; so too does Kassapa.' Other teachers, however, say that in the word 'yāvade', the construction should be made by the power of the object of the word 'ta' (that) brought forward, such as: 'Whatever first jhāna I wish, that first jhāna I enter and dwell in' in the context of attainments and the higher power of psychic sorts (iddhividha-abhiññā); and by the power of the instrument (karaṇa) in the context of the remaining higher powers, such as: 'Whatever divine ear element I wish, with that divine ear I hear sounds.'

In the phrase 'vivicceva kāmehi' (secluded indeed from sensual pleasures), the word 'eva' has the sense of restriction (niyama) and should be applied to both terms. What needs to be said here will become clear further on.

In the phrase 'navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhede' (the nine successive dwellings and the six higher powers), the 'nine successive dwellings' are the eight attainments together with the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), so named because they are to be attained in successive order. The 'six higher powers' are the five mundane higher powers together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). In some books, the word 'ādi' (etc.) is found here. That 'ādi' is not desired because the meaning to be taken from the aforementioned Pali is complete without remainder. It is called 'superhuman state' (uttarimanussadhamma) because it is the state (dhamma) of those who are superior among humans, or superior to humans, or of those humans who are meditators and noble ones (ariyas); or because it is a state superior to the [ordinary] human state. Here, the ten courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha) are called 'human state' (manussadhamma) because they are to be accomplished by humans naturally even without the mental development of meditation (bhāvanā), and because they lead to the human state of existence. States such as the jhānas, which are superior to that human state, should be known as 'superhuman states.'

'By placing on an equal footing' (samasamaṭṭhapanena) means by placing [him] as an exact equal, thus: 'For as long as I, or with as many dwellings of attainment and as many higher powers as I use, so too does Kassapa.' It is said 'by placing on an equal footing' with reference to placing him [on par] in more than one instance, or the absolute equal placement of any superhuman state without remainder. This placing on an equal footing with the Teacher should be understood as mere praise by way of the commonality of possessing the nine successive dwellings and the six higher powers. For the Venerable Mahākassapa did not, like the Blessed One, enter into two hundred and forty thousand crores (240,000,000,000) of attainments daily, nor did he exercise the higher powers by way of the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and so on. It should be understood that this 'placing on an equal footing with himself in the superhuman states' is a mere illustration (nidassana). For that reason—
50:
“Kassapa, exhort the monks. Kassapa, give a Dhamma talk to the monks. Either I, Kassapa, shall exhort the monks, or you shall. Either I, Kassapa, shall give a Dhamma talk to the monks, or you shall.” By saying this, the Buddha indeed placed the Elder on an equal footing with himself. Just as he favored him in due order, so too did he praise him. 

Regarding the phrase “moving his hand in the sky,” the Blessed One moved his own hand in the sky, and this is connected to his praise based on the state of having a mind unattached to families. Alternatively, the phrase “because of the state of having an unattached mind” is in the locative sense of support (ādhāra). It means that just as one moves a hand in the sky, a monk who visits families should have a mind unattached to them; thus, the Buddha praised the Elder, using Kassapa himself as a witness. 

As the Blessed One taught: “Bhikkhus, then the Blessed One moved his hand in the sky.
