Bhikkhus, just as this hand is not stuck, not caught, and not bound in the sky, even so, bhikkhus, when any bhikkhu approaches families, his mind is not stuck, not caught, and not bound among those families, thinking, ‘May those who desire gain receive gain; may those who desire merit perform merit.’ Just as he is delighted and glad with his own gain, so too is he delighted and glad with the gain of others. Bhikkhus, a monk of such a nature is worthy of approaching families. Bhikkhus, when Kassapa approaches families, his mind is not stuck, not caught, and not bound among those families, thinking, ‘May those who desire gain receive gain; may those who desire merit perform merit.’ Just as he is delighted and glad with his own gain, so too is he delighted and glad with the gain of others.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.146).

In that Pāḷi text, “moved his hand in the sky” means he moved his hand in the lower part, upper part, and on both sides, like a pair of lightning flashes moving in the middle of the dark blue sky. Furthermore, this word “cālesi” (moved) is known as an “undivided word” (asambhinnapada) in the Buddha’s words of the Tipiṭaka. “Attamano” (self-delighted) means having one’s own mind, not a mind that has been seized and destroyed by dejection (domanassa). “Sumano” (glad-minded) means having a satisfied mind. Now, those of low inclination and wrong practice...
51:
...might say: “The Blessed One, by saying ‘Approach families with an unattached mind like the simile of the hand moving in the sky,’ is placing us in an impossible position, imposing an unbearable burden, and making us do what cannot be done.” To refute such a view and to show that “it is indeed possible to do so, and there is such a monk,” the Buddha spoke the words beginning with “Bhikkhus, Kassapa...” using the Venerable Mahākassapa himself as a witness.

He also spoke another praise: “And by the practice of being like the moon.” This means he was praised because of his practice which is comparable to the moon; or it means he was praised by the Buddha using himself as a witness in that practice. As the Blessed One taught:

“Bhikkhus, approach families like the moon. Drawing back the body, drawing back the mind, always being like a newcomer among families, not being forward. Bhikkhus, just as a man might look down an old well, a mountain precipice, or a river abyss, drawing back his body and drawing back his mind; even so, bhikkhus, approach families like the moon. Drawing back the body, drawing back the mind, always being like a newcomer among families, not being forward. Bhikkhus, Kassapa approaches families like the moon. He draws back his body, draws back his mind, and is always like a newcomer among families, not being forward.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.146).

In that Pāḷi, “like the moon” (candūpama)—if one asks if it is like the moon because of its roundness, the answer is no. Rather, just as the moon, while traversing the expanse of the sky, does not form intimacy, affection, attachment, longing, or obsession with anyone, yet remains dear and pleasing to the multitude of people; so too should you, by not forming intimacy and so forth with anyone, be dear and pleasing to the many, being like the moon when approaching the four types of families, such as the Khattiya families. Furthermore, just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, one should be understood as being like the moon by dispelling the darkness of defilements and spreading the light of knowledge.

“Drawing back the body, drawing back the mind” means withdrawing, pulling back, and removing the body and mind by that very absence of intimacy and so forth. “Always like a newcomer” (niccanavakā) means always being like a newly arrived guest.
52:
A guest (āgantuka) enters a house reached in order. If the householders see him and, out of compassion, think, 'Our sons and brothers, having gone abroad, have also wandered like this,' and make him sit and feed him, but as soon as he has eaten, he says, 'Take your dishes,' and gets up and leaves, without forming a friendship with them or attending to their affairs; in the same way, you should enter a house reached in order, receive the almsfood given by people who are inspired by your postures, and then depart, severing ties and not being concerned with their affairs. This is what is shown. 'Appagabbha' means not being impudent. It means approaching families while being free from physical impudence of eight kinds, verbal impudence of four kinds, and mental impudence of many kinds.

'Jarudapāna' means an old well. 'Pabbatavisama' means an uneven precipice on a mountain. 'Nadīvidugga' means a difficult, broken bank of a river. Here, the phrase 'evameva kho' (just so) is a comparison of the simile. The four families are like the old well and so on. The monk is like the man looking at them. Just as a man looking at those wells without guarding his body and mind falls into them, so a monk approaching families with unguarded body and so on becomes entangled in the families, and because of that entanglement, he meets with various misfortunes such as the breaking of the legs of virtue (sīla). Just as a man who guards his body and mind does not fall into those wells, so a monk who approaches families with a guarded body, guarded speech, and guarded mind, with well-established mindfulness, and with body and mind withdrawn, does not become entangled in the families. Then his legs, hands, belly, and head, which are virtue (sīla), faith (saddhā), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), do not break. The thorns of lust (rāga) and so on do not pierce him. Having attained happiness, he goes to the region of Nibbāna, where he has never gone before. To cut off the path of argument of those with low inclinations or those who practice wrongly, the Buddha showed Mahā Kassapa Thera as a witness, saying, 'Monks, Kassapa...' and so on. Thus, he is praised for the moon-like practice (candūpama-paṭipadā), which is characterized by a detached mind. Or, he is praised by making the Buddha himself a witness to that practice. If this is the meaning, the words 'ceva' and 'ca' should not be used, because the two terms are coordinate (appositional). This meaning and this reading seem more appropriate because it is stated in the Commentary to the Parinibbāna Sutta: 'Waving his hand in the sky and teaching the moon-like practice, he taught it making me a personal witness.'
53: The intended meaning is: 'What other freedom from debt (repayment of gratitude) will there be for that Venerable Mahā Kassapa other than the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya?' In that context, 'tassa' is used to show the cause; because of the word 'yaṃ', the word 'tasmā' should be added, meaning 'for that me'. In terms of referring to the action, it should be understood as the connection to that favor and that praise. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading 'tassa me' is found; in that case, another word 'tassa' should be added when referring to the action. One who has no debt is 'anaṇa'; the state of being debtless is 'āṇanya'. The meaning is: 'Apart from the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya, what other freedom from debt could there be for me? There can be none.' The meaning already stated in 'nanu maṃ bhagavā' and so on is clarified through a simile. In the phrase 'sakakavacissariyānuppadānena', 'kavaca' means armor that covers the chest; the chest is covered by that armor. That armor should be understood as referring to the robes (cīvara). 'Issariya' (sovereignty) should be understood as referring to the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti). 'Kulavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpakaṃ' means one who establishes the family lineage. Since the word 'me' always depends on another word, it should be compounded as 'saddhammavaṃsappatiṭṭhāpako' (the establisher of my lineage of the True Dhamma). The meaning is this: Just as a king favors a son who establishes the royal lineage by suppressing a host of enemies, by giving him his own armor and sovereignty, so too the Buddha, seeing far ahead, thought, 'This Kassapa will be the one who establishes my lineage of the True Dhamma,' and favored me with this extraordinary favor—giving me his robes and appointing me to a status equal to himself—in order to establish the lineage of the True Dhamma by suppressing the host of enemies of the Dispensation. Did he not favor me? And did he not praise me with this noble praise? This is the meaning. In the phrase 'iti cintayanto', the word 'iti' points to the three sentences beginning with 'ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati', preceded by the words 'they might disappear, I shall rehearse them, what other freedom from debt will there be?'. Now, to prove the aforementioned meaning with the Saṅgīti-khandhaka of the Pali Canon, he said 'yathāha' and so on. In that phrase 'yathāha', it means: 'What did he say? What word did he speak as proof of the meaning I have stated?' Alternatively, it means: 'In whatever way I have spoken, in that same way it is stated in the Pali Canon.' Alternatively, it means: 'Whatever word he spoke in the Pali Canon, the word spoken by me coincides and agrees with that word, just as the water of the Ganges and the water of the Yamuna merge.' This is because the fact of it being cited as proof from the Pali Canon is clearly perceived, and when using a word with a clear meaning, one may act according to one's wish. Indeed, the connection of the meaning is for the purpose of clarifying the intention. Alternatively, in whatever way, for the purpose of rehearsing the Dhamma and Vinaya...
54:
He inspires the monks to make an effort; it means he spoke in the Pali text in that manner. In such matters, it should be understood thus.

In the phrase "Ekamidāhaṃ", "idaṃ" is merely a particle. The term "ekaṃ samayaṃ" is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, meaning "at one time". "Pāvāyā" means from the city of Pāvā. After wandering for alms in that city of Pāvā, he set out on a long journey, thinking "I will go to the city of Kusinārā". "Addhānamaggo" refers to a long road. Here, the word "addhāna" is a synonym for "dīgha". "Mahatā" means great either by virtue or by number. The phrase "pañcamattehi" etc. shows greatness in number. The word "matta" denotes measure, as in "bhojane mattaññutā" etc. The Pali starting with "Atha kho", which is brought to fulfill the meaning "he inspires effort for the purpose of the Dhamma-Vinaya rehearsal", does not fulfill the stated meaning. To dispel the objection that the manner of inspiring effort does not appear in this Pali, it is said: "The entire Subhadda-kaṇḍa should be understood in detail". Since this objection still remains at that moment, it says "Tato paraṃ āha" etc. Alternatively, because the Pali that fulfills the stated meaning is very extensive, to avoid the burden of a large text, he showed only the beginning and the end of the Pali by way of an ellipsis in the middle, saying "The entire Subhadda-kaṇḍa should be understood in detail". By that passage "Sabbaṃ subhaddakaṇḍaṃ vitthārato veditabbaṃ", it shows the Subhadda-kaṇḍa starting from the Pali "Friends, at that time I, having left the road, sat at the foot of a certain tree" up to the end of the Pali "We shall not do what we do not desire".

By the passage "Tato paraṃ" etc., it shows the remaining Pali that demonstrates the manner of inspiring effort, starting with "Come, friends", etc. Therefore, in "Tato paraṃ āha", it should be understood that after the Subhadda-kaṇḍa, he spoke the words showing the manner of inspiring effort. This same meaning is stated in the Mahāgaṇṭhipada. The teacher Venerable Sāriputta also intended the same. However, the teacher Venerable Dhammapāla said: "Tato paraṃ means after inspiring the monks to make an effort". This statement should be examined because the manner of inspiring effort was not previously mentioned in the Pali. This manner of inspiring effort is indeed this: "Come, friends, let us rehearse the Dhamma and Vinaya before unrighteousness shines", etc.
55:
If it is said that the Subhadda-kaṇḍa itself inspires effort because it reveals the words spoken by the old monk Subhadda, which are the cause for inspiring effort, then there is nothing to be examined in Venerable Dhammapāla's statement. In "Pure adhammo dippati", "adhamma" refers to the unrighteousness that is the opposite of the ten courses of wholesome action. Or, in the context of inspiring effort for the Dhamma-Vinaya rehearsal, it could be the collection of faults that cause the failure to hold that rehearsal. Because it is said "Those who speak unrighteousness become powerful, and those who speak righteousness become weak", teachers also say that "adhamma" refers to the collection of faults such as evil desires caused by the failure of virtue, etc. "Pure dippati" means it might shine or will likely shine. The word "pure" is used in the sense of doubt. Alternatively, it means "earlier than the time when unrighteousness is able to obstruct the Dhamma". This word "pure" is not desired in the sense of "near". "Dippati" means "dippissati" (will shine), referring to the future; because it is associated with the word "pure", the present tense is used in the sense of the future, like "Pura vassati devo". Thus it is said: "In deciding the future, and likewise in the distant past, in both these times, the wise use the word pure". And: "When associated with pure, yāva, or purā, or always with karahi or kadā, even when the future suffix is not used, the present tense becomes the future".

Some teachers explain here: "Pure" means later in the future. Just as the road to be traveled by a traveler is called "pure" (ahead), so here too, the future time is called "pure" by way of traveling a path. In this case, the use of the present tense is possible in consideration of that time. In "Dhammo paṭibāhiyyati", the meaning should be understood according to the method mentioned in association with the word "pure". Likewise, "Dhamma" should be understood as the opposite of "adhamma". This same method applies hereafter. "Avinaya" is the non-discipline that is the opposite of the discipline of abandonment and the discipline of restraint. The passage "Those who speak the Vinaya become weak" should be seen as connected with the word "āha" in "Tato paraṃ āha" along with the word "iti".

"Tena hi" is a particle in the sense of urging. The monks, urging the selection, said to the Elder Mahākassapa: "Let the monks be selected". It means: "Please select, examine, and take the monks suitable for the rehearsal". By the words "Sakala... pariggahesi", it shows that although the attainment of learning and realization is possible for those individuals mentioned up to the dry-insight Arahants, the attainment of learning and realization of those endowed with qualities such as the three knowledges along with the analytical insights is superior, and thus they can be of great benefit in the rehearsal. Since this Dispensation has nine factors such as Sutta and Geyya, it is called the complete nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher. By this Dhamma...
56:
Although the attainment of the scriptural tradition (āgama) and the realization of the paths and fruits (adhigama) are possible, it shows that the attainment of learning and realization of those endowed with qualities such as the threefold knowledge (tevijjā) along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) is of great benefit to the Council (Saṅgīti) because it has reached the pinnacle. In this Dispensation, because all nine branches (aṅga) such as Sutta and Geyya exist, or because this Dispensation possesses all nine branches, it is called 'Sakalana-vaṅga' (complete ninefold). Because it is the instruction of the Buddha, it is called 'Satthusāsana' (the Teacher's Instruction). Because one is instructed by this Dhamma, it is called 'Sāsana'. Since that instruction itself is the instruction of the Buddha, it is called 'Sakalana-vaṅga-satthusāsana' (the Teacher's Instruction complete with nine branches). Or, in this Dispensation, there are nine branches such as Sutta and Geyya; therefore, it is called 'Navaṅga'. That ninefold teaching itself is the Teacher's Instruction. And because that instruction is complete and does not omit even a single part, it is so called (Sakalana-vaṅga-satthusāsana).

Because it should be mastered and practiced by those desiring their welfare, or because it should be mastered to accomplish human welfare such as benefits in the present life, it is called 'Pariyatti' (scriptural learning). Those who bear the Pariyatti, which is called the Teacher's Instruction consisting of all nine branches, namely the three Piṭakas, are called 'Sakalana-vaṅga-satthusāsana-pariyatti-dhara'. Regarding the phrase "Worldlings... (etc.) ... dry-insight Arahant monks" —

"The Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun,
Spoke of two kinds of worldlings:
One is the blind worldling,
And the other is the noble worldling."

Among the two kinds of worldlings mentioned, here only the noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is intended. This is because the specific meaning can be understood by its proximity to other words. Because of the absence of the moisture of tranquility meditation (samatha-bhāvanā), their insight (vipassanā) is dry, rough, and not unctuous. Therefore, they are called 'sukkhavipassaka' (dry-insight practitioners). They themselves are the Arahants whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). The word 'bhikkhū' (monks) should be applied to all categories. For it is said:

"Whatever word is heard from a meaningful term,
Or from a term where one remains from similar ones (ekasesa),
That word is to be connected to each,
Whenever applicable."

In the term 'Tipiṭaka-sabba-pariyatti-pabheda-dhara', the collection of the three Piṭakas is called 'Tipiṭaka'. Those who bear the entire variety of scriptural learning, which is divided into many parts by way of the nine branches etc., and is known as the three Piṭakas, are so called (Tipiṭaka-sabba-pariyatti-pabheda-dhara). Because that power causes one to develop repeatedly, it is called 'anubhāva'. That 'anubhāva' itself is 'ānubhāva' (majesty/power). Those who possess great majesty are called 'mahānubhāva'. Because it arose based on the words spoken by the Blessed One, "Monks, this monk is the foremost," the term 'etadagga' is an imitative name (anukaraṇa-nāma), like the term 'yevāpanaka'. The specific rank mentioned by virtue of that name is what is meant here by 'etadagga'. Or it can be said that it refers to one who has been appointed to the position of 'etadagga' (foremost), as in "This monk is the foremost." To show that there were also monks present in that Council who, though not appointed to an 'etadagga' position, were selected because they were endowed with other remaining qualities, the word "yebhuyyena" (mostly) is used. The three knowledges are called 'tevijjā'.
57:
The threefold knowledge (tevijjā) and so forth refers to the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā) and so forth. Because there are many varieties of these threefold knowledges and so forth, they are called those with varieties such as the threefold knowledge. Alternatively, an Arahant is called 'tevijja' because he possesses the three knowledges. These three knowledges and so forth refer to the six supernormal powers and so forth. Because these very threefold knowledges and so forth have varieties, they are called those with varieties such as the threefold knowledge. This refers specifically to Arahant monks who are distinguished by many varieties through the power of the threefold knowledge, the six supernormal powers, and so forth. The phrase "ye sandhāya vuttaṃ" (concerning whom it was said) asks: concerning which monks was the statement beginning with "Atha kho" in the Saṅgītikhandhaka spoken? By this, although it is spoken generally in the Pali text without distinction, it shows the correlation with the Pali text by stating that it was spoken specifically concerning the aforementioned Arahant monks.
## 
Are there not hundreds and thousands of Arahants who bear the scriptures (pariyatti), the ninefold teaching of the Teacher? Nevertheless, why did the Elder Mahākassapa make it one less (than five hundred)? To resolve this objection by showing a special reason, the passage beginning with "Kissa pana" was spoken. In that context, "kissa" means "why". The word "pana" indicates another aspect. "Okāsakaraṇatthaṃ" means for the purpose of making an opening (giving permission). The word "attha" is a word expressing cause, as in sentences like "He left the city and climbed Mount Missaka for the sake of (atthā) the festival." It is in the nominative case with the sense of cause, as in Pali passages like "Kissa hetu" (for what reason). Indeed, they explain: "Channatthaṃ means for the sake of the festival, because of the festival." Only when this is so does the answer become suitable for the question. In such matters, it should be understood in this way.
## 
Regarding the question "Why did he give permission to the Venerable Ānanda?", the passage beginning with "Tena" was spoken. The word "hi" is used in the sense of cause. By the words beginning with "So hāyasmā", he shows the individual reasons in the statement "It is not possible either with him or without him." Some teachers say that this explains that very meaning. That is not appropriate. This is because the causal word "tasmā" is found. In places where the cause is shown by "tasmā" and so forth, the word "hi" indeed illuminates the cause. Particles like "hi" are like broken branches placed on a path; they merely indicate a sign. In such matters, it should be known thus.
## 
He is called a "sekkha" (trainee) because he trains (sikkhati). Alternatively, training is called "sikkhā", and because that training is his habit, he is called "sekkha". Because his training is not yet completed and because his mind is inclined toward that training, he is truly one whose habit is training. He is not like an asekha (one beyond training) whose training is finished and whose effort has subsided. Nor is he like a worldling (puthujjana) who has discarded training and whose mind is not inclined toward it. Whether by the power of the "kita" suffix or the "taddhita" suffix, the meaning of his natural habit should be taken here, as in the word "kāruṇika" (compassionate). Alternatively, because he is born in the three trainings through the noble birth, or in those trainings...
58:
...he is a "sekkha". Furthermore, one sees (ikkhati) by means of it, thus it is "ikkhā", referring to the right view (sammādiṭṭhi) associated with the paths and fruits. Because he is with that "ikkhā", he is called "sekkha". Because the tasks of the three higher paths are not yet completed, he is "sakaraṇīyo" (one with tasks to be done). The word "assa" (to him) connects with the phrase "appaccakkhaṃ nāma" (known as not personally witnessed). Alternatively, the word "assa" is a word ending in the dative case (sampadāna) that receives the verb in the phrase "natthi" (there is not). Due to the state of having practiced repeatedly, there is nothing that is not personally witnessed by the Venerable Ānanda.
## 
In the Vinaya Commentary, however, it is said: "There is nothing that was received in the absence of the Blessed One." Although it is said "two thousand from the monks," it was spoken with the intention that they were indeed received in the presence of the Blessed One. For that reason, even a Sutta spoken by a disciple is called "the Buddha's word" (Buddhabhāsita).
## 
By the words beginning with "Yathāha", he shows the very verse spoken by the Venerable Ānanda as evidence. This verse was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda himself in the Gopaka-moggallāna Sutta when he was providing an answer to a brahmin named Gopaka-moggallāna, who asked: "You are famous as one of great learning in the Buddha's Dispensation. How many teachings were spoken by your Teacher and retained by you?" It was also spoken in the Theragāthā for the purpose of showing his own qualities.
## 
The summary of the meaning in that verse is: "I received and mastered eighty-two thousand Dhamma aggregates (dhammakkhandha) from the Teacher, the Buddha. I received two thousand Dhamma aggregates from the monks, such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and others. Those teachings which are on the tip of my tongue or proceed in my heart, which have been practiced and memorized—combining both of these, they are eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates."
## 
Some teachers, however, split the word "yeme" into "ye ime" and explain the connection as: "Among these teachings which were set in motion by the Buddha and the monks, I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha and two thousand from the monks; thus there are eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates." This connection is designated as "kecivāda" (the view of some) because the conclusion "only this many are the Dhamma aggregates" is not clearly evident.
## 
The reason stated as "it is not possible even without him" is stronger than the reason "it is not possible even with him," because he is of great benefit to the Council. Therefore, to show and resolve the objection in that statement, the passage beginning with "Yadi evaṃ" was spoken. In that context, "yadi evaṃ" means "if it is not possible without him in this way, if that were the case." "Sekkho pi samāno" means even though he is a trainee (sekkhapuggalo). Here, the word "māna" is used in the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇa). "Bahukārattā" means because of being of great benefit. The word "kāra" is a word expressing benefit (upakāra).
59:
It is like in the words beginning with, “Even a small deed of merit performed brings great fruit.” “Assa” means “should be.” The word “atha” is used in the sense of inquiry. In questions, the usage “Atha tvaṃ kena vaṇṇena” (How is it, for what reason do you release yourself?) is cited as an example. It should also be interpreted as “When it is so.”

“Parūpavādavivajjanato” means because of the desire to avoid the blame and reproach of others who do not know the aforementioned reason. This point is explained by the words beginning with “Thero hi.” “Ativiya vissattho” means one who is exceedingly intimate. Since one might ask how this is known, the words beginning with “Tathā hi” are spoken. Alternatively, this statement is for the purpose of confirmation. Experts in grammar say that these words “Tathā hi” are used in the sense of confirmation. “Naṃ” refers to the Elder Ānanda and is connected as the object of the verb “ovadati” (admonishes).

When the Elder Ānanda’s retinue, who were mostly junior monks, disrobed, the Elder Mahākassapa said, “This boy does not know his measure.” Indeed, when the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, sitting in the midst of the gathered Saṅgha of monks, selected five hundred monks for the purpose of reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya (Saṅgāyana). He said, “Friends, let us spend the rainy season in Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and Vinaya. Before the commencement of the rainy season, sever your own impediments (palibodha) and assemble in Rājagaha.” Having said this, he himself went to Rājagaha.

The Elder Ānanda also took the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, and while informing the great multitude of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, he went to Sāvatthī. Departing from there and heading towards Rājagaha, he wandered on a walking tour in the Dakkhiṇāgiri district. At that time, about thirty of the Elder Ānanda’s co-residents—who were mostly young men, monks of one or two years’ standing, and novices—disrobed.

Why did they ordain, and why did they disrobe? It is said that their parents thought: “The Elder Ānanda is intimate with the Teacher; he requested eight boons and serves Him. He is able to take the Teacher and go to any place he desires. Let us ordain our sons in the presence of this Elder. In this way, he will bring the Teacher and come here. When He comes, we will have the opportunity to perform great honor and offerings.” For this reason, their relatives first had them ordained. However, when the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, that expectation was cut off, and so they had them disrobe in a single day. Then, seeing the Elder Ānanda arrive in Rājagaha after wandering in Dakkhiṇāgiri, the Elder Mahākassapa spoke thus. This is stated in the Kassapa Saṃyutta—
60:
“Friend Ānanda, why do you now wander on a walking tour with these nine junior monks who do not guard their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness? I think you wander like one destroying crops; I think you wander like one destroying families. Friend Ānanda, your retinue is breaking up. Friend, the junior monks and novices under you are mostly perishing. This boy does not know his measure,” (said the Elder Mahākassapa).

“Venerable Mahākassapa, grey hairs have grown on my head, yet even so, we are still not free from being called a ‘boy’ by the Venerable Mahākassapa,” (replied the Elder Ānanda).

“Friend Ānanda, why do you wander on a walking tour with these nine junior monks who do not guard their sense faculties, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not devoted to wakefulness? I think you wander like one destroying crops; I think you wander like one destroying families. Friend Ānanda, your retinue is breaking up. Friend, the junior monks and novices under you are mostly perishing. This boy does not know his measure,” (he said again).

In that Pali text, “Sassaghātaṃ maññe carasi” means wandering as if destroying crops. “Kulūpaghātaṃ maññe carasi” means wandering as if destroying the families of lay supporters. “Olujjati” means to be destroyed or to break up. “Palujjanti kho te āvuso navappāyā” means, friend Ānanda, the monks of one or two years’ standing and the novices under you are mostly perishing. “Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī” means this boy surely does not know his own measure; this was said as a rebuke to the Elder. “Kumārakavādā na muccāmā” means not being free from the designation of being a “boy.” The phrase “Tathā hi pana tvaṃ” is spoken to show the reason for speaking in such a manner. The meaning here is: because you wander with these junior ones who lack sense restraint and are immoderate in eating, you, wandering with boys, deserve to be called a “boy.”

In the phrase “Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī,” the word “vā” is used in the sense of a filler (padapūraṇa). The word “vā” is seen in many senses such as comparison (upamā), conjunction (samuccaya), doubt (saṃsaya), abandonment (vissagga), alternative (vikappa), and filler (padapūraṇa). It is like in the words, “Paṇḍito vāpi tena so,” and so on.
61:
It is found in the sense of comparison (upamāna), meaning 'the state of being similar.' In passages such as 'Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti' (Sn 213), it is used in the sense of aggregation (samuccaya). In passages such as 'Ke vā ime kassa vā' (Pārā 296), it is used in the sense of doubt (saṃsaya). In passages such as 'Ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho' (DN 181), it is used in the sense of distinction (vavassagga). In passages such as 'Ye hi keci bhikkhave samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā' (MN 1.170, SN 2.13), it is used in the sense of alternative (vikappa). In passages such as 'Na vāhaṃ paṇṇaṃ bhuñjāmi, na hetaṃ mayha bhojanaṃ,' it is used in the sense of a verse-filler (padapūraṇa). Here too, it should be understood as a verse-filler.

For this very reason, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla, when extracting the meaning of the word 'vā,' stated that in passages such as 'Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī,' it is a verse-filler. This is also stated in the Saṃyutta Commentary: 'Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī means the Elder spoke rebuking him, saying, "This boy truly (vata) does not know his own measure."' Here, the word 'vata' is used for the sake of euphony. Alternatively, having split the word 'na vāyaṃ' as 'na ve ayaṃ,' the word 'vata' (indeed) is used to show the meaning of the word 've.' Because the word 've' has the sense of certainty (ekaṃsa), experts in grammar cite this very Pali passage as an example. However, the Elder Vajirabuddhi says: 'In the word na vāyaṃ, vā has the sense of option (vibhāsā); he might know, or he might not know.' That is merely his opinion, as it is not stated thus in the Saṃyutta Commentary. This is one reason for the possibility of others' criticism, and it should be connected with the sentence beginning with 'Tattha keci.'

Another reason is stated as 'Sakyakulappasūto cāyasmā'—this Venerable Ānanda was born in the Sakya clan, or was famous for being of the Sakya clan. In that context... [the monks] might criticize—this is the connection. Another reason is stated: 'Tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto'—the brother of the Tathāgata, the son of his paternal uncle. Here, 'bhātā' (brother) means a younger brother by virtue of being the son of a paternal uncle, but not by being born on the same day in terms of age.

'Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, Sukkodana, and Amitodana; Amitā and Palitā—these are the five [princes] and these two [princesses].'

Among these aforementioned Sakya princes, Venerable Ānanda was the son of the youngest, King Amitodana. Indeed, it is stated in the Manorathapūraṇī Commentary:
62:
'Having given gifts for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. Then, because he was born making all his relatives joyful and delighted, they gave him the name "Ānanda."' 

It is stated likewise in the Papañcasūdanī Commentary:

'Others, however, say: Venerable Ānanda was not co-natal (sahajāta) with the Blessed One; he was the Blessed One's younger brother only by age and by being the son of his paternal uncle. For in the explanation of the Ekanipāta in the Manorathapūraṇī, he is not mentioned in the enumeration of those who were co-natal.'

Whichever statement is made, that should be accepted. 'Tattha' means when there is that state of intimacy and so on. It means: because of being the brother of the Tathāgata, born of the Sakya clan, and being extremely intimate. In some places, when one action is marked by another action (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa), the sense of cause (hetu) is achieved. Thus, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla stated in the explanation of the verse 'Gunañce taramānānaṃ' in the Netti Commentary:

'"Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchantī" means all those cows go crookedly. Why? "Nette jimhagate sati" means when the leader goes crookedly; the meaning is because the leader has gone crookedly.'

In the Udāna Commentary as well, in the explanation of the sutta phrase 'Iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti,' it is stated: 'It should be understood that the locative case (sattamī) has the sense of cause (hetu); by the existence of the cause, the existence of the effect, which is invariably connected with it, is characterized.' Alternatively, 'tattha' means in that intimacy and so on which serves as the cause. Some also say it means 'in that selection.' In the phrase 'chandāgamanaṃ viya,' the word-split is 'chandā āgamanaṃ viya.' The word 'chandā' is in the ablative case (nissakka) in the sense of cause; the meaning is 'like the proceeding (āgamana) because of desire.' It means 'as if doing what should not be done because of desire.' Or, 'chandāgamana' means desire comes (āgacchati) by way of association (sampayoga); such is the arising of unwholesome thought (akusala-cittuppāda) that leads to the lower realms.

Alternatively, 'agamana' means improper conduct (going). 'Chandāgamana' means improper conduct because of desire. It means like improper conduct due to the affection of desire, as if doing what should not be done. The analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of one beyond training (asekha)...
63:
“Taṃpattā” means those who have reached the asekha-paṭisambhidā (analytical insights of an Arahant). Alternatively, it means those monks who are both asekha (Arahants) and have attained the paṭisambhidā; it refers to those of such nature. In the term “Sekha-paṭisambhidāppatta” as well, it should be understood in this same manner. In the word “Parivajjento”, the suffix “anta” carries the sense of cause (hetu), meaning “because of wanting to avoid”. “Anumatiyā” means by permission or by request.

The phrase “Even though he is a sekha” is said because only Arahants (asekha) were selected for the Council, not because sekhas are capable of going to the wrong paths (agati). This is because the four wrong paths are abandoned even by the first path (sotāpatti-magga). Therefore, the connection should be: “Even though he is a sekha, may the Elder select the Venerable Ānanda.” It should not be connected as: “Even though he is a sekha, he is incapable of going to a wrong path.” By using the word “Abhabbo” (incapable) and so on, it shows the suitability of Venerable Ānanda for the Dhamma-saṅgīti (Dhamma Recitation) by mentioning his existing virtues. This indicates that when deciding on the Dhamma and Vinaya at the Council, he would not speak otherwise due to favoritism (chanda) etc., but would speak only according to the truth. It is called “agati” because it is a path that should not be gone to, or because it is an improper going. “Pariyatta” means attained or learned.

The words starting with “Evaṃ” show the counting of the final decision. “Uccinittena” means taken by selection. The words “Api ca evaṃ... uccini” are the conclusion. Some teachers say the words starting with “Tenāyasmata” show the counting of the final decision.

After showing the manner of selecting the reciters for the Council, the words starting with “Atha kho” are said to show the selection of the location for the Council. In that context, “Etadahosi” means “this thought occurred”. The word “nu” indicates reflection. In the Gaṇṭhipada texts, it is said that “Rājagahaṃ” refers to the vicinity of the city of Rājagaha. It is called “gocara” because it is a place where cattle roam. Similarly, it is called “gocara” because it is a place where monks wander for alms. Because that alms-resort is large, it is called “mahāgocara”. There are many lodgings (senāsana) because there are eighteen great monasteries.

“Thāvarakammaṃ” means work that lasts a long time (repairs or renovations). “Visabhāgapuggalo” refers to a person of a discordant nature, like the old monk Subhadda. “Ukkhoṭeyya” means he might object or prevent. The word “iti” is used in this sense. It means “this thought occurred because of this reasoning as a cause.” To generate a sense of gravity, the Saṅgha was informed through a ñattidutiyakamma (a formal act with a motion), not merely by an apalokanakamma (an act of notification).

Regarding the question of when this kammavācā was performed, the words starting with “Ayaṃ pana” are said. That it was performed in this way is known by this counting, as shown by the words starting with “Bhagavā hi”. The particle “atha” is in the sense of “immediately after” (anantara). It means “immediately after the Parinibbāna”.
64:
“Seven days” is said including the day the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. “Assa” means “of the Blessed One” and should be connected with the word “sarīraṃ” (body). The days of good play are called “sādhukīḷana days” because of the celebration through worship, singing songs related to impermanence (aniccatā), and repeatedly proclaiming the grounds for spiritual urgency (saṃvegavatthu). Alternatively, it is appropriate to say they are days of celebration by proclaiming the grounds for spiritual urgency of the virtuous ones (sappurisa), who are called “sādhu” because they fulfill the welfare of themselves and others.

During this first week, the sādhukīḷana (homage festival) was performed only partially. Specifically, it was performed on the days of relic worship (dhātupūjā). This is stated in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta Commentary: “During these first two weeks, those monks were busy preparing places for the Saṅgha to stay and sit, and arranging food and snacks, so they did not get the opportunity for sādhukīḷana. Then they thought, ‘We will celebrate the sādhukīḷana for this week. It is possible that someone, knowing our negligence, might come and take the relics. Therefore, we will celebrate after placing a guard.’ Thus they did so.”

Even though they did so, because they also performed relic worship, these are also called relic worship days. Since there was no other specific duty to be performed for the Blessed One, the term “sādhukīḷana days” became well-known based on the homage festival performed partially. Thus it was said, “In this way, there were seven days of sādhukīḷana.”

“Citakāya” refers to the sandalwood funeral pyre, which was one hundred and twenty cubits high. It is said that “the fire burned the pyre for seven days” only in terms of the main activity. It did not burn continuously for seven days in an absolute sense, because it burned only on the last day of those seven days. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as “within seven days”. If it burns on any day within the seven days between the two weeks (the former and the latter), it is appropriate to say “it burned for seven days”. As it is said: “At that time, four Malla chiefs, having bathed their heads and wearing new clothes, tried to light the Blessed One’s funeral pyre but were unable to light it,” and so on.
65:
## Explanation of the First Great Council

The phrase 'sattipañjaraṃ katvā' (having made a cage of spears) is spoken by way of indication (upalakkhaṇa) to describe how the Malla kings provided protection for the Blessed One’s relics using men holding spears, swords, and so forth. Men holding weapons such as spears are called 'satti'. Just as in the phrase 'kuntā pacaranti' (the spears go about), the act of having these armed men provide protection from all sides is called 'sattipañjara' (spear-cage) because it resembles a cage.

'Santhāgāra' refers to a great hall (assembly hall) of kings. This is because, at times such as when departing for war, the kings would stay in that hall and make arrangements and establish boundaries, saying: "Let this many soldiers go in front, let this many go behind, let this many go on both sides, let this many mount the elephants, let this many mount the horses, and let this many mount the chariots." Therefore, that place is called 'santhāgāra'.

Alternatively, it is called 'santhāgāra' because kings, after returning from the battlefield, would stay there for two or three days to rest and dispel dangers while their homes were being prepared with treatments such as being smeared with fresh cow-dung water. Or, it is called 'santhāgāra' because it is the house (agāra) where kings provide instruction (atthānusāsana) on what is beneficial (by changing the letter 'ha' to 'dha' and adding the anusvāra). Or, it is called 'santhāgāra' because kings would assemble in that hall and consult on household matters, such as: "At this time it is proper to plow; at this time it is proper to sow." Thus, they sustain (sandhārenti) their interrupted household affairs in that place.

The teacher stated that twenty-one days had passed, consisting of sixteen days from the full moon of Vesākha to the new moon of Vesākha (taken according to the Sinhalese usage) and five days of the waxing moon of Jeṭṭhamūla. The relics were distributed only on that twenty-first day, and this Kammavācā was performed on that very day. Therefore, it is said: "jeṭṭhamūlasukkapakkhapañcamyaṃ" (on the fifth day of the waxing moon of Jeṭṭhamūla). In that phrase, the month is called 'Jeṭṭhamūla-māsa' because either the Jeṭṭha nakshatra or the Mūla nakshatra is associated with the moon on the full moon day of that month. 'Anācāra' refers to the improper conduct mentioned below.

If this is so, why is it stated in the Vinaya Commentary and the Maṅgala Sutta Commentary: "When the seven days of sacred festivities (sādhukīḷana) and the seven days of relic worship had passed"? It seems that when the seven days of relic worship are taken, the seven days of the funeral pyre's burning in the middle—which is inseparable from it—are also included, and thus not mentioned separately.

If this is so, why is it stated: "Half a month has passed, half a month remains"? There is no fault in this. A slight deficiency or excess is usually not included in the count. Therefore, even if a collection is slightly in excess, it is treated as if it were not; thus, although it was five days more than half a month, it is said: "Half a month has passed." This is like how the eighty-two Khandhaka duties are in some places called "eighty Khandhaka duties." Similarly, even if a collection is slightly deficient, it is treated as if it were not...
66:
...because a collection can appear as if it is not in excess even when it is, it is said that 'half a month has passed' even though it was five days more than a month and a half. This is like the eighty-two Khandhaka duties being called 'eighty Khandhaka duties' in some commentaries. Likewise, because a collection can appear as if it is not deficient even when it is, it is said that 'a month and a half remains' even though it was five days less than a month and a half. This is like the statement in the Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga Commentary: 'Recitation should be performed for six months,' even though it was half a month less than six months. Otherwise, there would be contradictions between the commentaries.

Alternatively, according to the view of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas (Reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya), it is stated here as 'twenty-one days have passed' based on three weeks. However, in the commentaries on the Vinaya, Suttanipāta, and Khuddakapāṭha, according to the view of the Khuddaka-bhāṇakas (Reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya), they count only one day for the burning of the pyre and, based on the remaining two weeks, state: 'Half a month has passed, half a month remains.' It should be understood that, as with the 'First Word of the Buddha' and so forth, there are differences in statements in the commentaries according to the views of the respective reciters.

In this regard, teachers say: Starting from the day of Parinibbāna, the first four days were only for sacred festivities (sādhukīḷana). The next three days were both for sacred festivities and the burning of the pyre (citakajhāyana). The next one day was for the burning of the pyre only. The next three days were both for the burning of the pyre and relic worship (dhātupūjā). The next four days were for relic worship only. Thus, by counting according to the respective tasks, three weeks are completed. However, by not counting what was already taken (or by taking what was not yet taken), it is only half a month. The statement 'twenty-one days have passed' mentioned here is also only by counting according to the respective tasks. It should be accepted after reflecting that only in this way do the statements in all four commentaries agree.

Elder Vajirabuddhi, however, said: 'In this context of half a month having passed, one day is lost; that is the first day of the waning moon, called the day of commotion (kolāhala), and therefore it is not taken here.' That statement is not good. This is because in the Parinibbāna Sutta Pāḷi, seven days are preached starting from the first day of the waning moon, and in the commentary, three weeks are counted including the day of Parinibbāna. Indeed, only by counting three weeks including the day of Parinibbāna does the fifth day of the waxing moon of Jeṭṭhamūla become the twenty-first day.

The phrase 'forty days' is stated by counting from the sixth day of the waxing moon of Jeṭṭhamūla until the full moon of Āsāḷha. 'Within this' means within those forty days. Illness itself is the impediment of illness (roga-palibodha). Only the duties to be performed for teachers and preceptors are called the impediment of teachers and preceptors (ācariyupajjhāya-palibodha). Similarly, the duties to be performed for parents are called the impediment of parents (mātāpitu-palibodha). It is called an impediment (palibodha) because it can oppress, cause failure, or prevent the arising of other desired benefits or tasks.
67:
The duty to be performed towards teachers and preceptors is called the impediment of the teacher and preceptor (ācariya-upajjhāya-palibodha); likewise, the duty to be performed towards parents is also called the impediment of parents. It is called 'palibodha' because it obstructs, impairs, or does not allow the occurrence of the desired benefit or action; here, the letter 'r' is changed to 'l'. With the intention that the one who will perform the rehearsal should cut off that impediment and perform the necessary task, let him cut off all impediments and perform only that necessary task known as the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

'Other great elders' refers to Elder Anuruddha and others. 'Pierced by the arrow of grief' means entered or pierced by the arrow known as grief. Because of the underlying tendencies of ignorance and craving that have not yet been eradicated, one is called 'jana' (being) because one produces or brings into existence the selfhood (attabhāva) known as the five aggregates in the realms of existence (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (ṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) through kamma prepared by ignorance and craving. Alternatively, one is called 'jana' because one is producing, has produced, or will produce defilements (kilesa). A great multitude of people is called 'mahājana'; it refers to that mahājana. 'Whenever they came' is like saying 'one by one'.

In this context, there might be an objection: "The Elder, surrounded by his retinue of five hundred, went to Rājagaha; other great elders also, taking their respective retinues, departed for various regions desiring to console the great multitude who were pierced by the arrow of grief"—this statement in this (Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā) and the statement in the Samantapāsādikā which says, "Venerable sirs, let us go to Rājagaha; saying thus, Elder Mahākassapa took half of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and went by one route, and Elder Anuruddha also took half and went by one route," seem to contradict each other. This is because in this (Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā), it implies that Mahākassapa and others went to various regions only with their own personal retinues of monks, whereas in that (Samantapāsādikā), it implies that only Elder Mahākassapa and Elder Anuruddha went by separate routes, each with half of the Saṅgha.

To that objection, it is replied: Both statements do not contradict each other because they are consistent in meaning. In this (Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā), only the individual departures of the elders are mentioned without exception, but in that (Samantapāsādikā), it is shown by way of method. Here, the statement about going with their own retinues is the same as the statement there about going with half of the Saṅgha. Indeed, 'half of the Saṅgha' refers to the group of monks who were their own respective retinues, because the word 'upaddha' (half) is also used for an unequal portion. If one were to take the meaning as half of the entire Saṅgha that had assembled, it would not be appropriate because the number of the Saṅgha was beyond counting. If one were to take the meaning as half of the five hundred monks selected for the rehearsal, it would also not be appropriate because those monks were selected as the leaders of their respective groups. These elders were each leaders of a group. For it was said: "There were seven hundred thousand monks; among them..."
68:
The phrase "pāmokkha-bhikkhavo" (leading monks) is consistent in meaning when compared, so both statements in those two commentaries do not contradict each other. Some also say that this statement was made according to the views of the respective reciters of the collections (nikāya-bhāṇaka).

It should be connected with the words "aparinibbutassa bhagavato" and so on. In the phrase "taking the bowl and robes," it means taking the stone bowl made of blue gem offered by the Four Great Kings and the robes of the Sugata. Indeed, the Buddha always used that very bowl. For it was said in the commentary to the Samacittappaṭipadā Sutta: "Desiring to show that he used only that bowl for a period of over twenty years following the conclusion of the rains retreats, having performed the morning bodily cleansing, properly dressing in the undergarment and donning the Sugata's robes, taking the stone bowl, and surrounded by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, he entered the city through the southern gate to wander for alms." "Gandhamālādayo nesaṃ hatthe" means those who have perfumes, flowers, and so on in their hands (gandhamālā-hattha).

"Tatra" means in that city of Sāvatthī. "Sudaṃ" is merely a particle. "Aniccatādipatisaṃyuttāya" means a discourse connected with the nature of impermanence, such as "All conditioned things are impermanent." "Dhammī" means a talk connected with the Dhamma or suitable for the Dhamma. "Saññāpetvā" means having made them understand well; "samassāsetvā" means having consoled them. The compound "vasitagandhakuṭiṃ" is a compound (samāsa) because of its constant dependence. Because it is a shrine of use (paribhoga-cetiya), it is said, "having paid respects to the Gandhakuṭi." Between the words "vanditvā" (having paid respects) and "vivaritvā" (having opened), paying respects is the preceding action. Thus, Elder Ācariya Sāriputta said: "'Having opened the door of the Gandhakuṭi' means it should be understood that he paid respects to the Gandhakuṭi because it is a shrine of use, and then opened the door of the Gandhakuṭi."

"Milātā mālā" means withered flowers, which are themselves refuse. Or it means refuse known as withered flowers. "Atiharitvā" means having carried them towards the place where they were originally placed. "Yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā" means having placed them back in the original position without exceeding the place where they were first kept. The statement "He performed all the duties that were to be done while the Blessed One was still alive" is said in reference to the duties to be performed in the monastery. "Kurumāno ca" means while he was performing all those duties. Here, the suffix "-māna" is in the sense of an attribute (lakkhaṇa). It means at the times of sweeping the bathroom, preparing water in that bathroom, and so on, as well as at the times of Dhamma teaching, giving exhortations, and so forth.

The sleep of the lion, the king of beasts, is called "Sīhaseyyā." By way of a term similar to that of a lion, the Buddha's reclining is also called "Sīhaseyyā." Or it is called the supreme sleep (uttamaseyyā) because it is a posture of great power and majesty. In reference to that supreme sleep, it was said: "Then the Blessed One, lying on his right side, in the lion's posture..."
69:
The Blessed One lay down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, performing the noble sleep (the lion's posture). It should be understood by connecting the sense that: Is this not the time for such an action?

With the words "Yathā taṃ" and so forth, he clarifies the aforementioned meaning with a simile. In those words, the connection should be made thus: Just as another person, other than the Venerable Ānanda, who knew the nectar-like medicine of the Blessed One’s collection of virtues, possessed established love, had not yet exhausted the taints (āsavas), and—due to mutual benefits rendered over many lifetimes—possessed a gentleness of mind, acted accordingly; so too did the Venerable Ānanda, because of the Blessed One’s virtues, possess established love, had not yet exhausted the taints, and possessed a gentleness of mind born of benefits rendered, and thus he acted. The word "taṃ" is merely a particle. Alternatively, by this, he shows the reason for acting so. Just as others, being of the aforementioned nature, acted, so too did the Venerable Ānanda act because of his established love for the Blessed One, because his taints were not yet exhausted, and because of the gentleness of mind produced by benefits rendered over many lifetimes; this is because the causal meaning is obtained. Indeed, these words carry the causal meaning within themselves, as their meaning itself is the cause for acting in such a way. In this matter, it should be clearly understood through the accounts of the taming of the elephant Dhanapāla, the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka, the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka, the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, and others. 

The collection of virtues is called "Amata-rasa" (the nectar of the deathless) because it is like the essence that produces the deathless. The sense of having the nature of knowing that nectar of the deathless is the cause (hetu) in the word "patiṭṭhita." "Upakāra... maddavo" means having a gentleness of mind well-produced by having rendered benefits in previous lives. Thus, desiring to show that the Venerable Ānanda endured for this reason, he spoke the words beginning with "Tamenaṃ." In that phrase, "Tamenaṃ" refers to that Venerable Ānanda. The word "ena" is merely an ornament of the term. Among the two pronouns, it is the nature of the grammar that only the meaning of the preceding term is expressed.

Regarding "Saṃvejesi," the teacher Venerable Dhammapāla stated: "Did the Blessed One not say beforehand, 'There must be division, separation, and parting from all those who are dear and beloved,' and so forth, thus generating spiritual urgency (saṃvega)?" If this is so, it should be connected with the remaining text: "Having first said, 'Venerable Sir... please provide comfort.'" However, according to the direct literal meaning of the Pali, it is also appropriate to connect it using the word "iti" as "He caused agitation with such words and so forth." This is because whatever words were used to generate spiritual urgency, all of them can be the cause of that agitation.

"Santhambhitvā" means restraining and composing oneself, being free from weeping and lamentation. "Ussannadhātukaṃ" refers to having an excess of the faults (dosas) such as bile and phlegm. Indeed, in this context, the three elements (dhātus) by way of bile, phlegm, and wind...
70:
...intended for their suitability for medical treatment, which are called "faults" (dosas) and "impurities" (malas) in the world, are each of five kinds by way of division into earth, water, fire, air, and space. For it is said:

"Wind, bile, and phlegm are called faults (dosas), and likewise elements (dhātus) and impurities (malas);
Therein, each is said to be fivefold, sustaining the body.
They are called faults because they corrupt the body, impurities because they make it soiled,
And elements because they sustain it; thus they are named according to their meaning."

"Samassāsetuṃ" means to comfort or to soothe. It was on the second day from the day the deity caused the agitation, or from the day he entered the Jetavana monastery. It is called "virecana" (purgative) because one is purged by it; likewise, milk infused with medicine is a purgative. "Yaṃ sandhāya" refers to that specific medicinal intake. He is called "Subha" because he is beautiful in his major and minor limbs. He is called "Māṇava" because he is a descendant of Manu; when the dental 'n' is changed to the retroflex 'ṇ', it becomes "Māṇava." Manu refers to the man who stood in the position of a parent to humans at the beginning of the aeon, who is called "King Mahāsammata" in the Dispensation. He is called "Manu" because he knows (man-ati) the welfare of the entire world. In this regard, teachers say: "The word 'mānava' with the dental 'n' is a term common to all beings, while the word 'māṇava' with the retroflex 'ṇ' is a term for a base or deluded lineage." Even in the Commentary to the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta, the meaning of the word "māṇava" with the retroflex 'ṇ' is explained. In its sub-commentary (ṭīkā), teachers say: "Whatever lineage is base or deluded, the world uses the designation 'māṇava' for it; and since beings are mostly of a deluded nature in their youth, that very meaning is clarified."

In other texts, a youth within twenty years of age is called a "māṇava," but here, he is called "māṇava" even though he is old, because of that common usage. For it is said in the Commentary to the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta: "They called him 'māṇava' in his youth, and he is still called by that same designation even in his old age." This means the youth named Subha obtained the designation "māṇava." When that Subha Māṇava heard, "The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna; Venerable Ānanda is said to have arrived carrying his bowl and robes, and a great crowd is approaching to see that Venerable One," he thought: "If I go to the monastery, it will not be possible to converse comfortably or to listen to the Dhamma in the midst of a great crowd; only when he comes to my house will I be able to converse with him comfortably."
71:
“I will have a conversation (with Venerable Ānanda); I also have a doubt, and I will ask Venerable Ānanda about that doubt,” he thought and sent a youth. With reference to the sending of that youth, it is said, “Pahitaṃ māṇavakaṃ.” In the word “māṇavaka,” the suffix “-ka” is used in the sense of smallness (youth). “Etadavoca” means that Venerable Ānanda spoke these words beginning with “Akālo.”

“Akālo” means it is an inappropriate time to go today. Why is it inappropriate? He said, “Atthi me,” etc. “Bhesajjamattā” means a small amount of medicine. Here, the word “matta” has the meaning of “a small amount,” as in “mattā sukhapariccāgā,” etc. “Pītā” means having drunk. Regarding the word “svepi,” Elder Vajirabuddhi said that the word “api” has the sense of expectation (apekkhā) and slight permission. The Elder’s intention is that if one only says “appeva nāma” (perhaps), the state of permission is not clear; therefore, the word “api” is used to accomplish that permission. By that word “api,” he shows this meaning: “Perhaps we might approach tomorrow; if we are able to approach, we shall approach.”

“Dutiya-divase” means the second day from the day the milk-purgative was drunk. “Cetakatherena” means with the Elder named Cetaka because he was born in the Cetiya country. “Pacchāsamaṇena” means with a monk who follows behind (an attendant). Here, the instrumental case denotes “together with” (saha). Subha the youth thought, “The Blessed Gotama established this world in certain dhammas; have those dhammas disappeared after his passing, or do they still exist? If they exist, Venerable Ānanda will know; let me go and ask him.” Then he asked, “O Venerable Ānanda, of which dhammas was the Blessed Gotama a praiser? In which dhammas did he urge, settle, and establish this generation?” etc. Then, Venerable Ānanda, wishing to show the three Piṭakas by encompassing them within the three aggregates such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), etc., spoke the tenth sutta in this Sīlakkhandhavagga, beginning with, “O youth, the Blessed One was a praiser of three aggregates,” etc. With reference to that sutta, it is said, “Imasmiṃ... abhāsi.”

“Khaṇḍaṃ” means something broken. “Phullaṃ” means something cracked, or the blossoming of moss, mushrooms, etc. The proper repairing of those things to their original state is called “paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ,” which means renewing. “Upakaṭṭhāya” means when it is near. The time that has arrived for entering the rains-retreat is called “vassūpanāyikā.” Although it is spoken generally in the Saṅgīti Pāḷi...
72:
## Explanation of the Account of the First Great Council

Even the words spoken generally in the Saṅgīti Pāḷi are said with reference only to the monks who travel in this way; thus, he said “Evañhi,” etc., in order to connect or to complete the meaning.

“Rājagahaṃ parivāretvā” (surrounding Rājagaha) is said in the sense of staying outside the city. “Chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā” means rubbish that is discarded, fallen, and dirty. The meaning is this: the monks who were going to the place of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna discarded [the dwellings]; because they were discarded, they were eaten by termites, etc., and thus fell here and there; because there was no sweeping, they were dirty, being strewn with rubbish. He clarifies that very meaning with “Bhagavato hi,” etc. “Avakuthi” means it reached a state of putridity. In the word “uklāpo,” the letter ‘th’ has been changed to ‘l’; or it is called “uklāpo” because it is a heap of discarded rubbish. It is spoken thus by way of letter transformation, just like the words “upakkleso,” “sneho,” etc. It is called “pariveṇa” (precinct) because it is seen by way of its boundaries.

“Kurumānā” means desiring to do. Because the duties regarding dwellings (senāsana-vatta) were prescribed, and because many words connected with dwellings were spoken in the Senāsanakkhandhaka, the repairing of dwellings is indeed a form of worship to the Blessed One; thus he said, “Bhagavato vacanapūjanatthaṃ” (for the purpose of honoring the Blessed One’s words). “Paṭhamaṃ māsaṃ” means throughout the first month of the rains. Here, the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) is in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga). He said “Titthiyavādaparimocanatthañca,” etc., to clarify the meaning “and for the sake of release from the arguments of sectarians.”

“Yaṃ” refers to the making of an agreement (katika). In such places, the word “yaṃ” does not need to depend on the word “taṃ” because the meaning is complete by itself. Or, it means: whatever agreement was referred to by the words “Atha kho,” etc., that very agreement I also speak of. In such places, it should be understood in this way. The Blessed One praised [this] when he prescribed the duties regarding dwellings and when he spoke words connected with dwellings in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. In the phrase “saṅgāyissāma,” the word “iti” should be connected with both “vuttaṃ” and “ahosi”; or it should be understood that one “iti” word has been elided.

“Dutiya-divase” means on the second day from the day of such thought; and that is indeed the second day from the day of entering the rains-retreat. For the Elders assembled on the first day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, entered the rains, and then thought in this way. “Rājadvāre” means at the gate of the King’s palace in Rājagaha. “Hatthakammaṃ” means performing manual labor (handiwork). “Paṭivedesuṃ” means they informed. “Visaṭṭhā” means having minds free from doubt.
73:
Authority itself is called a 'wheel' (cakka) because it proceeds with unobstructed activity; therefore, it is called the 'Wheel of Authority' (Āṇācakka). Similarly, the Dhamma itself is a wheel; therefore, it is called the 'Wheel of Dhamma' (Dhammacakka). Here, that Wheel of Dhamma is appropriate in both senses: by way of the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedhañāṇa). This is because the Recital (Saṅgīti) was conducted through both these types of knowledge. It is stated in the Commentaries: "This name 'Wheel of Dhamma' is a name for the knowledge of teaching and also for the knowledge of penetration."

'Sannisaññajjaṭṭhāna' refers to a place for sitting together in assembly. A tree that has seven leaves is called 'Sattapaṇṇi' (the seven-leaf tree). That tree is also called 'Chattapaṇṇi' or 'Visamacchada.' The meaning is: at the entrance of the cave where that Sattapaṇṇi tree grows.

'Vissakammunā' refers to the celestial son Vissakamma, who manages the major and minor affairs of Sakka, the lord of devas. In the phrase 'suvibhattabhittithambhasopānaṃ,' the word 'suvibhatta' (well-apportioned) is placed before the compound (dvanda) and thus connects with all members of the compound. The same applies to 'nānāvidha... vicittaṃ' and so on. 'Rājabhavanavibhūtiṃ' means the abundance of the royal palace or the splendor of the royal palace. 'Avahasantamiva' means as if mocking [other palaces] with laughter. 'Siriyā' means with glory, which is described as beauty. 'Niketanamiva' means like a dwelling place. There is also a variant reading 'jalantamiva' (as if blazing). It is said 'ekanipāta... vihaṅgānaṃ' because the eyes of all people fall upon the pavilion just like birds descending upon a single watering place. 'Nayanavihaṅgānaṃ' means of the birds that are the eyes. 'Lokarāmaṇeyyakamiva sampiṇḑitaṃ' means as if all the delightful things existing in the world were brought and gathered in one place. Or it means as if every delightful object in the world that is worthy of enjoyment were gathered together. 'Daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḑaṃ' means the essence that is like heartwood free from sapwood, or like clarified butter free from dregs; it is the essential and pure part among things worthy of being seen. Alternatively, it is called 'daṭṭhabbasāramaṇḑa' because it possesses a decoration (maṇḑana) that is worthy of being seen, essential, and superior. It is called 'maṇḑapa' (pavilion) because it wards off (pāti) the sun's rays (maṇḑa), or because it protects (pāti) the clarity (maṇḑa) of all people, or because it takes up (pāti/pivati) suitable ornaments (maṇḑana) for the purpose of decoration.

'Kusumadāmolambakāni' refers to flower garlands that are hanging down. In this term, the adjective (vissessana) is placed at the end, as in the word 'agghāhita.' It is so called because there is a beautiful canopy in that pavilion where various hanging flower garlands are particularly prominent, as if they were emerging. It is called 'kuṭṭima' or 'koṭṭima' because it is made smooth by being worked with a hammer (or stone-cutting tool). Being a floor of rubies of such a nature, it is called 'maṇikoṭṭima'.
74:
'Maṇikoṭṭima' refers to a floor of rubies intricately inlaid with various jewels. Alternatively, it is called 'maṇikoṭṭima' because the floor is made by cutting and carving gems; thus, it is produced by gem-cutting (maṇikoṭṭa). That very floor is 'maṇikoṭṭimatala,' which is variegated with various jewels. It should be understood that it is connected [to the next phrase] as: 'a well-finished ground-work variegated with various flower offerings like that [floor].' Here, the mention of being variegated with various jewels illustrates the variegation with various flower offerings, and the mention of the ruby-inlaid floor (maṇikoṭṭimatala) illustrates the well-finished ground-work.

'Naṃ' refers to the pavilion. 'Brahmavimānasadisaṃ' (like a Brahma mansion) is an adverbial use. The meaning is that it was decorated just as a Brahma mansion shines. It is called 'vimāna' because it is especially to be honored (mānetabba). However, grammarians say: "It is called vimāna because devas travel (māyanti/gacchanti) through it in the sky (vihe/ākāse)." Or it is called 'vimāna' because it is specially created (nimmīyati) by virtuous deeds (sucarita-kamma). Or 'vi' refers to a bird, and it is called 'vimāna' because it is created in the shape of that bird, and so on. In the Vimānavatthu Commentary, however, it is said: "It is called vimāna because it possesses specific dimensions such as one league or two leagues, and because it is especially to be honored due to its excessive beauty."

'Anagghāni' (priceless) means they are of immeasurable value and thus cannot be priced. There are hundreds of 'paccattharaṇa' (coverings/rugs) that are suitable or spread out individually. A Dhamma seat (Dhammāsana) facing North was prepared. Because the Dhamma itself performs the function of the Teacher after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, it is said: "having prepared a Dhamma seat worthy of the seat of the Blessed Buddha." Just as the Buddha said: "The Dhamma I have taught... shall be your Teacher after my passing," this is also said to show that the one who teaches the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata is performing the Teacher's function and is thus worthy to sit on such a seat. 'Worthy of the seat' (āsanārahaṃ) means worthy of sitting. 'Dhamma seat' (Dhammāsana) means the seat of a Dhamma preacher or a seat suitable for speaking the Dhamma. 'Dantakhacitaṃ' (inlaid with ivory) means made with ivory, specifically elephant tusks. For it is said: "Danta refers to elephant ivory." In this context, "my task" (mama kiccaṃ) means: "The task to be performed by me, King Ajātasattu, is completed."

Now, to show the attainment of the stage of the Beyond-learner (Arahantship) by the Venerable Ānanda, [the text] says: "And on that day..." and so on. "On that day" means on the day informed by the King, which is the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa. Defilement (kilesa) is called 'poison' (visa) because it is suspected of being like poison due to its producing harm. After becoming an Arahant, there is a power (satti) characterized by the transformation [of those defilements], which is called 'scent' (gandha). Indeed...
75:
That Venerable Ānanda performed lamentations and so forth at the time of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. Alternatively, defilement (kilesa) is called 'poisonous scent' (visagandha) because it is similar to the scent of poisonous flowers and the like, and because it produces actions that are the cause of various kinds of suffering. Indeed, that defilement is described (in the Mahāniddesa) as: 'It is called visattikā because it carries poison; it is called visattikā because it has poison as its root; it is called visattikā because it has poison as its fruit; it is called visattikā because it consumes poison,' and so forth. Furthermore, 'poisonous scent' (visagandha) refers to the foul smell of decaying flesh and the like; defilement is so called because of its similarity to that. In the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā, it is stated: 'The word vissa refers to a foul appearance.'

'Addhā' means certainly. 'Saṃvega' means spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega). The phrase 'of those who have laid down the burden' (ohitabhārānaṃ) is spoken generally and primarily. However, in such contexts, the spiritual urgency of others is also intended. Thus, in the Rajjumālā-vimāna-vaṇṇanā, it is stated: 'Saṃvega is knowledge accompanied by moral dread (ottappa); that knowledge arose in her upon seeing the Blessed One.' At that time, she was one who did not yet know the Dispensation and whose fruition was yet to come. Otherwise, if saṃvega were taken only as anger (dosa) occurring by way of mental terror, it would be a fault. If that were the case, that saṃvega could not be the certain cause for reaching the stage of the non-trainee (asekkha-bhūmi/Arahantship). Since such (anger-associated) saṃvega is not intended here, there is no need for further elaboration.

'Tena' means because the assembly of the Sangha is to take place tomorrow, or because as a trainee (sekkha), there is still work to be done. 'Te na yuttaṃ' means it is not proper for you, or it is not suitable for you to go to the assembly. 'Metaṃ' means this going of mine. 'Yvāhaṃ' means 'I who,' or it is the use of the word 'yaṃ' to refer back to the action. By that word 'yaṃ,' the action of going in the phrase 'gaccheyyaṃ' is referred to. It is seen in various places that the nature of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' when referring to an action is to remain in the neuter gender and singular number. Indeed, grammarians desire the neuter and singular for the nature of an action. 'Āvajjesi' means he inclined (leaned). 'Muttā' means they were released. 'Appattañca' means before reaching, meaning before [his head] was placed on the pillow. 'Etasmiṃ antare' means in this interval. It means in the middle moment of the times shown by these two words, or in the gap between those two shown times. It is said:

'The sound (word) "antarā" is used in the senses of cause, mind, moment, gap, and middle, etc.'

'Anupādāya' means without grasping any phenomena by way of craving or views, or without grasping even a trace of those defilements from which he was being liberated.
76:
"Āsavehi" means from the defilements called taints (āsava) because they flow from the beginning of existence up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), and according to their nature, up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). This is merely a metonymic expression (upalakkhaṇa). This is because the mind is truly liberated from all defilements and all evil unwholesome states that exist in the same thought-arising as those taints. "Cittaṃ vimucci" means the mind, being in the process of being liberated from the taints at the moment of the Path of Arahantship, became liberated at the moment of the Fruition of Arahantship. That meaning is explained by the words beginning with "ayañhi."

"Caṅkamena" means by the act of walking meditation. "Visesaṃ" means a Path and Fruition higher than the Path and Fruition already attained by himself. He is called "katapuñño" because he has performed and accumulated merit which is a powerful support for the turning away from Saṃsāra (Nibbāna). It means one who has made the necessary effort for the attainment of Arahantship. "Padhānamanuyuñja" means apply energy; it means make a repeated effort for the attainment of Arahantship. "Hohisi" means you will become. "Kathādoso" means a fault in speech, an inaccuracy. "Accāraddhaṃ" means excessively exerted. "Uddhaccāya" means for the sake of restlessness and agitation. "Handa" is a word expressing relinquishment or determination. By that, he makes a resolution: "I will join (balance energy and concentration) right now; I will not delay any longer." "Vīriyasamataṃ yojemi" means because the energy of walking meditation was excessive, I will join the balance of energy by reducing it and making it equal with concentration; or it means I will join concentration, known as tranquility (samatha), with energy. Both readings are found. "Vissamissāmi" means I will rest or I will take a breather.

Now, to show that Venerable Ānanda is worthy of special praise, the words beginning with "tena" are spoken. "Tena" means because of the reason of being free from the four postures. The words such as "anipanno" are in the present tense. Even when he attained Parinibbāna (final passing), he did so in the air. Therefore, the Elder's attainment of the Nibbāna of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna) and the Nibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna) is especially worthy of praise, being truly marvelous and wonderful (acchariya-abbhuta).

"Dutiya-divase" means on the second day from the day the Elder attained Arahantship. "Pañcamiyaṃ" is said with regard to the lunar day (tithi), and it has the same meaning as the phrase "dutiya-divase." Words with different genders but the same meaning are sometimes seen, such as "guṇo pamāṇaṃ," "vīsati cittāni," and so forth. "Kāḷapakkhassa" means of the dark fortnight of the month of Sāvaṇa. For the first month, they performed the repairs of broken and dilapidated parts; the status of the first month is according to the usage of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). For there, they designate one month from the previous full moon to the next full moon. After that month, the King built the pavilion for three days. On the second day after that, the Elder realized Arahantship. On the third day, the Elders assembled and performed the Recitation (Saṅgīti). Therefore, from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha until...
77:
Up to the 5th day of the waning moon of Sāvaṇa, it is one month and five days (starting from the 1st day of the waning moon of Āsāḷha). 'Samāno' means 'arisen' (having attained Arahantship). 'Haṭṭhatuṭṭhacitto' means having an extremely joyful mind, or a mind gladdened by joy, or a mind satisfied with delight. 'Ekaṃsaṃ' means on one shoulder, specifically the left shoulder. Thus, in the Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta, it is said: 'In this context, "ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ" is said again regarding the proper adjustment of the robe. "Ekaṃsaṃ" is a term for the robe as it stays covering the left shoulder.
