The meaning should be understood as: in whatever manner it stays covering the left shoulder, having made (worn) the robe in that manner.'

'Bandhanūpaghāti' and so forth means like a well-ripened palm fruit that has fallen from its stalk. 'Paṇḍukambalavighāti' and so forth means like a genuine gem placed on a pale yellow woolen blanket from the Paṇḍu region; here, the word 'jāti' (genuine/birth) excludes imitation gems. 'Samuggatapuṇṇacando viya' means like the full moon with all sixteen phases complete, rising on the 15th day Uposatha of the waxing fortnight. 'Bālasūriya' and so forth means like a paduma lotus filled with golden-colored pollen that has bloomed upon contact with the light of the young rising sun. "The word 'piñjara' is a synonym for golden color," it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā. 'Pariyodātena' means with a radiant color. 'Sappabhena' means endowed with physical radiance and the radiance of virtue (sīla). 'Sassirikena' means extremely endowed with glory, such as the beauty of the body. 'Mukhavarena' means with a noble face, because it is adorned with the aforementioned qualities of beauty. Indeed, although he did not announce, "I have attained Arahantship," because he walked with such noble and graceful demeanor, all who saw him knew that fact. Therefore, because it was as if he were announcing it, it is said: "He went as if announcing his own attainment of Arahantship."

For what purpose did he go as if announcing it in this way? It is answered—that Venerable Ānanda, reflecting that "The Blessed One praised the declaration of Arahantship in other ways without directly referring to oneself," went as if announcing it for the purpose of causing joy by letting the Great Elders—who were sitting and thinking, "Although it is not suitable to include him in the Dhamma-Vinaya Council because he is still a sekha (one in training), we shall include him because he is of great learning"—know of his attainment of Arahantship, and for the purpose of showing the fruitfulness of the advice given by the Blessed One, "Be diligent."
78:
The thought occurred to Venerable Mahākassapa because [Ānanda] had reached a state comparable to the Teacher for the reasons mentioned above. He gave a 'Sādhu' (well done), saying, 'Friend Ānanda, your attainment of Arahantship is truly beautiful.' This is the view of the Dīghabhāṇakas (Reciters of the Long Discourses). Among the Khuddakabhāṇakas, it is also fitting to say it is the view of the reciters of the Suttanipāta and Khuddakapāṭha, as it is stated thus in those commentaries.

Those teachers who habitually recite the Majjhima Nikāya are called Majjhimabhāṇakas. 'Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ' means according to seniority (the order of elders and juniors) or without overstepping that order. 'Ānanda's seat' should be connected to 'in that assembly of monks.' At that time of speaking, the Elder thought that when he showed himself to the monks who were asking 'Where has Ānanda gone?', it would be very manifest. This is also the view of some Majjhimabhāṇakas. Therefore, it should be connected as 'Thus some say.' Some of those same Majjhimabhāṇakas say, 'Having come through the air, he showed himself right in his own seat.' In the context of the masculine gender, when 'eke' (some) is said, the meaning should be understood as 'ekacce' (certain ones) in all places.

In all these three views, apart from the mere fact of arrival in those various ways by those various reciters, there is no other special reason for their separate statements. In the Dhamma-Vinaya Council which was conducted for seven months, because he arrived sometimes in the normal way, sometimes by diving into the earth, and sometimes through the air, they speak in those various ways based on his arrival. Alternatively, it is also said that on the first day of the Council, he first came in the normal way, then flew into the air, and upon reaching the assembly, descended from there and, without disturbing the row of monks, dived into the earth and showed himself in his seat.

In whatever way he may have come, the mere manner of arrival is not the standard (the main point). Only the giving of 'Sādhu' by Venerable Mahākassapa after he had arrived is the standard. This is because, by the giving of 'Sādhu' which should be given by the Teacher, the attainment of Arahantship was made known to others, and because the Elder accepted the praise that should have been received while the Blessed One was still alive. Therefore, desiring to show that meaning, he said 'Yathā vā' and so forth. 'Sabbatthāpi' means in all three views.

'Bhikkhū āmantesi' means he called the monks; this is the meaning here. In other places, however, it is also seen in the sense of informing, as in: 'Monks, I inform (āmantesi) you; I notify (paṭivedayāmi) you.'
79:
The word "Bhikkhave" is found in the sense of calling (pakkosana), as in the passage, "Come, bhikkhu, in my name, address Sāriputta" (A. Ni. 9.11). It is also found in the sense of addressing (ālapana), as in the passage, "There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying, 'Bhikkhus'" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.249). In this context as well, it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā that it is in the sense of addressing. However, it is not merely an address; since it is accompanied by a specific meaning to be made known, such as "What shall we chant first?", it is more appropriate in the sense of informing (ñāpana). Therefore, the word "āmantesi" should be interpreted as "informed" or "viññāpiyamānattha" (the meaning of making known). In the Pāḷi texts such as "There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, saying, 'Bhikkhus'; 'Venerable Sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One," only the address is found, and no specific meaning to be made known is seen. That specific meaning is undertaken individually in passages like "Formerly, bhikkhus..." Therefore, it should be considered that the sense of addressing is appropriate only in such instances. Scholars, however, say that the meaning of "āmantesi" is "consulted," because the word "manta" exists in the sense of speaking secretly, as in "The Lord of Devas, having consulted Vissakamma of great power..."

"Āvuso" and so on indicate the manner of addressing and consulting. In the phrase "dhammaṃ vā vinayaṃ vā," the word "vā" is in the sense of alternative (vikappa), showing "Which of these two shall we chant first?" As to why the Vinaya is chanted first, it is stated as "vinaye ṭhite" (when the Vinaya stands), etc. Here, "yasmā" (because) and "tasmā" (therefore) should be supplied and connected. "Tasmā" means because of being like that life. "Dhuraṃ" means the chief or the head. In "no nappahoti," the double negation indicates the meaning of being very capable.

"Etadaggaṃ" means "This venerable one is the foremost." This is a designation with a reversal of gender (liṅgavipallāsa). "Yadidaṃ" should be connected as "yo ayaṃ" (who is this) or "yadidaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ" (which is this group of five aggregates). If one regards the five aggregates in this way, the neuter form "etadaggaṃ" is consistent with the Pāḷi text. The nature of the word "yadidaṃ" is that it should be connected according to the gender of the meaning being expressed, as "yo ayaṃ," "yā ayaṃ," or "yaṃ idaṃ," as shown in various places. "Bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharānaṃ" is a partitive genitive (niddhāraṇa chaṭṭhī) distinguishing (the foremost) among the bhikkhus who are masters of the Vinaya.

"Attanāva attānaṃ sammanni" means he himself performed the designation (selection) of himself. "Attanā" is an instrumental of specification (tatiyā-visesana), which excludes designation by others. Alternatively, "attanā" is an indeclinable word (avyaya) that resembles a word with a case ending.
80:
## Avyayasaddo.
Some teachers say, "Because it is an expressed agent, the third case ending is used in the sense of the base (liṅgattha)." That statement is not appropriate, because the agent "thero" is clearly present. For the purpose of answering, it should be construed as "he designated himself by himself." Since the root *puccha* (to ask) is a ditransitive (dvikammika) root, two objects are mentioned: "Upāliṃ vinayaṃ" (Upāli and the Vinaya).

In the phrase "taking the fan," it should be understood that taking a fan is the custom (dhammatā) of Dhamma preachers. With that fan, Dhamma preachers can conceal fidgeting of the hands, facial expressions, and so forth in the midst of the assembly. The Blessed One also took the variegated fan only to demonstrate the custom of Dhamma preachers. Otherwise, there would be no need to conceal the moon-like face of the Buddhas, which is an ornament to the whole world and possesses the highest training and restraint. Why was it said, "Venerable Upāli, where was the first Pārājika prescribed?" Is it not inappropriate to call it "first" at a time prior to the Council? It is not inappropriate; it is appropriate. Because its being first is established according to the order in which the Blessed One prescribed them and according to the order of the Pātimokkha recitation. Generally, the three Piṭakas were recited in the same order as they existed during the Blessed One's lifetime; specifically, the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas should be understood in this way. In the phrases "in what matter" and "in the act of sexual intercourse," the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimittattha). To include and show the remaining offenses, supplementary regulations, etc., along with the sequence shown by "where was it prescribed?" and so on, it is said "he also asked about the matter (vatthu)," and so forth.

To dispel doubt as to whether it is mixed with the words of the Elders who conducted the Council or is the pure word of the Buddha, and to show that only what was recited in the Council is the standard (pamāṇa), he extracted the question and answered, saying "What then is here?", etc. "In this first Pārājika" means in the text (Pāḷi) of the first Pārājika as recited there. Therefore it is said, "Tathāgatas do not speak even a single syllable that is useless." "Words to be removed" refers to words that should be discarded because they are redundant and useless, or because they are incorrect and inappropriate. "Words to be added" refers to words that should be brought in because of incompleteness. Why? He said, "For not...", etc. The speech of disciples or deities refers to speech uttered by way of questioning or praising the Blessed One. In all places, even in the speech of the Blessed One, disciples, and deities, such additions are only for the sake of connecting the words (sambandha), and not because the meaning is inappropriate in its nature. He shows this by saying "What then is that?", etc. "Sambandhavacana" means merely the words that connect the preceding and following parts. Having defined "This is the first Pārājika," they established it in this way of recitation for the purpose of accomplishing the tasks of learning and memorizing. For that very purpose, they performed group chanting (gaṇasajjhāya), saying "By that... dwells."

Teachers say that at the very moment the chanting began, the earth shook. To make it known that this earthquake was due to the power of the Elders' Dhamma recitation, the teacher said "as if giving applause." "Ending at the water" means it shook as far as the water that supports the earth. In truth, only when that water moves does the earth move. By this phrase, partial shaking is excluded (showing the whole world shook). Even if the number of Sekhiya training rules is not mentioned in the Pāḷi, it is said "seventy-five training rules" to make it known that there are seventy-five such Sekhiya rules presented by number. By the phrase "just as in the previous method," he speaks of it being like giving applause. To show the meaning that the earth shook not just by defining the Vibhaṅga of the training rules, but also by defining the extent and measure, it is said "four Bhaṇavāras." In that word "Bhaṇavāra," eight syllables make one foot (pāda). Four feet make one verse (gāthā). One verse is also to be understood as a "gantha." In one gantha, there are thirty-two syllables. Five hundred ganthas of thirty-two syllables each are to be understood as one Bhaṇavāra. That...
81:
To make it known that [the earth shook] by the power of the communal recitation of the Dhamma, it is said, "as if giving applause." "Bounded by water" means up to the water that supports the earth. Indeed, only when that water moves does the earth move; by this [phrase "bounded by water"], it excludes the shaking of only a part of the earth.

Although there is no count [of the Sekhiya rules] in the Pāḷi text, it is said, "seventy-five training rules," to show that these are the only training rules included in the Council. By the phrase "in the same manner as before," it expresses the meaning "as if giving applause." It is said, "sixty-four bhāṇavāras," to show [that the earth shook] not only because of the division of the Sikkhāpadakaṇḍa Vibhaṅga but also because of the extent of its measurement. Here, a bhāṇavāra is defined as:

Eight syllables make one foot (pada), four feet make one stanza (gāthā).
One stanza is known as a gantha; one gantha has thirty-two syllables.
Five hundred ganthas of thirty-two syllables each
Are known as one bhāṇavāra; that one bhāṇavāra has eight thousand syllables.

Thus, a portion of the Pāḷi text measuring eight thousand syllables is called a bhāṇavāra. It is called bhāṇavāra because it has a turn (vāra) to be recited (bhaṇitabba); the meaning is a portion to be recited in a single session of chanting. "Khandhaka" refers to the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. It is called Khandhaka either because it is a collection of Vinaya regulations or because it explains them. Here, "khandhas" refers to the regulations known as Vinaya acts such as going forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā), and the regulations known as training rules of conduct (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta). Since the Buddha prescribed acts such as going forth, they are called prescriptions (paññatti). The word "khandha" is found in the sense of a collection in prescriptions, as in "dārukkhandha (a heap of wood), aggikkhandha (a mass of fire), udakakkhandha (a body of water)," etc. Furthermore, the meaning of "portion" (bhāga) or "collection" (rāsi) is also appropriate because those prescriptions are divided into portions and collections. Thinking that "this Vinaya Piṭaka, being protected and guarded by the reciters (bhāṇakas), will remain without disappearing for a long time according to the method established in the Council," they entrusted it to the Venerable Upāli Thera, saying, "Friend, teach this to your pupils."

"Wishing to recite the Dhamma" means wishing to perform the recitation of the Suttanta and Abhidhamma. This is because, as in passages such as "the Dhamma and Vinaya have been taught and prescribed," the word "Dhamma" refers only to the Suttanta and Abhidhamma by the method of elimination (pārisesanaya). This meaning will become clear later.

In the phrase "he informed the Saṅgha," the meaning should be understood according to the method mentioned below. "Friend, which Piṭaka [shall we recite first]?" means which of the two remaining Piṭakas after the Vinaya. Since the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are also included in the Khuddaka Recitation, it is said, "There are four recitations in the Suttanta Piṭaka," excluding them. By "recitations" (saṅgīti), the Nikāyas themselves are meant, because they were separately defined as Dīgha, etc., at the time of the Council. Therefore, it is said, "Dīgha-saṅgīti," and so on. To show that there are only three vaggas (divisions) formed by grouping the suttas together and no others, it is said, "thirty-four suttas, three vaggas." Therefore, the thirty-four suttas constitute three vaggas; or there are thirty-four suttas, and by grouping them, they become three vaggas; it should be connected as "among those three vaggas [the Brahmajāla Sutta is first]."

When it was said, "There is a sutta named Brahmajāla, let us recite that first," since there might be the question "Why?", the phrase "adorned with the three types of virtue" and so on was said. These are indeed phrases containing reasons. It is called "adorned" or "beautified" by virtue because it explains the three types of virtue: the minor (cūḷa), the middle (majjhima), and the major (mahā) virtue. Likewise, it is said to "destroy various forms of wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana) and talk (lapana)" because it eliminates them. Therein, "scheming" (kuhana) means deception; the meaning is astonishing others by the three types of conduct: pretending to reject requisites, indirect talk regarding the acquisition of requisites, and the posturing of one's deportment. "Talk" (lapana) refers to speaking to people who have come to the monastery in such a way as: "O lay devotees, for what purpose have you come? Have you come to invite monks? If so, go ahead; I will bring the monks and follow after you," and so on. By the word "ādi" (and so on), it includes giving flowers, acting as a messenger (nemittikatā), etc. Furthermore, here, the term "wrong livelihood" (micchājīva) includes other forms of improper search (anesana) apart from scheming and talk. By the word "ādi," other forms of immorality such as great greed should be understood. The sixty-two views themselves are called a "net" (jāla) because they are like a net in the sense of entangling; the disentangling of that net of views is likewise [explained].

In the phrase "between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā," the word "antarā" (between) is used in the sense of an interval, as in the passage, "Monks, this Tapodā river flows through the interval between two great hells." Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "in the interval between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā." Because it is used with the word "antarā," the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used. In such places, grammarians use the word "antarā" only once, as in "antarā gāmañca nadiñca yāti" (he goes between the village and the river), but that word must also be connected with the second term. If not connected, the accusative case would not be achieved, as the accusative case is desired in connection with the word "antarā" instead of the genitive case (sāmivacana). In that place, they built a house decorated with various imaginative paintings for the king's amusement; it is called "Rājāgāraka" (the royal pavilion). "Ambalaṭṭhikā" means...
82:
Since the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are also included in the Khuddaka collection (Khuddaka Nikāya), he stated parenthetically, "There are four collections (saṅgīti) in the Suttanta Piṭaka." By "saṅgīti," the Nikāyas themselves are meant, because at the time of the Council, they were defined and recited collectively as the Dīgha Nikāya and so on. Therefore, he said "Dīgha Saṅgīti," etc. To show that there are only three groups (vaggas) by grouping the suttas, and no others, he said: "Thirty-four suttas, three vaggas." Therefore, the thirty-four suttas constitute three vaggas; or, there are thirty-four suttas, and by grouping those suttas, there are three vaggas. It should be understood as: "Among those three vaggas (the Brahmajāla Sutta is the first)."

When it is said, "There is a sutta named Brahmajāla Sutta; let us recite that first," since the question "Why?" might arise, he said: "Adorned with the threefold virtue," and so forth. These qualifying terms represent the reasons. Because it shows the threefold virtue by way of the minor, middle, and major virtue (cūḷa, majjhima, mahā sīla), it is said to be "adorned" or "decorated" with that virtue. Furthermore, because it destroys various forms of wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana) and talk (lapana), it is said to "destroy various forms of wrong livelihood like scheming and talk." Therein, "scheming" (kuhana) means trickery; it is the act of impressing others through three types of conduct: pretending to refuse requisites, indirect talk regarding the acquisition of requisites, and posturing of the physical postures. "Talk" (lapana) means, upon seeing people coming to the monastery, speaking in such a way as: "O lay followers, for what purpose have you come? Have you come to invite the monks? If so, you go ahead; I will bring the monks and follow later," and so on. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), giving flowers, making signs (nimitta), and so on should be included. Alternatively, in this context, by the term "wrong livelihood" (micchājīva), other forms of improper search (anesana) apart from scheming and talk are taken. By the word "ādi," other forms of moral failure such as great greed (mahicchatā) should be understood. The sixty-two views themselves are called a "net" (jāla) because they are like a net in the sense of entangling; the "disentangling" (viniveṭhana) of that net of views means making it non-entangling.

In the phrase "between (antarā) Rājagaha and Nāḷandā," the word "antarā" is used in the sense of "in between," as in such Pali passages as: "Bhikkhus, this Tapodā river flows between two great hells." Therefore, it should be understood as the space between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā. Because it is associated with the word "antarā," the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used. In such places, grammarians usually use the word "antarā" only once, as in "He goes between the village and the river," but that word must also be connected with the second term. If it is not connected, the accusative case cannot be achieved, because the accusative case is desired instead of the genitive case (sāmivacana) when associated with the word "antarā." In that place, they built a house decorated with various imaginative paintings for the king's amusement; that is called "Rājāgāraka" (the royal pavilion). "Ambalaṭṭhikā" means...
83:
It is the King's garden. It is heard that near the gate of that garden, there is a young mango tree; people call that tree "Ambalaṭṭhikā." Because it is situated near that tree, the garden also came to be known as "Ambalaṭṭhikā." This is similar to how the name "Varuṇanagara" is used. Therefore, it means [the meeting took place] at the royal pavilion within the garden named Ambalaṭṭhikā. These two names are mentioned to make it known to those who do not yet know. Alternatively, it is called Rājāgāraka (the garden with the royal pavilion) because it is a garden that possesses a royal pavilion. Some teachers say that although the grammatical genders (liṅga) are different, it can still be an adjectival phrase (visesana); however, if that were the case, Rājāgāra could not be the location (ādhāra). The Elder Vajirabuddhi, however, states: "In the garden named Rājāgāraka, there is also a delightful royal pavilion; it is because of that royal pavilion that this garden receives this name." If that is so, it would mean that the name Ambalaṭṭhikā qualifies the young mango tree, and the name Rājāgāraka refers to the garden itself, which would lead back to the same fault mentioned above.

Suppiya the Wanderer (Paribbājaka) refers to the clothed wanderer who was a disciple of Sañjaya. Regarding the term "Brahmadatta Māṇava," the word "māṇava" is used for a young person, just as in "Ambaṭṭha Māṇava," "Aṅgaka Māṇava," and so on. Therefore, it means [the discourse was] concerning the youth named Brahmadatta. "Vaṇṇāvaṇṇā" refers to praise and dispraise. Alternatively, merit is called "vaṇṇa" and lack of merit is called "avaṇṇa"; speaking of these two is called "vaṇṇāvaṇṇā" by dropping the subsequent word, similar to how "rūpabhavo" is called "rūpabhava."

In the words beginning with "After that," there is this sequence of words: "Friend Ānanda, where was the Sāmaññaphala Sutta spoken?" asked the Elder Mahākassapa. "Venerable Sir, it was spoken in Jīvaka's Mango Grove in the city of Rājagaha," the Elder Ānanda replied. "With whom was it spoken?" he asked. "It was with King Ajātasattu, the son of the Videhan princess," he replied. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda regarding both the origin (nidāna) and the person (puggala) of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Here, the reason why one should say "with whom" instead of "concerning whom" is because this sutta was not spoken by the Blessed One alone; King Ajātasattu also made several petitions, such as "Venerable Sir, just as these various crafts..." and so on. In this same manner, it should be understood that the Council (Saṅgīti) was conducted by saying "concerning whom" or "with whom" as appropriate in all places. "Tanti" refers to the Pāḷi text as defined by the collection of sutta groups (vaggas). By doing so, the statement "composed of thirty-four suttas, organized into three vaggas" becomes appropriate and complete. "Bear it in mind" (pariharatha) means to maintain it through learning and recitation. The connection should be made as: "after that, having conducted the Council."
84:
The compound is formed as "Dhamma-saṅgaho ca," and so on. This means it was explained (and praised) by the ancient commentators (Porāṇas). By this word "saṃvaṇṇitaṃ," the view of the Vitandavādins (Sophists)—who claim that "the Abhidhamma Piṭaka consists of seven books together with either the Mahādhammahadaya or the Mahādhātukathā"—is rejected. Instead, it shows the view of the Samānavādins (those of the same/orthodox view), who state that "the Abhidhamma Piṭaka consists of seven books only with the Kathāvatthu." It is called "Sukhumañāṇagocara" (the domain of subtle knowledge) because it is the object of subtle knowledge, or because it is the range of those who possess subtle knowledge.

There are two types of Niddesa: Cūḷaniddesa and Mahāniddesa. The Dīghabhāṇakas (reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya) say that the Jātakas and other such texts included in the Khuddaka Nikāya—which for the most part demonstrate the ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma)—should be categorized only within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. They argue it is not appropriate to include them in the Suttanta Piṭaka like the Dīgha Nikāya, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka which demonstrates designations (paññatti). The Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa are not included here [in the Abhidhamma] because they share the same nature as the Jātakas. The Netti and Peṭakopadesa are also not included here because they share the same nature as the Niddesa and Paṭisambhidāmagga. However, the Majjhimabhāṇakas (reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya) say that the Jātakas and others, which were preached according to specific circumstances (aṭṭhuppatti), are teachings given in a natural sequence (yathānuloma-desanā); therefore, it is appropriate to include them in the Suttanta Piṭaka. They argue it is not appropriate to include them in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which is a teaching of ultimate nature (yathādhamma-sāsana), nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is a teaching based on offenses (yathāparādha-sāsana). Thus, they claim the Jātakas and others belong to the Suttanta Piṭaka. Between these two views, one should investigate and accept the one that is most fitting.

Having thus shown the First Council through the aspects of cause (nimitta), purpose (payojana), time (kāla), place (desa), performer (kāraka), and method (karaṇa), the author now says "Evametaṃ," etc., to show the singlefold (ekavidha) and other classifications for the sake of various types of proficiency in the Dhamma and Vinaya established in that First Council. In that Pāḷi, the word "evaṃ" points to the aforementioned method of conducting the Council, which is referred to by the word "etaṃ." The passage beginning with "Yañhi" is an elaboration. "Unsurpassed Supreme Enlightenment" (Anuttara Sammāsambodhi) refers to the Path-knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) which has the Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa/Omniscience) as its proximate cause, and the Unobstructed Knowledge which has the Path-knowledge as its proximate cause. "Etthantare" (in this interval) refers to the period between the penetration of the Four Noble Truths and the Parinibbāna. That interval is defined by time as "45 years (vassa)." The phrase "or by one who is reviewing" (paccavekkhantena vā) refers to the Dhamma that occurred through the power of inspired utterances (udāna) and so on. The connection is: "all that word which was spoken." To the question "What is that [Dhamma]?", he says "Vimuttirasaṃ eva" (it is only the taste of liberation). This means it has no other taste than the taste of liberation. It is called "Vimutti" because it is liberated from defilements. It is called "Rasa" because it is to be known and enjoyed. Because it has the taste known as liberation, it is called "Vimuttirasa." It means the blissful taste of the Fruit of Arahantship. This is the opinion of the Elder Sāriputta, the author of the Sāratthadīpanī. (Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Commentary on the Great First Council). The Elder Dhammapāla, however, treats that view as a "kecivāda" (the view of some teachers) and...
85:
The sub-commentator states this meaning: "It is called vimutti (liberation) because one is being liberated or has been liberated; this vimutti is indeed the Path and the Fruit as appropriate. Rasa means excellence or the accomplishment of success; the compound should be understood according to the method mentioned. It means having the benefit of liberation because it produces the Path and Fruit, or having the accomplishment of liberation, or having the function of liberation because it brings about the absolute liberation from defilements" (from the Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā, Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā). However, in the Aṅguttara Commentary, it is said: "Among attharasa and so on, attharasa refers to the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), dhammarasa refers to the four Paths, and vimuttirasa refers to the deathless Nibbāna."

In particular, without distinction, the entire word of the Buddha is called Vinaya because it disciplines defilements, and it is also Dhamma because it upholds those who practice according to the instruction from falling into the lower realms and so forth. Nevertheless, with the intention of referring only to the Dhamma and Vinaya desired in this context, He taught by distinguishing them, saying "Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka," and so on. The word of the Buddha remaining after the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Dhamma because it extensively teaches the ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) by way of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth. Alternatively, although Vinaya is also Dhamma due to being the scriptures to be studied (pariyatti) and so on, when used in conjunction with the word Vinaya, the word Dhamma refers only to the Sutta and Abhidhamma Pāḷi other than the Vinaya Pāḷi. This is like the expressions "puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra" (the accumulation of merit and wisdom) and "go-balībadda" (cattle and bull). To show this point, it is said, "Therefore it is said," and so on. For whatever reason the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Vinaya and the remaining word of the Buddha is called Dhamma, for that very reason, their nature as such is taught in the Saṅgītikhandhaka.

The Buddha uttered this verse, "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ," while reviewing the attainment of Arahantship, which is the basis of His Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), immediately after the nineteenth reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Therefore, it is called the "First Word of the Buddha" (paṭhamabuddhavacana). It is said that this is an inspired utterance (udāna) not forsaken by any of the Buddhas. The brief meaning of this verse is: "Searching for the house-builder, the carpenter of craving (taṇhā) who builds this house called the individual existence (attabhāva), for the sake of that Enlightenment Knowledge (bodhi-ñāṇa) by which that craving can be seen, I have wandered and circled through the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) for this long a time, numbering many hundreds of thousands of births, without yet finding that knowledge. Because it is mixed with aging, sickness, and death, this being born (jāti) repeatedly is indeed suffering; and as long as that craving is not seen, birth does not cease. Therefore, searching for that craving, I have wandered." Now, O house-builder, the carpenter of craving who builds the house of individual existence, I, who have penetrated the Omniscient Knowledge, have seen you. You shall not build this house of my individual existence again. I have broken all your rafters (phāsukā), which are the remaining defilements.
86:
"I have broken [them]. The ridge-pole (kaṇṇikā) of this house of individual existence built by you, which is called ignorance (avijjā), has been shattered and destroyed. Now my mind has reached and entered the unconditioned (visankhāra), Nibbāna, by way of making it the object. And I have reached and attained the Path of Arahantship or the Fruit of Arahantship, which is called the destruction of cravings." In the Gaṇṭhipadas, however, the meaning is stated as: "Only the mind that has reached the unconditioned Nibbāna has attained the Path of Arahantship or the Fruit of Arahantship, which is called the destruction of cravings."

In the word "sandhāviissaṃ," grammarians say that in the verse, the suffix -issaṃ is used in the sense of the past tense. Some say that with the desire to express that past time, the future tense suffix (bhavissanti) is used even for the past. "Punappunaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta) meaning repeatedly. Regarding "phāsukā," it is called phāsu because it should be protected (pātabba), changing 'p' to 'ph', or it is called phāsu because it should be touched (phusitabba); that phāsu itself is phāsukā. In the word "ajjhagā," it is also said that the suffix -i or -aṃ in the past tense is changed to -ā. If the mind alone is the agent, then it would be the perfect tense (parokkhā). Since the Buddha uttered the two verses beginning with "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ" as an internal utterance, this is the beginning of the teachings produced by the mind. However, it is said that the passage beginning with "Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā" is the beginning of the teachings produced by speech.

"Keci" (some) refers to the Khandhaka-bhāṇaka elders (reciters of the Khandhaka). The first-mentioned view is the doctrine of the Dhammapada-bhāṇaka elders. In the place "Yadā ... dhammā," it should be understood that the word "iti," which has the meanings of illustration (nidassana) and beginning (ādi), is elided. Without the meaning of illustration which shows the limit, the meaning that causes a change in the sense of the word is not complete. Taking the word "iti" in the sense of 'beginning' in that context, Ācariya Sāriputta Thera stated in the Sāratthadīpanī: "By that word 'iti' meaning 'beginning', it includes the three verses beginning with 'Tena ātāpino ... sahetudhammaṃ'." "Khandhake" refers to the Mahāvagga. "Udānagāthaṃ" is a singular noun by class, or it should be understood as being said by taking only the first verse.

In this matter, the Khandhaka-bhāṇaka elders say: "Because the verse of the Dhammapada-bhāṇakas was taught only by the mind, it did not benefit the great multitude at that time. But because our verse was taught by breaking into speech, it benefited the devas and brahmas who heard it then. Therefore, this alone is the First Word of the Buddha." The Dhammapada-bhāṇakas, however, say: "Whether a teaching benefits people or not is not the characteristic of being the First Word. Because the Buddha taught it first with the mind, this alone is the First Word of the Buddha."
87:
Thus it is said. Therefore, it should be understood that the statements of both Elders are appropriate in both ways. If the verse beginning with "Aneka jāti saṃsāraṃ" was taught only mentally, then why is it stated in the Dhammapada Commentary: "The Teacher, while seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, uttered this Dhamma teaching as a joyous utterance (udāna) by the power of his joy, and later, when asked by the Elder Ānanda, he spoke it"? This is because it should be understood in that manner (as a mental utterance) by the power of its meaning. In that Dhammapada Commentary as well, only the meaning of uttering it mentally should be taken. For, like a teaching (desanā), a joyous utterance (udāna) is also understood to be of two kinds: a mental utterance and a vocal utterance. If this joyous utterance were a vocal one, it would have been included in the Udāna Pali. Therefore, the very fact that it is not included in the Udāna Pali should be seen as the reason for it being a mental utterance without being vocally expressed.

The phrase "paṭipada-divase" (on the first day of the waning moon) should not be connected with the phrase "sabbaññubhāva-ppattassa" (of one who has attained the state of omniscience); rather, it should be connected with "paccavekkhantassa uppannā" (arisen while reflecting). For the Blessed One attained omniscience only at the time of dawn on the full moon day of Vesākha. Although such a connection might be possible according to worldly custom, it should not be taken so, as it is not the custom used in the Sasana. Just as one says "dānamaya" or "sīlamaya," "somanassa" itself is called "somanassamaya." The meaning is: "by the knowledge associated with that joy." Alternatively, it is also proper to say: "by such knowledge produced by the feeling of joy through the power of conascence (sahajāta) and so forth."

"Handa" is a particle in the sense of exhortation. He exhorts, saying, "Come now... fulfill [the practice]." "Āmantayāmi" means "I inform" or "I awaken [you]." The word "vo" is the object of the verb "āmantayāmi." Grammarians demonstrate that in the sense of addressing or informing, only the second case (accusative) is used, not the fourth case (dative). By the word "vayadhammā," through the heading of the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), he also clarifies the characteristics of suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta) of conditioned things (saṅkhāra). This is because it is taught: "Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self."

By the method of clarifying the three characteristics, he shows the insight (vipassanā) that has those three characteristics as its object. It should be understood that he reveals the practice leading to Nibbāna, which is unerring, established in the meditation on the Four Truths, a unique quality of the Buddhas, and not within the scope of all sectarians. Now, he urges them toward that right practice with the words "appamādena sampādetha." The meaning is: "Fulfill with heedfulness (appamāda) that unerring practice leading to Nibbāna, which is established in the meditation on the Four Truths." Furthermore, having caused spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in brief with the words "vayadhammā saṅkhārā," he shows the entire right practice without remainder, also in brief, with the words "appamādena sampādetha."
88:
(The Blessed One) shows [the practice in brief]. The word "appamāda" (heedfulness) encompasses the entire, perfectly complete Sasana, which is comprised of the three trainings (sikkhattaya). The meaning is: "Fulfill with heedfulness the right practice called the Sasana, which is perfectly complete and comprised of the three trainings."

"Ubhinna-mantare" means in the middle, between the two statements (the first and last words of the Buddha). In this context, it should be understood that the time-possessing phenomena (kālavanta) and the time (kāla) itself are also indicated, because they are inseparable.

In the term "Suttanta Piṭaka," just as in the words "kammanta" and "vananta," the Sutta itself is called Suttanta. By the words "saṅgīta (recited in council) and asaṅgīta (not recited in council)," he speaks of the entire nature [of the teachings]. "Asaṅgīta" refers to works such as the Saṅgītikkhandhaka and the Kathāvatthu. Some teachers say, "The Subha Sutta was not recited in the First Council." That statement is not appropriate. For Ācariya Dhammapāla stated that the Elder Ānanda preached it to the youth Subha while residing at Jetavana, even before the First Council was held.

The Subha Sutta begins with: "Thus have I heard: At one time, shortly after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery." In that Subha Sutta, it would not be fitting for the Venerable Ānanda himself to say "Thus have I heard" (evaṃ me sutaṃ) during the First Council. For the Elder Ānanda, having preached the Subha Sutta himself, would not say "Thus have I heard" and so forth. It should rather be said: "Venerable sirs, at one time I was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery," and so on. Therefore, it appears as if the Subha Sutta was placed into the recital with the words "Thus have I heard" by the makers of the Second and Third Councils.

However, if the intention of Ācariya Dhammapāla was: "Although it was preached by the Elder Ānanda, the Elders such as Mahākassapa, wishing to place the Subha Sutta into the First Council and establish the text, established the text with 'Thus have I heard' according to the method found in other Suttas," then it would be appropriate. Alternatively, even if the intention is that the Venerable Ānanda, though preaching the Subha Sutta himself, preached it according to the method taught by the Blessed One in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and others; and because he preached it based on the method received in the presence of the Blessed One, he did not attribute the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to himself, but said "Thus have I heard," then it is also appropriate. There is also a reading "anusaṅgītañca." In the Second and Third Councils, by the power of the meaning of being recited again, there is simply no difference. The construction (yojanā) should be made as: "By combining these, it should be known as the Vinaya Piṭaka... the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka."
89:
By way of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, there are two types of Pātimokkha. By way of the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, there are two types of Vibhaṅga. There are twenty-two Khandhakas found in the Mahāvagga and Cūḷavagga. It is said there are sixteen Parivāras because each is characterized by sixteen vāra (modes).

In fact, in the Parivāra Pāḷi, there are sixteen vāra in the Mahāvibhaṅga and sixteen vāra in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, totaling thirty-two vāra. Although some palm-leaf manuscripts only show 'Parivārā,' many other manuscripts, as well as the Vinaya Commentary and Abhidhamma Commentary, show 'sixteen Parivāras' (soḷasa parivārā). Therefore, considering that this reading should not be rejected, only the meaning of that reading is stated.

'Iti' indicates the aforementioned Word of the Buddha, and the word 'idaṃ' refers to that Word of the Buddha. Alternatively, the word 'iti' is used in the sense of 'idaṃ' (this), where 'idaṃ' is merely for the sake of euphony. Or both synonyms 'iti' and 'idaṃ' are used only in the sense of 'this,' as in 'it exists now' and so forth. In such cases, it should be understood in this manner.

In this Dīgha Nikāya, thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta are collected; or they are collected by this Dīgha Nikāya; or the collection of those thirty-four suttas is in this Dīgha Nikāya. Therefore, it is called the Brahmajālādi-catuttiṃsa-sutta-saṅgaha (the collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with Brahmajāla). The same applies to the other Nikāyas.

Among the views of the Dīghabhāṇakas and Majjhimabhāṇakas mentioned below, the view of the Majjhimabhāṇakas is more appropriate. Therefore, wishing to show that the Khuddakapāṭha and others are also included in the Suttanta Piṭaka, it is said: 'The Khuddaka... [pe]... is called the Suttanta Piṭaka.' Among those, since it is said, 'Listen to the verses of those of developed selves, which lead to the goal' (Theragāthā, Introductory Verse), the reading 'Theragāthā Therīgāthā' is appropriate.

Having thus defined the three Piṭakas by their nature, the word 'tattha' and so forth are stated to show the etymological definition (nibbacana).

'Tattha' means 'among those three Piṭakas.' 'Vividhavisesanayattā' means because of having various methods (vividha-naya) and because of having distinguished methods (visesa-naya).

'Vinayanato' means because of the nature of disciplining (vinayana). This is an exposition where the state (bhāva) is primary, or there is an elision of the word 'state' (bhāva). Otherwise, the substance (dabba) alone would be primary. In that case, it would follow that it is called 'Vinaya' only because of the 'Vinaya-substance' which possesses the quality of disciplining as a cause, and not because of the quality of disciplining itself—which is an undesired meaning. In such cases, it should be understood in this manner.

Alternatively, disciplining is called 'vinayana'; because of that [disciplining], it is called 'Vinaya.'

'This is the Vinaya' means this Pāḷi text, which is the object of designation (saññī) and a concept of meaning (atthapaññatti), is the Vinaya. 'It is called Vinaya' means it is known as 'Vinaya,' which is the designation (saññā) and a concept of name (saddapaññatti). Indeed, the clarification of a name-concept (nāmapaññatti) by means of a meaning-concept (atthapaññatti) is called an etymological definition (nibbacana).
90:
Now, wishing to clarify the meaning of this verse, he said "Vividhā hi" and so forth. It should be construed as: "In this Vinaya Piṭaka, there are various methods; because of the fact of having various methods, it is called Vinaya." He personally demonstrates the state of having various methods by saying "it is of five kinds" and so forth. Similarly, he demonstrates the state of being distinctive by saying "strengthening" (daḷhīkamma) and so forth. In training rules concerning worldly faults (lokavajja), there is the benefit of strengthening; in training rules concerning conventional faults (paṇṇattivajja), there is the benefit of relaxation.

Conduct that occurs by overwhelming the boundary of restraint is called transgression (ajjhācāra). That transgression occurs in both body and speech. He demonstrates that the prohibition of such transgression in body and speech, or the training of body and speech through such prohibition, is figuratively called discipline (vinayana).

Having said "Tasmā" (therefore), he refers to that statement in various ways by saying "Vividhanayattā" (because of various methods) and so forth. To show that the aforementioned verse was spoken to clarify such an etymology, he said "Tena" and so forth. Some say "Tena" means because of the reason of having various methods, or because it is the instrument. Alternatively, they say the connection is made by saying "Tena" to show the quality of the sentence "Vividhā hi" and so forth. In this case, "Tena" means because of the reason of having various methods. Otherwise, they also say "Tena" is said to correlate with the words of the ancient teachers (porāṇā) who spoke this verse in reference to the aforementioned statement. The meaning of the word "Tena" should be understood as in the second method. "Etam" refers to the words of the verse. "Etassa" connects with the word "vacanattha" (meaning of the word), which is the meaning of the word "Vinaya." Even though the connection "meaning of the word" is stated, "Etassa" is said again to show the distinction from common usage. Grammarians (neruttikā), however, desire distinction by another word in such instances because of commonality and being nouns when compounds (samāsa) and derivatives (taddhita) are formed.

The word "Atthānaṃ" (of the meanings) should be connected as an object with the words "sūcanato...pe... suttāṇā" as appropriate. He explains that meaning with "Tañhi" and so forth. Regarding the meanings divided into one's own benefit, others' benefit, and so forth, for whoever recites, hears, teaches, reflects on, or preaches that Sutta, the benefit of virtue and so forth contained in that Sutta accrues to that person. Since he accomplishes it for others, it also accrues to others. Therefore, that Sutta indicates or illuminates both those benefits. Similarly, benefits of the present life, benefits of the future life, mundane benefits, and supramundane benefits are included by the word "ādi" (etc.). Here, the word "attha" is a synonym for welfare (hita), not the meaning of the spoken Pali text. If it were the meaning of the Pali, it would result in an unintended meaning, such as the Sutta indicating its own spoken meaning and the meaning of others. The meaning revealed by a Sutta is the meaning of that Sutta alone. Therefore, that Sutta does not reveal the meaning of another. Since there is no such "meaning of another" revealed, one should not take the meaning of the word "lakkhaṇa" (characteristic). Since there is no meaning of that Pali text apart from one's own benefit and others' benefit, the word "ādi" should not be used. Therefore, since the aforementioned welfare (hita) of oneself and others cannot directly exist in the Sutta, they are called "one's own benefit" and "others' benefit" by virtue of the person who bears the Sutta.

Alternatively, following the Sutta Piṭaka in order, in the explanation of the phrase "nanyadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā," the terms are: one's own benefit, others' benefit, both benefits, present benefit, future benefit, manifest meaning, profound meaning, hidden meaning, concealed meaning, meaning to be inferred, meaning to be understood directly, blameless benefit, stainless benefit, pure benefit, ultimate benefit (paramattha)...
91:
A Sutta indicates its own meaning and benefit. Therefore, that Sutta does not indicate the meaning of another Sutta. Since there is no meaning of another Sutta to be indicated, one should not take the meaning of the word 'lakkhaṇa' or the word 'ādi'. Thus, because the aforementioned benefits in the sense of welfare (hitapariyāya), namely one's own benefit (attattha) and others' benefit (parattha), are not possible within the Sutta itself, they are spoken of in terms of the person who bears the Sutta.

Alternatively, following the Sutta Piṭaka, in the explanation (niddesa) of the phrase 'na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā', one should take the meaning that it indicates various types of benefits: one's own benefit (attattha), others' benefit (parattha), the benefit of both (ubhayattha), benefit in the present life (diṭṭhadhammika-attha), benefit in the future life (samparāyika-attha), clear meaning (uttāna-attha), profound meaning (gambhīra-attha), hidden meaning (gūḷha-attha), concealed meaning (paṭicchanna-attha), meaning to be inferred (neyya-attha), direct meaning (nīta-attha), blameless benefit (anavajja-attha), benefit free from defilements (nikkilesa-attha), pure benefit (vodāna-attha), and the ultimate benefit (paramattha). Although attattha and so on are mentioned without excluding other Suttas because they are shown only as meanings within a Sutta, not one of these varieties of meaning exceeds the state of being shown by a Sutta. In this classification of meanings, the word attha is also a synonym for the 'spoken meaning' (bhāsitattha). Here, the first five varieties of meaning are synonyms of welfare (hita), the next six are varieties of spoken meaning (bhāsitattha), and the last four possess both natures. Among them, the state that is clear because it is easily understood is called uttāna. The state that is deep because it is difficult to comprehend is called gambhīra. A meaning that is not open is called gūḷha. A meaning concealed by the arrangement of words and sentences, like roots and water hidden by dust, is called paṭicchanna. A meaning that must be drawn out to be known is called neyya. A meaning to be understood according to the direct literal Pali is called nīta. Anavajja, nikkilesa, and vodāna are spoken of as synonyms; or they should be applied respectively to the states of wholesome (kusala), resultant (vipāka), and functional (kiriya). The ultimate benefit (paramattha) is either Nibbāna or the unerring true nature of phenomena.

Alternatively, it indicates one's own benefit (attattha) as 'being few-wished oneself,' and others' benefit (parattha) as 'being one who speaks to others about having few wishes.' In this way, Suttas such as 'He is himself one who abstains from taking life, and he encourages others in the restraint from taking life' should be applied. Other teachers, however, say that the meaning spoken according to its true nature is attattha, while the doctrines of sectarians like Pūraṇa Kassapa are parattha. Or, the meaning contained within a Sutta is attattha, and what is in accordance with the Sutta is parattha. Or, the method of the Suttanta is attattha, and the methods of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are parattha. The meaning of the word 'Sutta' as distinct from Vinaya and Abhidhamma is stated. In the teaching that occurs according to the inclinations of those to be trained (veneyya), one's own benefit, others' benefit, etc., are especially shown. Since such showing is primary, the teachers say this Suttanta Piṭaka is called 'Sutta' because it indicates meanings and benefits. In this context of 'atthaṃ sūcanato', the 'u' of the word 'sūca' is shortened. Because it is so made, it is said, 'This much of the Blessed One's... included in the Sutta (suttapariyāpanna)' and 'five hundred Suttas in the entire Suttanta'...
92:
...it is also said that it indicates the benefit of others (parattha). The meaning of the word 'Sutta' should be stated by distinguishing it from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. Therefore, in the teaching that proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be trained (veneyya), one's own welfare, others' welfare, and so on are pre-eminently manifested because that is its primary purpose. It is not like the teaching that proceeds by the power of authority (āṇā) or the nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva); thus it is said, 'It is a Sutta because it indicates meanings (atthānaṃ sūcanato).' Here, the 'u' of the word sūca is shortened. Having done so, the Elder Teacher Sāriputta said: 'In such passages as "This much of the Blessed One's text has come in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta" and "five hundred Suttas in our own tradition," the word Sutta should be understood as being used figuratively.' Other teachers, however, say that by the same type of definition as mentioned, the word Sutta also refers to the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.

In the Sutta, the nature of authority and the nature of ultimate reality follow the inclination of those to be trained. It is not like in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, where the inclination of those to be trained follows the nature of authority and ultimate reality. Therefore, the Suttanta teaching is that which leads to the attainment of the absolute welfare of those to be trained; thus the commentator said, 'And herein the meanings are well-spoken (suvuttā),' and so on. This statement, 'The Suttanta teaching leads to the attainment of the absolute welfare of those to be trained,' is also said with reference to the fact that the Suttanta teaching is solely intent on accomplishing the welfare of those to be trained. This intentness should be seen as being in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained. Therefore, he said, 'Because it is spoken in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.' For this reason, he resolves the inquiry: 'Are not the Vinaya and Abhidhamma also well-spoken? Why then is only this Sutta spoken of in this way?'

To show the accomplishment of the benefit after a period of time through gradual training and so on, it is said, 'Like the fruit of a crop.' This is what is meant: Just as a crop does not bear fruit at the very moment of sowing or planting, but bears fruit only after a period of time through gradual tending and so on, so too this [Sutta] does not produce benefits at the very moment of hearing or memorizing, but produces benefits only after a period of time through gradual training and so on. 'Pasavati' means 'it bears fruit' or 'it accomplishes.' Accomplishing is indeed bearing fruit. To show that the benefit is accomplished only for those endowed with the right means, he said, 'Like the milk of a cow.' The intention here is: Just as a cow causes milk to flow only for those who possess the means, such as taking the teat and milking at the proper time when the calf is born, and not at an improper time when no calf is born; or even at the proper time, not for those who lack the means, such as taking the horn and milking; so too, this Sutta [yields results] for those who practice hearing and memorizing with the motive of liberation...
93:
Only for those with the right means does it cause the benefits of virtue and so forth to flow. For those who hear and memorize without the right means, like the simile of the water-snake (alagaddupa), it does not cause the benefits to flow. Although the word "sudati" means to flow or pour, because it is a transitive verb, it is stated with a causative meaning as "paggharapeti" (causes to flow). It is like saying "tarati" (crosses) means "nipāteti" (causes to fall/settle). "Suttāṇā" is so called because it protects well. "Ne" refers to welfare (attha/benefit).

The similarity to a thread (sutta) is shown with "Yathā hi" and so forth. Just as the carpenter's string (kāဠသုတ္တံ/kāḷasutta) is a measure (pamāṇa) because planing is done according to that string, so when disputes arise, by merely bringing forth a Sutta, it becomes clear that "this should be accepted, this should be rejected," and the dispute is settled. Therefore, the Sutta is a measure for the wise, like a carpenter's string.

Furthermore, just as flowers tied with a strong thread (sutta) do not scatter or get destroyed even when the wind blows, so the meanings tied together by a Sutta do not scatter or get destroyed by false views (micchāvāda). Because it is a teaching (desanā) delivered according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those to be guided (veneyya), and because it excellently reveals one's own benefit and others' benefit, it is called "Sutta" (thread) specifically in this Sutta Piṭaka, unlike the Vinaya which is the teaching of authority (āṇā-desanā) or the Abhidhamma which is the teaching of ultimate realities (paramattha-desanā). The connection and meaning should be stated as appropriate according to the method mentioned earlier. In this context, although "Suttanta Piṭaka" was mentioned below, the word "anta" is not used here to show that it has no separate meaning.

The particle "Yaṃ" is used in the sense of cause. Because the great/exalted dhammas are taught in the Abhidhamma, it is called "Abhidhamma." To show the various meanings of the prefix "Abhi," he said "Ayañhi" and so forth.
94:
The word 'abhi' expresses the sense of excellence, known as the increase in the act of going; therefore, in words such as 'abhikkamanti', it is said to occur in the sense of increase. 'Abhiññātā' means known, recognized, or made manifest by some sign such as the half-moon. Indeed, the state of the half-moon etc. is a sign by way of marking the night: 'Because the moon is half, it is the eighth day. Because it is waning, it is the fourteenth day. Because it is full, it is the fifteenth day.'

In this word 'abhilakkhitā' as well, this same meaning should be understood. However, in the Bhayabherava Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, it is stated that the word 'abhiññāta' is a synonym for 'abhilakkhita' in the sense of a sign, saying 'abhiññātā abhilakkhitā' etc. If it is asked, 'If only the word lakkhita expresses the sense of marking, would the word abhi not be useless?', it should not be regarded so. This is because the word 'abhi' also illuminates that very meaning. In the presence of a word that expresses a meaning, prefixes and particles merely illuminate that meaning. Therefore, because it illuminates the very sense of marking expressed by the word 'lakkhita' which has the nature of expressing it, it should be understood that the word 'abhi' also occurs in the sense of a sign. 'Rājābhirājā' is a king worthy of being honored by other kings. 'Pūjita' means worthy of honor. This is taught in the Sela Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta.

'Abhidhamma' refers to the Dhamma that is unmixed with Vinaya regulations, such as 'even though there is no offense for the emission of semen in a dream, unwholesome intention is found.' Teachers also say it refers to the Dhamma unmixed with one another because the aforementioned ultimate realities (paramattha) do not contradict each other. Alternatively, in passages such as 'killing (pāṇātipāta) is unwholesome,' the intention (cetanā) that originates the effort to cut off the life-faculty of one who desires death is unwholesome, not the 'atipāta' which is the cutting off of the life-faculty called a living being. Likewise, 'the physical intimation (kāyaviññatti) called taking what is not given and belongs to another is an indeterminate (abyākata) dhamma; the intention to steal that originates that intimation is an unwholesome dhamma.' In this way, the meaning should be understood as the Dhamma unmixed with one another.

In the word 'abhivinaya', one who says 'gold and silver should not be accepted' is said to discipline in the Vinaya. Here, one who says 'for one who accepts in this way, there is a Pācittiya offense; for one who accepts in this way, there is a Dukkaṭa offense' is said to discipline in the Abhivinaya. Therefore, for one who takes gold and silver belonging to another with the intention to steal, one of the offenses among Pārājika, Thullaccaya, or Dukkaṭa is incurred according to the object. For one who takes it as a treasurer, a Pācittiya or Dukkaṭa is incurred. For one who accepts it, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya is incurred. For one who merely handles it out of playfulness, an Anāmāsa Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. For one designated as a monk who discards gold and silver, there is no offense. In this way, it should be understood that one is able to discipline in the Vinaya which is distinct and unmixed. By this statement, the definition is shown only in essence and in brief. The phrase 'aññamañña... visiṭṭhehi' should be understood. In the word 'abhikkantena', it is said that 'abhi' shows the excellence of delight. In the word 'abhikkamantံ', the word 'abhi' shows the excellence of the act of going.
95:
According to the case, one should be understood as being capable of disciplining even in the Vinaya, which is free from mutual confusion, such as: one of the offenses among Pārājika, Thullaccaya, and Dukkaṭa; a Pācittiya offense for one who takes [something] in the capacity of a storekeeper; a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense for one who takes [something] for oneself; an Anāmāsa Dukkaṭa offense for one who handles [something] out of mere greed; and no offense for one who is appointed as a discarder of money. Desiring to show this defined nature in essence and in brief, he said: "Aññamañña... pe... hotī."

In this word "Abhikkantena," the word "Abhi" is said to show the excellence of pleasure, as indicated by the word "Adhike." In the word "Abhikkamanti," the word "Abhi" shows the increase and excellence of the action of going. In the words "Abhiññātā Abhilakkhitā," it shows the distinct prominence of the actions of knowing and marking. In the word "Abhikkantena," it shows the surpassing distinction of pleasure. Thus, this statement is appropriate because the prefix (upasagga) qualifies the action. In the grammar treatises, it is also said: "Words such as 'parā' and others are called prefixes (upasagga) only when they are associated with an action." However, in the words "Abhirājā" and "Abhivinaya," where the word "Abhi" exists in [the context of] a worshipped king and a defined Vinaya, how could this be appropriate? Is it not true that a word expressing a substance (dabba) cannot be a word expressing an action? There is no fault here. This is because it also indicates the actions of worshipping and defining, and because it occurs in [the context of] the king and the Vinaya associated with those actions. With the meaning "a king who is greatly worshipped," making the connection between action and agent (kāraka) the cause, the word "Abhi" primarily expresses the substance (dabba) of the king as a passive derivative (kammasādhana), while it expresses the action of worshipping secondarily. Similarly, with the meaning "a Vinaya that is greatly defined," making the connection between action and agent the cause, the word "Abhi" primarily expresses the substance of the Vinaya as a passive derivative, while it expresses the action of defining secondarily. Therefore, just like the word "Ati" in words such as "Atimālā," the word "Abhi" here expresses the action along with the derivative (sādhana); thus, it is clear that the words "Abhirājā" and "Abhivinaya" are formed with a prefix. In this way, it should be understood that in the word "Abhidhamma," the word "Abhi" also expresses the action of growth and so forth along with the derivative.

Let the word "Abhi" remain in the aforementioned meanings; however, if the dhammas characterized by growth, etc., expressed by the word "Dhamma" associated with that "Abhi," are not included here, how would this be appropriate? To answer this question, he said "Ettha ca," and so forth. There, "Ettha" means in this Abhidhamma. The word "ca" is used in the sense of reference. By the word "Bhāveti," the growth of the mind is meant; by the word "Pharitvā," the expansion of the object is meant; therefore, the dhammas that have reached growth through that development (bhāvanā) and expansion are also mentioned.
96:
The meaning is: "Ārammaṇādīhi" means by way of object, associated states, doors of action, practice, and so forth. Since only supramundane dhammas are truly and invariably worthy of worship, he showed that those very dhammas are worshipped through the teaching beginning with "Sekkhā dhammā." By this word "Pūjāraha," he excludes the agent (kattar) and other derivatives (sādhana), the past and other times, and the sense of capability (sakkuneyyattha). The intention shown is that in this Abhidhamma Piṭaka, only those dhammas that are worthy of worship and should be worshipped, free from the restriction of a specific time, are mentioned.

"Sabhāvapariccinnattā" means because they are defined by their own nature, such as contact (phusana) and so forth. He shows that because they are superior to sense-sphere dhammas, the sublime (mahaggata) dhammas are excellent, and because there is no dhamma higher than them, the unsurpassed (anuttara) dhammas are even more excellent, through the words beginning with "Mahaggatā." "Tena" refers to the words beginning with "Vuḍḍhimanto," which function as either the instrument (karaṇa) or the cause.

"Yaṃ panettha" means that among the three Piṭakas such as the Vinaya, which are mutually distinct, that which is non-distinct and common is the word "Piṭaka." Indeed, the three terms such as Vinaya are distinct because they are not shared with one another. The word "Piṭaka," however, is called a "non-distinct term" because it is common to all three. "Pariyattibbhājanatthatō" means because of the meanings of learning (pariyatti) and container (bhājana), which function as either the instrument or the qualifier. Alternatively, it should be understood that "Pariyattibbhājanatthatō" means they say it has the meaning of being the container of what is to be learned. In fact, the word "tō" occurs in the sense of the nominative case (paccatta) because it is indicated by the word "iti." Grammarians desire the word "tō" in places indicated by the word "iti." For example: "They contemplate as impermanent (aniccato), as suffering (dukkhato), as non-self (anattato)." By this, he shows the meaning of "Piṭaka" as that which is to be learned and as the container of various meanings. This word "Piṭaka" is an underived primary stem (anipphanna-pāṭipadika) that is not formed by compound, derivative, verb, or primary derivative. Grammarians, however, say that the word "Piṭa" occurs in the senses of sounding and collecting, and they cite only the example "Mā piṭakasampadānena" already mentioned in this commentary. Therefore, according to those teachers, the grammatical definition (vigga-ha) should be: it is called "Piṭaka" because it is learned (piṭīyati/saddīyati), or it is called "Piṭaka" because various meanings are collected (piṭīyati/saṅghāṭīyati) in this word of the Buddha. By the words beginning with "Tena," he shows the compound (samāsa).

"Mā piṭakasampadānena" refers to the Pali text found in the Kālāma Sutta and the Sāḷha Sutta. In the commentary on that Sutta, the meaning is given as: "Do not accept it [merely] because it agrees with our Piṭaka Pali text." The Elder Sāriputta, however, said: "Do not accept it by way of the completeness of the Pali text." "Kudālapitakamādāya" means...
97:
In the phrase 'taking a hoe and a basket,' the earth is called 'ku.' Because it breaks or splits that earth, the specific iron tool is called 'kudāla' (hoe). Because it serves as a container for various objects, the specific vessel made of palm leaves, rattan, and so forth, is called 'piṭaka' (basket). This statement (regarding mā piṭakasampadānena) is mentioned in the Kakacūpama Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi.

Extracting the verse 'Tena... pe... ñeyyā,' it is explained with the words starting with 'Tena.' Pronouns such as 'sabba' usually take the gender of either the preceding word or the following word. However, in this context, according to the intended meaning, it takes the gender of the already mentioned (Vinaya); therefore, it is said, 'Vinayo ca so piṭakañca' (The Vinaya is that, and it is a Pitaka). By the phrase 'yathāvutteneve nayena,' it refers to everything stated as 'evam duvidhatthena... pe... katvā' and 'pariyattibhāvato, tassa tassa atthassa bhājanato ca.' In the word 'tayopi,' the particle 'api' or 'pi' has the meaning of aggregating parts. By saying 'pi' instead of 'api,' it demonstrates that 'pi' also exists as a separate particle just like 'api.'

'Desanā' (Exposition) is the act of making known through the method of authority and so forth, in relation to the Blessed One who preaches the meanings to be told. 'Sāsana' (Instruction) is the admonition according to the faults of the person to be taught. 'Kathā' (Discourse) is the telling of meanings such as restraint and non-restraint, and the formation of a sequence of words. The intended meaning is this: 'Desanā' is in reference to the Blessed One who preaches; 'Sāsana' is by virtue of the person to be taught; 'Kathā' is by virtue of the meaning to be told. Thus, the distinction between them should be understood.

In this context, although 'Desanā' and the others are not independent of the meanings to be preached, 'authority' and so forth specifically depend on the Preacher. Therefore, the distinction of 'Desanā' etc. is stated based on those specific connections. Just as the exercise of authority depends on the Blessed One's skill in that area—He being the one worthy of authority—so too the methods of conventional and ultimate truth depend on the Preacher who prescribes them. Thus, the exercise of authority etc. is said to be related to the Preacher. Just as admonition according to faults and intentions depends on the person to be taught, so too admonition according to the Dhamma specifically depends on the person to be taught. Therefore, it is called 'Sāsana' by virtue of the person to be taught. Like restraint, non-restraint, and mind-and-matter, the preaching of the views to be unraveled occurs only when there is a subject matter of speech (vaca-vatthu) and does not occur when there is none; thus, it specifically depends on that meaning. Therefore, it is called 'Kathā' by virtue of the meaning to be told. In this regard, there are the following verses:
98:
“In this context, by virtue of the Exalted One who taught, the Three Piṭakas are called 'Desanā' (Exposition).
By virtue of the person to be instructed, these Three Piṭakas are called 'Sāsana' (Instruction).
By virtue of the meaning to be expressed, they are also called 'Kathā' (Discourse).
In this way, one should demonstrate the distinctions of Desanā, Sāsana, and Kathā.”

Combining these three terms and making them the 'distinctions' of that Desanā, Sāsana, and Kathā, the word 'bheda' (distinction) should be applied to each respectively, as it is heard after the dvanda compound. One should apply it thus: "One should demonstrate the distinction of Desanā, the distinction of Sāsana, and the distinction of Kathā as appropriate." 'Bheda' means difference or specific characteristic. In those Piṭakas, one should demonstrate the training (sikkhā), the abandoning (pahāna), and the state of profundity (gambhīra-bhāva) as appropriate.

By the second verse, one should explain the distinction of the scriptures (pariyatti), the manner of learning, and the specific qualities. In whichever Piṭaka, such as the Vinaya, etc., a monk reaches such success (sampatti) and failure (vipatti), all that should be connected and explained in that Piṭaka. Alternatively, it should be applied thus: in whichever Piṭaka a monk reaches such a distinction of learning, success, and failure, all that should be explained in that Piṭaka. 'In such a way' means by such modes as learning for the sake of refuting others, etc.; it means by these modes: learning for the sake of refuting others, for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, for the sake of guarding the treasury of the Dhamma (Brahmacariya), and right practice and wrong practice. Although others also reach such states, they are called 'monks' (bhikkhus) because they are the eldest, the most excellent, always present nearby, and because they establish the Dhamma by practicing rightly according to the instruction.

In those verses, 'tatra' means in those verses. 'Ayaṃ' refers to the discourse that is about to be spoken. 'Paridīpanā' means illuminating from all sides, meaning to analyze without leaving even a small portion. 'Vibhāvanā' means making it clear for the listeners to understand easily, without keeping it hidden or concealed, even when it is illuminated from all sides. Teachers also say that illuminating in brief is 'paridīpanā', and explaining in detail is 'vibhāvanā'. Furthermore, although these two terms are spoken in accordance with what was said above, they are the same in meaning. Therefore, 'paridīpanā' should be applied to the first verse and 'vibhāvanā' to the second verse. The word 'ca' (and) connects both to each other. If one asks why they are so called, he said, "In this context..." and so on. The word 'hi' is a particle indicating cause, as in "akkharavipattiyamaṃ hi," etc. It carries the meaning of 'because' or 'why'. He is called 'Āṇāraha' because he is worthy of exercising authority, being the Sammāsambuddha...
99:
Because He possesses great compassion and because He points out the undistorted benefit, the Blessed One is worthy of authority (āṇā) and His words are the standard (pamāṇa). In these two teachings, because of the presence of both conventional (vohāra) and ultimate (paramattha) realities, it is said 'āṇābāhullato' (due to the abundance of the teaching of authority). By this, the general method is shown. This same method applies to the teachings that follow. Specifically, it is called 'vohāra' (convention/designation) because it carries away (avaharati) the minds of beings; He is skilled in that convention.

Those who have many faults or transgressions are called 'pacurāparādha' (those of many offenses), such as the Elder Seyyasaka and others. 'Yathāparādhaṃ' means according to the offense. In terms like 'anekajjhāsaya', 'āsaya' is indeed 'ajjhāsaya' (inclination). In essence, it consists of view (diṭṭhi) and knowledge (ñāṇa), and it is of four types. It is said:

'Eternalist view, annihilationist view, conformable patience (insight knowledge),
And the knowledge of things as they really are (knowledge of ownership of deeds)—these four are called inclinations (āsaya).'

Among these, since all views are included in the eternalist and annihilationist views, all beings with wrong views rely only on these two views. As it was said: 'Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on a duality: existence (atthitā) and non-existence (natthitā).' Existence refers to the eternalist view, and non-existence refers to the annihilationist view. This is the inclination of worldlings (puthujjana) who rely on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). For pure beings who aim for the end of the round (vivaṭṭa), there are two inclinations: conformable patience and knowledge of things as they really are. Among these, conformable patience is insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), and knowledge of things as they really are is knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa).

Beings dwell in these four inclinations, or the mind comes to rest there; thus it is called 'āsaya', like a deer's lair (migāsaya). Just as a deer goes for food but returns to sleep in that same thicket, so the mind, though it may function elsewhere, returns to rest in that view or knowledge. That view or knowledge is the 'āsaya' of that mind. The seven tendencies like sensual lust are called 'anusaya' (latent tendencies). Like rat poison that appears when it finds a cause, past, future, and present defilements that are fit to arise are called 'anusaya' because they have that nature. This is because there is no difference in the nature (sabhāva) of dhammas merely by the difference in time. 'Cariyā' (conduct) refers to the six root conducts like the greedy conduct, etc. Though there are many varieties, there are sixty-three through combination. Alternatively, conduct is of two kinds: good conduct and bad conduct. This is explained in the 'Carita-niddesa' of the Vibhaṅga.
100:
'Adhimutti' (resolve) is the decision that arises by inclining towards a state, such as 'I will ordain this very day, I will attain Arahantship this very day,' as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā and other Ganthipada texts. However, the teacher Dhammapāla stated in the Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā that 'adhimutti' is the preference (abhiruci) arising from the power of beings' past habits; it is of two types: low and superior.

This is indeed true: because of that resolve, beings of low inclination associate only with those of low inclination, and those of superior inclination associate only with those of superior inclination. If the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous but the students are, those students do not approach their own teachers but approach only suitable monks similar to themselves. If the teachers and preceptors are suitable monks but the students are unsuitable, those students do not approach their teachers but approach only unsuitable monks similar to themselves. This meaning should also be explained by way of the Dhātu-saṃyutta. Thus, this preference and disposition (āsaya-dhātu) determined by mutual association, etc., of those with low inclinations and so on, should be known as 'adhimutti'.

Those who have many inclinations and so on, or those whose property is many inclinations and so on, are called [anekāsayānusayacariyādhimuttika], similar to the terms 'bahukattuka' or 'bahunadika'. 'Yathānulomaṃ' means without overstepping the conformity of inclinations, etc., or by means of whatever inclinations are conformable. Teachers also say it means in accordance with the conformity of inclinations and so on.

Because of the inability to analyze the compact (ghana), beings have perceptions arising through the power of views, conceit, and craving, such as 'I' or 'mine'. In contrast, 'yathādhammaṃ' (according to the Dhamma) means in accordance with the nature of things (dhammasabhāva), such as 'There is no self here, nor what belongs to a self; it is merely a phenomenon (dhamma).'
