Restraint is 'saṃvara', which is non-transgression by body and speech. Great restraint is called 'asaṃvara'. Here, the prefix 'a-' denotes 'increase' (vuḍḍhi), as in the term 'asekhā dhammā'. Because of its association with that 'a-', the remaining restraint is called 'saṃvara' (lesser restraint). Therefore, it means lesser restraint and great restraint. Thus it is said 'saṃvarāsaṃvaro', etc. 'Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanā' means liberation from views; in essence, it refers to states like right view which are the direct opposites of those views. Thus it is said, 'being the opposite of the sixty-two views.' The distinguishing of mentality, materiality, or both is 'nāmarūpapariccheda' (definition of mentality-materiality). Since it is said to be 'the opposite of greed, etc.', it is indeed the knowledge that functions in that way.
101:
With the words beginning with "Tīsu pi," the author explains the latter half of the verse [which illustrates the depth of the trainings and abandonings]. Since the teaching of these three trainings is possible in all three Piṭakas, the word "visesena" (specifically/especially) is used. This term "visesena" should be applied to all the sentences. Among those three trainings, because it is taught in the Pārājika Pali, "There is this training in higher virtue; this training in higher virtue is intended in this context [the first Pārājika]," it is said: "Training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) in the Vinaya Piṭaka." In the Suttanta Pali, because there are many discourses teaching concentration (samādhi) with such words as "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (vivicceva kāmehi) and so forth, it is said: "Training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) in the Suttanta Piṭaka." Because the discernment of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) is the proximate cause for higher wisdom, and because the other mental and material phenomena known through higher wisdom are taught there, it is said: "Training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka."

"Kilesānaṃ" refers to the corruptions (saṅkilesa-dhamma) that torment beings, or to the corruptions of action (kamma-kilesa). This expression regards both types. It is also said: "The transgression (vītikkama) of defilements through the doors of body and speech is such; the abandoning of that transgression is [the function of virtue], because it is the opposite of virtue." The word "vītikkamo" should be connected with the word "paṭipak-kha" (opposite), while the word "sīlassa" is connected in the sense of the state [of virtue]. This should be understood in all instances. Defilements that follow the mind-stream by way of latent tendencies (anusaya) do not get the chance to transgress even when they are aroused upon meeting a cause, because of the fear of breaking virtue; therefore, it is said: "It is called virtue because it is the opposite of transgression."

The arising of defilements by taking over the occurrence of wholesome states in the mind through not giving them an opportunity is called obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna); it refers to the abandoning of that obsession. It means the abandoning of the outburst of defilements that have arisen in the mind-stream. The word "kilesānaṃ" (of defilements) also applies here. Since the abandoning of that obsession occurs by way of properly composing the mind (concentration), it is said: "It is called concentration because it is the opposite of the obsession of defilements."

The seven defilements, such as sensual lust (kāmarāga), which lie dormant in the mind-stream because they have not yet been abandoned, which are liable to arise when meeting a suitable cause, and which have gained strength, are called latent tendencies (anusaya). It refers to the abandoning of those latent tendencies. Since those latent tendencies are abandoned absolutely only by the wisdom of the Noble Path, it is said: "It is called wisdom because it is the opposite of latent tendencies."

Just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp, the abandoning of a particular unwholesome state by a particular wholesome factor occurring in the bases of meritorious action such as giving (dāna) is called abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). However, in this context, since it is the place where the training in higher virtue is taught, the abandoning of a particular factor of immorality (dussīlya) by a particular factor of possessing virtue should be taken as "tadaṅga-pahāna." Just as moss on the surface of water is pushed away by striking it with a pot, the abandoning by way of keeping away the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and other such states through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), which prevent the occurrence of defilements, is called abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). Because the four Noble Paths have been developed, in the mind-stream of the person possessing those respective paths...
102:
The abandoning by way of absolute cutting off, characterized by the total non-occurrence of the collection of defilements belonging to the side of origination (samudaya) [or the cause of suffering], is called abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Misconduct (duccarita) means conduct that is performed badly, or conduct corrupted by defilements. That same misconduct is called corruption (saṅkilesa) because, when it arises in the mind-stream [of a person], it thoroughly oppresses, torments, and afflicts that mind-stream; its abandoning is [referred to here]. Since virtue (sīla) is the opposite of misconduct, the abandoning of the corruption occurring by way of bodily and verbal misconduct through the substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) is mentioned. This meaning should be understood by following the instruction of the three trainings. It is called craving (taṇhā) because it torments [or causes trembling]; that craving is also called corruption in the manner already stated. Since concentration (samādhi) is the opposite of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), the abandoning of that corruption of craving through suppression (vikkhambhana) is mentioned. Wrong view (diṭṭhi) is also called corruption in the manner already stated. Since wisdom (paññā) reveals the nature of phenomena (dhamma) liberated from the notion of "self" (attā) and so forth, the abandoning of that corruption of wrong view through eradication (samuccheda) is mentioned.

"Ekam-ekasmiñ-cettha" means in each one of these three Piṭakas. The word "ca" is used either at the beginning of a sentence or to indicate another side. The word "api" is used in the sense of combining parts; by that, it combines the fact that not only is there depth in the fourfold [Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, Paṭivedha], but there is also depth in each of their parts. This is the method in such places. Now, to show those things in their own form, the words beginning with "Tattha" are said. In that context, "Tanti" refers to the Pali. It is called "Pali" because it makes known noble meanings such as virtue, because it has the nature of natural linguistics (sabhāva-nirutti), and because it is a lineage or row (āḷi/panti) of noble words spoken by the Buddha and others.

In this context, however, according to the opinion of the teachers who composed the Vinaya-gaṇṭhipada and the teachers of grammar (Saddavādī), the Tanti (Pali), which is the sequence of ultimate sounds/words (paramattha-sadda-pabanda) previously determined by the mind, is called Dhamma. The word "iti" is used in the sense of a name, thus it is also called "Dhamma." "Tassāyeva" refers to the meaning of that very Tanti (Pali) as already described. "Manasā vavatthāpitāya" refers to that Tanti, which is the sequence of ultimate sounds, previously determined by the mind occurring by way of learning, memorizing, and so forth. "Desanā" is that very Tanti, the sequence of ultimate sounds, called a teaching for the purpose of making others understand at a later time. Alternatively, Desanā is the mental volition (cittuppāda) that produces the sounds called the aforementioned Tanti. "Tantiyā tantiatthassa ca" means the penetration of the two types of Tanti as they are, and of their meanings; this is how the sense should be understood. For those teachers say that the sound itself, which illustrates the meaning and the usage spoken by the Blessed One, is called Tanti. If it is asked, "In their view, since Dhamma also has the nature of sound, what is the difference between Dhamma and Desanā?"—[the answer is:] that which is known by the nature of making known those respective meanings...
103:
The sequence of ultimate sounds (paramattha-sadda) determined beforehand by means of learning and so forth is called Dhamma. The sound that arises later for the purpose of making others understand, which expresses those respective meanings, is called Desanā. This is the distinction between this Dhamma and Desanā.

Alternatively, the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that produces the aforementioned sound is called Desanā. Because the sound is produced by this arising of consciousness, it is called Desanā, just like the case of false speech (musāvāda) and so forth. Indeed, in those terms such as false speech, the intention (cetanā) that produces the false speech is referred to by the term 'false speech' and so on.

Although only the conceptual sound (paññatti-sadda) in the form of a sequence of letters makes the meaning known, because it is the root cause, as in 'known by the perception of letters' (akkharasaññāto) and so forth, it should be understood that only the ultimate sound is said to be that which makes the meaning known, as it is the meaning of those letters. The statement 'the teaching of that Pali text (tanti)' is also spoken by way of similar usage (sadisūpacāra), just as it is said, 'The arisen wholesome states (kusalā dhammā) lead to further growth and abundance.'

However, according to the view of the proponents of concepts (paññatti-vādī) such as the author of the Abhidhamma-gaṇṭhipada, the Pali text, which is a sequence of name-concepts (nāma-paññatti) determined precisely by the Buddha's mind in ultimate sounds according to the meanings distinguished by convention (sammuti) and ultimate reality (paramattha), is called Dhamma, or is referred to as 'Dhamma'. The phrase 'tassāyeva' means the meaning of only that Pali text which is a name-concept. 'Manasā vavatthāpitāya' means (the meaning) of that Pali text which is a sequence of name-concepts determined by the Buddha's mind in ultimate sounds according to the meanings distinguished by convention and ultimate reality. 'Desanā' is the Pali text known as the sequence of ultimate sounds, which is the breaking into speech (vaci-bheda) that manifests through vocal utterance, excellently arranged for the purpose of making others understand. 'Tantiyā tantiatthassa ca' means the penetration and knowledge as it really is of both kinds of Pali text and the meaning of that Pali text as mentioned. Those teachers say: In this context, the concept determined by the Buddha's mind only by way of being appropriate to the ultimate meaning and ultimate usage is called 'Pali' (tanti). If, according to the view of the proponents of sound (sadda-vādī), only sound were called Pali in this context, there would have to be a distinction between Pali and Desanā. Apart from the mere act of vocal utterance, there is no distinction between Desanā and the Pali text determined by the mind. Therefore, the commentator, wishing to show Desanā, stated the non-difference of Pali and Desanā, apart from the mere act of vocal utterance, by saying that the Pali text determined by the mind is itself Desanā. Likewise, because it is stated above that 'Desanā is a concept (paññatti)', the conceptual nature of the Pali text is also stated by way of its non-difference from Desanā.
104:
Furthermore, if the teaching (desanā) were indeed something other than the Pali text (tanti), it should have been stated as 'the knowledge as it really is of the Pali text, the meaning of the Pali text, and the teaching.' But since it is not stated thus, but rather as 'the knowledge as it really is of the Pali text and the meaning of the Pali text,' the non-difference between the Pali text and the teaching is shown. By doing so, the teacher who shows above that 'what is called teaching is a concept (paññatti)' has stated the conceptual nature of the Pali text because it is non-different from the teaching.

In the ultimate sense, both of these are merely sound (sadda), because there is no convention (sammuti) that is liberated from ultimate reality. Taking this very method, some teachers say, 'Dhamma and Desanā are, in the ultimate sense, only sound.' Their statement is also not blameworthy. Just as the sense-sphere resultant rebirth-linking consciousnesses (kāmāvacara-paṭisandhi-vipāka) are called 'having limited objects' (parittārammaṇa), this should be understood in the same way here. It cannot be said that sense-sphere resultant rebirth-linking consciousnesses have only ultimate realities as their objects, because they arise even by taking the objects of unwholesome states like greed (rāga) or wholesome states like loving-kindness (mettā), which are preceded by thoughts of forms such as 'woman' or 'man'. However, because that thinking is rooted in ultimate realities, it is possible to designate it as having ultimate objects. In this case also, it should be understood in the same way.

Let this be the view of the proponents of concepts (paññatti-vādī). Even in the view of the proponents of sound (sadda-vādī), the distinction between Dhamma and Desanā has been manifested by teachers such as the Elder Dhammapāla in the manner already stated. There is a summary verse here:

'Some teachers say that sound is both Dhamma and Desanā.
Others say that Dhamma is a concept, while sound is Desanā.'

Among these three, in the context of 'Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, Paṭivedha', these three—the meaning of the Pali text, the teaching of the Pali text, and the penetration of the meaning of the Pali text—are the objects (visaya) of the Pali text. Therefore, it is appropriate for the Vinaya Piṭaka and so forth to be the support (ādhāra) for meaning, teaching, and penetration. However, the Piṭakas are themselves the Pali text (tanti); how then is it appropriate for them to be the support of Dhamma (Pali)? It is appropriate because the whole Pali text (tanti-samudāya) is the support for the constituent Pali text (avayava-tanti). Indeed, the whole is said to be the support of the parts by way of a support established merely by conceptualization, just as it is said, 'There are branches in a tree.'

In this context, because Dhamma and so forth are difficult to plunge into, it is stated that the Vinaya and so forth are profound (gambhīra) by means of those Dhamma and so forth. Thus, the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and so forth has already been stated. Therefore, it should not be objected that only Dhamma and so forth are profound because they are difficult to plunge into, and that the Vinaya and so forth are not profound. This is because the profundity of the Vinaya and so forth is stated by way of the object (visaya) and the possessor of the object (visayī). Indeed, Dhamma is the Vinaya and so forth themselves, as they are not different. Their meaning (attha) is the object (visaya) because it is the sense to be expressed by those which are the expressers (vācaka). As for the possessors of the object...
105:
Desanā and Paṭivedha (penetration) are called profound (gambhīra) because they are the objects (visaya) of Dhamma and Attha. Among those four, it should be understood that Dhamma and Attha are difficult to plunge into because Paṭivedha is difficult to achieve, and Desanā is difficult to plunge into because the knowledge of Desanā is difficult to achieve. It should be understood as being plunged into with difficulty because of the inability to produce Paṭivedha and because of the difficulty of arising knowledge that takes those Dhamma, Attha, and Desanā as objects.

Because Dhamma, Attha, and Desanā are profound, the Paṭivedha that takes them as objects is also profound. Just as in measuring the depth of deep water, there must be a long measure, so this entire fulfillment should be understood; thus said the Elder Vajirabuddhi. When the profundity of the parts of the Piṭaka, such as Dhamma, etc., is spoken of, the profundity of the Piṭaka, which is the collection of those parts, is also said to be spoken of. Therefore, teachers say that one should not object in that way. This statement should be investigated. Why? Because all those—Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha—are parts of the Piṭaka.

The connection should be made as: "Like the great ocean is difficult to plunge into and like no footing can be found." Due to the power of the meaning, there is the transformation of case endings, number, and gender. They are called 'dukkho-gāha' because they are plunged into with difficulty, or because there is a difficult plunging (entering into) those teachings. 'Alabbhanīya' means that which cannot be obtained; that itself is 'alabbhaneyya'. Alternatively, obtaining is called 'labbhana'; because it is not worthy of that obtaining, it is called 'alabbhaneyya'. 'Patiṭṭha' means that which stands in this place, or standing is called 'patiṭṭha'. Because that footing cannot be found in those teachings, they are called 'alabbhaneyya-patiṭṭha'. This is said again to show that even those with dull wisdom who plunge in partially cannot find a footing. The words beginning with 'evaṃ' are the conclusion.

Now, wishing to show the profundity by way of cause, result, etc., he said "aparo nayo" (another method) and so on. In that context, 'hetu' means cause. That cause is called 'dhamma' because it bears (dahati) or ordains (vidahati) its own result, by changing the letter 'd' to 'dh'. If one asks how it is known that the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for 'hetu' here, he said "vuttañhetaṃ" and so on. It is taught in the Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga. If one objects, "How is the causal nature of Dhamma known by this statement: 'Knowledge of the cause is Dhamma-paṭisambhidā'?"—it is known because he said "knowledge of the cause" (hetumhi ñāṇaṃ) wishing to show the meaning of the component word of the compound 'Dhamma-paṭisambhidā'. For in the phrase 'dhamme paṭisambhidā dhammapaṭisambhidā', he said 'hetumhi' (in the cause) to show the meaning of 'dhamme', and 'ñāṇaṃ' (knowledge) to show the meaning of 'paṭisambhidā'. Therefore, the words 'hetu' and 'dhamma' have the same meaning, and the words 'ñāṇa' and 'paṭisambhidā' also have the same meaning; thus the commentator, expressing this meaning, established the causal nature of Dhamma. Likewise, by the statement "Knowledge of the result of the cause is Attha-paṭisambhidā," the nature of Attha as the result of a cause is established.
106:
It should be understood as the state of cause and result (hetu-phala-bhāva). The result of a cause is 'hetu-phala'. Because that result is known or attained in accordance with the cause, it is called 'attha'.

In the phrase 'teaching is a concept (paññatti)', according to the view of the Saddavādī teachers, the Pali (tanti), which expresses the meaning, is an unerring utterance, constitutes the linguistic expression of Dhamma (dhamma-nirutti), and is described as a succession of ultimate sounds, is called 'desanā'. Or it means it is named 'desanā'. For it is called 'desanā' because the meaning is taught by that Pali. It is called 'paññatti' because the meaning is known in various ways by that Pali, or because it makes the meaning known in various ways. To show that very concept in its specific form, it is said: 'It means the expression of Dhamma according to the Dhamma (yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpo)'. In this word 'yathādhammaṃ', the word 'dhamma' includes all causes and results of causes. This word 'dhamma' is a term expressing intrinsic nature (sabhāva), not a term expressing scriptural learning (pariyatti) or cause, etc. Therefore, it means 'in such and such a nature' like ignorance (avijjā), formations (saṅkhāra), etc., that exists. Or, 'yathādhammaṃ' means in accordance with those various natures like ignorance and formations. Like penetration, teaching also proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma because it clearly manifests the intrinsic nature which is its own object without error. For that very reason, it is called an 'unerring utterance' (aviparitābhilāpa). 'Dhammābhilāp' is a succession of ultimate sounds called Pali, which expresses the meaning, is an unerring utterance, and constitutes the linguistic expression of Dhamma. Because that sound is uttered, it is called 'abhilāpa'. The uttered sound which is the unerring ultimate nature is called 'dhammābhilāpa'. By this term 'dhammābhilāpa', he shows the 'dhamma-nirutti' mentioned in the Vibhaṅga Pali: 'Knowledge in the utterance of that dhamma-nirutti is Nirutti-paṭisambhidā'. This is because teaching has the nature of sound. Indeed, because teaching has the nature of sound, the Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga Pali states that Nirutti-paṭisambhidā has objects such as the limited (paritta) and so on. In its commentary as well, the state of having sound as an object for that Nirutti-paṭisambhidā is shown by saying 'making that sound of natural expression (sabhāva-nirutti) the object'. Having defined the word and its meaning as 'this sound is the expresser of this meaning', the sound that proceeds by way of clearly manifesting the meaning of various words is called 'desanā'. By the word 'adhippāyo' (the intention), he shows that the statement 'teaching is a concept' is said with reference to the utterance of the linguistic expression of Dhamma (dhamma-niruttābhilāpa), and not with reference to a mere concept apart from that. This is because, although various meanings are possible, only the intended meaning is stated. This is the decision according to the view of the Saddavādī teachers.

However, in the view of the Paññattivādī teachers, the name-concept (nāma-paññatti) called Pali, which was defined in the mind by the Blessed One among ultimate sounds by way of being an appropriate expresser of the meaning divided into conventional (sammuti) and ultimate (paramattha), is called 'desanā'. Or it is said to be 'desanā'. That very name-concept...
107:
It is said, "The expression of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma is the intention," in order to show, by way of metonymy of cause, the manifestation of the sound which is the root cause. Even if here in the term "Dhamma-abhilāpa" (expression of the Dhamma), the word "abhilāpa" refers to the ultimate sound (paramattha-sadda) because it is uttered or pronounced, and not to the concept (paññatti), nevertheless, when the sound is uttered, one grasps the conventional usage (vohāra) corresponding to it and understands the meaning indicated by that usage. Therefore, when the sound is spoken, the concept corresponding to that sound is also spoken by way of metonymy of cause.

Alternatively, by saying "Dhamma-abhilāpa is the intention" instead of "Dhamma-abhilāpa is the meaning," it is shown that what is called "teaching" (desanā) is not merely sound. Therefore, only the intention is spoken of by way of the sound which is the root cause; the meaning of this term "desanā" to be grasped here is not spoken of—this is the decision according to the view of the teachers who uphold the doctrine of concepts (paññattivādī).

Another meaning is stated as "Anuloma...pe... kathanaṃ" (the preaching in accordance...). By this, it shows the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that produces the teaching mentioned below. Because the meaning is preached by this consciousness, it is called "preaching" (kathanaṃ). By the word "ādi" (etc.), the ways of the Pali such as nīta and neyya, and the methods based on the Pali such as the method of unity (ekatta-naya) and the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, are included.

Knowledge is called "penetration" (paṭivedha) because it penetrates by itself, or because associated states penetrate by means of this knowledge. That same knowledge is also called "realization" (abhisamaya) because it realizes, or because associated states realize by means of this knowledge. Now, to make that penetration clear by way of the divisions of realization, the mode of realization, the object, and the nature, the passage beginning with "So ca" is stated. Therein, it is made clear: by division as "mundane and supramundane"; by mode as "by way of the object and non-delusion"; by object as "in the dhammas, in the meanings, and in the concepts"; and by nature as "in accordance with the meaning, in accordance with the dhamma, and in accordance with the path of concepts."

Therein, by way of the object, penetration in the dhammas in accordance with the effect means mundane realization, which has for its object the causes such as ignorance (avijjā), the effects such as formations (saṅkhāra), or the concepts that make both known. By way of non-delusion, penetration in the dhammas in accordance with the effect means supramundane realization, which has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the Path, and destroys delusion regarding the aforementioned causes, effects, and concepts. Indeed, mundane knowledge penetrates by way of the object through the process of taking as an object: "This is the cause, this is its effect, this is the conventional usage corresponding to both." However, supramundane knowledge penetrates by way of non-delusion because delusion regarding those causes, effects, etc., has been utterly cut off by knowledge. But the supramundane (penetration)...
108:
Some teachers also say that supramundane penetration (paṭivedha) penetrates by way of taking Nibbāna as the object, and by way of non-delusion regarding other states (other than Nibbāna).

"In the dhammas in accordance with the meaning" (atthānurūpaṃ dhammesu) means penetration in the causes in accordance with the accomplished effects, such as: "Ignorance is the cause, formations are the states arisen from the cause, ignorance produces formations." Alternatively, it means penetration in the causes in accordance with the effects, such as: "Among the three types of formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—ignorance assists the non-meritorious formations by way of the associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya), and assists the others as is appropriate," and so forth. "In the meanings in accordance with the dhamma" (dhammānurūpaṃ atthesu) means penetration in the effects in accordance with the causes, such as: "With ignorance as condition, formations come to be," and so forth. The path of the sixfold designation is called the "path of concepts" (paññattipatha). Penetration (avabodha) in the concepts in accordance with that path of concepts, or in accordance with the dhammas expressed by the concepts, is the meaning. To show another meaning of penetration other than realization (abhisamaya), the passage beginning with "Tesaṃ" is stated. It refers to the undistorted nature of those respective dhammas, such as matter (rūpa) and so forth, because they are penetrated; thus it is called "penetration" (paṭivedha). "There and there" (tattha tattha) means in this or that Piṭaka, or in this or that passage of the Pali. "Known as individual characteristics" (salakkhaṇa-saṅkhāta) means the nature known as their respective individual characteristics, such as being deformed (ruppana), bending (namana), and touching (phusana).

To show the profundity of the Piṭakas by way of the aforementioned dhammas and so forth, the passage beginning with "Idāni" is stated. "Dhamma-jāta" refers to the variety of causes or simply the cause. "Attha-jāta" refers to the variety of effects or simply the effect. "And this teaching" (yā cāyaṃ desanā) is the connection of words. It becomes present to the knowledge by way of understanding the meaning of that Pali. "And what is here" (yo cettha) means: whatever penetration there is in the dhammas, meanings, and teachings found in those respective Piṭakas, and whatever undistorted nature of those respective dhammas there is in those Piṭakas. This is the meaning. Because it should be fulfilled, only merit (kusala) is called "requisite" (sambhāra). Those by whom those requisites of merit have not been well accumulated are called "those with unaccumulated requisites of merit" (anupacita-kusala-sambhāra); for that very reason, they are "those of poor wisdom" (duppañña) or "those without wisdom" (nippañña). Indeed, for a wise person or for wisdom, a state of badness or corruption is impossible; therefore, one is called "of poor wisdom" (duppañña) simply because of the absence of wisdom, just as one is called "immoral" (dussīla) [for the absence of virtue]. In this context, it should be understood that because the dhammas and meanings such as ignorance and formations are difficult to penetrate, they are "difficult to fathom" (dukkho-ogāha). Because it is difficult to make those states known, the teaching of them is difficult to understand. Because it is impossible to produce and take as an object the penetration known as realization, and because the penetration known as the undistorted nature is difficult to know, they are "difficult to fathom" (dukkho-ogāha). In the word "evampi", the word "pi"...
109:
It summarizes the various distinctions previously mentioned. Thus, wishing to show that the meaning has been fully and completely expressed by the first verse, he said "Ettāvatā" and so on. By this statement of renewed effort—"When a matter is completed, a new beginning is made either to make known a specific meaning or for the sake of certainty"—he shows that the meaning has been fully and completely expressed. "Ettāvatā" is a particle in the sense of delimitation; it means "by this sequence of words." Or, because it has this measure, it is called "ettāvaṃ"; by that "ettāvaṃ," it means "by this sequence of sounds and meanings of such measure." Teachers say, "When the sound is uttered, its meaning is also said to be uttered." "Vuttatthā" refers to the verse whose meaning has been well-explained.

"Ettha" means "in this verse." The remaining words such as "this is the meaning" or "this is the decision" should be added and understood. In the phrase "in the three Piṭakas," it should be understood as "in each one" according to the context or the subject matter. For it was said below, "And in each one here." Or else, because the occurrence of words follows the speaker's intention, here the locative (ādhāra) is stated without intending specification (niddhāraṇa). One should not object here, saying, "The three types of learning should be seen only in the three Piṭakas," because even when a statement is made by way of a whole, it can imply its parts. Indeed, the completion of a partial sentence is seen in sentences such as "Let the Brahmins and others eat"; therefore, enough with excessive elaboration. It should be taken only in a way that the meaning is not contradicted. This applies everywhere.

"Pariyattibhedo": learning is called "pariyatti." Here, the word "pariyatti" is a term denoting the act of learning, not a synonym for the Pāli text; therefore, it means the "mode of learning." Alternatively, the Pāli texts themselves, which are to be learned in three ways, are called "pariyatti." Teachers say that it is so stated in the Sinhalese glossary (Gaṇṭhipada) of the Abhidhamma Commentary. Even if the Pāli text is called "pariyatti" in this way, it can also be called "alagaddūpamā pariyatti" (water-snake simile learning) because it is associated with learning that is like catching a snake. By doing so, the subsequent detailed statement—"The learning that is badly grasped and learned for the sake of criticizing others and so on is like catching a water-snake"—becomes appropriate. In that sentence, it is proper to refer to the Pāli text itself as "badly grasped" and "learned."

It is called "alagaddūpamā" because a snake or the catching of a snake is the simile for this learning. In this term "alagaddūpamā," it should be understood that the word "alagadda" refers to the catching of a snake. Just as in the word "āpūpika," the word "āpūpa" (cake) refers to the eating of cakes, and in "veṇika," the word "vīṇā" (lute) refers to the playing of the lute. By catching a snake, the learning...
110:
...is compared, not by the snake alone. Although it should be said as "alagaddagga-haṇūpamā" (the simile of catching a water-snake), the middle term is elided and it is called "alagaddūpamā," as in "oṭṭhamukho" (one with a face like a camel's face) and so on. A venomous snake is also called "alagadda." For "gada" is a name for poison, and that snake has it fully; therefore, because it has full poison, the vowel "a" and the "niggahīta" are dropped and the letter "da" is inserted to call it "alagadda." Or, it is called "alagadda" by the aforementioned method because it has poison capable of taking life. It is called "nissaraṇattha" because it has the benefit of escaping from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). One appointed to a storehouse is a treasurer; being like that treasurer, an Arahant who protects the Treasure of Dhamma is like a treasurer. Learning that is like a treasurer, without regard for other benefits, is called "bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti."

"Duggahitā" means badly grasped. To specifically define that "duggahita" itself, he said, "They learn for the sake of criticizing others and so on." It means the meaning learned for the sake of escaping from others' doctrines and so forth. Learning for the sake of gains, honors, and so on should also be understood as included here. This is stated in the Commentary to the Alagaddūpama Sutta: "If someone learns the Buddha's word thinking, 'In this way I shall obtain robes and so on, or they will know me in the midst of the fourfold assembly,' and learns for the sake of gains and honors, that person's learning is called alagadda-pariyatti. Indeed, rather than learning the Buddha's word in this way, it is better to fall asleep without learning it."

Learning that has the simile of catching a snake is called "alagaddūpamā." If so, it is proper to call even well-grasped learning "alagaddūpamā," because in the Pāli text, even that well-grasped learning is taught as a simile of catching a snake. As it was taught: "Monks, suppose a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake, should see a large water-snake. He would press it down well with a cleft stick (ajapada-daṇḍa), and having pressed it down well with the cleft stick, he would grasp it well by the neck. Monks, although that water-snake might wrap its coils around that man's hand or arm or any other limb, yet that man would not on that account come to death or deadly suffering. Why is that? Because, monks, the water-snake was well-grasped. Monks, in the same way, some worthless men here learn the Dhamma: they learn the discourses (sutta) and the songs (geyya)..."
111:
...would coil around [him]. However, that man would not, on that account, suffer death or death-like suffering. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the snake was well-grasped. In the same way, bhikkhus, some clansmen here learn the Dhamma, such as discourses (sutta), songs (geyya), and so forth.

Therefore, how is this distinction known, that in this Dispensation, only the poorly learned scriptural study (pariyatti) is compared to a snake? Why is that poorly learned study, which is undertaken for the sake of criticizing others and so forth, called "the scriptural study like a snake"? This is true; however, it should be understood that this statement is made by way of the method of elimination (pārisesa-naya). Because the scriptural study for the sake of liberation and the treasurer-like scriptural study have been taken separately, by the method of elimination, only the scriptural study that is like the poor grasping of a snake is known as "the scriptural study like a snake." This is because the scriptural study that is like the well-grasped snake is either the scriptural study for the sake of liberation or the treasurer-like scriptural study. Therefore, this statement, "the poorly learned... scriptural study," is well-said.

Now, wishing to prove that meaning with the Pāḷi text, he says "Yaṃ sandhāya" and so forth. In that phrase, "yaṃ" refers to that poor learning of the scriptural study (pariyatti). The Blessed One taught this in the Alagaddūpama Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka in the Majjhima Nikāya.

"Alagaddatthiko" means one who desires a venomous snake. He is called "alagaddagavesī" because he habitually seeks out snakes. "Alagaddapariyesanaṃ caramāno" means one who goes about for the purpose of seeking a venomous snake. In this sense, this term is in the nominative case or the accusative case. Alternatively, it means one who wanders in a place where snakes are sought. This is because, since one seeks snakes in this place, that place is called "alagaddapariyesana." "Tamenam" refers to that snake. "Bhoge" means on the body. It is said in the dictionary, "The body of a snake is called bhoga." It is called "bhoga" because it can be made to coil or curve.

"Tassa" means of that man. It should be connected as "on the hand or on the arm." From the wrist to the tips of the fingernails is called the "hand (hattha)." The remaining part of the arm including the shoulder is called the "upper arm (bāhā)." In some places, however, from the elbow to the tips of the fingernails is called the "hand," because the upper arm is not intended separately. Excluding the hand and arm with the stated characteristics, the remaining parts of the body are called "limbs and extremities (aṅgapaccaṅga)." "Tatonidānaṃ" means because of that cause, namely the snake bite. Since the biting on the hand and so forth is the cause of this suffering, while it should be said as "tannidānaṃ," it is expressed as "tatonidānaṃ" by applying the ablative suffix -to in the sense of the nominative in the preceding word without eliding that suffix; it is in the nominative case in the sense of cause (hetu). Teachers also say it is an indeclinable (nipāta) in the sense of cause. Alternatively, this term "tatonidānaṃ" is an adjective (visesana) according to the method mentioned in the phrase "death or death-like suffering".
112: What is the reason for that? As for what was said regarding the snake bite on the hand and so on, and the arrival at suffering such as death caused by that bite—if one asks, "For what reason, by what cause does that occur?" it is because that man caught the snake wrongly.## It means "in this Dispensation." "Empty men" (mogha-purisā) means they are empty men because they are devoid of the essence of virtues such as the Path and Fruition. "Dhamma" means the Pali Dhamma. "They learn" (pariyāpuṇanti) means they study, recite, and bear it in mind by heart. He shows the "Dhamma," which is spoken of generally, by specifying it as "Sutta" and so on. Indeed, there is no Dhamma other than the nine-fold division of Sutta and so forth. Therefore, He said, "of those Dhammas." In this context, the indication "the meaning" (attha) is an indication of connection. The word "meaning" refers to the meaning of the Pali as it was truly spoken, and also to the meaning as purpose or benefit, expressed either generally or by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa). It should be understood in all places that when a word, through commonality of hearing, points to many meanings, it is expressed generally or by the method of ellipsis. "They do not examine" (na upaparikkhanti) means they do not grasp or investigate with wisdom. Indeed, the word ikkha is used here in the sense of seeing. Among the types of seeing—grasping with wisdom and seeing with the eye—it is only grasping with wisdom. Among the two types of grasping—investigation and taking up—it is only investigation. That investigation is wisdom (vīmaṃsā) alone, not mere thought (vicāra). This vīmaṃsā is of two kinds: investigation of the meaning of what was spoken and investigation of the purpose or benefit; both are intended here. Among them, "In this place virtue is taught, in this place concentration, in this place wisdom; we shall fulfill that virtue, concentration, and wisdom"—this is the investigation of the meaning of what was spoken. "Virtue is the cause for concentration, concentration for insight," and so on—this is the investigation of the purpose or benefit. The meaning is that they do not perform these. "For those empty men who do not examine" is the meaning. "They do not endure scrutiny" (na nijjhānakkhama) means they do not delight in wisdom that looks thoroughly (nijjhāna). Indeed, the word jhe is used here only in the sense of looking, not in the sense of thinking or burning. That looking is only looking with knowledge, not looking with the eye. Or, it is only looking closely at the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna), not looking closely at the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Therefore, the intention should be understood as: they are not things to be taken up by seeing and delighting with wisdom. Because it looks thoroughly without remainder, it is called nijjhāna. By the power of euphonic combination (sandhi), the nasal (niggahīta) is dropped, resulting in nijjhānakkhama. There is also a reading nijjhānaṃ khamanti. By that reading, this meaning is shown: "Because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, those Dhammas do not become clear to them; they are unable to know thus: 'In this place virtue, concentration, insight, the Path, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.'"## It means "and for the benefit of being able to criticize the doctrines of others." "Upārambha" is the act of severely finding fault in the doctrines of others.
113: It means attacking and destroying others by relying on the scriptures (pariyatti). This statement is true; the commentator said that this upārambha (censure of others) "has the characteristic of not removing the faults of others, or the characteristic of bringing the faults of others near." "Vādappamokkhānisansā ca" means that by this pariyatti, there is the benefit of releasing oneself or one's own doctrine from the faults or refutations imposed by others. Here, the word iti is used in this sense; therefore, in the word pariyāpuṇanti, it refers to the act of learning. Because it oppresses with this fault, that fault is called vāda. Pamokkha means release or causing release. Those who have the benefit of release from the faults imposed upon them are called vādappamokkhānisansā. The doctrine that is imposed is simply called vāda, just as Devadatta is called Datta. Or, vāda means reproach or blame (nindā), as per the method mentioned before. This is what is meant: when others find fault in their own doctrine or when blame is imposed, they learn for the reason that "we shall release ourselves from that fault or blame in such and such a way."## Alternatively, various kinds of oppression are called iti-vāda, because the word iti occurs in the sense of the word ta (that). Those who have the benefit of release from those various kinds of oppressive faults are called iti-vādappamokkhānisansā. "Yassa catthāya" means for the benefit of fulfilling virtue and so on, or for the benefit of the liberation without clinging (anupādā-vimokkha) which is the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. Although there is no distinction, it is spoken of as if there were a distinction, like saying "the body of a statue." Or, it is a qualifying term like "the cloth brought for the purpose of the Kaṭhina." Is it not said, "and the meaning of that"? The word ca is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa); therefore, it should be decided that learning is possible only for that purpose, and not for any other purpose. It means that sons of good family (kulaputta), both by birth and by conduct, learn the Dhamma in the proper way. Those who grasp it wrongly do not experience or attain the benefit of that Dhamma, which is the fulfillment of virtue or the liberation without clinging known as the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.## Another method: those empty men who learn the Dhamma for the purpose of censuring others or for the sake of releasing their own doctrine from criticism—when others say "this is not the meaning," they are unable to establish that "this is indeed the meaning" because they have learned it wrongly. Therefore, being unable to find fault in others' doctrines or to release their own doctrine from fault, they do not experience or attain that benefit. This is how the meaning should be understood here as well. Here too, the word ca is used only in the sense of emphasis.
114:
In the words beginning with "tesaṃ" (for them), the meaning is that for those individuals, the Pali Dhamma they have learned leads to harm and suffering for a long time because it was wrongly grasped, serving as a cause for criticizing others, pride, deceit, depreciation of others' virtues, and rivalry. The word "duggahita" (wrongly grasped) is a term expressing the cause. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Monks, because those teachings were wrongly grasped..." (M. i. 238). Here, by way of figurative expression (phala-vohāra) where the effect is attributed to the cause, it is said: "Those teachings lead to harm and suffering." This is like saying "Ghee is life" or "Curd is strength." For although those learned Pali teachings do not themselves lead to harm and suffering, for those who learn them in the aforementioned way, many unwholesome states such as criticizing others—which are rooted in that wrong grasping—can arise during times of recitation and dispute. Thus it is said: "Those teachings... lead to [harm]." In the phrase "taṃ kissa hetu" (what is the reason for that?), the word "taṃ" refers to both the failure to experience the benefit of practicing virtue and the fact that those learned teachings lead to harm and suffering. "Kissa" is in the genitive case with a causal meaning. Similarly, "hetu" is in the nominative case.

In the phrase "yā pana" (but which), the meaning should be understood according to the aforementioned method by way of the Pali for the act of learning. Regarding the two aspects of action, the expression "that pariyatti-dhamma which is well-grasped" is used even where there is no distinction, similar to expressions like "he departs on a journey" or "he travels a journey" (D. i. 254, 300). This very meaning is explained starting with "the group of virtue" (sīlakkhandha), etc. Here, the word "ādi" (etc.) includes concentration (samādhi), insight (vipassanā), and so on. A person who learns the Buddha's word and, where virtue is mentioned, fulfills virtue; where concentration is mentioned, establishes concentration; where insight is mentioned, develops insight; and where the Path and Fruit are mentioned, learns with the intention: "I will develop the Path, I will realize the Fruit"—for such a person, that learning is called "learning for the sake of liberation" (nissaraṇattha). "Yaṃ" refers to that well-grasped pariyatti-dhamma. This is taught in the Alagaddūpama Sutta. "They lead to welfare and happiness for a long time" means that for those who fulfill virtue where virtue is mentioned, for those who, having attained Arahantship, teach the Dhamma in the midst of an assembly and use the four requisites offered by those inspired by the teaching, for those who point out faults in others' doctrines with reason, and for those who dispel faults attributed by others to their own doctrine—for all these, it leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. Indeed, not only are the development of the Path and the realization of the Fruit accomplished by relying on well-grasped pariyatti, but also the refutation of others' doctrines and the establishment of one's own doctrine are achieved. Thus it is said in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and others: "Having well refuted the arisen doctrines of others with reason, they will teach the Dhamma with marvels" (D. ii. 68).

## Regarding "yaṃ pana" here as well

In this phrase "yaṃ pana" as well, the meaning of the word "yaṃ" should be understood in two ways according to the aforementioned method. By fully knowing the Truth of Suffering, one has aggregates that are fully known; by abandoning the Truth of Origination, one has defilements that are abandoned; because of the state of the Fruit of Arahantship...
115:
In this phrase "Yaṃ pana" as well, the meaning should be understood in two ways according to the method already mentioned. By fully understanding the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), one has aggregates that are fully understood (pariññāta-kkhandha). By abandoning the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), one has defilements that are abandoned (pahīna-kilesa). Because of having penetrated the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), one has the unshakeable penetration (paṭividdhā-kuppa). This name "Akuppa" (unshakeable) is a name for the fruit of Arahantship.

Indeed, although the four paths and the four fruits are imperishable, the seven types of trainees (sekha) are not said to have "unshakeable" (akuppa) paths and fruits, because they relinquish their respective names and attain different higher names. However, since an Arahant is always called an Arahant, his fruit alone is called "unshakeable" (akuppa) by virtue of the person's name. By this, he shows this meaning: "Only the learning of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is called 'Treasurer Learning' (bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti)."

For that Arahant, there are no aggregates not fully understood, no defilements not abandoned, no path not developed, and no fruit or Nibbāna not realized. Therefore, even when he learns the Buddha’s word (Buddhavacana), he learns it only as a bearer of the text (tantidhāraka), a protector of the lineage (paveṇīpālaka), and a preserver of the tradition (vaṃsānurakkhaka). Therefore, it is said, "For the sake of protecting the lineage," and so forth. Here, "paveṇī" (lineage) refers to the continuous succession of the Dhamma (dhamma-santati). The "vaṃsa" (lineage) of the Blessed Buddha is also this aforementioned succession.

If learning the Buddha’s word for the sake of protecting the lineage is "Treasurer Learning," then why is it specifically said "one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava)? For this method is also found in some worldlings (puthujjana). Indeed, a certain worldling monk, when others are unable to stay in one place due to the danger of famine and so forth, himself undergoes great hardship while wandering for alms, and learns with the thought: "May the extremely sweet Buddha’s word not perish; I will bear the text, I will establish the lineage, I will protect the tradition." Therefore, why is his learning also not called "Treasurer Learning"?

The answer is stated: Even if this is so, the learning of a worldling cannot be called "Treasurer Learning." For although a worldling learns with the intention "I will protect the tradition," because he himself has not yet crossed over the wilderness of existence (bhava-kantāra), that learning of his is only for the sake of escape (nissaraṇattha). Therefore, the learning of a worldling is either "like the simile of the water-snake" (alagaddūpama) or "for the sake of escape" (nissaraṇattha). The learning of the seven types of trainees (sekha) is only for the sake of escape, whereas it should be understood that only the learning of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is "Treasurer Learning." One whose taints are destroyed is called a "Treasurer" (bhaṇḍāgārika) because he is like a treasurer. For just as a treasurer, having stored away the stock of ornaments, presents the appropriate ornaments to the king at the time of decoration and adorns him, so too, the one whose taints are destroyed, having received the treasure-stock of the Dhamma...
116:
...having seen beings who are capable and possess the necessary conditions for the attainment of liberation (mokkha), he develops the Dhamma teaching appropriate to them and adorns them with supramundane ornaments known as the path-factors (magganga), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhanga), and so forth.

Having thus analyzed the three types of learning, now, wishing to extract and analyze the respective accomplishments (sampatti) and failures (vipatti) in the three Piṭakas, he said the words beginning with "In the Vinaya, however" (Vinaye pana). In the passages such as "Depending on the accomplishment of virtue, one attains the three knowledges" (Sīlasampadaṃ nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇāti), the meaning should be understood as follows: When virtue (sīla) is being purified, it becomes pure from the stains of defilement and reaches fulfillment through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) and through the power of the knowledge that beings are the owners of their actions (kammassakatā-ñāṇa). Therefore, when the accomplishment of virtue is achieved, it brings forward the power of mindfulness and the power of knowledge as the accomplishment of a strong support (upanissaya-sampatti). Thus, its status as a strong support for the three knowledges should be understood because of the achievement of the cause of the same nature.

Indeed, through the power of mindfulness, the first knowledge, the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), is accomplished. Through the power of clear comprehension, by the habit of seeing clearly in all tasks, the second knowledge, which follows the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa), is accomplished. Through the absence of transgression, because of the presence of the abandoning of defilements, and through the purity of intention by way of being a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya), the third knowledge, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), is accomplished.

The status of virtue as a strong support for the knowledge of the destruction of taints, even without the prior fulfillment of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā), should be illustrated by those who are dry-insight Arahants (sukkhavipassaka-khīṇāsava).

According to the statement, "One who is concentrated knows things as they really are," the accomplishment of concentration is the strong support for the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā).

According to the statement, "From application, wisdom is born," the accomplishment of wisdom—cultivated through prior application, living with a teacher, skill in local languages, learning, and inquiry—is the strong support for the different types of analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

Here, because it is said "Depending on the accomplishment of virtue," even if a person does not achieve the complete six higher powers which are the manifestations of concentration, and even if it is said that he does not have the accomplishment of concentration in its highest sense, since the knowledges are a part of the higher powers, only the three knowledges arising from the accomplishment of virtue are taken. Just as the four analytical insights arising from the accomplishment of wisdom are achieved only through the Path for one who possesses the strong support, because they are acquired at the very moment of the Path; so too, the three knowledges arising from the accomplishment of virtue and the six higher powers arising from the accomplishment of concentration are achieved only through the Path for one who possesses the strong support. Therefore, their attainment should be understood as occurring only through the attainment of the Path. For the attainment of these special distinctions by these noble ones (ariya) is similar to the attainment of the individual enlightenment (paccekabodhi) of Paccekabuddhas and the perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas.
117:
In this context, the restrictive term (avadhāraṇa) "tāsaṃyeva" is stated with reference to the fact that there is no detailed exposition of the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) in the Vinaya Piṭaka. This is because in the Verañja Section, only the three true knowledges (vijjā) are analyzed and taught. The conjunction with the word "ca" is also stated with reference to the partial teaching of those higher powers and analytical insights in this Vinaya Piṭaka. This is because a portion of the higher powers and analytical insights is taught in that Vinaya Piṭaka. In the second, the Sutta Piṭaka, the restriction "tāsaṃyeva" is made with regard to the four analytical insights, not with regard to the three true knowledges. Since those three true knowledges are included within the six higher powers, they have already been analyzed and taught in the Suttas. The word "ca" also combines and shows the partial teaching of the analytical insights. In the third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the word "ca" in "tāsañca" shows that the remaining dhammas are also present in that Abhidhamma. In the Abhidhamma, the three true knowledges, the six higher powers, and the four analytical insights have already been taught. Wishing to show both the absence of a detailed exposition of the analytical insights elsewhere (in the Vinaya and Sutta) and their thorough analysis only in that Abhidhamma, the restriction is placed by changing it to "tattheva" instead of using the restriction in the manner mentioned below. "In the Abhidhamma, however, the three true knowledges, the six higher powers, the four analytical insights, and other special qualities such as the right efforts (sammappadhāna) are analyzed and taught. Although they are taught, for the purpose of showing that they pertain specifically to the four analytical insights because of their nature of wisdom, the restriction is changed to 'tāsañca tattheva'," says the Elder Vajirabuddhi. The words beginning with "Evaṃ" are the conclusion.

Because those rugs, coverings, and so forth have a pleasant touch, they are called "sukhasamphassa" (pleasant to the touch). Such rugs, coverings, and so forth are indeed permitted. Because they are similar to the touch of women, the pleasant touch is also [considered]; and since that pleasant touch is permitted for those rugs and coverings, they are called "anuññātasukhasamphassa" (permitted pleasant touch). This is because such rugs, coverings, and so forth are similar to the touch of those women.

The touch of women is called "upādinnaka-phassa" (clung-to contact); it is nothing but the practice of sexual intercourse (methunadhamma).

It was once said by the monk named Ariṭṭha, who was formerly of the vulture-killer caste. Although that monk was a learned Dhamma-preacher, among the five kinds of obstacles—obstacles of action (kammantarāya), obstacles of defilement (kilesantarāya), obstacles of result (vipākantarāya), obstacles of disparagement (upavādantarāya), and obstacles of transgressing authority (āṇāvītikkamantarāya)—he did not know the obstacle of transgressing authority, but knew only the remaining obstacles. Therefore, that monk went into seclusion and thought thus: "These laypeople, while enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, can become Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. Monks also see pleasing forms cognizable by the eye. ... They touch tangible objects such as rugs and robes cognizable by body-consciousness. They use soft and delicate rugs and garments made of silk and wool. All of that is allowable. Why is it that only the sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches of women are not allowable? Those sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches of women should also be allowable."
118:
...they see. ...p... they touch tangible objects cognizable by body-consciousness, and they use soft rugs and garments. All this is allowable. Why is it that only the sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches of women are not allowable? They too are certainly allowable (he thought). In this way, by mixing the flavor of using blameless requisites with the flavor of using blameworthy sensual pleasures, and by making the use accompanied by lustful desire and the use free from lustful desire into one, as if joining a coarse thread with an extremely fine thread, or as if comparing a mustard seed to Mount Meru, he gave rise to a wicked wrong view. "Why did the Blessed One, with great effort as if damming the great ocean, prescribe the first Pārājika training rule? There is no fault in this (sexual intercourse)," he said, acting in opposition to the Omniscient Knowledge, obstructing the Knowledge of Fearlessness (vesārajja-ñāṇa), and as if placing stumps and thorns on the path of the Noble Path. By saying "There is no fault in sexual intercourse," he struck at the wheel of authority (the Vinaya teaching) of the Victorious One. Therefore, it was said beginning with "Tathāhaṃ."

They are called "antarāyika" (obstructive things) because of the sense that they should not be transgressed, or because they deserve to become obstacles, or because they have the nature of creating obstacles. It means they create obstacles to heaven and Nibbāna, as well as to the jhānas, paths, and fruits. Those obstacles are of five kinds: action (kamma), defilement (kilesa), result (vipāka), disparagement (upavāda), and transgressing authority (āṇāvītikkama). The details should be sought in the commentary on the Ariṭṭha training rule and so forth. The connection of the meaning of the words here is: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: 'Those things which are called obstructive things by the Blessed One, for one who indulges in them, those things are not able to create an obstacle to heaven and Nibbāna'." Because of perceiving them as blameless in that way, he transgressed the training rule and became an immoral person (dussīla).

With the words beginning with "Cattāro...", he points to the Sutta Pali associated with the teaching on persons (puggaladesanā) taught by the Blessed One. Here, by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the following Sutta should be taken: "Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit; one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. ...p... Bhikkhus, (these four persons exist) in the world."
119:
With these words and so forth, he shows the Suttanta Pali connected with the teaching in terms of persons (puggala-desanā). 'Intention' means the intention of the Blessed One as follows: "This teaching is by way of conventional worldly usage (loka-vohāra-paññatti); it is not a teaching in terms of ultimate reality (paramattha)."

Indeed, it is said:
"The Buddha, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional (sammuti) and the ultimate (paramattha); a third is not found. Conventional speech is true because of worldly convention; ultimate speech is true because of the actual nature of phenomena (dhamma). Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in worldly usage, no false speech (musāvāda) arises when he speaks in terms of convention."

The Blessed Buddhas do not abandon worldly convention; they teach the Dhamma while remaining within the worldly designation, worldly language, and worldly expression. Furthermore, he is one who does not know the intention that the Blessed One speaks a discourse on persons (puggala-kathā) for eight reasons, such as "for the purpose of illustrating moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), and for the purpose of illustrating the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa)." This meaning will be made clear later on.

'Grasps wrongly' means he grasps it incorrectly and perversely, saying, "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness (viññāṇa) that runs and wanders [through rounds of rebirth], not another," and so forth. The word 'duggahitaṃ' is a neuter designation of a state (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa) because it must be indicated by the neuter gender as a qualifier of the action. This is the nature of a term that is a neuter designation of a state: being indicated by the neuter gender, having the state (bhāva) as the primary focus, being associated with transitive and intransitive verbs, and having the endings of the nominative and accusative cases. Therefore, it is said, "having grasped wrongly."

'Yaṃ' refers to the view that is wrongly grasped. In the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka, Majjhima Nikāya, this was spoken by the Blessed One concerning the monk named Sāti, the fisherman's son, who held such a view. The rest of the Pali should be supplemented as "by the Dhamma wrongly grasped by himself," meaning "by way of a false nature." Alternatively, 'duggahaṇaṃ' (wrong grasping) is called 'duggahitaṃ'. The word 'attanā' (by oneself) is either a term with an instrumental ending in the sense of the possessive (sāmī), or an indeclinable word (avyaya) resembling a term with a case ending. Therefore, it means "by his own wrong grasping" or "by his perverse grasping."

'Misrepresents' means he makes a false accusation. One who digs up and destroys his own roots of merit is said to dig up and destroy himself. 'Tato' means because of that wrong grasping.
120:
Reflection on the Dhamma (dhamma-cintana) means investigating and contemplating the nature of phenomena. 'Overreaching' (atidhāvanta) means not remaining within the established limits and proceeding by surpassing the nature of the Dhamma, such as thinking, "Giving occurs even by a mere arising of thought (cittuppāda); the mind itself is its own object; and every mind has only the ultimate nature of phenomena as its object." To show those things that are impossible to think about or unworthy of thinking about, which are called 'inconceivables' (acinteyya), the commentator said "vuttañhetaံ" and so forth. In that passage, the word 'acinteyyāni' shows the nature of those things. The word 'na cintetabbāni' shows the duty to be performed regarding them. The words 'yāni' and so forth show the reason for that. One who thinks about those inconceivables would partake of madness, distraction of mind, vexation, and distress. Therefore, these four inconceivables should not be thought about. Or, these four are called inconceivables and should not be thought about. Or, if one thinks about which things... he would become... Therefore, the construction is: these four which are of a nature not to be thought about are called inconceivables.

By the word 'iti'—"Monks, what are the four? Monks, the range of the Buddhas (Buddha-visaya) is inconceivable and should not be thought about; one who thinks about it would partake of madness and vexation. Monks, the range of one in meditative absorption (jhāna-visaya) is inconceivable... Monks, the result of kamma (kamma-vipāka) is inconceivable... Monks, speculation about the world (loka-cintā) is inconceivable... these four... would become..."—he includes the entire Pali text illustrating the nature of the inconceivable, starting with the Acinteyya Sutta taught in the Catukka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. Although the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) and so forth are indeed inconceivable, they should be thought about because they are a cause for the arising of merit in one who recollects them. However, these four inconceivables are not like that because they are fruitless; therefore, they should not be thought about.

By the words "dussīlya... pabhedaṃ", he shows the failure (vipatti) in its specific form. To show the connection between preceding and following words (pubbāpara-sambandha) through the linking of such words as "How? By way of the Piṭaka," the commentator said "In this way, by many methods" and so forth. Indeed, speech devoid of connection between preceding and following words is confused. It is not capable of making the meaning known to the listeners. Such scrutinized speech is the domain only of the wise who know the preceding and following context.

The Blessed One taught thus:
"One who knows the preceding and following, who knows the meaning,
Who is skilled in the language (nirutti) and terms,
Grasps well what is learned,
And investigates the meaning."

'Tesaṃ' refers to the Piṭakas. 'Etaṃ' refers to the Word of the Buddha.
121:
Because it is a collection (counting) by way of the three groups known as the Sīlakkhandhavagga, Mahāvagga, and Pāthikavagga, these suttas are called the Tivagga-saṅgaha. In the verse, however, in whichever Nikāya there are only thirty-four suttas by count, and because the counted groups of that Nikāya are three by virtue of the group-collection, it is called 'Tivagga-saṅgaha' (the Nikāya collected into three groups). This first Nikāya has the non-contradictory name 'Dīgha Nikāya'. It means a Nikāya whose name is consistent with its meaning, or whose name follows the meaning, because it accords with the meaning.

In that verse, this term 'Tivaggo saṅgaho' is a compound (samāsa) even though the word 'yassa' intervenes; it should be understood that it is not a sentence. It is just like the term 'navacīvaralābhena' in the Pācittaya Pali, which appears as 'navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhena'. Regarding this, the Commentators explain: 'It is called lābha because it is obtained; labha itself is lābha. What is obtained? A robe. What kind of robe? A new one. Thus, although it should be said as "navacīvaralābhena", the nasal sound (anusvāra) was not dropped, and it was stated as "navaṃcīvaralābhena", meaning one who has obtained a new robe. Among the two middle words, the word "pana" is merely a particle. The word "bhikkhunā" is the term that points out the person who obtained it.'

In this context as well, it can only be a compound because it is not logically suitable as a sentence, either by word or by meaning. If the word 'Tivaggo' were in the instrumental sense (karaṇa) in relation to the word 'saṅgaho', it would only be a word ending in the instrumental case. If those two words were appositional (tulyādhikaraṇa), it would only be of neuter gender, like the word 'Tilokaṃ' and so on. Furthermore, this word 'Tivaggo' cannot be connected to any other word except the word 'saṅgaho'. Even there, connecting it with such a sentence is not appropriate. Therefore, the fact that the word and meaning do not conflict despite the intervening word is the reason for it being a compound; thus, it should only be a compound.

'Tivaggo saṅgaho' means 'in that collected Nikāya, there are three groups'. By changing the 'a' to 'o' or by the arrival of 'o', it is like the words 'sattāhaparinibbuto' (seven days since parinibbāna), 'acirapakkanto' (not long since departed), 'māsajāto' (one month since birth), and so on. 'Assa saṅgahassa' means 'of this collected Nikāya'. Other teachers, however, resolve the compound as 'tayo vaggā yassa' and say it can be appositional with the word 'saṅgaho', and that saṅgaha means counting (number). They say the Sub-commentators also showed only the appositional nature of the two words as 'tayo vaggā assa saṅgahassa'. That statement is inappropriate because of the mixing of the number (saṅkhyā) and the numbered (saṅkhyeyya), and because it is not clear.

To clarify the consistency with the meaning, he said 'Kasmā' and so on. By way of metaphorical quality (guṇūpacāra) or by the power of the derivative (taddhita), by the word 'Dīgha', only suttas of long measure...
122:
...are taken. Furthermore, he shows that the word 'Nikāya' by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī) occurs in the senses of 'collection' (samūha) and 'dwelling' (nivāsa) with the words 'Dīghappamāṇānaṃ' and so on. Because the word 'Nikāya' with its stated meaning is established by the convention of ancient wise men, the Commentator, wishing to make known its establishment by convention in those senses of collection and dwelling through examples, said 'Nāhaṃ' and so on. 'Eka-nikāyaṃ' means even in one collection. 'Evaṃ cittaṃ' means so diverse. 'Yathayidaṃ' means just as these animals are diverse. The dwelling place of the Poṇika kings and Cikkhallika kings is called 'Poṇika-nikāya' and 'Cikkhallika-nikāya'. Here, because they fulfill the intended meaning in the sense of the word 'Nikāya' expressing collection and dwelling, these examples are called 'sādhakāni' (proving factors). The connection of this word 'sādhakāni' with the remaining text 'samānītāni' is made as an object-verb relationship. Or else, they are witnesses (sakkhī) that fulfill the meaning in the aforementioned logical way. Those examples which are extracted to fulfill the intended meaning are called 'sakkhī' (witnesses). Therefore, it is said in the Manorathapūraṇī, the Aṅguttara Commentary: 'The Pañcagaru Jātaka should be brought and told for the sake of being a witness.' 'Sāsanato' means by way of scriptural example or in the Dispensation. 'Lokato' means by way of worldly example or in the world. This example of 'Poṇika-Cikkhallika-nikāya' is not found in the Tipitaka; therefore, teachers say it is stated as 'lokato'. Among these two examples, the first is a proving statement by way of the Dispensation, and the second should be understood as a proving statement by way of the world.

By virtue of the Mūlapariyāyavagga and so on, it is counted by fifteen groups. 'One hundred and a half' means there are one hundred and fifty suttas. 'Yattha' means in whichever Nikāya. 'Pañcadasavagga-pariggaho' means counted or encompassed by fifteen groups.

It is called 'Saṃyutta' because they are joined (connected) in this Nikāya. What is the joining? It is the joining of groups of suttas. Just as there is the designation 'word' (pada) in a collection of syllables (byañjana), 'sentence' (vākya) in a collection of words, 'sutta' in a collection of sentences, and 'group' (vagga) in a collection of suttas, so too there is the designation 'Saṃyutta' in a collection of groups. Because of the connection of the groups of suttas etc. taught by the Blessed One when asked by deities, there is the state of 'Devatā-saṃyutta' and so on. Therefore, he said 'Devatā-saṃyuttādi-vasena' and so on. In the text 'Suttantānaṃ sahassāni satta suttasatāni ca', it should be connected as seven thousand and seven hundred suttas. There is also the reading 'Satta suttasahassāni satta suttasatāni ca'. 'Saṃyutta-saṅgaho' means the counting (enumeration) of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
123:
The term 'Aṅguttara' is so called because it exceeds [the previous] by one factor at a time, as stated: 'By way of exceeding by one factor at a time,' and so forth. In that Aṅguttara Nikāya, [discourses] are taught starting from one up to eleven factors. 'Aṅga' means a portion of the Dhamma (dhammakoṭṭhāsa).

'Pubbe' refers to the description of the Suttanta Piṭaka. To show it concisely without making distinctions, it is said: 'Excepting (ṭhapetvā),' and so forth. This is a concise way of showing what has already been stated as 'the entire Vinaya Piṭaka,' and so on. Furthermore, it should be understood that all other words besides those mentioned above—taught by the Buddha or according to the method given by the Buddha, and approved by the Buddha, such as the Netti and Peṭakopadesa—are included only in this Khuddaka Nikāya, expressed in a way that encompasses everything without remainder. Although the intended meaning is already established, a new sentence is undertaken either to make a special meaning known or to make the meaning firm. In this Khuddaka Nikāya, unlike the mention of 'Dīghappamāṇa' (long measure) and so forth, only the nature of the Khuddaka Nikāya is mentioned because long texts such as the Vinaya and Abhidhamma are also included within that Khuddaka Nikāya. Therefore, it should be understood that this name is not always literally true for all texts included in the Khuddaka Nikāya, but it is called so in some places because its nature is common in being opposite to the nature of the Dīgha Nikāya and others. 'Tadaññaṃ' means the remainder other than those four Nikāyas.

Regarding 'navappabhedaṃ' (ninefold division), how does this Dispensation have nine divisions? The nine factors must exist separately without overlapping with one another. If that were the case, factors such as Geyya would not have the nature of a Sutta. Or, if Geyya and others were only of the nature of a Sutta, then there would be no separate 'Sutta-aṅga' (Sutta factor). In that case, the fault would arise that the Dispensation has only eight factors. Furthermore, it is stated in the Commentary: 'A Sutta with verses is Geyya; a Sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa.' Since a Sutta can be either with or without verses, both are already encompassed by the two factors of Geyya and Veyyākaraṇa. Therefore, there would be no separate 'Sutta-aṅga' that is free from those two and lacks special names such as Udāna. Alternatively, if there were a separate Sutta-aṅga, then the Maṅgala Sutta and others would not be included in the Sutta-aṅga because they consist of verses like the Dhammapada. Or they would be included only in the Geyya-aṅga because they have verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. Likewise, should not the parts containing verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others also be called Geyya-aṅga? To this question, we shall reply:
124:
The name 'Sutta' is a general rule (sāmañña-vidhi), while the others such as Geyya are specific rules (visesa-vidhi) accompanied by their respective causes. Because the Maṅgala Sutta and others are well-known as Sutta-aṅga, they are included only in the Sutta-aṅga and not in the Geyya-aṅga despite being associated with other verses.

The aforementioned fault does not apply here; therefore, the Teacher's Dispensation indeed has nine divisions without overlap.

Calling the entire Buddha-word 'Sutta' is a general rule. This is because the term 'Sutta' is seen even in the specific divisions of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas, as in: 'This much of the Blessed One's word has come in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta,' 'In the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī,' and 'Five hundred Suttas in the Sakavāda,' and so forth. For this very reason, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said in the Netti: 'The ninefold Suttanta search (pariyeṭṭhi).' There, the search, seeking, and investigation of the meaning of the ninefold Dispensation by way of Sutta and so forth is called 'the ninefold Suttanta search.'

However, in the parts of that Dispensation, others such as Geyya are specific rules established by their respective causes. For instance, the presence of verses in Geyya is the cause for it being Geyya. Even in the world, people call a prose text (cuṇṇiya) that is accompanied by verses 'Geyya.' But when verses are absent, the state of being a question and answer is the cause for Veyyākaraṇa. Indeed, questioning and answering is called 'Byākaraṇa' (exposition), and Byākaraṇa itself is Veyyākaraṇa.

If this is so, would not the teachings that arise by way of questioning and answering while also having verses become Veyyākaraṇa? No, they would not, because the names such as Geyya have no room [to be overridden]. For a specific rule (anokāsa-vidhi) is stronger than a general rule (sa-okāsa-vidhi). Furthermore, it is because of the qualification 'in the absence of verses.' A qualification is used to exclude an unintended meaning from the intended meaning.

This is how it is: in the pure verse compositions such as the Dhammapada, in the specific Suttas associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge even if they have verses, in the Suttas connected with words such as 'vuttaṃ hetaṃ' (for this was said), and in the Suttas connected with wonderful things (abbhutadhamma), the names Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are established respectively.
