'Citta-santānassa' (of the stream of mind) means of the aforementioned stream of consciousness. 'Nānākāra-ppavattiyā' means because of the occurrence in various modes regarding the object. The taking of various meanings and syllables, or the taking of meanings and syllables in various ways, is 'tathā' (thus). Because of that very taking, it is called 'designation of manner' (ākāra-paññatti). That very meaning is established by the passage beginning with 'evaṃ hi'. 'Ākāra-paññatti' is also just a 'derivative designation' (upādā-paññatti). However, because it is designated based on the manner of occurrence of phenomena, it is called 'ākāra-paññatti' to distinguish it from other derivative designations. 'Visaya-niddesa' (description of the sphere) means the description of the locus of occurrence. Indeed, the Dhamma which is to be heard is the locus of occurrence for the person, who is the agent of the act of hearing, through the act of hearing. Because the action resides in the agent and the object, and because by that power the state of being a locus for the substance (dabba) which is its support is desired, and since in this context the state of being the locus of the agent's occurrence is desired, the object (kamma) itself is spoken of as the locus (ādhāra). Therefore, it is said, 'the conclusion of taking the sphere (visaya) of the agent.' Alternatively, the object itself is the 'visaya' (sphere/object). This is because the object is the locus of occurrence for the mind that has that object. In this way, the meaning is even easier to understand.

To show the collective meaning of the aforementioned statement, the passage beginning with 'ettāvatā' is stated. 'Ettāvatā' (by this much) means by the three words having the aforementioned meaning, it is 'done' (connected). 'Nānākāra-ppavattena' means by that which occurs in the object in various modes. 'Citta-santānena' means by the stream of mind characterized by the aforementioned cognitive process. This word is the instrument (karaṇa) for the word 'gahana' (taking). Although in the ultimate sense (paramattha) there is no agent separate from the stream of mind, because of the desire to express a distinction conceived by the intellect through conventional language, the person possessing that mind is treated as if he were different from the stream of mind; thus, even though there is no difference, it is said by conventional usage of difference: 'by the stream of mind, of the person possessing that mind.' This is because language has conventional designation (vohāra-paññatti) as its sphere...
153: Indeed, 'not absolutely ultimate' (existing only in the realm of conventional usage) (refer to the verse 'Yo kāreti sahetu' in the Kārakarūpasiddhi) means that the Dhamma to be heard, which is the object of the act of hearing, is also the object of the mental continuum that arises by the power of the act of hearing, because in this context, that mental continuum is the agent in the ultimate sense. Therefore, it is said to be 'the decision in grasping the object of the agent.' Alternatively, since the arising of consciousness by the power of hearing is itself the act of hearing, the agent of that action—which is the collection of other mental and physical phenomena—is also considered the object by the power of that action; thus it is so stated. The meaning is this: In the former method, the act of hearing and its agent are ultimately just the mental continuum that occurs in that way; therefore, even the object of the action is called 'the object of the agent.' In the latter method, however, the mental continuum occurring in that way is the action, while the collection of other phenomena is the agent. Therefore, although this Dhamma is strictly the object of the action, it is called 'the object of the agent who possesses that action' by the power of the action. 'Taṃsamaṅgino' refers to one who is endowed with that mental continuum. 'Kattū' means 'of the agent.' 'Visayo' refers to the place of occurrence by way of the object, or the object itself. Because the Elder (Venerable Ānanda), who has the manner of hearing, has made a firm decision, it is called 'the decision in grasping.' Another method: 'Yassa... pe... ākārapaññatti' means that by connecting with the word 'Evaṃ' which has the sense of 'manner' (ākāra), and also taking the sense of 'emphasis' (avadhāraṇa), it should be noted that in this very method, instead of saying 'grasping is performed,' it is said 'the decision in grasping is performed' to facilitate the connection. This is because, in this context, decision by way of emphasis is intended. Therefore, it should be understood that by taking the word 'Evaṃ' in the sense of emphasis, as in 'ettāvatā' etc., this very construction (yojanā) is shown. In this construction, it should be noted that the demonstration of the specific object of the one who grasps the manner of grasping is performed. Another construction is also stated with 'Atha vā' etc. The word 'Evaṃ', which has the nature of showing the manner of reflecting on the various meanings and sounds called Suttas previously heard by oneself, or showing emphasis, is called 'the designation of the person's function' because it is the activity of the continuum of phenomena based on the designation of a person who performs such reflection. The repeated reflection on the meanings and sounds heard by oneself is the collection of the three—manner (ākāra) and so forth—and that is the meaning of the word 'Evaṃ.' That meaning, which arises based on whichever continuum of phenomena the designation of a person occurs, is the activity of that continuum of phenomena...
154: Since the meaning of the word 'Evaṃ' is merely a function, the function of the person is indicated by the word 'Evaṃ.' Although the act of hearing and noting is generally the activity (byāpāra) of a person, it is specifically the activity of consciousness; thus, it is called 'the indication of the function of consciousness.' This is because even in the view of the Personalists (Puggalavādins), there is no act of hearing that is independent of consciousness, as hearing and so forth are specifically desired as the activity of consciousness. Because the occurrence of the word 'Me' (by me) exclusively takes a being (satta) as its object, and because the function of consciousness is also to be integrated into that being without distinguishing between the being and the consciousness, it is called 'the indication of the person endowed with both functions.' The phrase 'Ayaṃ' etc., is to make that meaning clear. Here, it is said with reference to the function of the person indicated by the word 'Evaṃ.' To show that this function is called the person's function because the person is endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing, it is not said 'one endowed with the person's function' but 'one endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing.' Therefore, it means 'one endowed with the consciousness that has the indicated function of hearing.' The function of consciousness indicated by the word 'Sutaṃ' (heard) is intended. Consciousness that has only hearing as its function is called 'savana-kicca.' It means by the power of the consciousness which has obtained the designation of 'the function of hearing.' The connection (yojanā) is this: 'I, the person endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing, have heard by means of the consciousness which is the instrument (karaṇa) and which has obtained the designation of the function of hearing.' Alternatively, the meaning of the word 'Evaṃ' is a designation of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti), and the meaning of the word 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti). Therefore, desiring to show the meanings of those words only as the activity of the person who is the basis of such designations, it is said: 'Evaṃ indicates the function of the person; Sutaṃ indicates the function of consciousness.' This is because if one were to define them strictly by the ultimate sense (paramattha), this distinction between the person's function and the consciousness's function would not be obtained. In this construction (yojanā), it should be understood that the indication of the agent's activity and the instrument's activity is performed. Since all meanings to be understood through words must be approached through the medium of designations (paññatti), and since all designations are included within the six types of designations such as the designation of the existent, etc., the phrase 'Evañca' etc., is stated to specifically determine and show the nature of designations such as 'Evaṃ.' In that statement, the meaning of 'Evaṃ' and 'Me', such as 'manner' (ākāra) etc., is a designation of the non-existent because those things are not distinct ultimate realities. Thus it is said: 'It is a designation of the non-existent by the power of the ultimate reality in the true sense (sacchikaṭṭhaparamattha).'
155:
"By way of the real and ultimate sense" (saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena) means by the power of the true, non-distorted meaning and the highest meaning. The intended meaning is this: it is not an unreal meaning like a magic trick or a mirage, nor is it an inferior meaning like something to be accepted through hearsay. Rather, it is the nature that is clearly present as an ultimate reality, such as form (rūpa) and sound (sadda), or the nature characterized by change (ruppana) and experience (anubhavana). Such a meaning is called 'saccikaṭṭha' (real sense) and 'paramattha' (ultimate sense). However, the meaning of the words 'evaṃ me' cannot be called so, because they are neither real nor ultimate. Therefore, by the qualifier 'saccikaṭṭhaparamattha'—meaning the true and highest sense—it is only a non-existent concept (avijjamānapaññatti) that does not exist in the ultimate sense. With this qualifier, it refutes the mere concept imagined as 'existing' by foolish people. He makes that very meaning clear, or establishes it with a reason, starting with 'kiñhettha taṃ'.

Whatever phenomenon (dhamma) or meaning (attha) receives the designation 'evaṃ' or 'me', it should be construed as not existing in the ultimate sense, whether in the collection of phenomena such as form (rūpa) and contact (phassa), or in the meaning of the words 'evaṃ me'. The meaning designated by the nature of form, contact, etc., does exist here in the ultimate sense. But the meaning designated as 'evaṃ me' does not exist in the ultimate sense. Regarding the word 'sutaṃ' (heard), he refers to the sound-base (saddāyatana) and calls it an 'existent concept' (vijjamānapaññatti). Here too, the phrase 'saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena' is the governing principle (adhikāra). The words starting with 'yañhi' serve to clarify that (sutaṃ) or to show the reason. It means that the sound-base is known through the ear-door or through the consciousness dependent on that ear. Therefore, he shows that here the word 'suta' takes the sound-base in the objective sense (kammasādhana).

Having thus determined the nature of concepts according to the method of the Commentaries, he now wishes to determine the nature of concepts such as 'evaṃ' among the six types of concepts mentioned even by methods not directly in the Commentaries, and so he says 'tathā', etc. Concepts such as 'derivative concept' (upādāpaññatti), though absent from the ancient Commentaries, were stated only by the author of the Compendium (Saṅgahakāra). Details should be sought in the Abhidhamma Commentary. 'Taṃ taṃ' refers to those various phenomena. It means that 'evaṃ' is said by way of reviewing the mode, indication, and determination of those phenomena that have come into the range of the ear, and 'me' is said by way of depending on the aggregates (khandhas) included within one's own continuity. A concept made by depending on or based on various phenomena such as form (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā) is called a 'derivative concept' (upādāpaññatti). For example, 'chariot' or 'house' based on various parts; 'pot' or 'cloth' based on various forms, tastes, etc.; 'time' or 'direction' based on the revolution of the moon and sun, and so on. This (derivative concept) is called a concept only in the sense of 'that which is made known' (paññapetabba), not in the sense of 'that which makes known' (prajñāpana). The act of making that meaning known (prajñāpana) is indeed a non-existent concept (avijjamānapaññatti). Objects that are seen, etc...
156:
"*Upanidhāya vattabbato*" means because it is spoken of by depending on, supporting, and considering the objects seen, heard, and cognized. Even though it occurs in the sound-base which is devoid of the nature of seeing, etc., the usage "second, third", etc., is called "comparative designation" (*upanidhāpaññatti*) because it occurs in consideration of the first, etc., which are seen, heard, and cognized.

That comparative designation is of many kinds: comparative designation considering something else (*tadanyapekkhūpanidhā*), comparative designation of what is in the hand (*hatthagatūpanidhā*), comparative designation of what is associated (*sampayuttūpanidhā*), comparative designation of what is attributed (*samāropitūpanidhā*), comparative designation of what is near (*avidūragatūpanidhā*), comparative designation of what is similar (*paṭibhāgūpanidhā*), comparative designation based on majority (*tabbahulūpanidhā*), and comparative designation based on distinction (*tabbisiṭṭhūpanidhā*), and so on. Among those designations, this designation "second, third", etc., is called "comparative designation considering something else" (*tadanyapekkhūpanidhāpaññatti*) because it is spoken of by considering the first, etc., which are seen objects, in relation to one another.

Having thus shown the benefit to be shown, namely the state of the meaning being understood through designation, he now wishes to distinguish and show the meaning to be shown by the power of the words "*Evaṃ me sutaṃ*", and so he says "*Ettha ca*", etc. "*Ettha*" means in this group of three words. The word "*ca*" is used because he wishes to begin another meaning. When it is said "*sutaṃ*", it shows the meaning that it is not "unheard". Therefore, the Elder reflected on the specific modes of the discourse (*sutta*) which he himself had penetrated and which are shown by the word "*suta*" in that manner of being heard, using the word "*evaṃ*". By that word "*evaṃ*", non-confusion (*asammoha*) is said to be shown. Therefore, it is said: "By the word *evaṃ*, he shows non-confusion".

Non-confusion (*asammoha*) means non-confusion regarding the discourse that was heard. He establishes that very meaning by way of suitability and by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) with the words "*Na hi*", etc., because the discourse to be mentioned is of various kinds and difficult to penetrate. In such a discourse that is of various kinds and difficult to penetrate, how could a confused person be able to penetrate it in its various ways? By this suitability and by this contrast, the meaning to be shown, namely the Elder's state of non-confusion therein, is understood. In such matters, it should be understood accordingly.

Because the Elder shows the truth of the manner of hearing from the presence of the Blessed One, it is said: "He shows the non-forgetting (*asammosa*) of the discourse". "*Kālantarena*" means by a time subsequent to the time of hearing. For someone to whom the heard Dhamma is forgotten, that person cannot acknowledge "I have heard it" after a long time. But for the Elder, it remains without disappearing and without forgetting, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel. Therefore, it means that the Elder acknowledges it in this way.

As to what is shown by the meaning thus shown, he says "*Iccassa*", etc. There, "*iccassa*" is "*iti assa*". Therefore, because non-confusion and non-forgetting are shown, it is connected with "the accomplishment of the wisdom (*paññāsiddhi*) of that Elder", and so on. "*Asammohena*" means by the absence of confusion. The accomplishment of wisdom associated with phenomena such as concentration (*samādhi*) devoid of wisdom, etc., [is meant].
157:
In the wisdom of the Elder Ānanda, the teachings remain without being lost or forgotten, like lion's oil kept in a golden vessel. Therefore, it means that the Elder made such an admission.

The perfection of wisdom (paññā) is achieved through powers (satti) such as conascence (sahajāta) and so forth. Or, it is achieved through the collection of dhammas called wisdom, which is the opposite of delusion (sammoha). Indeed, due to the wisdom that arises at the time of hearing and learning, the perfection of wisdom that occurs in subsequent times is achieved through the peak of decisive support (upanissaya) and so forth. In other matters as well, the method should be applied accordingly.

What is clarified by the meaning thus shown? He said, "Tattha," and so forth. "Tattha" means in those two dhammas. The manner of penetrating the phrasing (byañjana) is not very profound; one should only maintain it as it was heard. Therefore, in that maintenance, the activity (byāpāra) of mindfulness (sati) is predominant, while wisdom (paññā) is subordinate. Thus, it is said, "paññāpubbaṅgamāya," and so forth. The etymological meaning of "paññāpubbaṅgamā" is "having wisdom as the precursor." Here, being the precursor means being primary (padhāna), as in "manopubbaṅgamā dhammā" (mind is the precursor of all things). Alternatively, just as in eye-consciousness and so forth, advertence (āvajjana) and so forth are precursors but not primary in cognizing the object; even if it is a precursor but not primary, the etymological meaning "mindfulness preceded by wisdom" is also appropriate. Here, being a precursor means the nature of going before (purecāri). Thus, both types of precursors—conascent precursor and pre-nascent precursor—are possible here. Just as the method is shown here, in the case of "pubbaṅgamāya," this method should also be understood accordingly.

What is shown by the word "capability" (samatthatā) thus clarified? He said, "tadubhayasamatthatāyogena," and so forth. Therein, "atthabyañjanasampanna" refers to the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-dhamma) which is endowed with meaning and phrasing, or endowed with the six terms of meaning such as "saṅkāsana" and the six terms of phrasing such as "akkhara," or having a good taste through the flavors known as meaning and phrasing. Because the Dhamma of learning is the source of the nine supramundane treasures, and like a treasury that is the source of seven or ten kinds of jewels, it is called "Dhamma-kosa" (Dhamma-treasury); likewise, it is called "Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgāra" (Dhamma-storehouse). Because he is the person appointed to that storehouse, he is called "Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika" (Treasurer of the Dhamma). Or else, because he is like a treasurer who guards various royal treasures, he is called a treasurer. Because he is the treasurer who preserves the Dhamma, he is specifically called "Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika" by showing that reason for similarity. The Blessed One said:

"O Sage, in the Dispensation, the one named Ānanda is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, capable of reciting all the texts, and the guardian of your Dhamma."

He also showed the meaning through another method starting with "aparo nayo." Since the meanings of manner (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa) expressed by the word "evaṃ" are within the scope of the true Dhamma, it is appropriate to show wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) through meanings that take those dhammas as objects. By the words "ayoniso" and so forth, the indicative cause (ñāpaka-hetu) is shown through the method of exclusion (vyatireka). Here, the word "hi" is used in the sense of showing a reason. By these words, since various penetrations can occur for one with much wise attention, just as fire (the cause) is known by smoke (the effect), wise attention (the cause) should be known by penetration (the effect). Therefore, he also showed the meaning of wise attention, which is suitable for that knowledge, by way of implication. In all the first parts, this method is the connection (anusandhi) of the questions in the Brahmajāla Sutta and so forth.
158:
Considering it appropriate to show wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) through the meanings of manner (ākāra), illustration (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa), which have the undistorted true Dhamma as their object, it is said: "Yoni... pe... dīpeti." By the words beginning with "ayoniso," the indicative cause (ñāpaka-hetu) is shown by way of contrast (vyatireka). In that text, the word "hi" is found in some places; it should be understood that this word "hi" occurs in the sense of cause, indicating the meaning "why?" By this very statement, since various kinds of penetration are possible for one who has much wise attention, just as the cause (fire) is known by the effect (smoke), it is shown by implication (atthāpatti) that the cause (yoniso manasikāra) can be known by the effect (various kinds of penetration), and the meaning suitable for such knowledge is also shown. This method applies everywhere as appropriate.

By the power of the question, "Friends, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?" and so forth, it is considered that the hearing in the presence of the Blessed One, expressed by the word "suta" (heard) regarding the Sutta now arrived in the text and about to be spoken, is not possible without non-distraction (samādhi). Therefore, it is said: "It shows non-distraction (avikkhepa)." Having shown the indicative cause (ñāpaka-hetu) by way of the contrary cause with the words beginning with "vikkhittacittassa," that very cause is supported by the words beginning with "tathā hi." "Sabbasampattiyā" means by the fulfillment of everything, such as the meaning, the phrasing, the teacher, and the purpose. What is shown by this statement? It says, "Yoniso manasikārena cettha," and so forth. "Ettha" (herein) refers to these two factors: wise attention and non-distraction (samādhi).

By the words beginning with "na hi vikkhittacitto," which act as the cause, only the accomplishment of the effect—hearing the true Dhamma—due to non-distraction and associating with good people (sappurisa-upanissaya) is stated. However, the accomplishment of associating with good people due to non-distraction is not stated. Why? Because the fact that those with distracted minds cannot attend upon good people is already established by the sense of the meaning. Since that meaning is clear by its very implication, it is not stated separately.

Here, an objector says: Just as it is stated that the causes—right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) and having performed merit in the past (pubbekatapuññatā)—are accomplished through the effect, wise attention, because they are inseparable from it; so too, it should be stated that the causes—hearing the true Dhamma and associating with good people—are accomplished through the effect, non-distraction. For non-distraction cannot exist for one who does not hear the Dhamma and does not associate with good people. Even so, by the supporting statement beginning with "na hi vikkhittacitto," only the accomplishment of the effect—hearing the true Dhamma—due to the causes of non-distraction and associating with good people is stated. Why is it stated in this way? I shall provide the answer: It is stated thus because there is another specific intention. The meaning here is that hearing the true Dhamma and associating with good people are not the absolute causes of non-distraction because they are external causes (bāhira-kāraṇa). Non-distraction, however, like associating with good people, is an absolute cause (ekanta-kāraṇa) of hearing the true Dhamma, because it is an internal cause (ajjhattika-kāraṇa). Therefore, while an absolute cause exists, for what purpose would one conceive of a non-absolute cause as an effect?
159:
The fulfillment of hearing that Dhamma is stated in that way. Between wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and non-distraction (avikkhepa), first, demonstrating the fulfillment of the causes—right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) and merit performed in the past (pubbekatapuññatā)—through the result of wise attention is like demonstrating the existence of rain upstream through the result of a full river. Second, in the case of non-distraction, demonstrating the fulfillment of the result of non-distraction through the causes of hearing the true Dhamma (saddhammasavana) and reliance on a good person (sappurisūpanissaya) is like demonstrating the occurrence of rain through the cause of rising clouds.

With the words "Another method" (aparo nayo), etc., the meaning is explained in another way. It is connected as "because it does not happen." As for "Thus" (evaṃ), etc., the "description of various modes" (nānākāraniddesa) was mentioned below. That mode is the manner of entering into the fulfillment of the entire Dispensation (sāsana) by means of distinguishing the varieties of meaning and phrasing of the Buddha's words, which is called the grasping of various meanings and phrasing due to the occurrence of the mental continuum—known as the process of mind-consciousness following the ear-door—in various modes regarding the object. It is called "auspicious" (bhaddaka) because it is the cause for the complete fulfillment of others' welfare without remainder, and because it is excellent due to the grasping of various meanings and phrasing as mentioned. Alternatively, as a compound word, it is "auspicious" (bhaddaka) meaning one who has such an auspicious mode.

For that person who does not have an ill-directed mind but has a well-directed mind, the "fulfillment of the two latter wheels" means the fulfillment of the two qualities called right self-direction and merit performed in the past. These qualities themselves are called "wheels" (cakka) because they occur in succession. Or, they are called "wheels" because by them beings reach a fortunate state of existence, or they occur in fortunate states of existence. Regarding these wheels, it was said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: "Monks, there are these four wheels; possessed of these four wheels, the four-wheeled [blessing] rolls for devas and humans," etc. Here, "latter" is only according to the order of the teaching. The "fulfillment of the two former wheels" means the fulfillment of the two qualities called living in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa) and reliance on a good person (sappurisūpanissaya). The rest is as previously stated. Therefore, the former cause is stated with the words "For not..." (na hi), etc.

What is revealed by those wheels? It is stated with "Of this" (iccassa), etc. Because of the fulfillment of these four wheels which act as causes, there is the "purity of inclination" (āsayasuddhi) through the fulfillment of the two latter wheels for that Elder Ānanda. Purity of inclination means the purity through the removal of defilements that cause impurity in the two types of inclination: conformable patience (anulomika-khanti) known as insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), and knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa) known as the knowledge of ownership of kamma (kammassakata-ñāṇa) and path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). These two are indeed the inclination of pure beings who rely on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). One who has a well-directed mind and has performed merit in the past possesses a pure inclination. Thus it was said: "A well-directed mind can do one better than that [which parents or relatives can do]," and "Ānanda, you have performed merit; strive in meditation, and you will soon become an Arahant, free from taints."
160:
"Strive in meditation; you will soon be free from taints" (in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta). Although some teachers say, "The desire to perform wholesome deeds (kattukamyatā-chanda) is called inclination (āsayasuddhi)," that statement is inappropriate because it contradicts the commentary's statement: "Through that purity of inclination, the proficiency in attainment (adhigama-byatti) is fulfilled." If one argues that the purity of inclination known as path-knowledge is inappropriate because it is not mentioned in the result of fulfilling proficiency in attainment, that is not so. It is appropriate because the preceding path is the cause for the subsequent paths and fruits.

Purity of application (payogasuddhi) is the purity through the clarity of the application of hearing the Dhamma preceded by wise attention. Or, it is the purity through the faultless nature of all bodily and vocal applications. One who lives in a suitable locality and relies on good people possesses the aforementioned pure application. With such pure application of hearing the Dhamma preceded by wise attention, and with bodily and vocal applications that bring about the absence of remorse, the Elder Ānanda, whose mind was undistracted, became proficient in the scriptures (pariyatti). Therefore, it should be understood that the Elder's purity of application was fulfilled through the fulfillment of the two former wheels (living in a suitable locality and reliance on a good person).

What meaning is shown by that purity of application? It is stated with "Through that purity of inclination," etc. Fulfillment of proficiency in attainment (adhigama-byatti-siddhi) means the fulfillment of skillfulness in attainment known as penetration (paṭivedha). In the commentaries, penetration is called "attainment" (adhigama) because it is what is to be penetrated and attained. Scripture (pariyatti) is called "tradition" (āgama) because through this scripture, one's own benefit, others' benefit, etc., arrive, or because it is to be known thoroughly.

What is demonstrated by that fulfillment of proficiency in attainment? It is stated with "Thus," etc. "Thus" refers to the method already mentioned or is an indication of the cause. To make that meaning known through a simile well-known in the world and in the Dhamma, it is said, "Like the rising of the dawn," etc. "Wise people understand the meaning through a simile," is it not so? Just as the rays of the dawn that appear before the sun rises are fit to be the precursor to the sun's rising, so the introductory words of the Elder, who is endowed with proficiency in scripture and attainment, should be understood as having reached the status of a precursor to the words of the Blessed One.

Now, to clarify the meaning previously mentioned as non-delusion (asammoha) and non-forgetfulness (asampajañña), he speaks again with "Another method" (aparo nayo), etc., using the words "Thus" (evaṃ) and "Heard" (suta). In that passage, by showing the penetration of various meanings (nānappakāra-paṭivedha) with the word "Thus," and the penetration of the varieties of what is to be heard (sotabbappabheda-paṭivedha) with the word "Heard," he clarifies the non-delusion and non-forgetfulness mentioned earlier.
161: Intending to explain the meanings to be revealed, known as non-confusion (asammoha) and non-forgetfulness (asammosa), which were previously mentioned, through the words 'evaṃ' and 'suta', the Commentator stated 'Aparo nayo' (Another method) and so forth. This is because through non-confusion, the penetration of various aspects is accomplished, and through non-forgetfulness, the penetration of the distinctions of what is to be heard is accomplished. By the words 'Attano' and so forth, the meaning to be revealed is shown. Therefore, the Teacher Dhammapāla stated: 'By the words evaṃ and suta, which indicate the penetration of various aspects, the Elder shows the connection of meanings by way of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), because they indicate non-confusion and non-forgetfulness regarding the meanings and phrasing of the Elder.' These two terms (nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpaka and sotabbappabhedapaṭivedhadīpaka) are terms that contain the cause (hetu-gabbha). This is meant because they indicate the meanings to be revealed, namely the penetration of various aspects and the penetration of the distinctions of what is to be heard. The state of being evident is called sabbhāva. The presence of the attainment of the analytical insights of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) and perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) is likewise. There is also a variant reading 'sambhavā'; sambhava means arising. The arising of the attainments of the analytical insights of meaning and perspicuity is likewise. This should also be understood in the same way for the remaining analytical insights of doctrine (dhamma) and language (nirutti). By the term 'sotabbappabhedapaṭivedhadīpaka,' it is shown that this word suta, whether because of its proximity to the word evaṃ or because it looks forward to what will be said later, although spoken in a general sense, refers to the specific Dhamma to be heard. Here, regarding the meanings of the spoken word (bhāsitattha) and the purpose (payojanattha) to be shown by the Pāḷi text known as the Dhamma to be heard, and because the knowledge occurring in the three analytical insights is of various kinds, it is appropriate to show the presence of the attainment of the analytical insights of meaning and perspicuity by the word evaṃ, which indicates the penetration of those aspects. However, because the Dhamma to be heard is the cause for the realization of meaning, and because through it the remaining distinctions of causes are grasped, and because it is of the nature of language (nirutti), it should be understood that it is appropriate to show the presence of the attainment of the analytical insights of doctrine and language by the word suta, which indicates the distinctions of what is to be heard. To make only that meaning known, he spoke thus without directly saying 'indicating non-confusion' (asammohadīpaka) or 'indicating non-forgetfulness' (asammosadīpaka). Thus, after explaining the meanings to be revealed, known as non-confusion and non-forgetfulness, by the words evaṃ and suta, the Teacher now speaks the words 'Evañca' and so forth, intending to explain the meanings to be revealed, known as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and non-distraction (avikkhepa), by those same words evaṃ and suta. In that context, by the words 'Evaṃ... bhāsamāno, sutaṃ... bhāsamāno,' he states the meanings to be revealed, known as wise attention and non-distraction, previously indicated by those words evaṃ and suta. By the words 'Ete mayā' and so forth, he explains the meaning to be revealed, and because the application to hearing (savanayoga) is accomplished by way of non-distraction, he refers to that non-distraction...
162: ...intended to say. For this reason, the Teacher Dhammapāla stated: 'Hearing, retaining, and verbal practice of the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) are particularly connected with attentive listening (sotāvadhāraṇa); therefore, they are joined with the word suta, which indicates non-distraction' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1). Repeated reflection and good penetration of the scriptural Dhamma by the wisdom occurring at the mind-door are particularly connected with attention (manasikāra). Therefore, by the word (evaṃ) which indicates that meaning, he shows this meaning: 'These teachings have been repeatedly reflected upon by me with the mind, and well-penetrated with wisdom,' as stated in 'Evañca...pe... dīpeti.' In that context, 'teachings' (dhammā) refers to the scriptural Dhamma. 'Repeatedly reflected upon by me with the mind' means reflecting with the mind through distinctions such as: 'In this Sutta, virtue (sīla) is taught; here, concentration (samādhi); here, wisdom (paññā); and these are the only sequences (anusandhi) here.' 'Well-penetrated with wisdom' means having well-defined and penetrated the material and immaterial phenomena (rūpa-arūpa-dhamma) taught in that scriptural Dhamma, starting from 'This is matter, this much is matter,' through the wisdom known as intellectual receptivity (nijjhānakkhanti) or the wisdom known as full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). Hearing, retaining, and verbal practice are also particularly connected with the reception at the ear-door of the scriptural Dhamma. Therefore, by the word suta, which indicates that meaning, he shows this meaning: 'Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and practiced verbally,' as stated in 'Sutaṃ...pe... dīpeti.' In that context, 'heard' means known through the sequence of the ear-door. 'Retained' (or 'borne') means held in mind, achieving a state of being well-established in the mind, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel. 'Practiced verbally' means practiced and recited with the tongue, achieving proficiency. Now, intending to explain the meaning to be clarified by the two aforementioned words (evaṃ, sutaṃ) which indicate the two meanings to be revealed, he stated 'Tadubhayenapi' and so forth. In that context, 'by both of those' (tadubhayena) means by those two kinds of words which indicate the meaning to be revealed as mentioned in both the previous and subsequent methods. 'Showing the completeness of meaning and phrasing' (atthabyañjanaparipūri) is a statement of the reason for generating respect. He explains that same reason by way of negation (vyatireka), or strengthens it with logic, saying 'Atthabyañjanaparipūṇṇaṃ hi' and so forth. In the word 'asuṇanto' (not hearing), the suffix 'anta' is used in the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇa) or a cause (hetu). 'Mahatā hitā' means from a great benefit. 'Paribāhiro' means one who has gone outside in every respect (an outsider). By these two words indicating the meaning to be clarified, while making the meaning to be experienced felt, he stated 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ...'. To make it known that these words, which were previously applied to separate meanings, are taken here as indicating a single significant meaning (anubhāva-attha), he said 'sakalena' (with the whole). In fact, the word 'me'...
163:
In this context, it should be connected according to the previous method. However, even if not connected in that way, it should be understood that this word 'me' is stated thus (as 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ') because of its association and inseparability with the words 'evaṃ' and 'sutaṃ'. 'Tathāgata-pavedita' refers to the Dhamma known in various ways or spoken by the Tathāgata. 'Not attributing to oneself' means not regarding it as 'this is mine' within oneself. Here, the genitive case (sāmivacana) is used in the sense of the locative (bhummatttha). 'Asappurisa-bhūmi' (the ground of the ignoble) refers to the domain of the ignoble, which is essentially ingratitude. The Blessed One spoke of this as being like a 'great thief' (mahācora), saying: 'In this teaching, a certain evil monk, having learned the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, attributes it to himself' (Pārājika 195). This is a state of ignoble speech (anariya-vohāra). Therefore, it is said, 'not attributing to oneself the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata.' Here, the word 'hutvā' (having been) is an elliptical term. Likewise, 'professing the status of a disciple' (sāvakatta-paṭijānana) describes the entry into the ground of the virtuous (sappurisa-bhūmi).

One might ask: Since Elder Ānanda did not have the overestimation (adhimāna) of thinking 'this is my word,' and since Elder Mahākassapa and others had no such suspicion, is the statement about 'transcending the ground of the ignoble' not useless? It is not so. By saying 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' he intends to make this meaning clear as well; thus, it is shown for the sake of the meaning itself. Therefore, it should be concluded here that he shows only the meaning to be realized through that statement, and not because of any overestimation in Elder Ānanda or suspicion in Elder Mahākassapa and others.

However, some teachers say: 'This statement was made in consideration of the thoughts of the devas; therefore, such an objection is groundless.' It is said that at the time of the Council, a thought arose in the minds of some devas: 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna. This Venerable Ānanda is skilled in preaching and is now teaching the Dhamma. He is born of the Sakyan clan, a brother of the Tathāgata, and the son of his paternal uncle. Is he preaching the Dhamma realized by himself, or is he preaching the words of the Blessed One exactly as he heard them?' Knowing their thoughts, he made the meaning of 'transcending the ground of the ignoble' clear in order to dispel their doubts. The aforementioned state of ignoble speech is 'asaddhamma' (false Dhamma), and professing the status of a disciple, characterized by not entering that state, is 'saddhamma' (true Dhamma). In this way, it should be understood that he shows the previous meaning through another method. Furthermore, the mass of unwholesome states arising through scheming (kuhana), talkativeness (lapana), etc., is 'asaddhamma,' and the state of being free from them is 'saddhamma.' The meaning already stated with words like 'kevala' is shown through another method, liberating one from the aforementioned state of ignoble speech. By professing the status of a disciple, he points to the Teacher (the Buddha). Furthermore, he liberates himself from acting as if he were the Teacher.
164:
Because there is the possibility of suspicion regarding such an act (acting as the Teacher), he makes the specific meaning clear by pointing to the Blessed One, saying: 'I have heard only the words of the Teacher, the Blessed One.' The term 'Jina-vacana' (the word of the Conqueror) and others are also shown as another method or to clarify a specific meaning. 'Appeti' means 'points out.' It is called 'Netti' (guide) because it leads beings appropriately to welfare in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (paramattha). Likewise, the Dhamma itself is called 'Netti.' In this context, the meaning should be understood in both ways according to the method mentioned.

With the words 'Api ca' (Furthermore), etc., he clarifies another meaning to be understood. In that context, 'uppādita-bhāva' refers to the state of being brought forth through the power of teaching. When explaining the previous statement, Elder Ānanda, wishing to make clear the words of the Blessed One that existed previously as preached by the Blessed One, should connect it as 'this word.'

[This is the word] of that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), who is intrepid through the fourfold knowledge of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), or who is endowed with the fourfold knowledge of intrepidity which is the cause of intrepidity; who bears the ten powers of knowledge (dasa-ñāṇa-bala); who stands at the supreme height known as the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One, or who stands in a state of unshakable nature known as 'āsabha' (bull-like) in that sense; who utters a lion's roar (sīhanāda) in many ways as found in the Sīhopama Sutta, etc., beginning with: 'Bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata arises in the world... he teaches the Dhamma' (A.N. 4.33); who is supreme among all beings (here, in the term 'sabba-sattuttama,' it is not a 'niddhāraṇa' compound because the characteristic of 'niddhāraṇa' is absent, and it is stated thus in both Sanskrit and scriptural texts); who is the Lord of beings through Dhamma, or who is the Lord of the Dhamma itself by way of producing it (as some teachers say); the remaining two terms (Dhammarāja, Dhammādhipati) illustrate that same meaning through other methods; who is like a lamp to the world through Dhamma, or who is endowed with the lamp of Dhamma by way of producing it (for it is said: 'Bhikkhus, "Dhamma-kāya" is a designation for the Tathāgata' [D.N. 3.118]); who is the refuge of the world through Dhamma, or who is endowed with the refuge known as Dhamma (for it is said: 'What if I... should dwell depending on that very Dhamma, honoring it, respecting it, revering it, and worshipping it?' [A.N. 4.21, S.N. 1.173]); who sets in motion the excellent wheel (vara-cakka) known as the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) consisting of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), etc., or who sets in motion this excellent wheel of authority (āṇā-cakka) of the True Dhammas. It should be connected as: 'This word of that Blessed One was received by me in his very presence.'

'Byañjana' (syllable/phrasing) refers to a sentence which is a collection of words. In the phrase 'kaṅkhā vā vimati vā,' 'kaṅkhā' (doubt) is a deeply rooted uncertainty. 'Vimati' (perplexity) is a mere difference of opinion without excessive trembling. The statement 'This was received by me in his presence' is a speech that makes one's conduct non-harsh in that manner. This statement, which explains the previous words without claiming the state of a Buddha for oneself, is a speech that states the reason for dispelling doubt and producing the fulfillment of faith. Therefore, he shows the aforementioned meaning through the power of an inspired verse (udāna-gāthā) beginning with 'Tenetaṃ'.
165:
The Venerable Ānanda, who is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One of the Gotama clan, or a disciple related to the Gotama clan, by saying "Thus have I heard," indicates that it was spoken by the Blessed One and that he himself received it in the presence [of the Buddha]. By such indication, he establishes the absence of faults such as slips, poor pronunciation, or wrong memorization, thereby dispelling lack of faith in the Dispensation (Sāsana) and increasing faith (saddhā).

Here, the three types of interpretations (atthayojanā) starting from the fifth are shown by taking the word 'evaṃ' without specifying its particular meaning among 'mode' (ākāra), etc. The next three interpretations are explained by taking the word 'evaṃ' only in the sense of 'mode' (ākāra). The last three interpretations should be understood as being construed by taking the word 'evaṃ' respectively in the senses of 'mode' (ākāra), 'illustration' (nidassana), and 'emphasis' (avadhāraṇa).

There are also verses here:
"The wise one who knows the methods, in these three words 'evaṃ me sutaṃ',
Shows in five ways through connection with the verb:
Direct showing (dassana), indirect showing (dīpana),
Manifestation (pakāsana), clarification (vibhāvana), and making experienced (anubhāvana).
The meaning established by tradition and by multiple applications
Is explained by the one skilled in methods in the three words 'evaṃ me sutaṃ'."

The word 'eka' is found in the senses of 'other', 'excellent', 'solitary', 'number', etc. Thus, it is found in the sense of 'other' (añña) in passages such as: "Some (ittheke) say, 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, any other is vain.'" In the sense of 'excellent' (seṭṭha) in "unification of mind" (ekodibhāva); in the sense of 'solitary' (asahāya) in "dwelling alone and secluded"; in the sense of 'number' (saṅkhyā) in "Monks, there is only one (eko) moment and one occasion for living the holy life." Wishing to show that here too it is only in the sense of 'number' (saṅkhyā), he said: "'Eka' is a designation for a numerical limit." This means that this word 'eka' is a designation of a numerical limit, indicating that this occasion is only one, not two or three, without being less or more. If one inquires, "What is delimited by such delimitation?"...
166:
To show that the word "samaya" is a designation of limitation, it was said: "Samaya is a designation of limitation." Even though the limited "samaya" is spoken of by way of limitation, because it is not specifically defined as "such and such a samaya," it is shown to be an indefinite expression by the words "Ekaṃ... pe... dīpanaံ."

Now, having shown the occurrence of the word "samaya" in many meanings by extracting those meanings, and wishing to define the intended meaning here, he said "Tattha," etc. "Tattha" means that in those two words "ekaṃ samayaṃ," the word "samaya" is included; this is the connection. It does not show all meanings because here it occurs in only one of those meanings. "Samavāya" means in the concordance of conditions; the meaning is the concordance of causes. "Khaṇe" means in opportunity. "Hetudiṭṭhīsu" means in cause and in view. These are the meanings of the word "samaya."

In the phrase "taking time and occasion" (kālañca samayañca upādāya), "kāla" is the suitable time for approaching. "Samaya" is the concordance of conditions of that time. In terms of meaning, it is the possession of physical strength suitable for that time and the absence of dangers arising from those causes. "Upādāna" means grasping those things with knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is: having grasped with wisdom and reflected upon the aforementioned time and occasion. This is what is meant: "If there be a suitable time for our going tomorrow, if there be strength in the body, and if no other discomfort arises from going, then, having reflected upon that time and the occasion known as the concordance of causes for going, we might perhaps come even tomorrow."

"Khaṇa" means opportunity. The arising of a Tathāgata, etc., is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path, because it is the cause for attaining that Path. "Khaṇa" itself is "samaya." The meaning is that what is called "khaṇa" and "samaya" is one and the same. The remaining month and a half of the summer is the "hot season" (uṇha-samaya). The first month of the rainy season is the "season of oppressive heat" (pariḷāha-samaya). "Mahāsamaya" means a great multitude. It can be a compound (samāsa) or an expansion (byāsa). A thriving forest is called "pavana"; the meaning is in that forest grove known as the Mahāvana near Kapilavatthu.

In the phrase "Samayopi kho," "samaya" is the cause for fulfilling a training rule. "Bhaddāli" is the name of that monk. This is what is meant: "Bhaddāli, there is one reason that you ought to have penetrated, but you have not penetrated or noted that reason." To answer what that reason is, he said "Bhagavāpi kho," etc.

In the words "Uggahamāno," etc., "Māṇa" is the original name of that wanderer. Because of his ability to learn various arts little by little, he is called "Uggahamāna."
167:
People recognize that wanderer; therefore, he is called 'Uggahamāna'. Because he is the son of Samaṇamuṇḍika, he is called 'Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta'. It is heard that this wanderer Uggahamāna was an attendant of Devadatta. Because doctrines (views) are specifically spoken of in this place, it is called 'Samayappavādaka'; it means the place where doctrines are discussed. In that place, brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, and ascetics such as Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Paribbājakas gather and specifically speak, show, and clarify their own doctrines; therefore, that park is called 'Samayappavādaka'. Because that same park is surrounded by a row of Tinduka trees, it is called 'Tindukācīra'. Because there is one hall in this place, it is called 'Ekasālaka'. In truth, although there was originally only one hall in that place, later many halls were built depending on the meritorious wanderer Poṭṭhapāda; however, based on the first single hall that was built, it is called 'Ekasālaka' according to its former name. That park, which is the garden of Queen Mallikā, the queen of King Pasenadi of Kosala, and is covered with flowers and fruits, is referred to as 'in Mallikā’s park'. Because he lives there comfortably, it is said 'he dwells'.

'In this life' (diṭṭhe dhamme) means in the present existence. 'Benefit' (attha) means growth. Because one reaches the next life through the power of kamma and defilements (kilesa), it is called 'samparāya', meaning the world beyond; the benefit associated with that world beyond is 'samparāyika', the benefit occurring in the world beyond. 'Because of attaining the benefit' means the attainment of both the aforementioned benefits of this life and the future life. Since the future benefit is also said to be attained because of the completion of its cause, these two benefits are combined and called 'atthābhisamaya'. Because one takes up various benefits with wisdom, or because one possesses wisdom, one is called 'dhīra' (wise). Wisdom is called 'paṇḍā'. Because that wisdom goes into very subtle meanings, or because it knows the manner of oppression of suffering etc., it is called 'paṇḍā'. Because one is characterized by that wisdom, one is called 'paṇḍita' (learned/wise). Alternatively, one is called 'paṇḍita' because one has good wisdom or because one proceeds with knowledge. 'By the right realization of conceit' means by the right abandonment of conceit. Here, 'rightly' (sammā) refers to the abandonment by eradication through the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa). 'End' (anta) means the conclusion. 'Oppression' (pīḷana) means the harming of one who is possessed of that suffering, or making the effort unsuccessful. That very meaning is the nature; in the word 'attha', by changing 'ta' to 'ṭṭha', it becomes 'saṅkhatattha'. The state of being produced by the harmony of causes is the meaning of the conditioned (saṅkhatattha). The burning or distress through the power of the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkhata), etc., is the meaning of burning (santāpattha). It is made to change in two ways: by aging and by death.
168:
## Vipariṇāmattha
The meaning of change (vipariṇāmattha). Because it is to be penetrated and known, it is called the meaning of realization (abhisamayattha). Only oppression (pīḷana) and so forth, being unified by the state of being to be penetrated, are called 'the meaning of realization' (abhisamayattha). Or else, because they are the objects of realization (abhisamaya) or penetration (paṭivedha), those very things like oppression are collectively called 'the meaning of realization' due to the commonality of becoming the object of that [realization]. In this context, since prefixes (upasagga) only serve to illuminate the meaning, the word 'samaya' itself expresses those various meanings. Therefore, even when extracting the meaning of the word 'samaya', it is stated as 'abhisamaya' along with the prefix 'abhi-'.

Among those meanings, the word-definition (vacanattha) is: It is called 'samaya' (samavāya - concordance) because it comes together or combines by the power of cooperating causes. In this occasion, the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariya) arises well by the power of the person who is the locus of that Path; therefore, it is called 'samaya' (khaṇa - occasion). At this time, or by this [time], dhammas or beings come together (arise) well through [conditions] such as co-nascent (sahajāta) and through [stages] such as arising (uppāda); therefore, it is called 'samaya' (kāla - time). In reality, although time does not exist in the ultimate sense as it is just the occurrence of dhammas, it is referred to by a form established merely by conceptualization, as if it were the locus or the instrument for the occurrence of dhammas.

Because of the concordance or the right occurrence and persistence of parts, it is called 'samaya' (samūha - group), just as 'samudāya' is said. Only the coexistence of parts is called a group; there is no such thing as a 'group' in the ultimate sense that is separate from the parts. When there is a meeting of other causes, the fruit arises or proceeds from it; therefore, it is called 'samaya' (hetu - cause), just as 'samudaya' is said. That [cause], only by meeting with other causes, brings about the state of being possessed of the arising and persistence of its own fruit.

Because it is a fetter (saṃyojana), it proceeds in its own object by being a connection; or because of the state of firm grasping, beings associated with it proceed according to their inclination by means of it; therefore, it is called 'samaya' (diṭṭhi - view). Indeed, beings are extremely bound by the fetter of views. Meeting and coming together is called 'samaya' (paṭilābha - acquisition). The reaching of the peaceful cessation (nirodha), or the right departure, non-occurrence, is called 'samaya' (pahāna - abandonment). Because it is to be rightly known face-to-face by knowledge, it is called 'abhisamaya' (the undistorted nature of dhammas). Because it rightly goes to, reaches, or understands each nature by being face-to-face, it is called 'abhisamaya' (the penetration of the nature of dhammas as they really are).

Question: Do not words settle only upon the intended meaning? Therefore, a single word cannot express many meanings. If so, why are many meanings of the word 'samaya' stated here? Answer: That statement is true if one considers the specific word...
169:
If one considers the specific linguistic nuance, it is not possible for a single word to express many meanings simultaneously. This is because the word *samaya*, which has meanings such as 'time' (kāla), does not itself express meanings such as 'assembly' (samūha) and so forth. However, in this context, the polysemy of the word *samaya* is stated by taking the commonality of what is expressed by the word *samaya* for those various meanings. Thus, it should be understood in the extraction of all meanings. In this regard, there is this verse:

“Based on the commonality of what is expressed, it expresses meanings in various ways.
A single word would not [ordinarily] be one that expresses multiple meanings.”

In this context, because meanings such as 'conjunction' (samavāya) are not possible, and because only 'time' (kāla) is to be indicated, it is said, “In this context, the meaning of this word *samaya* is time.” Just as the place of teaching, the person teaching, and so forth are intended, time is also intended as the origin (nidāna); therefore, time is also indicated here. To the question, “What kind of time is shown by this word *samaya*?”, the passage beginning with “*tena*” is stated. “*Tena*” means by the word *samaya* which has the meaning of time. A half-month (*aḍḍhamāsa*) is stated by way of the fortnight (*pakkha*); the morning and so forth are stated by way of the parts of the day; the first watch (*yāma*) and so forth are stated by way of the watch (*pahāra*). By the word “*ādi*” (and so forth), moments (*khaṇa*), measures of time (*laya*), and so forth are included; the meaning is that it shows a certain time by way of an indefinite manner.

Why is time indicated here in an indefinite manner, and not in a definite manner by way of season (*utu*), year (*saṃvacchara*), and so forth? To this question, the passage beginning with “*tattha kiñcāpi*” is stated. Although it is known by wisdom and well-distinguished, it should be connected with “*tathāpi*” (nevertheless). Because of the various and diverse nature of time, because much must be said, and because it would have to be spoken for as long as there are divisions of time, it is not possible to maintain it by speech, to indicate it oneself, or to have it indicated by others. By the phrase, “by consolidating that meaning with only a single word,” it is shown that when “*ekaṃ samayaṃ*” (at one time) is said, such divisions of time that would be included within it do not exist.

Thus, having shown the meaning of the word *samaya* by way of time as conventionally recognized in the world, the passage beginning with “*ye vā ime*” is now stated to show the meaning of the word *samaya* by way of time as well-known in the Dispensation (*Sāsana*). Alternatively, showing that this quality is also obtained when the word *samaya* is spoken without making a definite restriction by way of season, year, etc., he said the passage beginning with “*ye vā ime*”. For a general indication resides in the specific, because its scope is to encompass the specific. In that context, it should be connected as “*ye ime samayā*”. Herein, the time of the Blessed One’s descent into His mother’s womb is the *gabbhokkanti-samaya*. The time of being stirred by spiritual urgency upon seeing the four signs is the *saṃvega-samaya*. For six years, in order to attain the Supreme Enlightenment...
170:
...the period of practice is called the *dukkarakārika-samaya* (the time of austerities). The period of passing time daily through the attainments of Jhana and Fruition is called the *diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra-samaya* (the time of dwelling in happiness in the present life); specifically, it is the period of practicing the meditative attainments throughout the seven weeks (*sattasattāha*). The period of teaching various Dhammas throughout the forty-five years is the *desanā-samaya* (the time of teaching). By the word “*ādi*”, the time of the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*) and so forth are included. *Pakāsa* means they are manifested by such events as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems and the appearance of radiance. When “*ekaṃ samayaṃ*” is said, it implies that there are other times as well; therefore, among those times, it is shown that the specific time known as the *desanā-samaya* is referred to here as “*ekaṃ samayaṃ*”. This is the intention.

In order to show a portion of the aforementioned various types of *samaya* by grouping them in another way, the passage beginning with “*yo cāyaṃ*” is stated. In that statement, the time of the function of knowledge (*ñāṇa-kicca-samaya*) and the time of practicing for one's own benefit (*attahita-paṭipatti-samaya*) are simply the *abhisambodhi-samaya* (the time of Enlightenment). The time of the Noble Silence (*ariya-tuṇhībhāva-samaya*) is called the *diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra-samaya*. The time of the function of compassion, practicing for the benefit of others, and giving Dhamma talks is the *desanā-samaya*. Therefore, it should be understood that among those aforementioned various types of *samaya*, only a portion is shown in another way. With reference to the occasion when it was said, “Monks, for you who have assembled, two things should be done: either Dhamma talk or Noble Silence,” it is said, “in the times of the two duties of those who have assembled.” Even in those times means even in the times of the function of compassion, practice for the benefit of others, Dhamma talk, and teaching. With reference to one of those times, it is said “*ekaṃ samayaṃ*”, because there is no difference in meaning.

Unlike in other texts, where the indication is made using the Locative case (*bhumma-vacana*) or the Instrumental case (*karaṇa-vacana*), here, wishing to bring out the purpose of indicating with the Accusative case (*upayoga-vacana*), he raises an objection indirectly with the passage beginning with “*kasmā panettha*”. “Herein” (*ettha*) refers to this term “*ekaṃ samayaṃ*”; it should be connected as “as if the indication were made with the Instrumental case.” It is called *bhumma* or *okāsa* (location) because things exist in it; the case ending occurring in that sense of location is the Locative case (*bhumma-vacana*). It is called *karaṇa* or the cause for the completion of an action because the action is accomplished by means of this; the case ending therein is likewise. It is called *upayoga* or *kamma* (object) because it should be employed for the action; the case ending occurring in that sense of object is also the same. With the passage beginning with “*tattha*”, he resolves the aforementioned objection. “*Tattha*” means in the Abhidhamma and in the other Suttas and Vinaya. “*Tathā*” should be joined as “because the meaning can be accomplished by the Locative and Instrumental cases,” in the sense of the container (*adhikaraṇa*) and the characteristic of an action by another action (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa*)...
171:
It means because the meanings of cause (hetu) and instrument (karaṇa) are possible. "Idha" means in this sutta passage. "Aññathā" means by the second case inflection (accusative). "Atthasambhavato" means because the meaning of continuous connection (accanta-saṃyoga) is possible.

The passage beginning with "Tattha hi" is an explanation of that statement. "Ito" refers to the sutta passage "Ekaṃ samayaṃ". The meaning of locus (adhikaraṇa) is the meaning of support (ādhāra). Arising is called state (bhāva) or action (kriyā). The marking of one action by another action is called "characterization of an action by another action" (bhāvena bhāva lakkhaṇa). That very bhāvena bhāva lakkhaṇa is the meaning, and it is just so.

If there is an inquiry as to by which meaning of the word "samaya" these two meanings are possible, he said "Adhikaraṇañhi" etc., wishing to strengthen that meaning with the meaning of samaya that is consistent with the possibility of those two meanings. Indeed, the two aforementioned meanings are established by the meaning of the word itself; the case inflection is merely an illuminator (jotaka). Among those words, whichever word "samaya" has the meaning of time (kāla) is called "kālattha" (having the meaning of time). Whichever word "samaya" has the meaning of assemblage (samūha) is called "samūhattha" (having the meaning of assemblage). What is that? It is samaya itself.

This means that samaya with the meaning of time and samaya with the meaning of assemblage are the locus (adhikaraṇa) or support for the states such as contact (phassa) mentioned in that Abhidhamma. At whatever time, or in whatever group of states, the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises, at that very time, or in that very group of states, contact and other states also occur—this is the meaning there. One might ask: Is not this time merely a derivative concept (upādā-paññatti), and is not the assemblage merely a conventional usage (vohāra)? How then could they be the locus for the states mentioned in that Abhidhamma? This is not a fault.

For just as time, though not existing in the ultimate sense (paramattha), is known as a support because it is delimited by natural states (sabhāva-dhamma); and time delimited by natural states is evident in such phrases as "it arises in the morning, he comes in the evening," because it does not exist before or after the states occurring at that moment; and just as an assemblage, though not existing separately from its parts, is designated as the support of the parts in such passages as "a branch in a tree, seen in a heap of grain," because it is established merely by mental construction; so too in this Abhidhamma, because they are delimited by natural states and established by mental construction, both are designated as the locus of the mentioned states.

The passage beginning with "Khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa" is a statement showing the possibility of the meaning of characterization of an action by another action (bhāvena bhāva lakkhaṇa). Among those moments (khaṇa), what is called a moment is the ninth moment of a Buddha's arising (buddhuppādakkhaṇa), which is free from the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa). Alternatively, there are these wheels which the Blessed One taught: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels...
172:
“For gods and humans endowed with these wheels, the four wheels revolve” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.31). In this Pali passage, the four wheels are taught as: dwelling in a suitable locality (patirūpadesavāsa), association with good people (sappurisūpanissaya), right self-direction (attasammāpaṇīdhi), and having performed merit in the past (pubbekatapuññatā). These four wheels, taken together, are to be understood as a “moment” (khaṇa) in the sense of an opportunity (for the arising of wholesome states). Indeed, these four wheels are the opportunities for the arising of the wholesome.

Concordance (samavāya) is the harmony (sāmaggī) of causes such as the eye and forms, which is established by the fact of producing common results such as eye-consciousness, as indicated by “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises,” and so on. In fact, the common result of the eye, forms, and so forth is eye-consciousness and the like. Cause (hetu) refers to the producing cause such as wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

The meaning is that by the presence of the occasion (samaya) known as moment (khaṇa), concordance (samavāya), and cause (hetu) as mentioned before, the presence of those states such as contact (phassa) is characterized or known.

This is what is meant: Just as in the statement, “He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked,” the action of going is characterized by the action of milking; so too here, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the occurrence of contact and other states are characterized by the action of the presence of the aforementioned occasion (samaya).

One might ask: Since the action of presence (of the samaya) does not actually exist here, how can it be a characterizer? It is true; nevertheless, when it is said “yasmiṃ samaye” (at which occasion), the meaning “when it exists” is already understood. Even if there is no connection with another action, the meaning of the word is not devoid of presence. Therefore, the arising of consciousness is characterized by that action of presence which is understood through the sense.

The meaning here is: When the aforementioned moment, concordance of conditions (paccaya-samavāya), or cause (hetu) exists, the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness arises; and at that very moment, when that concordance of conditions or cause exists, contact and other states also occur. This meaning is taught by way of illustration only in the Abhidhamma; this method should be applied accordingly to other sutta passages as well.

Therefore, it is because the meaning of locus (adhikaraṇa) and the meaning of characterization of an action by another action (bhāvena bhāva lakkhaṇa) are possible. “Tadattha-jotanatthaṃ” means for the purpose of showing those two meanings, which exist as the meanings of the word samaya, by means of the locative case (sattamī vibhatti). Indeed, case inflections, like a lamp, only illuminate a meaning that already exists in the object; this fact is well-known in the treatises on grammar.

The meanings of cause (hetu) and instrument (karaṇa) are also possible. The meaning of cause is seen in such examples as “He lives because of food, he lives because of knowledge”; and the meaning of instrument is seen in “He cuts with an axe, [he digs] with a hoe...”
173:
The instrumental sense (karaṇattha) should also be applicable, as in examples like 'he digs the earth.' How is this possible? It is said, 'For that which...' and so on. In the Vinaya, regarding the request for the laying down of training rules, it is stated with reference to the Elder Sāriputta, 'It is difficult to understand even for those such as Sāriputta.' In the phrase 'at that time as a cause, as an instrument,' the transgression of a particular matter is both the cause (hetu) and the instrument (karaṇa) for the laying down of a training rule.

Indeed, when the Blessed One, for the purpose of laying down a training rule, first dwells looking toward the transgression that is the cause for laying down that training rule in various places, his dwelling for that purpose while looking toward the transgression makes the transgression's status as a cause for laying down the training rule evident—just as in 'he lives because of food,' where food is the cause because he lives for that purpose looking toward food. At the time of laying down the training rule, however, he lays it down by means of that previously established transgression. Therefore, because it is the most effective means (sādhakatama) for laying down the training rule, the status of the transgression as an instrument is also evident—just as in 'he cuts with a sword,' where the sword is the instrument because it accomplishes the act of cutting.

Even so, the Blessed One, while looking toward the transgression, also dwells looking toward the time associated with it; thus, the status of time as a cause is mentioned here. When laying down the training rule, he does not exceed the time of that transgression and lays down the rule by means of that very time; thus, the status of the time, which is the support for the transgression, as an instrument is also mentioned. Therefore, because the status of time as a cause and an instrument is obtained through this figurative method (pariyāya), it is said, 'at that time as a cause, as an instrument.' In the primary sense (nippariyāya), however, only the transgression is the cause and the instrument.

Indeed, that transgression becomes the cause at the moment of transgression and later becomes the instrument at the moment of laying down the training rule. When laying down the training rules, having inquired about the transgression, having caused the Saṅgha of monks to assemble, having questioned the person regarding the matter that has come to the Saṅgha, and having rebuked them, he lays down the training rules by means of that very time as the instrument, without exceeding the time when that matter occurred. 'Looking toward the cause for laying down the training rule' means, as in the third Pārājika and others, looking toward the time of the transgression of the matter which is the cause for laying down the training rule; the meaning is that the Blessed One dwelt in various places at that time which was the cause.
174:
The phrase 'laying down the training rules, and looking toward the cause for laying down the training rule' is a statement that establishes the status of instrument (karaṇa) and the status of cause (hetu) respectively. Therefore, although it should be said 'by that time as an instrument, as a cause' in accordance with that status, the reversed order 'as a cause' first is used because the status of cause is particularly intended. It is said in all three Ganthipada texts: 'The Blessed One, while dwelling in Verañjā, dwelt with that time as a cause, looking toward the time when the thought arose, which was the cause for the request by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, to lay down training rules.'

Some say: 'What is the use of logical reflection here? Since the teachers do not intend a specific order here, this sequence of words should be taken as previously stated.' This same sequence is also mentioned in other commentaries. In those commentaries, regarding the Vinaya Pāḷi term 'tena samayena verañjāyaṃ viharati,' it is stated this way because the causal sense is particularly intended, or because it is not the proper scope, or because the words are connected as far as possible: 'He dwelt with the time as a cause and an instrument, desiring to lay down training rules; he dwelt with the time as a cause, looking toward the cause for laying down the training rule.'

'Tasmā' (therefore) means because both types of meanings mentioned are possible. 'Tadattha-jotanatthaṃ' means to illuminate both the causal and instrumental meanings by the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) in the manner stated. 'Tattha' means in that Vinaya. Here, since the time of transgression (vītikkama-samaya) is the most effective means for laying down the training rule, its status as an instrument should be connected with the supplied word 'laying down the training rules' (sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto). As for its status as a cause, since it is merely looking toward that time of transgression, it should be understood to connect only with the word 'dwells' (viharati). Thus it is said: 'Laying down the training rules by that time as a cause and an instrument, and also looking toward the cause for laying down the training rule, the Blessed One dwelt in various places.' For the instrument has the sense of the action; it is not the reason for the action like the cause. The cause, however, is the reason for the action; it is not the sense of the action like the instrument.

By the words 'Idha pana' and so on, the possibility of the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) for the accusative case is shown. 'Accantasaṃyoga' means constant association with substance, quality, or action; it means the state of being continuously connected with them. That very meaning is 'tathā' (so). 'Evaṃjātika' means having such a nature. To show how it is possible, he says 'Yanhī' and so on. 'Accantam-eva' means from the beginning of the effort to teach until the end of the discourse, it is certainly constant and continuous. 'Karuṇāvihārena' means dwelling with compassion, which is defined as the practice for the welfare of others. Indeed...
175:
Because it has compassion as its root, in this Dispensation, the practice for the welfare of others is called 'karuṇāvihāra' (dwelling in compassion); however, it does not refer to dwelling in the meditative attainment of compassion (karuṇāsamāpatti). The reason is that at the time of teaching, it is impossible for the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa), which has the Dhamma to be taught as its object, and the great compassion (mahākaruṇā), which has sentient beings as its object, to arise simultaneously because their objects are different. Therefore, the practice for the welfare of others, which is a dwelling occurring through compassion, should be understood here as 'karuṇāvihāra'. The word 'tasmā' is used because the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) is possible. To manifest that sense, the designation is made with the accusative case (dutiyā vibhatti) according to the method already mentioned, just as in 'māsaṃ sajjhāyati' (he recites for a month) or 'divasaṃ bhuñjati' (he eats for a whole day). The word 'tena' means: for whatever reason the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) has the sense of locus (adhikaraṇa) and the sense of an action characterized by another action (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa) in the Abhidhamma and in other Sutta passages, and the instrumental case (tatiyā vibhatti) has the sense of cause (hetu) and instrument (karaṇa) in the Vinaya, in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the accusative case has the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga); for that reason, it is so understood. The word 'etaṃ' is a verse-foot that encompasses the meaning already stated. The word 'aññatra' refers to the Abhidhamma, other Sutta passages, and the Vinaya. The word 'samayo' is the word 'samaya' itself. Since the case ending cannot be attached to the meaning, the case ending follows the word itself. The word 'so' refers to that very word 'samaya'.

Having thus shown his own opinion, he now says 'porāṇā pana' etc., to show the opinion of the ancient teachers. 'Porāṇā' refers to the original commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas). Whether it is 'tasmiṃ samaye' or 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', it should be connected as being merely a difference in terminology. 'Abhilāpamattabhedo' means a difference only in the mode of expression, but there is no difference in meaning; therefore, it is said, 'In all places, the meaning is only that of the locus (ādhāra)'. By this statement, he shows the interchange of case endings in the Sutta and Vinaya, or he shows the accomplishment of the accusative and instrumental cases in the sense of the locus. With the words 'tasmā' etc., he speaks of the excellence in showing the opinion of those teachers.

He is called 'Garu' because of the sense of being heavy (venerable). He supports that very meaning by way of worldly convention with the words 'garuṃ hi' etc., because a word that is a subject of convention conveys the meaning only according to that designation. 'Garuṃ' refers to a person who should be respected. By the word 'loke', he shows that the designation of the Buddha as 'Bhagavā' is established by convention because of the sense of being one who should be respected, not only in the Dispensation but also in the world. If he is called 'Bhagavā' because of the sense of being one who should be respected, then to show that this Buddha alone is the 'Bhagavā' in the highest sense, he says 'ayañca' etc. For that Lord of the World, being endowed with the special qualities of infinite and incomparable power, virtue, and so forth,
176:
