Because He is preceded by the dispelling of all harm, because He is intent on providing complete welfare and happiness, because He is endowed with unsurpassed effort and application, because He is of ultimate benefit to the generation of beings including devas and humans, and because He is the supreme object of veneration for infinite beings in infinite world systems. He shows with the words 'porāṇehi' etc., that the name 'Bhagavā' is due to the sense of being venerable not only in the world but also in the Dispensation. 'Porāṇehi' means the Commentators. It is said, 'The word Bhagavā is noble,' because a word expressing the noble is itself noble due to its association with noble qualities. It is called 'vacana' (word) because the meaning is spoken (vuccati) by it; it is a sound. Or, it is called 'vacana' because it is spoken; it is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning expressed by the word 'Bhagavā' is noble. In the phrase 'The word Bhagavā is supreme,' the same method applies. 'Gāravayutto' means being endowed with the state of being venerable (garu) because of association with venerable qualities, or being endowed with reverence because of being worthy of the highest respect; it means one worthy of reverence. It is connected thus: because of these three reasons, that Tathāgata is 'Garu' in the sense of being heavy (venerable), and therefore He is called 'Bhagavā'. These three words are for showing the reasons for His venerability.

Some teachers say, 'Teachers who teach arts and sciences are also called Garu (teachers), but they are not Gāravayutta (endowed with supreme reverence); this Blessed One, however, is not like that; therefore, being Garu, He is called Gāravayutta.' In that case, that word 'Bhagavā' would be a mere epithet, and only the first two words would be the demonstration of the reason.

'Api ca' is a particle used in the sense of an alternative meaning, meaning 'another way'. Therein—

'The addition of a letter, the transposition of letters,
the other two: the transformation and deletion of letters,
and association with an excellence of the roots' meanings—
these five are called Nirutti (linguistic derivation).'

Taking this characteristic of Nirutti, or taking the characteristic of inclusion in the 'pisodarādi' class of words according to the grammatical method stated as 'pisodarādīni yathopadiṭṭhaṃ', He is called 'Bhagavā' where He should be called 'Bhāgyavā' because He possesses fortune (bhāgya) in the form of the perfection of virtue and so forth, which brings about mundane and supramundane happiness; thus he shows this with the word 'Bhāgyavā'. Likewise, He is called 'Bhagavā' where He should be called 'Bhaggavā' because He has broken (abhañji) hundreds of thousands of defilements of various kinds, or briefly, the five Māras; thus he shows this with the word 'Bhaggavā'.
177:
In the world, the word 'Bhaga' occurs in relation to six things: lordship (issariya), doctrine (dhamma), fame (yasa), glory (sirī), wish (kāma), and effort (payatta). To show the meaning that 'He is the Bhagavā because these things called Bhaga exist in that Blessed One,' it is said: 'And because He is endowed with the qualities of Bhaga.' Because He divided, revealed, and taught all dhammas through many divisions such as the wholesome and so on, it should be said 'Vibhattavā' (The Divider), but it is said 'Bhagavā'; this is shown by the word 'Vibhattavā'. Because He frequented, associated with, and practiced extensively the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra), the Brahma abidings (brahma-vihāra), and the noble abidings (ariya-vihāra), as well as physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka), and the void (suññata), signless (animitta), and undirected (appaṇihita) deliverances (vimokkha), and other mundane and supramundane higher human states (uttarimanussadhamma), it should be said 'Bhattavā' (The Associator), but it is said 'Bhagavā'; this is shown by this word 'Bhattavā'. Because He has discarded (vomited) the 'going' known as craving in the three realms of existence, it should be said 'Vantagamano bhavesu'. By taking the letter 'Bha' from the word 'bhava', the letter 'Ga' from the word 'gamana', and the letter 'Vā' from the word 'vanta', and by making that 'Vā' long (dīgha) and through the transposition of letters (vaṇṇa-vipariyāya), it is said 'Bhagavā'. To show this, it is said: 'And because He has vomited the going in the realms of existence.' It should be understood by connecting each individually as 'Since He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), therefore He is Bhagavā,' and so on. 'Of that word' means of the word 'Bhagavā'. 'Detailed meaning' means the meaning that is extensive. By the words 'And that [meaning]...' and so on, the author avoids making the text too bulky. The meaning has already been stated, but it should not be stated here again because this Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā is a part of the Visuddhimagga; this is the intention.

Furthermore, He is called 'Bhagavā' because He associated with (vani) or discarded (vami) the Bhaga qualities. For He associated with (vani), frequented, and practiced the Bhaga qualities such as virtue and so on. Or, He desired (vani), requested, and aspired for those qualities called Bhaga, such as virtue and so on, to arise in the continuities of those to be led (vineyya-satta), thinking, 'How indeed might they arise?' Thus, He is 'Bhagavā' because He desired (vani) the Bhaga qualities. Alternatively, He vomited (vami) and discarded like a lump of spit the Bhaga qualities such as glory, lordship, and fame. Indeed, the Blessed One discarded without regard the glory of a Universal Monarch (cakkavatti) that had come into His hands, the lordship over the four continents, and the fame associated with the prosperity of a Universal Monarch, which shines with the seven treasures. In another way, 'Bhā' is the name for stars; those that go or proceed together with those stars are called 'Bhagā' (by shortening the 'ā' sound), which refers to the beauty of the receptacle world (bhājanalo-ka) situated on Mount Sineru, Mount Yugandhara, and so on. He vomited (vami) and abandoned those 'Bhagā' by abandoning the desire and lust (chandarāga) connected with them. Thus, He is 'Bhagavā' because He vomited the 'Bhagā'. The meaning of this word should be stated by such methods as found in various texts. However, we have overlooked those meanings for the sake of favoring those who fear long texts and to avoid the burden of an excessively large book.

Having thus shown the meaning of the individual parts of those words, now, wishing to show the collective meaning, and to show it together with the preceding three words by way of the opposite of the meanings already stated in their collective sense, the author says 'By this much' (ettāvatā) and so on.
178:
The word 'Ettāvatā' (by this much) is connected with the words 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā'. 'Ettha' means in this introductory statement. In the phrase 'teaching the Dhamma as it was heard' (yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ desento), the word 'anta' has the sense of cause. Indeed, by teaching in such a manner, one is said to make it manifest (paccakkha). This method applies to other places as well.

According to the words, 'Ānanda, the Dhamma I have taught... is your teacher,' the Dhamma is considered to exist in the capacity of the Teacher; thus it is said, 'He makes the Dhamma-body (dhamma-sarīra) manifest.' 'Dhamma-kāya' means the body consisting of the Dhamma that is associated with the Blessed One. And so it was said, 'Bhikkhus, Dhamma-kāya is a designation for the Tathāgata.'

If it is asked what the benefit of such manifestation is, the answer is given starting with 'Tena'. 'Tena' means by such manifestation. This discourse (sutta) which is about to be taught is the Pāvacana, the sublime and supreme word of the Buddha, the Blessed One. Therefore, it means that the state of having a teacher who has passed away (atītasatthuka) does not exist for you.

Indeed, this description is one where the abstract state (bhāva) is primary, or where the word 'bhāva' is elided. Otherwise, only the Pāvacana would be that which has a teacher who has not passed away, and for the people who are weary because they do not see the Teacher, the meaning would result in them having a teacher who has passed away. If that were so, teachers say there would be a contradiction with the statement, 'This [Dhamma] is your teacher, thus reassuring the people who are weary because they do not see the Teacher.' This Pāvacana is not one whose teacher has passed away because it fulfills the functions of the Teacher. 'Satthu' is either the genitive case in the sense of the object (kamma), or it is a compound word (samāsa) as in 'satthu-adassanena' (by not seeing the Teacher).

'Ukkaṇṭha' means weariness or living with difficulty. Indeed, they say the root 'kaṭha' is used in the sense of living with difficulty. One who has reached that state is called 'ukkaṇṭhita'. Alternatively, according to the method of derivative analysis (nirutti), one is called 'ukkaṇṭhita' because, being oppressed by a lack of delight (anabhirati) and having a distracted mind, one raises one's head, stretches the neck (kaṇṭha) upwards, and wanders or lives looking here and there. This is merely the meaning obtained through the power of the word itself; in common usage, however, it means being oppressed by a lack of delight. This method applies everywhere. 'Samassāseti' means to bring about reassurance.

'Tasmiṃ samaye' (at that time) means at the time of the Council (saṅgīti) for this sutta. Although it would be proper to speak thus even while the Blessed One was still present, here it is said while He is no longer present. Therefore, wishing to show that meaning by way of an intentional utterance (sandhāyabhāsita), the author says, 'Wishing to show the state of His no longer being present'. 'Parinibbāna' refers to the Parinibbāna of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna) by way of the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). 'Tena' means by such accomplishment. 'Evaṃvidhassa' means of such a kind.
179:
"To one of such a nature" is also a suitable meaning. The word "nāma" is a particle used in the sense of reproach, as in: "Ānanda, how can you remain indifferent while a senior monk is being harassed?" By this word "nāma," it highlights the sense of reproach: "Even the Blessed One, who is of such a nature, has attained Parinibbāna; what then is there to say of others?"

"Ariyadhammassa" means the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, or the Dhamma that is noble. He is the "Possessor of the Ten Powers" (Dasabaladharo) by virtue of the ten kinds of physical strength and intellectual power. He is called "Vajirasaṅghātasamānakāya" because his body is like a solid mass of the special gem called diamond (vajira). The meaning is this: just as a mass of diamond cannot be broken by any other gem or stone, but rather it alone can break other gems or stones—as it is said, "There is no gem or stone that cannot be broken by a diamond"—likewise, the Blessed One has a body that cannot be broken by anyone. This is because no one is able to cause harm to the Blessed One's physical body (rūpakāya).

Since the word "nāma" indicates reproach, the word "pi" indicates the sense of inclusion: "Not only the Blessed One, but others as well (attain Parinibbāna)." In this context, although it is fitting for one endowed with such qualities to be of a nature not to attain Parinibbāna, the Elder Ānanda said "Evaṃ" (Thus) and so forth to show the meaning in accordance with the context, that he has indeed attained Parinibbāna. Who should generate longing? It should simply not be generated. The conceit that arises through the power of intoxication, thinking, "I have lived long, I live long, I shall live long; I have lived happily, I live happily, I shall live happily," is called "intoxication with life" (jīvitamada). He causes one who is negligent due to that intoxication with life to be stirred (saṃvejeti). By causing such stirrings, he generates effort in the True Dhamma for that person. For stirring is the cause of effort, according to the saying: "One who is stirred strives wisely."

By pointing to the entire Sutta that is to be spoken with the word "Evaṃ" (Thus), he indicates the "Perfection of the Teaching" (Desanāsampatti). He indicates the "Perfection of the Disciple" (Sāvakasampatti) by showing that "It was heard by me, a Great Disciple (Ven. Ānanda), who has attained the Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā), who was placed in the foremost rank (Etadagga) in five categories by the Blessed One, and who was praised in five kinds of proficiency by the General of the Dhamma (Ven. Sāriputta)." Furthermore, it was heard directly by himself, not by hearsay or through a lineage of transmission. He indicates the "Perfection of Time" (Kālasampatti) by the word "samaya" (occasion/time) used in proximity to the word "Bhagavā," showing it to be a time adorned by the arising of a Buddha. Indeed, the arising of a Buddha is the supreme perfection of time. Therefore, it is said:

In the age called Kaliyuga, which arrives through the counting of the collection of time called aeons (kappa), the arising of a Buddha occurs as a supreme wonder, like a lotus blooming without mud (or without smoke/flame) in the midst of a bonfire. This is just a brief explanation for easy understanding. The detailed meaning should be understood as shown in the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā). The meaning of that verse is: In the collection of years and so forth designated as the era (Sakkara) called Kaliyuga, which proceeds by way of the recording of the accumulation of time called aeons, the collection of days called the moment of the Buddha's arising is a great wonder, because it occurs only occasionally, like a blind man climbing a mountain, and because it is worthy of snapping one's fingers in amazement. For example, how does it occur? ...
180:
"In the Kaliyuga of the dregs of the aeon, the arising of a Buddha—oh, what a great wonder! Like a lotus full of nectar, blooming perfectly in the midst of fire."

The meaning of that is: In the collection of years and so forth designated as the era called Kaliyuga, which proceeds by way of the recording of the accumulation of time called aeons, the collection of days called the moment of the Buddha's arising is a great wonder, because it occurs only occasionally, like a blind man climbing a mountain, and because it is worthy of snapping one's fingers in amazement. Like what does it arise? It arises like a water-born flower called a lotus, full of honey and perfectly bloomed in the midst of the fire called "hutavaha."

He indicates the "Perfection of the Speaker" (Desakasampatti) by using a title of great respect for the Supreme Being who is distinguished by his qualities. Having thus explained the meaning of the six words in various ways according to the sequence of words, he now says "Antarā ca" and so forth, wishing to explain the meaning of the words "Antarā ca Rājagahaṃ" and so on. In this context, "Antarā ca Rājagahaṃ antarā ca Nāဠandaṃ," the well-placed word "antarā" disregards the general meaning and, through the power of the context and so forth, becomes clear in the sense of "in between."

Wishing to show that this word "antarā" has various meanings according to usage (payoga), he says "Tadantaraṃ" and so forth. There, "tadantaraṃ" means "that reason." "I and he are consulting; what is the reason (kiṃ antaraṃ)?" is the meaning. "Vijjantarikāya" means in the moment of a lightning flash. It should be connected as: "The woman washing the bowl saw it." "Antarato" means in the heart (mind). "Kopā" refers to lust (rāga) and so forth, which destroy the mind because they cause mental turbidity. "Antarā vosānaṃ" means reaching the end in the middle of the beginning and the completion. "Api ca" means "even so" or "even though it is endowed with such an origin."

The phrase "Dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ" (Between two great hells) is said with reference to the Lohakumbhī hell. "Antarikāya" means "in between." It is said that the great realm of Petas exists by piercing through the city of Rājagaha. There, this Tapodā River comes from between two great Lohakumbhī hells. Therefore, that river flows boiling. Here, the word "antarā" occurs in the sense of an interval (vivara), as other meanings are not possible.

In this regard, words like "antarā" occurring in the sense of "reason" and "middle"—as in "Who could know that reason?", "Between those aeons, the intermediate aeons are incalculable by number," and "He drops a word in between"—should be cited as examples. However, words (like antarikā or antara) occurring in the sense of "mind" and "moment" should not be cited as examples.
181:
The words *antarika* and *antara* are derivations of the meaning of the word *antarā*. The intention here is as follows: since the words *antarika* and *antara* occur in the same meanings as *antarā*, they are cited as being present in the sense of *antarā* due to their synonymity. Alternatively, the word *antarā* itself is expressed with a short vowel as *antara* in the verse "Yassantarato" for the sake of metrical ease.

"In whom there are no angers within, who has transcended the states of existence great and small, that one who is free from fear, happy, and sorrowless, the gods do not [sufficiently] experience even by seeing (they cannot be satiated by the sight)."

This verse appears in the Bhaddiya Sutta of the Udāna Pāḷi. That same word *antarā* is expanded into the term *antarikāya* by adding the suffix *-ika* in its own sense. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no contradiction between the example cited and the subject being illustrated. To explain why a specific meaning is restricted, the text says "Tasmā," etc. Since one might ask why the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is used here when it refers to a relational sense (*sambandhattha*), or why the accusative is used in a relational context, the phrase "Antarā-saddena pana," etc., is stated to resolve this. It shows that although the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) would normally be expected in a relational sense, the accusative case is obtained here due to the connection with a specific word (*antarā*). To show that this is found not only in the Dispensation (*Sāsana*) but also in worldly usage, "Īdisesu ca," etc., is said. This meaning is also shown by way of demonstrating the connection with specific terms. Because of the connection with even a single word *antarā*, two accusative cases should be used. What more need be said when there is a connection with two words, as the meaning is already established?

Those who reflect on syllables (*akkhara*) through gender, case, etc., are called *akkhara-cintakā* (grammarians). In this term *akkhara-cintaka*, words and other elements based on syllables should also be included. Although grammatically it connects only once, in terms of meaning, that word *antara* should be connected twice. This is shown by "Dutiyapadenapi," etc., because even a single word can fulfill multiple meanings through methods such as repetition (*āvutti*). If it were not so connected, what would be the fault? It says, "Ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti," meaning it would not reach the second word. This is because the accusative case is desired where the genitive would normally occur due to the influence of a specific word. The use of cases follows the grammatical context of the words.
182:
The word *addhāna* has the meaning of "long," thus it is called a "long journey" (*dīghamaggi*). To answer the question of how much distance constitutes a "long journey," the text says "Addhānagamanasamayassa hi," etc. The "Vibhaṅga of the *addhānagamanasamaya*" refers to the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*) found in the *Gaṇabhojana* training rule and others, where the term *addhānagamanasamaya* is defined. Even half a *yojana* is a long journey; how much more so if it exceeds that? Half a *yojana* is two *gāvutas*. However, in this context, one *yojana* measuring four *gāvutas* should be taken. Therefore, it means "one who has entered upon a long journey."

The word *mahanta* implies both "noble" and "many," which is why "Mahatā," etc., is said. "Greatness of virtue" refers to being great through virtues such as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*). "Greatness of number" refers to the large number of monks. This meaning is clarified by "So hi," etc. "That community of monks" (*so bhikkhusaṅgho*) refers to the community of monks who were the retinue of the Blessed One at that time, as mentioned in this sutta. *Mahā* means "noble." In sentences, this noble meaning is also desired depending on the usage. Fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) means the absence of greed. Here, while the word *appa* (small/few) might suggest a remainder, the meaning is the total absence of greed. This is because the Commentaries state, "It is not fit to praise 'little greed' (*appolobhatā*)."

However, the Elder Dhammapāla, author of the *Majjhima Nikāya* Sub-commentary, says: "Considering the meaning of the word *appa* as 'small,' the Commentary says 'the syllable is as if there is a remainder' (*byañjanaṃ sāwasesaṃ viya*). But here, the word *appa* can also be understood in the sense of 'absence' (*abhāva*), just as in passages like 'I perceive the absence of illness' (*appābādhatañca sañjānāmi*)."

In terms of number, they were also many. Since the word *bhikkhusaṅgho* as a term-ending (*padāvatthikantavacana*) seems to cut off the word to be explained, instead of taking that word directly, it is made consistent with the word to be explained as a sentence-ending (*vākyāvatthikantavacana*) by saying "Tena bhikkhusaṅghena." This is the natural practice of commentators: to explain the meaning of the word to be explained as appropriate without regarding the case ending, and then to restate it according to the case ending present in that word.

Desiring to clarify the meaning that it is called a *Saṅgha* because of being united by commonality of view (*diṭṭhi*) and virtue (*sīla*), it says: "By a group of recluses united by commonality of view and virtue" (*diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātena samaṇagaṇena*). Here, "view" refers to that which is said: "That view which is noble and leading out, which leads the one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering; he dwells having attained commonality of view with such a view." "Those virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblotched, unmottled..."
183:
Being an assemblage united by the commonality of those virtues described as: “Those [virtues] that are liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped [by craving and views], and conducive to concentration,” it is called “diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghāto.” It means a group of monks united by the commonality of view and virtue. There is also a reading “diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghāṭasaṅkhātena,” which means the sense as stated.

In truth, because view and virtue and so forth are of a fixed nature, even Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) are united by the power of commonality in view and virtue; what then need be said of Once-returners (sakadāgāmi) and others? Therefore, it is said: “The Stream-enterer is fixed [in destiny], bound for enlightenment,” and “Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person attained to [right] view should intentionally deprive a living being of life; such a case does not exist,” and so forth.

An Ariya person, even if staying in an indefinite distant place, is indeed united by the harmony of their own qualities. Because of the statement: “With such a view, he dwells attained to commonality of view; in such virtues, he dwells attained to commonality of virtue,” the state of being united by the power of commonality in view and virtue is also applicable to worldlings (puthujjana).

The word “saddhiṃ” is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of “together.” In the phrase “pañca... pe... mattāni,” the word “matta” is elided with the word “pañca” to form a bahiratthasamāsa (exocentric compound). “Etesaṃ” refers to those hundreds of monks. Furthermore, “pañca mattā pamāṇā” is the expanded sentence; here, since it is of the neuter gender, the elision of the nasal (niggahīta) should be understood.

“Suppiya” is merely his name, not a title of quality and so forth. It was not only the Blessed One who was traveling with the Saṅgha of monks; rather, the wanderer (paribbājaka) Suppiya also went together with the youth Brahmadatta—thus it combines the individuals. This combination is only because of the similarity in being travelers on the road, not because of similarity in virtue or conduct; thus it is said with “pi-kāro” and so forth.

For the sake of ease of pronunciation, intending only the connection between the preceding and following words, it is said “he makes a word-junction (padasandhi)”; it does not mean the types of sandhi such as vowel or consonant sandhi. Therefore, it is said: “It is spoken by way of the smoothness of consonants”; by this, it shows that it is merely a word-filler (padapūraṇa). Alternatively, the word “kho” is also appropriate in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), as in the passage “The brahmin Verañja heard (assosi kho).” By that word “kho,” it is shown that he was indeed traveling on the long road, and there was no obstacle to his journey.

“Sañjayassa” refers to the wanderer named Sañjaya who lived in Rājagaha, in whose presence Upatissa and Kolita also first went forth as wanderers.
184:
(Sañjaya) was a clothed wanderer (paribbājaka), not a naked ascetic (acelaka). By the words “yadā” and “tadā,” it shows that they were traveling on the long road at the same time. The word “hoti” in the Pali text denotes the past tense through grammatical division (yogavibhāga); or it is spoken in consideration of that past time, meaning “at that time, he was [traveling]."

“Ante” means “near.” The word “vasati” (dwells) is a general term applicable to all postures because of performing major and minor duties and so forth; it means he moves about (avacarati). Therefore, it was said: “A student who moves nearby, who stays in the presence.” “Coditā devadūtehi” means although they were urged, exhorted, and moved to spiritual urgency (saṃvega) by these five divine messengers: a young child, an old person, a sick person, one undergoing punishment (or one associated with punishment), and a dead person. They are called divine messengers (devadūta) because they are messengers like devas, or because they are messengers of the devas of purity (Buddhas and Arahants). “Hīnakaayūpagā” refers to those who have reached the woeful planes (apāya). The connection should be made as: “those youths (beings) called men (nara).” Here, a being is called “māṇava” (youth) in a general sense, while others like thieves or young people are meant specifically. This is the extraction of meaning according to the scriptures. “Katakammehi” means by the acts of theft that were committed.

“Taruṇa” refers to one who has reached twenty years of age starting from sixteen. For in the Udāna Commentary, it is said: “Beings from the day of birth until fifteen years are called ‘kumāraka’ and ‘bāla’; after that, those of twenty years are called ‘yuvāno’.” The terms taruṇa, māṇava, and yuvā are identical in meaning. In worldly usage, however, they also say “taruṇa” from twelve years until one reaches old age.

In the phrase “tesu vā,” the locative case is used in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa), meaning “among those two persons.” Alternatively, the word “tatra” refers back to the time previously mentioned as “ekaṃ samayaṃ” (at one time); for at the time when the Blessed One was traveling on the long road between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, at that very time Suppiya also, while traveling on that road, spoke in dispraise of the Buddha, and Brahmadatta spoke in praise of the Buddha. In the phrase “nipātamattaṃ,” the word “matta” shows the state of being a word-filler (padapūraṇa) because there is no special meaning. “Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyo” means “Remember this discourse (sutta) as the Honeyball Discourse.” By the word “rājañña,” he addresses the king named Pāyāsi Rājañña. It is called “pariyāya” because it revolves or recurs, meaning a turn (vāra). It is called “pariyāya” because it presents the meaning to be taught, meaning a teaching (desanā). It is called “pariyāya” because it proceeds after taking its own result, meaning a cause (kāraṇa). By the word “aneka” (not one) alone, the meaning “in many ways” is understood.
185:
The term "Adhippāyamattena" means "anekavidhena" (in many ways). Here, "cause" (kāraṇa) refers only to a pseudo-cause (kāraṇapatirūpaka) and is not a true cause, because the reason for dispraising is false. Therefore, "kāraṇena" means "by a pseudo-cause." This is indeed the truth. The Commentary will state later: "Having called what is not a cause a 'cause'." This term shows the singular inflection in a plural sense (jātivase) through the phrase "bahūhi," etc.

"Avannavirahitassa asamanavannasamannagatassāpi" is said to show that the reason to be mentioned later is not a true cause. It means "even of one who is free from faults and endowed with incomparable qualities." The connection should be made as "dispraising the dispraise (fault) of the Blessed Buddha." With "Yaṃ loke," etc., the pseudo-causes of being tasteless (arasarūpa), the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda), the doctrine of annihilation (ucchedavāda), being loathsome (jegucchī), being a nihilist (venayika), being an ascetic (tapassī), and being barren (apagabbha) are shown. Therefore, the word "tasmā" should be connected with the words "arasarūpo ... apagabbho."

This is what is meant: The "taste of concord" (sāmaggīrasa), consisting of salutation, rising from one's seat, joining hands in reverence, paying respect, and invitation with a seat, which is recognized in the world, does not exist for the ascetic Gotama. Therefore, that ascetic Gotama is of a nature not endowed with the taste of concord; he is not possessed of the enjoyment called the taste of concord. There is the view that one should not pay respect to those elders, and the view that [such customs] should be cut off. A man who loves ornaments loathes all that, just as he loathes excrement. He destroys those acts of salutation, etc. Because of not doing so, that ascetic Gotama should be disciplined. Because of not doing so, he causes distress to the elders. Or, because he is devoid of such conduct, he is a wretched man. Because of not doing so, he does not take rebirth in the womb of the deva world; or because of not doing so, he has a low rebirth. Thus, the very act of not performing salutations, etc., should be understood as the pseudo-cause for being "tasteless," etc.

In the sentence "Natthi ... viseso," pseudo-causes such as "not knowing the death of the female wanderer named Sundarī, the admission of not knowing the beginning of Saṃsāra, and answering questions that should be set aside" should be determined. Likewise, in the sentence "Takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo ... sayampaṭibhānaṃ," pseudo-causes such as "preaching the Dhamma here and there in such and such a way through self-realization without a teacher, questioning others in some places, and answering only in the manner reported by Mahāmoggallāna and others" are shown. In the sentences "Samaṇo ... na aggapuggalo," [it says] "of all dhammas..."
186:
...not knowing in sequence, not knowing the end of the world (Nibbāna), and the absence of the practice he himself desires, and so forth. States such as Jhāna and Vimokkha are called "Uttarimanussadhamma" (superhuman states), which are superior to the ten wholesome courses of action of humans, as mentioned below. The vision called pure or noble knowledge is "dassana." Because of having that noble knowledge and vision (ariyañāṇadassana) capable of destroying defilements, or because that state has noble knowledge and vision, it is called "alamariyañāṇadassana." That very "alamariyañāṇadassana" is specifically the superhuman state. Or, because of having the distinction of noble knowledge and vision capable of destroying defilements as mentioned, it is the superhuman state called "alamariyañāṇadassana-visesa."

"Takkapariyāhata" refers to that which is brought from all around by mere imagination or that which is constructed by reasoning (vitakka). "Vīmaṃsānucarita" refers to that which is repeatedly examined by investigative wisdom. "Sayampaṭibhāna" refers to that which is manifest to oneself alone without a teacher. Such a Dhamma should be understood in connection with "sayampaṭibhāna." "Akāraṇa" refers to an improper or incomplete reason. This word is a modifier (visesana) of the word "kāraṇa." The reason is that faults such as [bad] form or sound do not exist in the Blessed One. In the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, too, there are no "non-causes" (akāraṇa) such as being badly proclaimed or badly practiced. Or, "akāraṇa" is a mere personal admission devoid of proper reasoning. This is a basic object (pakatikammapada). In this sense, in the phrase "kāraṇaṃ vatvā," the word "kāraṇa" should be applied in the sense of a metaphor (rūpaka) as "like a cause," because a pseudo-cause is intended. "Tathā tathā" means by such and such modes, such as not saluting those who are senior by birth. Since the word "vanna" occurs in the sense of quality and praise, it is said respectively as "avanna" for fault (dosa) and "ninda" (dispraise).

"Durakkhāta" means badly proclaimed, and likewise, badly understood. It is called "niyyāna" because it leads out from the round of rebirths (vatta); that very "niyyāna" is "niyyānika." Or, it is "niyyānika" because it is associated with the exit (nissaraṇa) from the round of rebirths. Or, it is "niyyānika" because it leads out from the round of rebirths; here, the letter 'ya' is changed to 'ka' and the 'ī' is made short. Grammarians say that the suffix "aniya" mostly expresses the agent (kattar), but here "niyyānika" is not like that. As mentioned, that which does not lead to the calming of the suffering of Saṃsāra is called "anupasamasamvattanika." "Paccanīkapaṭipadā" refers to the practice contrary to the right practice. "Ananulomapaṭipadā" refers to the practice inappropriate for good people. "Adhammānulomapaṭipadā" refers to the practice inappropriate for the supramundane Dhamma.

Why is the present tense used here, saying "he speaks dispraise, he speaks praise"? From the time of the Council (Saṅgāyana), is it not true that the time of speaking that dispraise and praise has passed? This is true. However, just as the word "is" (hoti) in the phrase "is one who has entered the path" expresses the past tense, the word "speaks" (bhāsati) should also be understood to express the past tense. Alternatively, it is spoken in the present tense in consideration of the time when they were speaking dispraise and praise. At the time when those people speak dispraise and praise...
187: Regarding the time currently being spoken of, it is said thus. By doing so, the alternative interpretation of the word 'tatra' as a temporal reference, though not mentioned in the Commentary, is well-established. In the Pali 'Suppiyassa pana... pe... bhāsati,' the demonstration of the connection is the statement beginning with 'Antevāsī panassa.' The kamma of reviling the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) should not be touched, nor should it be stepped upon (transgressed). 'Svāyaṃ' refers to that teacher. 'Asidhāraṃ' means the sharp edge of a sword. 'Kakacadantapantiyam' means it is like a person playing by striking with hands, feet, or any major or minor limb against the uneven row of teeth known as the edge of a saw. An elephant that is in rut in three ways through the parts known as eyes, ears, and trunk-cavity is called 'pabhinnamada.' 'Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsamāno' is due to the reason of speaking dispraise. Here, the word 'māna' has the sense of cause (hetu). The absence of welfare is called 'anaya.' That very absence of welfare means ruin, or extreme ruin; he will reach ruin because reviling the Triple Gem is an action of great fault. Therefore, it is said: 'He who praises the blameworthy, Or he who blames the praiseworthy, He accumulates evil with his mouth, Through that evil, he finds no happiness.' After showing the arising of Brahmadatta’s sense of urgency (saṃvega) and the arising of compassion for his teacher with the words 'Amhākaṃ ācariyo' and so on—although a pupil should follow the teacher’s will—because this Brahmadatta was wise by nature, he did not follow the teacher’s will in such a matter. Now, wishing to show the arising of his knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), the text says 'Ācariye kho pana' and so on. 'Halāhala' is a poison that kills instantly. It is called 'hala' because it kills (hanati) (changing the letter 'n' to 'l'). Among the lethal poisons, it is an extraordinary poison, so it is called 'halāhala' by lengthening the middle vowel. By this word, the other eight types of poison are also excluded. It is said: 'In the masculine and neuter: kākola, kāḷakūṭa, halāhala, sotthika, suṅkika, brahmaputta, padīpana, dārada, and vacchanābha—these are the nine varieties of poison.'
188: 'Kharodaka' means a rough current of water. There is also a reading 'khārodaka,' which means bitter water because it is extremely salty. 'Narakapapāta' means a cliff where thieves fall. 'Māṇavaka' is an address to admonish oneself, as in the words 'Bhaddāli, the time was not penetrated by you' and so on. 'Kammassaka' means that kamma alone is one's own property, and it is explained by saying 'beings go to a destination according to their own kamma.' 'Yoniso' means by way of means or method. 'Ummujjitvā' means not remaining submerged in the unwise reviling of Noble Ones like the teacher, but emerging from the reviling of Noble Ones through wise means; it means rising upwards. 'Maddamāno' means crushing or breaking. Wishing to show that only the certain cause is the cause here, it is said 'sammā' (rightly). With the words 'yathā taṃ' and so on, his state of well-initiated effort is shown; 'ca' and 'na' are merely particles. This is what is meant: Just as another wise person, a man of good birth by virtue of birth and conduct, would undertake to speak the praise of the Triple Gem in many ways, so too did this person undertake it. It also means: 'May this teacher desist from speaking dispraise of the Triple Gem even by this much.' 'Sapparājavaṇṇa' means the color of a king of snakes. 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means because of beauty of color or with a body endowed with color. It means 'I do not strike or break the water-born lotus, but only smell it from afar.' 'Atha' means 'even though it is so.' 'Gandhatthena' means a fragrance-thief. 'Saññūḷhā' means tied or bound. 'Gahapati' is the address of Nātāputta to the householder Upāli. Here, 'vaṇṇa' means shape (saṇṭhāna) because it is shown as 'this person is like this.' 'Vaṇṇa' means caste (jāti) because it is defined without confusion. 'Vaṇṇa' means the base of visual form (rūpāyatana) because it manifests the state of the heart when undergoing change. 'Vaṇṇa' means cause (kāraṇa) because the effect is made clear according to its nature by this means. 'Vaṇṇa' means measure (pamāṇa) because it is measured by way of small or great, etc. 'Vaṇṇa' means quality (guṇa) because it is praised. 'Vaṇṇa' means praise (pasaṃsā) because it is the recitation of qualities. Thus, the occurrence of the word 'vaṇṇa' in various places should be understood. By the word 'ādi,' meanings such as gold (jātarūpa), sand (puḷina), and letters (akkhara) are included. The statement 'Here, it means both quality and praise' is supported by the words 'ayaṃ kira' and so on. Here, the word 'kira' is used in the sense of hearsay or as a mere expletive. 'Guṇūpasañhita' means endowed with qualities. By saying 'praise endowed with qualities,' the speaking of qualities within praise is established, because praise is inseparable from qualities. Therefore, it shows that both these meanings are appropriate.
189: How is it said? He says "Tattha" and so forth. Because that person is both unique and a person, he is called "Ekapuggala" (Unique Person). In what sense is he Ekapuggala? He is Ekapuggala in the sense of being incomparable, in the sense of being distinguished by excellence of qualities, and in the sense of being equal only to the incomparable. Indeed, from the time of his initial aspiration (abhinīhāra), beginning with the reflection on the ten perfections (pāramī) in due order, he is incomparable to the rest of the great multitude by virtue of fulfilling the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and by the qualities of a Buddha. Whatever qualities he possesses, those qualities are also superior to the qualities of other beings. The previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddhas) are unequal to all beings; however, this Buddha alone is equal to those previous Buddhas in terms of the physical body (rūpakāya) and the mental body (nāmakāya). "In the world" means in the world of beings (sattaloka). The phrase "the person being born is born" (uppajjamāno uppajjati) is an incomplete statement because it refers to the present time of the action of arising. It should be understood here that the person being born is born for the welfare of many, and for no other reason. Here, the word "māna" (in uppajjamāno) is in the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇa); such a characteristic cannot be refuted by any other grammatical rule. Furthermore, the distinction between "being born" (uppajjamāno), "is born" (uppajjati), and "has been born" (uppanno) should be understood. Indeed, from the time at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), he is called "being born." At the moment of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), he is called "is born." At the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), he is called "has been born." For Buddhas, unlike disciples, qualities such as the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividhañāṇa) do not arise in succession; rather, the entire mass of omniscient qualities (sabbaññuguṇarāsi) arrives together with the Path of Arahantship. Therefore, because all tasks are completed, he is called "has been born" at the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship. Because those tasks were not yet completed, at other moments he is appropriately called "the person being born is born." In this sutta as well, referring specifically to the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship, it is said "is born." Since the present tense is sometimes seen used in the sense of the past, the meaning here is "has been born." This being so, the word "māna" in "uppajjamāno" has the sense of capacity (sāmatthiya). The meaning is: having become endowed with the complete capacity that constitutes the requisites of enlightenment, to the extent that the arising of Great Bodhisattas in their final birth is desired. Because of being associated with such capacity, he is called "being born." He is incomparable to all beings and equal only to the incomparable previous Buddhas, without distinction, like a gold coin (nikkha) split in the middle; this is the description of the term "Ekapuggala." He is called "Ālayasamugghāta" because he uproots the craving known as attachment (ālaya). He is called "Vaṭṭupaccheda" because he cuts off the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). "Pahontena" means by one who is able. Although saying "the five Nikāyas," because they have many parts, it is not possible to encompass everything by this alone, so he said "the ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher (navaṅga-satthusāsana)..."
190: It is said, "Eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates (dhammakkhandha)." "Atitthena" means by a place that is not a landing place (a non-ford). Because of the immeasurable virtues of the Buddha and others, and because the explanation of the Pali is completed by showing those virtues without remainder in this commentary, and because it is fruitful by way of fulfilling the meditation subject that gladdens the mind, he should not be called (a Dhamma speaker who enters a non-ford). Strength (thāma) should be understood because it is shown with all one's power. As to how that youth Brahmadatta spoke after entering (the discussion) in such a manner, he said "Brahmadatto pana" and so forth. Hearing in succession or hearing repeatedly is called "Anussava," meaning hearsay or oral tradition. By the word "ādi," he includes logical reasoning (ākāraparivitakka) and intellectual conviction (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti). Among those two, reflecting repeatedly on a reason by oneself, such as "This reason is good," is called ākāraparivitakka. Pondering with one's own wisdom and then accepting or liking it is called diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti, as stated in the commentaries. The meaning is that it is associated only with those (hearsay, etc.). Here, the word "matta" has the sense of excluding anything special. By that word "matta," he excludes the aforementioned reason. "Attano thāmena" means it is only by the power of his own knowledge, but not in accordance with the actual virtues of the Buddha and others. Indeed, the virtues of the Buddha and others have innumerable and immeasurable divisions. For it is said: "Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha, speaking nothing else for an entire aeon, the long and extended aeon would come to an end, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted." In this Brahmajāla Sutta as well, he will preach "Appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ" and so forth. The word "iti" has the sense of illustration (nidassana) and points to the manner already described. The syllable "ha" is merely a particle, so he says "evaṃ te." To show that this term "aññamaññassa" is a conventional term (ruḷhī) like the term "eko ekāya," he explains it using the conventional term "añño aññassa." Having stated that "ujumeva" is an emphatic compound (avadhāraṇa-samāsa) with the word "eva," he states the meaning excluded by that word "eva" as "without avoiding even a little" (īsakam pi apariharitvā), meaning without deviating even the slightest bit. As to how this is, he says "ācariyena hi" and so forth. Although the speaking of dispraise and praise was previously indicated as if it happened once, because it is said "ujuvipaccanīkavādā," it should be understood that they spoke in this way many times; to show this, it is said "again, one spoke dispraise, the other spoke praise." By saying so, he establishes that the prefix "vi" has the sense of variety. "Sāraphalake" means...
191:
(They sit) on two wooden planks or on an excellent plank. "Visarukkha-āṇi" refers to a peg made of poisonous wood or a sharpened wooden peg smeared with poison. They followed in terms of physical posture, not in terms of following the right practice.

"Sīthānulokino" means those looking with their heads, looking up and observing the path as they proceed. "Tasmiṃ kāle" (At that time) refers to the year, season, month, or fortnight in which the Blessed One set out on that long journey. Indeed, by the term "tasmiṃ kāle," the year, season, month, and half-month are indicated indefinitely. This is because "on that day" (taṃ divasaṃ) is specified separately, and moments (muhutta) etc., are included within a day. In the phrase "taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno," the word (implied by kāle) denotes the location (ādhāra). Therefore, to show the continuity of the action, it is stated in the present tense along with preceding actions: "He wanders for alms in Rājagaha." Otherwise, an unintended meaning would arise: "At that time he wanders for alms in Rājagaha and [simultaneously] has set out on that long journey." Indeed, actions with different locations cannot have the same basis. Here, the intended action is "setting out on the long journey," and it is understood that this action does not occur indefinitely.

"Rājagahaparivattakesu" means in the monasteries surrounding Rājagaha. By the word "aññatarasmiṃ" (in a certain place), it shows the Blessed One's non-permanent residence in those monasteries. "So" (He) refers to the Blessed One residing in Rājagaha in this manner. By mentioning "wandering for alms," it shows his residence there as being connected to the purpose. If one were to interpret it as "That Blessed One, while wandering for alms," the unintended meaning mentioned above would arise. "Taṃ divasaṃ" means throughout the day on which he set out on the journey. In the phrase "taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno," this term expresses continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). "Pacchābhatta" means after the mealtime. "Piṇḍapātapakkanto" means one who has departed from the place where they wandered for and ate alms-food.

"Taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno" means he set out on that long journey, reflecting: "Desiring the accomplishment of various benefits and happiness for those to be tamed in Nālandā, I shall preach the Brahmajāla Sutta—adorned with the threefold virtue, destroying wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy and flattery, disentangling the net of sixty-two views, and causing the ten thousand world systems to tremble." This reason is not explicitly stated because it is clear from the context. Thus, the objection "Why did the Blessed One set out on that journey?" is cleared.

Now, to clear the other objection, it is said: "Suppiyopi." The terms "tasmiṃ kāle," "taṃ divasaṃ," and "anubandho" should be connected and considered according to the method already mentioned.
192:
Food eaten in the morning is called pātarāsa (breakfast), and one who has eaten it is bhuttapātarāsa. "In this way" means having only this in mind, and not thinking, "I will follow behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." Therefore, it is said: "Not knowing that the Blessed One had set out on that path." It means he followed while being thus ignorant. That person (Suppiya the wanderer) did not follow because he wished to see the Blessed One; therefore, it is said: "If he had known, he would not have followed." By this much, the objection "Why did Suppiya follow?" is cleared. With the word "so" etc., another objection is cleared. Sometimes the Blessed One travels in a disguised form, as in the cases of taming Aṅgulimāla or approaching King Pakkusāti. Sometimes he travels with the Buddha's glory (buddhasiri). Here, to show that he travels with such glory, it is said: "buddhasiriyā sobhamānaṃ" etc. Here, "siri" refers to the perfection of the body's beauty and so on. This glory is shown through similes such as "as if wrapped in a red blanket." Because he moves, he is called "jangama" (mobile), similar to the word "caṅkama." It means like the peak of a moving mountain, a golden mountain.

"Tasmiṃ kira" etc., is an explanation of that point. Teachers say that because it is not shown in the Pali and not found in the ancient commentaries (porāṇaṭṭhakathā), the word "kira" (it is said) is used to show that this story is established by tradition (anussava). Whether it be so or otherwise, what is not seen, heard, or experienced by oneself should be regarded as tradition (anussava). There are six-colored rays: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant. "Samantā" means from all around the ten directions. "The measure of eighty cubits" refers to the natural extent of those rays. Therefore, it should be understood that the rays remain naturally dense in a space of about eighty cubits all around and above. In the Vinaya-ṭīkā, these rays are called "byāmappabhā" (fathom-wide radiance). Since the six-colored rays run in the ten directions like water from a lake into a channel, and that radiance appears to be about a fathom, it is called "byāmappabhā." In the Saṅgīti Sutta Commentary, it will be said: "A gold-colored ray arises from the front of the body and occupies a space of eighty cubits. From the back of the body, from the right hand, from the left hand, a gold-colored ray arises and occupies a space of eighty cubits. Starting from the top of the head, from all the curls of hair, a peacock-neck-colored ray arises..."
193:
In the expanse of the sky, it occupies a space of eighty cubits. From the soles of the feet, a ray resembling the color of coral arises and occupies a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. Thus, within a surrounding area of eighty cubits, the six-colored rays of the Buddha shine, vibrate, and stream forth (as stated in the Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3, 299). Some teachers speak of other versions based on mere imagination; such statements should not be accepted because they do not appear in other scriptures and lack logical consistency. To show that those rays were not concealed at that time, it is said, "at that time." There was no reason to conceal those rays then, as there was during the first visit to King Pakkusāti and others. 'Ādhāvanti' means running towards a particular direction. 'Vidhāvanti' means becoming diverse and running towards the intermediate directions.

Meaning that the beauty of those rays is known by the manner in which they appear within that forest, it says "ratanāveḷā" and so on. 'Ratanāveḷā' (or āveḷā) refers to a jeweled crest or head-ornament; it is so called because it protects (avati) the head (muddhaṃ), meaning a head-garland. 'Ukkā' refers to meteors or torches that are luminous; they are mingled together by falling in hundreds and thousands. It is called 'piṭṭha' because it is ground; red powder produced in the country of Cīna (China) is called 'cīna-piṭṭha' (vermilion), also known as 'sindūra'. It is like powder thrown here and there by the force of the wind. It is called 'indadhanu' (Indra's bow/rainbow) according to worldly convention; it is a special appearance in the sky caused by sunlight. It is called 'vijju' (lightning) because it is crooked and runs swiftly without lasting long; it is called 'vijjulatā' because it resembles a creeper, being a radiance produced by the clashing of clouds due to the force of the wind. It is called 'tārā' (stars) because it protects the sky without leaving it; the word 'gaṇa' (group) should be applied to each. The light of that rainbow, lightning, and stars is as if spreading diversely and shining brightly.

'Vanantara' refers to the interior of the forest, meaning the area of the Sattapaṇṇi grove where the Blessed One resided.

He is graced by the eighty minor marks, such as copper-colored nails and so on. The Paduma and Puṇḍarīka lotuses are called 'kamala', while the remaining blue, red, and white lotuses born in lakes are called 'uppala'; thus, the five kinds of lotuses are included. A lake that has both these kinds of lotuses in bloom is called 'vikkasita-padumuppala'. It is called 'sabbapāliphualla' because it blossoms all around in every way (changing the 'a' to 'ā' and 'r' to 'l', similar to 'pālibhadda'). It shines with the radiance of the stars. He is graceful with a fathom-wide circle of rays. Because the marks of a Great Man are interconnected, they exist in the manner of a florist's garland, hence called 'dvattiṃsa-vara-lakkhaṇa-mālā' (the garland of thirty-two excellent marks). Although it cannot be said that someone has strung thirty-two moons and placed them in order, it is said so by way of mere imagination, as in "a garland of thirty-two moons strung together."
194:
Just as it shines with the light of the stars, it has a surrounding circle of rays extending one fathom (byāmappabhā); He is elegant and beautiful with that fathom-wide radiance. Because the marks of a Great Man are interconnected like a garland made by a florist, it is called "the garland of thirty-two excellent marks." Although it cannot be said that someone has strung thirty-two moons and placed them in order, it is said by way of mere imagination (parikappanā), "a garland of thirty-two moons strung and placed." This is a hypothetical simile (parikappūpamā), which is also seen in the world:

"The moon's boasting that 'the beauty of the face exists only in me' is not proper,
Since that beauty of the face also exists in the lotus; this is a hypothetical simile."

It is connected as: "as if overwhelming the glory of a garland of thirty-two moons with His own glory." This method should be understood in the remaining cases as well.

Having thus shown the beauty of the Blessed One at that time, he now says "tañca pana" etc., to show the beauty of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. They are of few wishes (appiccha) by being endowed with the four kinds of fewness of wishes. They are contented (santuṭṭha) with the twelve kinds of contentment. They are secluded (pavivitta) by the three kinds of seclusion. They do not mix with kings, royal ministers, and so on. They are admonishers of those who practice wrongly. They are censurers of evil, unwholesome things. They are speakers for the welfare of others. They are patient with the words of others. 'Vimutti-ñāṇadassana' refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). With the words "tesaṃ" etc., he shows the beauty of the Blessed One in connection with that simile. A multitude or group of red lotuses is a forest; it is as if He moves in the midst of that forest of red lotuses. This is said without the restriction of petals, where "red lotus is paduma, white is puṇḍarīka." However, by the restriction of petals, a lotus with a hundred petals is a paduma, and one with fewer than a hundred petals is a puṇḍarīka. 'Pavāḷa' refers to coral; it is as if surrounded by a railing made of that coral. In the word "migapakkhīnampi," the word "pi" or "api" is used in the sense of commendation; therefore, he says, "not to mention gods and humans." 'Mahāthera' refers to the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka). Due to being well-adorned, they have a slightly dark hue, like the color of a rain cloud. "Ekaṃsaṃ karitvā" means placing the robe over one shoulder, specifically the left shoulder. The staff used as a support by the elderly is called 'kattara-daṇḍa'; this name is generally given because of its use by the aged. 'Suvamma' refers to a beautiful breastplate or cover; being girded with that is 'suvamma-vammita', which illustrates their wearing of rag-robes (paṃsukūla). Those elephants in whose bellies everything, even dry grass and leaves, becomes fragrant are called 'gandhahatthī' (scented elephants), also known as 'hemavata' elephants; those elders are similar to them because of the fragrance of their virtues such as morality (sīla).
195:
They are called 'vijatitajatā' because they have disentangled the tangle of craving, known as the internal and external tangles, by means of the Path. They are called 'chinnabandhanā' because they have severed the bonds of craving by means of the Path of Arahantship. The word 'so' and others are meant to show the qualities of the aforementioned words. 'Anubuddhehi' refers to the Arahants who realized the Four Noble Truths following the Buddhas who realized the Four Noble Truths. These Arahants also realize the Four Noble Truths partially, in the same manner as they were penetrated by the Blessed One. 'Pattaparivāritaṃ' means surrounded by petals. The lotus and such are called 'kaṃ'; because it is beautiful therein, it is called 'kesara' (pollen/filament). Because it is placed at the center, it is called 'kaṇṇikā'. Because it has a shape similar to a central ornament, the seed-pod is also called 'kaṇṇikā'. (The Buddha is beautiful) like the Dhataraṭṭha swan king, who is superior to the six tribes of swans, or like the Mahābrahmā named Hārita.

Seeing the Blessed One and the monks traveling in this manner, he looked at his own assembly—this is how the connection should be made. 'Kājadaṇḍaka' refers to a carrying pole that bears a load, or a stick on which a load is hung from a carrying pole. A small stool is called 'pīṭhaka'. A staff made into three prongs at the base and the tip is called 'tidaṇḍa'. 'Morahatthaka' is a bundle of peacock feathers. A small bag is called 'pasibbaka'. 'Kuṇḍikā' is a water-pitcher. It is called 'kuṇḍikā' by way of etymology because it increases water, or because it protects it. One is called 'gahitabhārabharitā' because they carry a load consisting of many requisites such as small stools, peacock-feather bundles, clay bowls, small bags, and water-pitchers, which are taken up as inferior items and are various and troublesome. The word 'iti' has the sense of pointing out. The word 'evaṃ' has the sense of 'this'. Because there is a speech beginning with 'this', it is called 'evamādi'. Because there is such profitless speech, it is called 'evamādiniratthakavacanā'. One is called 'mukharā' because they have a mouth. Although everyone has a mouth, this is said because this person has a mouth that speaks harsh words. This suffix 'ra' is used in the sense of reproach. Alternatively, one is called 'mukharā' because they take up unpleasant unwholesome kamma with their mouth. One is called 'vikiṇṇavācā' because they have various and scattered speech. 'Tassa' refers to Suppiya the wanderer. 'Taṃ' refers to the assembly of the aforementioned kind.

'Idāni' refers to the moment of seeing such an assembly. The word 'pana' has the sense of indicating displeasure, meaning 'even so'. It is because it is the cause of the loss of gain and honor. To answer the potential question 'How is there loss?', he said 'aññatitthiyānaṃ' and so forth. 'Nissirīkataṃ' means reaching the state of being without beauty; this meaning should also be understood through the Mora Jātaka and others. Through the words 'upatissakolitānañca' and so forth, the detail of the loss of the following should be understood. 'Tesu pana pakkantesu' is said with reference to the going forth of the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the presence of the Blessed One. At the very time those Venerables went forth, two hundred and fifty followers of the wanderers also went forth; after that...
196:
Furthermore, the words 'that assembly of theirs was also broken' show that the assembly of wanderers who followed them and went forth was immeasurable. It is said so because whenever any assembly of wanderers goes forth, the assembly of that Suppiya the wanderer is indeed considered broken due to being of the same sect. Through the words 'imehi' and so forth, the loss of the faction of gain is shown by way of conclusion. The vomiting of the poison known as envy is 'usūyavisuggāro'. Here, only through the words 'yasmā panesā' and so forth is the objection 'Why does that person speak dispraise of the Triple Gem?' resolved. Since all the words starting with 'sace' are merely peripheral to that speech, the objection is considered resolved by those words as well. They speak dispraise or praise to test the Blessed One's lack of resentment or favor (opposition or non-opposition). Although some teachers say, 'They speak thus because they are possessed by Māra,' that statement is inappropriate because it directly contradicts the Commentary. This meaning is quite clear.

The connection should be made as: 'Because the sun has set, it is now not the time to travel.'

'Ambalaṭṭhikā' is a metaphorical usage based on proximity, like 'Varuṇanagara' or 'Godāgāma'; this is stated with 'tassa kirā' and so forth. The word 'laṭṭhikā' is a synonym for 'taruṇa' (young/sapling) in the context of trees, as in 'Having entered the Great Forest, he sat for the day-rest at the foot of a young bael tree (beluvalaṭṭhikā)'; this is shown by the words 'taruṇambarukkho' (young mango tree). However, some teachers say that 'Ambalaṭṭhikā' is a village according to the method mentioned. In their view, the locative case 'Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ' expresses the sense of 'near'. 'Chāyūdakasampannaṃ' means being endowed with both shade and water. 'Mañjūsā' means a box or a casket. 'Paṭibhānacittavicittaṃ' means decorated with imaginative paintings such as the union of men and women. By this, it is shown that it refers to the king's house, and that very king's house is called 'rājāgārakaṃ'. Some say that 'rājāgārakaṃ' is the shrine of the Great King Vessavaṇa.

'Bahuparissayo' means having many dangers. If asked 'By whom?', it is said 'by thieves' and so forth. The particle 'handa' is used in the sense of relinquishing speech. The meaning is: 'By the power of the Blessed One, so that there may be no danger, I will now go to the park and travel tomorrow.' In the Sinhalese Commentary, it is only said 'together with the pupil Brahmadatta the youth.' That statement is also only according to what is recorded in the Pāḷi; it is not because Suppiya's assembly did not exist at that time. To show this meaning, it is said here 'together with his own assembly.' As to why only Brahmadatta the youth is included in the Pāḷi here, and not the rest of Suppiya's assembly...
197:
Why is it called an "assembly" (*parisā*)? Because it is not dependent on the teaching (*desanā*), it is without purpose. Just like this statement, other similar statements should be understood as not having been rehearsed by the Elders who performed the Rehearsal (*saṅgītikāraka*) because they lack purpose. Some teachers, citing "It is said in the Pāḷi," say, "This statement does not show the view of the Sinhalese Commentary (*Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā*), but only shows the fact that it was spoken in the Pāḷi." That is not appropriate. This is because the intended meaning of "It is said in the Pāḷi" is reached only through the fact of it being included in the Rehearsal of the Pāḷi. Therefore, the meaning should be taken only according to the method already mentioned. Alternatively, "*vuttaṃ*" means "it is said by us in this Commentary." Only if said this way is it appropriate to show that an assembly other than the Venerable's assembly was present at that time; however, by way of being included in the Pāḷi, the teachers say the meaning "it should be said here in another way" is also suitable.

Now, to show the connection of the Pāḷi beginning with "*tatrapi sudaṃ*," the passage beginning with "*evaṃ vāsaṃ upagato pana*" is stated. The connection should be made as "he was sitting surrounding [him]." The state of doing a loathsome deed is called remorse (*kukkucca*). It means a loathsome action, a trembling here and there. Remorse of the hands is the same. With the words "*sā hi*," etc., the cause for being so is shown. "*Nivāte*" means in a place free from wind. Because of the absence of the aforementioned faults, there is no trembling. "*Taṃ vibhūtiṃ*" refers to such splendor. "*Vippalapanti*" means they babble various things due to a lapse of mindfulness. "*Nillālita-jivhā*" means they have tongues protruding here and there. "*Kākacchamānā*" means making a sound similar to the sound of crows. "*Gharugharu-passāsino*" means breathing out and in while producing the sound "gharu-gharu" (or *chauk-chauk*). "*Issāvasena*" means by way of envy due to the two aforementioned reasons. By the words "*sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ*," it is shown that "this is the method of abbreviation (*peyyāla*)."

Because they are well able to perform various tasks, they are called "*sambahulā*"; it means "many." Therefore, it was said "*bahukānaṃ*." Because a Vinaya act (*vinayakamma*) must be performed by a Saṅgha of at least four members, the passage beginning with "*vinayapariyāyena*" is stated. The expression "*tayo janā*" (three persons) is a designation that indicates "many" (*sambahula*) even in the case of two persons. Because it appears exactly like that in various Pāḷi passages, the passage beginning with "*suttantapariyāyena*" is stated. This distinction is made only by the power of the terminology found in those various Pāḷi texts. Three persons are called "three" specifically; from then on, four, five, etc., are meant by "many" (*sambahulā*). The word "*tato*" is a limit (*avadhi*) showing the boundary. "*Maṇḍalamāḷo*" is a common name used in many senses, but here, wishing to restrict it to this specific kind of name, the passage beginning with "*katthaci*" is stated. The pinnacle (*kaṇṇikā*) is called the peak (*kūṭa*). "*Haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena*" means by way of a circular covering like a swan's wing. That very covering...
198:
In another text, it is said as "*supaṇṇavaṅkacchadana*" (covered like a Garuda's wing). A house joined with a peak is itself a hall, thus it is a gabled hall (*kūṭāgārasālā*). "Surrounding the row of pillars" means having made a row of pillars in a circular shape. An attendance hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) is a hall for waiting upon/service. In that hall, they only perform attendance; they do not sit for one or two nights, etc. However, in this context, such a sitting hall is shown by the words "But here," etc. Therefore, in the Pāḷi, it is not said merely as "those who assembled," but also as "those who were sitting." It is called "*māḷo*" because it should be honored (*mānitabbo*), or it is called "*māḷo*" because it is measured (*mīyati pamīyati*). A pavilion covered in a circular shape is a "*maṇḍalamāḷo*"; it is a special kind of shelter with many corners. "Those who were sitting" is said by way of the act of sitting, or the connection is made by inserting the word to be explained as "those who were sitting" by way of the act of sitting. By this, it is shown that these two words are spoken referring to the posture of sitting and the gathering by way of physical unity (*kāya-sāmaggī*). Conversation (*kathā*) is called "*saṅkhiyā*" because of being well-spoken or told. "*Kathādhammo*" is the nature of the talk; some say it is the method of investigation.

The passage beginning with "*acchariyaṃ*" is stated to show the manifestation of that *kathādhammo*, hence "What kind of *kathādhammo* is it?" etc. "*So*" refers to that *kathādhammo*. Venerable Dhammapāla Thera said, "It is called *naya* (method) because it is led; it is the meaning. A method that follows the science of grammar is *saddanaya* (linguistic method)." Or, it is called *naya* because the meaning is known by this; it is a means (*upāya*). The means of grasping the meaning found in the science of grammar is *saddanaya*. For in that *saddanaya*, the word "*acchariya*" is desired in the sense of something that does not occur frequently, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*). Therefore, it is said, "Like a blind man climbing a mountain," etc. For that blind man's climbing of a mountain is not constant; it might happen only once in a while; so too is this matter. It is called "*acchariya*" because it is worthy of a snap of the fingers (*acchara*), either because the word "*yogga*" (worthy) is elided according to the method of Nirutti (etymology), or because of the diverse meanings of the suffix *ṇiya* by way of Taddhita (derivative). That method is called "*aṭṭhakathānaya*" (the method of the Commentaries) because it appears only in the ancient Commentaries. That which has not happened before is called "*abhūtapubba*"; by this, the definition "not happened is *abhūta*" and the past sense of the word "*bhūta*" are shown. In "*yāvañcidaṃ*," the *niggahīta* (nasal) comes by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), so it is said as "*yāva ca idaṃ*"; this word is connected with the word "*suppaṭividitā*." The meaning, including the remaining text, is: "To what extent this diversity of dispositions (*nānādhimuttikatā*) has been well-penetrated [by the Buddha], we are not able to penetrate or to describe that wonder as 'it is only this much'." Therefore, it is said, "By its being so well-penetrated, he shows its immeasurability."
199:
Because it is stated in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with terms such as 'Bhagavatā', the word 'tena' (by him) in this context is a reflexive reference to its own meaning (sakattha-paṭiniddesa). Therefore, the Blessed One is well-known because of that state of being fully awakened; and wishing to show that state of being fully awakened, along with the practice for attaining it, as the meaning of that word 'tena', [the commentator] said 'yo so' (he who), and so on. For here, there is no previously mentioned meaning that should be referred to by the elders with the word 'tena'. Therefore, it should be understood that it primarily refers to its own meaning, which is the aforementioned quality (guṇa).

'Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment' (anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ) refers to the Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) which has the Knowledge of the Highest Path (aggamagga-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause, and the Knowledge of the Highest Path which has the Unobstructed Knowledge as its proximate cause. Because both of these understand correctly, without distortion, and by themselves, or because they understand excellently as praised, it is called 'Sammāsambodhi'. This Sammāsambodhi bestows the fulfillment of all qualities upon the Buddhas, just as the consecration (abhiseka) of kings bestows sovereignty over the whole world. Therefore, it is called 'Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment'. 'Abhisambuddho' means he has fully realized and penetrated; it means the Blessed One who is endowed with such qualities.

Although 'knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) are synonyms for wisdom (paññā) here, [the commentator] said 'of those various beings' (tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ) etc., wishing to show the occurrence of their specific objects through those respective distinctions. Here, the first meaning is shown by way of the Unique Knowledge (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). It means knowing through the Knowledge of Inclinations and Latent Tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and seeing through Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa).

The second meaning is shown by way of the Threefold Knowledge (vijjā-ttaya). 'By means of recollection of past lives, etc.' (pubbenivāsādīhi) means by the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives and the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). The third meaning is shown by way of Direct Knowledge (abhiññā) and Unobstructed Knowledge. Although included within Direct Knowledge, the phrase 'by the three knowledges' is used to show the distinction of those groups. It means seeing with the Eye of All-Round Vision (samanta-cakkhu), which is called Unobstructed Knowledge.

The fourth meaning is shown by way of Omniscience and the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu). 'By wisdom' (paññāya) means by Omniscience. He sees things that have reached the other side or the inside of a wall, etc., with the physical eye, which is extremely pure, endowed with five colors, adorned with beautiful eyelashes, and capable of seeing for one league (yojana) all around, both by night and by day.

The fifth meaning is shown by way of Penetrative Knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and Teaching Knowledge (desanā-ñāṇa). Although it is said primarily as 'accomplishing one's own benefit', figuratively it also accomplishes the benefit of others. For through that wisdom, which uproots the defilements that shroud the nature of things, Teaching Knowledge and so on arise. 'Penetrative wisdom' (paṭivedha-paññā) refers to the wisdom of the Noble Path. Concentration (samādhi) associated with insight (vipassanā)...
200:
Because the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of this penetrative wisdom is concentration, it is said to have concentration as its proximate cause (samādhi-padaṭṭhāna). 'Teaching wisdom' (desanā-paññā) refers to Omniscience which accomplishes the task of teaching. 'Arīnaṃ' (of enemies) refers to the enemies of defilements, or the five Māras, or the heretics who are enemies of the Dispensation. Their 'killing' (hanana) means overcoming them with miracles (pāṭihāriya), making them unable to respond (rendering them obscure), and looking on with equanimity. Here, the Caṅkī Sutta, chanted in the fifth vagga of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, is an illustration. By the grammatical method (nirutti-naya), the formation of the word is stated as 'the enemies were killed by him'. Therefore, it should be noted that the 'nā' suffix is indicated as 'tā' by the Mahāvisaya rule. Alternatively, the word is formed with the 'anta' suffix in the sense of 'he kills the enemies', and the letter 'i' is changed to 'a'. The teacher of the commentary shows the meaning 'Arahaṃ' by the phrase 'and because of being worthy of requisites, etc.', meaning he is worthy of receiving or accepting requisites and so on, which are the objects of donation. 'Sammā' means without distortion. 'Sāmaṃ' means by himself, meaning he understood without being led by others.

How is the specific term 'of all phenomena' (sabba-dhammānaṃ) obtained here? It is obtained because a general indication resides in the specific, and because one who desires the specific must apply the specific accordingly. If this is so, only the specific 'of phenomena' (dhammānaṃ) should be applied; why is the meaning 'of all phenomena' applied? It is because of not taking only a part, but wishing to take without remainder. Only when there is no taking of a part is the state of having no remainder of the meaning to be taken understood. For example, as in the saying 'The monk does not give'. This method should be understood in such cases.

Now, in order to show the sixth meaning, which is more intended by himself, by way of the Fourfold Intrepidity (vesārajja) through the four words, the commentator said 'or the obstructive states' (antarāyika-dhamme vā), and so on. For that reason, he makes the conclusion with the words 'thus' (evaṃ), and so on. In that passage, it should be applied respectively: knowing by the knowledge of states that cause obstacles, seeing by the knowledge of states that lead out [of saṃsāra], being worthy (arahaṃ) by the knowledge of the destruction of taints, and being perfectly awakened (sammāsambuddha) by knowing all phenomena without distortion by himself through Omniscience. Because they perform what is harmful, the defilements themselves are enemies; thus they are called 'enemies of defilements' (kilesāraya). Here, some teachers say: The Blessed One is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has known all phenomena correctly and by himself through the power of Omniscience. Does this Omniscience, when occurring by way of knowing all phenomena, occur in all objects at once, or sequentially? Furthermore, in this inquiry, state what remains. If it occurs in all objects at once, then when the conditioned phenomena, which are divided into past, future, present, internal, external, etc., and the unconditioned and conventional phenomena appear together, the understanding would be a confused one, like someone looking at a complex painting from a distance. If that were the case, 'all phenomena'...
201:
“All phenomena are not-self.” Just as those practicing insight perceive the mode of not-self, it might be argued that all phenomena become objects of the Blessed One's knowledge in an undefined manner. Some teachers also say, “The knowledge of the Buddhas exists at all times, without differentiation, regarding the present characteristic of all knowable phenomena; therefore, they are called ‘All-knowers’ (Sabbavidū).” By doing so, they say the words of the Nāgopama Sutta from the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which illustrates the constant occurrence of knowledge, are well-spoken:

“The Great Elephant (the Buddha) is composed while walking, the Great Elephant is composed while standing, the Great Elephant is composed while lying down, and even while sitting, the Great Elephant is composed.”

Even in the view of those teachers, the aforementioned fault cannot be avoided. Because of taking the present characteristic as an object, and because that present characteristic does not exist in past and future phenomena, the Blessed One's knowledge would only have a partial object. Therefore, the meaning that knowledge occurs for all objects at once is not tenable. If it is said that knowledge occurs for all objects sequentially, that is also not tenable. Indeed, when taking knowable things sequentially—which are divided into many types by way of plane of existence, direction, place, time, etc.—complete penetration without remainder is impossible because knowable things are infinite.
