However, some teachers say: “Because the nature of the meaning is consistent, by directly perceiving a portion of knowable things and determining that ‘it is the same for the rest,’ the Blessed One becomes known as ‘Omniscient.’ That knowledge is not called inferential (anumānika) because there is no doubt. In the world, only knowledge accompanied by doubt is called inferential.” The words of those teachers are also not tenable. This is because if everything is not directly perceived, it is impossible and unfeasible to determine that “it is the same for the rest” by merely perceiving a portion due to the consistency of the meaning. That which remains is indeed not directly perceived. If that remainder were also directly perceived, it would no longer be a “remainder.” Since knowable things are infinite, such a determination is simply not possible.

All of this is baseless. Why? Because it is an investigation into what is beyond one's range (avisaya). For it was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, the range of the Buddhas (Buddhavisaya) is unthinkable; it should not be thought about; one who thinks about it would partake of madness and vexation.” The conclusion here is: whenever the Blessed One wishes to know anything, whether the whole or a part, His knowledge occurs through direct perception because of its unobstructed nature in those various objects. He also has constant concentration because of the absence of distraction. Since all things to be known are not outside His range, the occurrence of that knowledge in connection with His wish would not be impossible (it indeed occurs). 

This is because it is said: “All phenomena are connected to the Blessed One's advertence, wish, attention, and thought-arising.” Even regarding past and future objects, the Blessed One's knowledge is direct perception because it is free from discursive reflection. There is no room for objection in this matter. In this view, at the time when all phenomena need to be known, the Omniscient Knowledge takes everything as an object at once, and in an indistinct manner...
202:
That omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is indeed to be desired. This is because it is stated: "All things are connected to the adverting (āvajjana) of the Blessed Buddha, connected to His desire, connected to His mental application (manasikāra), and connected to the arising of thought (cittuppāda)" (Mahāniddesa 69, 156; Cūḷaniddesa 85; Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.5). Even regarding objects of the past and future, the Buddha's knowledge is purely direct perception (paccakkha), as it is free from grasping through inference (anumāna), scripture (āgama), or logic (takka).

One might ask: In this case, when there is a desire to know everything, would not the Buddha's knowledge occur simultaneously with all objects in an indistinct manner? If so, would it not be impossible to escape the fault (dosa) mentioned previously? This is not so, because that fault has been cleared away. Indeed, it has been cleared by the fact that the range of a Buddha (buddhavisaya) is inconceivable (acinteyya). Otherwise, if it functioned similarly to the knowledge of ordinary people, the knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas would not be inconceivable. Therefore, although it takes all things as its object, that knowledge functions by clearly defining those things as if it were taking a single thing as its object; this point is inconceivable here. "As far as the knowable (ñeyya) extends, so far does knowledge (ñāṇa) extend. As far as knowledge extends, so far does the knowable extend. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not occur beyond the knowable; there is no path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These things stand within each other's limits. For example, of two well-fitted casket lids (samuggapala), the lower lid does not exceed the upper, and the upper lid does not exceed the lower; they stand within each other's limits. In the same way, the knowable and the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha stand within each other's limits... those things." Thus, by the power of that knowledge which occurs collectively, individually, simultaneously, or sequentially according to His desire, the Blessed Buddha is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because He has rightly and by Himself known all things.

Here, the method independent of the commentary (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka) is as follows: He is praised in four ways by the power of the Ten-Power Knowledge (dasabalaññāṇa): as one who knows the six objects such as the possible and the impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna) through the six knowledges; as one who sees beings according to their karma through the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapātaññāṇa) and the divine eye (dibbacakkhu); as an Arahant because the defilements (āsava) along with their residual impressions (vāsanā) have been exhausted by the knowledge of the destruction of the defilements (āsavakkhayaññāṇa); and as a Sammāsambuddha because He has rightly and by Himself understood things such as the jhānas in terms of their defilement and purification. Furthermore, He is praised: as one who knows with unimpeded knowledge regarding the three periods of time; as one who sees by acting with circumspection because His three types of actions (bodily, verbal, and mental) follow His knowledge; as an Arahant because of His attainment of abandonment (pahānasampadā) which effects the absence of playfulness, error, and so on; and because of His omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which effects the inexhaustibility that is the cause for the non-diminution of His zeal (chanda) and other qualities...
203:
The Blessed Buddha, who has personally penetrated and known all things without distortion, is thus to be understood as being connected with the Buddha-qualities enumerated through the meanings of knowing, seeing, abandoning, and penetrating, such as by the power of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadhamma) and by being praised in four ways.

The phrase "in four ways" is said with reference to the fourfold knowledge of fearlessness (catuvesārajja). By the word "praised" (thomitena), it shows that this is an attribute (visesana) of the word "by the Blessed One" (bhagavatā). Although inclination (adhimutti) is mentioned in the Pali only in two ways—as low and exalted—it is actually divided into many types according to the manner of its occurrence; therefore, it is said: "diversity of inclinations" (nānādhimuttikatā). That inclination is indeed the disposition (ajjhāsaya-dhātu). That disposition also makes known the meaning of seeing, liking, and desiring in various ways through the term "diversity of dispositions" (nānajjhāsayatā). For it will be said later: "diversity of inclinations, diversity of dispositions, diversity of views, diversity of preferences, diversity of likings." The term "yāvañcidaṃ" should be connected with "suppaṭividitā." Therein, the word "idaṃ" is a mere particle (padapūraṇa), or it has the same grammatical footing (samānādhikaraṇa) as the word "nānādhimuttikatā." Since its meaning is clear, it is said: "yāva ca suṭṭhu paṭividitā" (as far as it is well penetrated and known).

Showing the Dhātusaṃyutta Pali with the words "yā ca ayaṃ" and so on, and keeping that Dhātusaṃyutta in mind, [the author] shows that this nature of the discourse arose for the elders in connection with the speaking of blame and praise of those [teachers and pupils]. For that reason, it should be understood that the words "ayaṃ hi" and so on are spoken to establish the state of being well penetrated and known of those [inclinations, etc.] according to the method of the Dhātusaṃyutta teaching of the Blessed One. The statement beginning with "ayaṃ hi" is indeed a statement that establishes the state of being well penetrated and known. In that sentence, the words should be connected as: "yā ayaṃ nānādhimuttikatā ...pe... rucitā." "By way of elements" (dhātuso) means by the dispositional element (ajjhāsaya-dhātu). "They associate" (saṃsandanti) means they connect or become intimate. "They meet" (samenti) means they rightly or together exist. The passage beginning with "those of low inclinations" (hīnādhimuttikā) is an explanation of that state. "Even in the past time" (atītampi addhānaṃ) means in the past; this is an accusative of duration (accantasaṃyoga). The meaning of the word "nānādhimuttikatā" is "nānajjhāsayatā." "Diversity of views ...pe... likings" is the demonstration of the nature of that [diversity of inclinations]. "Diversity of views" (nānādiṭṭhikatā) is by the power of beliefs such as eternalism. "Diversity of preferences" (nānakkhantitā) is by the power of natures such as bad conduct and good conduct. "Diversity of likings" (nānārucitā) is by the power of states such as having evil desires or few desires. "By a nāḷi" (nāḷiyā) means by a tumba or by an āḷhaka [measures of capacity]. "By a balance" (tulāyāti) means by a scale which is a means of weighing.

In this context, regarding "knowledge of the diversity of inclinations," only omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is intended, not the knowledge of the ten powers (dasabalaññāṇa) (so says the commentator).
204:
The commentator says, "by omniscience" (*sabbaññutañāṇena*). In this way, the teacher Dhammapāla Thera also stated (in the Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā); it also appears thus in the Abhidhamma Commentary and the Dasabala Sutta Commentaries.

An opponent (*paravādī*), however, says: "There is no separate knowledge called the Ten-Power Knowledge; this division of the Ten-Power Knowledge is merely a division of Omniscience." That should not be regarded so. For the Ten-Power Knowledge is one thing, and Omniscience is another, distinct from it. Indeed, the Ten-Power Knowledge knows only its own function, whereas Omniscience knows both the function of that Ten-Power Knowledge and everything remaining beyond it.

Among the Ten-Power Knowledges, the first knowledge knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause (*kāraṇākāraṇa*); the second knows only the distinctions of karma and its results (*kammantara-vipākantara*); the third knows only the delimitation of karma (*kammapariccheda*); the fourth knows only the cause of the diversity of elements (*dhātunānattakāraṇa*); the fifth knows only the inclinations and dispositions of beings (*sattānamajjhāsayādhimutti*); the sixth knows only the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāva*); the seventh knows only the defilements and so on of the jhānas and so forth, along with those states; the eighth knows only the succession of aggregates lived in the past (*pubbenivuttha-kkhandhasantati*); the ninth knows only the death and rebirth of beings (*sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhi*); the tenth knows only the delimitation of the Four Truths (*saccapariccheda*). Omniscience, however, knows what is to be known by these Ten-Power Knowledges and also what is beyond them. Nevertheless, Omniscience cannot perform all the functions of those Ten-Power Knowledges. It cannot become a jhāna and attain absorption (*appetun*); it cannot become a psychic power and perform transformations (*vikubbitun*); it cannot become a Path (*magga*) and exhaust the defilements.

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked this: "Is this Ten-Power Knowledge with initial and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), with sustained thought only (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), or without initial and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*)? Is it of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)? Is it mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*)?" An opponent who understands will say that the first seven knowledges in sequence are "with initial and sustained thought"; then he will say the next two are "without initial and sustained thought"; and regarding the knowledge of the destruction of taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*), he will say "it may be with initial and sustained thought, it may be with sustained thought only, or it may be without initial and sustained thought." Likewise, he will say the first seven in sequence are of the sense sphere, the next two are of the fine-material sphere, and the final one is supramundane. Omniscience, however, is only with initial and sustained thought, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane.

Thus, the Ten-Power Knowledge is one thing, and Omniscience is another, distinct from it. Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is "known by both the knowledge of the diversity of dispositions (*nānādhimuttikatāñāṇa*), which is called the fifth power, and by Omniscience." Indeed, the particle "ca" (and) is also seen in some books. "Sā" (that) refers to the aforementioned diversity of dispositions. By the words beginning with "dvepi nāmā," he shows the meaning of the aforementioned sutta in brief; and by the words beginning with "imesu cāpī," he reveals the connection of those enumerated states in that sutta. In the phrase "iti ha me," the word "iti" has the meaning of "evaṃ" (thus), and the syllable "ha" is a mere particle (*nipāta*) or an augment (*āgama*).
205:
By the words "evaṃ ime," he shows the dropping of the letter 'i' or the substitution of 'a' for 'i' due to the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

In the word "viditvā" (having known), although the action of knowing, which is the meaning of the root, is generally without division, the words beginning with "bhagavā hi" are stated to show that it has many divisions because of its suitability for various instruments (*karaṇa*). "Vatthūni" refers to house-sites. The statement "He saw and knew with Omniscience" is merely a conventional expression (*vohāravacanamatta*). For there is no knowing other than the seeing by that knowledge. This knowledge proceeds by being connected to advertence (*āvajjana*), connected to wish (*ākaṅkhā*), connected to attention (*manasikāra*), and connected to the arising of thought (*cittuppāda*). To make the meaning easily understood by the listeners, he raises a challenge as if from another person by the words "What was the Blessed One doing when He knew?", implying: what action was the Blessed One performing when He knew with that knowledge connected to advertence and so on? It means that while performing the duties of the last watch (*pacchimayāmakicca*), that knowledge became connected to advertence and so on, and He knew thus by that Omniscience.

In response to the inquiry, "When there is a general statement, would a specific statement be meaningful?", he says the words beginning with "kiccañcanāmetaṃ" (this is indeed a duty). That mind has its defilements, which cause it to arise, eradicated by the Path of Arahantship; therefore, it is said among the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*), "There is no mind that is not engaged (*natthi abyāvaṭamano*)." The meaning here is that there is no occurrence of thought that is useless. He removes the objection that the aforementioned inquiry still stands even with this meaning, by the words beginning with "taṃ pañcavidhaṃ" (that is fivefold). Among those five duties, the first two should be taken as belonging to the daytime, and the other three as belonging to the nighttime, because they will be described in that very way.

By the words "for the sake of favoring the attendants and for the sake of physical comfort," he shows that although the Blessed One's noble mouth, produced by the accumulation of merit gathered over many aeons, has no defects such as bad odor, He performs the washing of the face and so on for those two purposes only. For the entire body of the Buddhas is undefiled by internal or external impurities, like a well-washed gem. "Viwittāsane" (in a secluded seat) means in a seat that promotes seclusion, suitable for the attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Vītināmetvā" (having passed the time) refers to passing the time with the attainments of fruition; even that is not because of a mere inclination toward seclusion, but for the sake of others following His example. The meaning is: having put on the well-dyed double-layered undergarment by way of changing the residence-wear, having fastened the waistband which is like a flash of lightning, having robed Himself in the cloud-colored robe of the Sugata, and having taken the stone bowl. For it is stated thus in various places. "Sometimes..."
206:
The phrase beginning with "Alone" (Ekako) shows the Blessed One's approach, which is suitable for the disciplining of various beings to be tamed (veneyya). In the phrase "to a village or to a market town," the word "vā" (or) has the sense of alternative (vikappa). By that word "vā," it also includes a city as an alternative. The connection of words is that he enters with many miracles occurring according to his wish.

With the words beginning with "As follows" (Seyyathidaṃ), he elaborates on the latter part. The word "Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle used in the sense of "What is that miracle?" Alternatively, the meaning "What is this entry accompanied by miracles?" is also appropriate. "Mudugatavātā" refers to winds that blow softly and gently. "Udakaphusitāni" refers to water droplets. "Muñcantā" means sprinkling or shedding. "Having settled the dust" means causing the dust particles to settle completely and remaining above like a canopy. This is because they fulfill the function of a canopy by removing harsh winds, the heat of the sun, falling snow, and so on. For that very reason, since the meaning can be understood that they bring flowers from various flowering trees in places like the Himālaya, such a statement was not explicitly made.

Just by making the ground even, low places rise up and high places sink down. Therefore, when he places his foot down, the ground is indeed level. This statement is merely an illustration, as it is also possible for pebbles, potsherds, thorns, stumps, mud, and so forth to be cleared away. Such leveling of the ground and removal of pebbles and so on is merely the natural result (nissanda-phala) of the mark of having well-placed feet; it is not a creation by psychic power. In the phrase "or lotus flowers," the word "vā" has the sense of alternative. By that word "vā," it shows how things occur according to the Blessed One's wish: "If the ground is level as stated, those lotuses do not receive [the feet]; only when the ground is not level do the lotuses receive [them]."

The Buddha's walking is always adorned with the minor mark (anubyañjana) of lifting the right foot first. Therefore, the commentator says, "as soon as the right foot is placed." The teacher Elder Dhammapāla and the teacher Elder Sāriputta say that this is said because the Buddhas are supreme over all beings. The meaning is that it is said thus because he is supreme over all beings. If this is so, it implies that it occurs due to the natural disposition of Great Men. The connection of words is that as soon as the right foot is placed, [the lotuses] emerge and spring forth.

This statement is made with reference to the sight of those beings, as it is a miracle of the Blessed One performed solely for the purpose of disciplining those to be tamed. Although it mentions "six-colored rays," the description "shining like liquid gold" should be understood as being due to the predominance of the golden hue on the Blessed One's body. It is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī: "Here, the word 'rasa' is a synonym for water, and the word 'piñjara' is a synonym for the color of gold; the meaning is that they have a golden color like a stream of liquid gold." Being those that adorn the mansions, gabled houses, and so on, that exist in various villages, market towns, and so forth.
207:
## 
With the words beginning with "In that way" (tathā), he shows the sounding of those instruments, such as drums and lutes, by the power of natural law (dhammatā) itself. At that time, because they are attached to the body, they are called "kāyūpagāni" (ornaments attached to the body); they are not ornaments situated just anywhere. By the word "antaravīthi" (inner street), he shows the path suitable for the Blessed One's journey for alms. Indeed, the Blessed One does not go just anywhere like a fickle alms-collector. It should be understood that those who go first, or those who are capable of giving almsfood suitable for the Blessed One, also receive the Blessed One's bowl.

"Paṭimānenti" means they worship with a devoted mind, or they cause others to worship the Blessed One, or they perform an act of worship. This word is a mere conventional expression; in reality, there is no one who does not worship (or revere) the Blessed One. "Cittasantānāni" refers to the mental continuums occurring in the past and at the present time. The connection is that the Buddha teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some are established in Arahantship.

"Some having gone forth" is said for the purpose of showing the transition to the monk's appearance of laypeople who have reached Arahantship; it is not for the purpose of denying the attainment of Arahantship by laypeople. Indeed, for laypeople who have reached Arahantship, it is their nature to either go forth or pass away (attain Parinibbāna) on that very day. Thus, it was said by the Elder Nāgasena: "Great King, the lay appearance is uneven (incompatible); because of the weakness of the appearance in that uneven state, a layperson who has reached Arahantship either goes forth or attains Parinibbāna on that very day. Great King, this is not a fault of Arahantship; it is a fault of the lay appearance, namely, the weakness of the appearance." This entire passage should be taken.

In this context, the benefit to the great multitude is shown only in connection with the entry for alms accompanied by miracles. Even in the entry for alms without miracles, the benefit to the great multitude should be understood through the meaning by appropriately connecting words such as "they, being well-dressed and well-robed." That entry for alms is also merely a pre-meal duty (purebhattakicca). Here, the assembly hall (upaṭṭhānasālā) is called the Maṇḍalamāḷa. In this commentary, the text is written as "tattha gantvā maṇḍalamāḷe" (having gone there to the circular pavilion). It is also found as "gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe" in the Manorathapūraṇī (Aṅguttara Commentary), and in its sub-commentary, it is said: "in the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa) which is prepared with four kinds of perfumes."

"Enters the Fragrant Cell" is said because of the connection with the action of entering and because of its proximity; therefore, the meaning should be understood as "he goes in order to enter," but not that he remains inside. Only if understood this way will the words beginning with "Then the Blessed One" (atha kho bhagavā) be well-established. "Atha kho" refers to the time when he is thus proceeding to enter the Fragrant Cell. "Upaṭṭhāne" means in the nearby area. In the passage "having washed his feet and standing on the footstool, he exhorts the Bhikkhu Saṅgha," it should be understood that he exhorts them while washing his feet and while standing on the footstool.
208:
## 
Indeed, for the purpose of exhorting those monks, he sits waiting for the conclusion of the monks' meal-duties. "Rare attainment" (dullabhā sampatti) means that although one obtains human status, the qualities known as attainments—such as living in a suitable locality, having unimpaired faculties, and the acquisition of faith—are rare. In palm-leaf manuscripts, however, there is the reading "the attainment of faith is rare"; that reading is simply improper. "In that place" (tattha) refers to the time when he exhorts them while standing on that footstool, or it refers to those monks. A place for staying at night is called a night-quarter (rattiṭṭhāna); likewise, a place for the day is a day-quarter (divāṭṭhāna). The words beginning with "keici" (some) are the explanation of that exhortation. "The realm of the Four Great Kings" (cātumahārājika-bhavana) is said with reference to the empty mansions in the heaven of the Four Great Kings. This method also applies to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and so on.

Then the Blessed One, having entered the Fragrant Cell and having divided the post-meal time into three parts, in the first part, if he so desires, he takes the lion's posture (sīhaseyya) on his right side; if he does not so desire, he enters the Fruition Attainment (phalasamāpatti) which is the constant practice of the Buddhas. Then, having emerged from that attainment according to the designated time, in the second part—as in the third portion of the last watch—he surveys the world to see the maturity of the knowledge of those who are to be guided (veneyya). Therefore, it is said: "if he so desires," and so on. The meaning of "lion's posture" and so on has already been stated below. Whatever word is not previously mentioned or is not clear, that alone we shall explain. "Well-supported" (sammā assāsitabbā) means supported by way of making one take [the right temperature]; thus he is called "samassāsita" (refreshed). He is so called because he has such a body.

They assemble for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. Having known the mental disposition of that assembly, and with reference to the performance of miracles, he said: "with a miracle suitable for the assembled audience." The place where they speak the Dhamma together is called the Dhamma Hall (dhamma-sabhā). "Timely" (kālayutta) means it is suitable for various times, such as "at this time, it should be spoken thus to this person." "Samayayutta" is a synonym for that same "kālayutta," or it means being suitable for the occasion that has arisen. Alternatively, "samayayutta" means being endowed with reasons and examples. The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma timely and with reasons. Having known the time, he dismisses the assembly; the intention is that he does not teach the Dhamma until it is dark. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading "having known the occasion (samaya), he dismissed the assembly" is found; that reading is just an error written through later negligence.

"Limbs" (gattāni) refers to the body itself, spoken of in the plural because of its many parts. By the phrase "makes one take the temperature," he shows that the pouring of water is only for the purpose of regulating the temperature, not for the purpose of washing away dirt. Indeed, dust and dirt do not smear the body of the Blessed One. A cell perfumed with four kinds of scents is called a Fragrant Cell (gandhakuṭi). Its surrounding area is likewise. He remains in seclusion for a moment through Fruition Attainments. After that, from his own...
209:
Coming from one's night-quarters or day-quarters and standing nearby is called upaᙩᙩhāna; it means attending or waiting upon. "There" (tattha) means in that place of residence, or in the first watch, or among those monks.

Fulfilling their desires by way of answering questions and so forth, the Buddha did not merely say "ten-thousandfold world system" (dasa-sahassi-lokadhātu), but said "the entire ten-thousandfold world system" (sakala-dasa-sahassi-lokadhātu) for the purpose of encompassing its many parts. It means that those who did not get the opportunity in the morning, afternoon, or the first watch due to the large crowds of people, now get the opportunity only in the middle watch, or they get the opportunity because the Blessed One has granted it to them. As for what kind of questions they ask, it is said: "even as few as four syllables, exactly as constructed." "Exactly as constructed" (yathābhisaṅkhataṁ) means in accordance with how it was prepared, or without deviating from that preparation. By this, it is shown that they ask questions according to their own intuition.

In the first of the three parts of the afternoon period, sleeping in the lion's posture is not always possible; thus it is said: "of the body fatigued by sitting since the morning." For this reason, it was previously said, "if he so desires," thereby clarifying that sleeping in the lion's posture at that time is not a fixed rule. Fatigue is called kilamatha. It should be connected as: he spends time in walking meditation to relieve the fatigue of the body, and then he takes the lion's sleep. The Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu) refers to looking with the Buddha-eye, which consists of the fifth and sixth powers known as the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayanusaya-āṇa) and the knowledge of the maturity of faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-āṇa). Because he frequently surveys the world with that knowledge, it is called the "Buddha-eye." This is said in reference to what the Blessed One habitually practices in the last watch. At other times, the Blessed One accomplishes the task of surveying the world with the remaining powers or with omniscience (sabbauta-āṇa) alone.

Wishing to support the meaning previously stated as "knowing while performing the duties of the last watch," he said "on that day, however," and so forth. Wherever the Blessed Buddhas reside, they never abandon these fivefold duties because they are always established in mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajaa). Therefore, it should be understood that the engagement with the fivefold Buddha-duties is mentioned here to show that he did not abandon those duties even on that day. "Caṅkama" refers to a place suitable for walking meditation in that location. It should be joined as "he knew while walking in meditation." Taking only the latter of the two meanings previously mentioned, it is said: "with reference to omniscience." This is because the former meaning is easily understood according to the context.
210:
‘Then the Blessed One, knowing this sequence of words of those monks, approached the circular pavilion (maṇḁalamāḷa).’ This Pali passage is one with a remainder. Therefore, to show that the meaning should be understood as ‘knowing that matter and having thought thus, he approached,’ it is said ‘atvā ca panassa’ and so forth. In that phrase, ‘assa etadahosi’ means this reflection occurred to the Blessed One, or this reflection of the mind occurred. Here, there is a gender reversal (liṅga-vipallāsa) as in ‘etadaggaṁ’ and so forth. The function of omniscience is not manifest in every way. ‘Nirantaraṁ’ means speaking without a gap by way of sequential narration, or speaking without distinction (completely) according to how it was preached. This is an adverbial neuter (bhāva-napuṁsaka).

‘Taṁ aᙩᙩhuppattiṁ katvā’ means making those spoken words the occasion for the arising of this Sutta, or making them the cause for the preaching of this Sutta. Here, the word ‘attha’ is used in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). Therefore, it shows the introductory origin (nikkhepa) of this Sutta arising from that cause. ‘Dvāsaᙩᙩhiyā ᙩhānesu’ means in the sixty-two grounds for views. ‘Appaᙩivattiyaṁ’ means that which cannot be turned back (overturned) by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. ‘Sīhanādaṁ nadanto’ means making a fearless roar, known as a noble roar.

As worldly people say:
‘When placed as a suffix, the words puṅgava, usabha, kujara, sīha, sādūla, nāga, and so forth, denote the meaning of "best" among men.’

That should be understood as being generally the case. Or, it is called a lion's roar (sīhanāda) because he utters a sound similar to a lion's roar. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta. Or, just as the king of beasts, the Kesara lion, is called ‘sīha’ because of enduring (sahana) danger and destroying (hanana) enemies, so too the Tathāgata is called ‘sīha’ because of enduring worldly conditions and destroying (abolishing) other doctrines. Therefore, the meaning should also be understood as making the roar of the Tathāgata who is like a lion.

Just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, being confident in all places and free from horripilation (fear), roars a lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the Tathāgata-powers, being confident in the eight assemblies and free from horripilation, utters a lion's roar endowed with various beauties of teaching in such ways as ‘these are the grounds for views.’ With reference to this, it was said: ‘Monks, "lion" is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. Monks, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma in an assembly, this is his lion's roar.’
211:
The teaching to be delivered in this Brahmajāla Sutta, beginning with “These monks stand in the sixty-two grounds for views,” is indeed the Lion’s Roar (sīhanāda). The connection of the mode of conditions (paṭiccasamuppāda) should also be understood through the method to be explained later, such as “with feeling as condition, craving arises.” By the two similes such as Mount Sineru, etc., he shows the extreme difficulty of the Brahmajāla teaching, as it is not shared by Paccekabuddhas or disciples.

Suvaṇṇakūṭa refers to completing a house with a special golden pinnacle; similarly, the Brahmajāla Sutta is concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship (arahatta). The term 'nikūṭa' also means an extremely high pinnacle that has reached its completion. This statement regarding the pinnacle of Arahantship is made because all virtues culminate in the fruit of Arahantship; thus, Arahantship alone is particularly superior to all virtues.

The word 'me' mentioned earlier refers to the teaching. Therefore, the meaning is appropriate that “even after my Parinibbāna, this teaching of mine will remain for five thousand years in the future.” It means that for one who practices through listening, learning, memorizing, and reciting, etc., and for one who practices accordingly, it will lead to Nibbāna.

'Yena' is an instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) indicating cause, and it should also be understood as 'tena'. Among these two words 'yena tena', 'tattha' means “in that assembly hall.” Alternatively, 'yena' is an instrumental case used in the sense of location (bhūmma). 'Tena' is an instrumental case used in the sense of the object (upayoga). Therefore, teachers also say 'tattha' means “to that assembly hall.”

'Upasaṅkami' (approached) means “is approaching” because the present time is intended. However, to indicate that such approaching is in the past, the past tense 'upasaṅkami' is used with regard to that past time. Only in this way is the word 'upasaṅkamitvā' (having approached) well-suited. Otherwise, if both words were in the past tense, it should not be stated thus.

In approaching (upasaṅkamana), there are two meanings: going and arriving. Here, only the meaning of going should be taken. A person who goes to a certain place because they wish to reach it can be said to “approach that place” by passing through various regions. Therefore, by saying “he went to that place,” the sense of arrival (upagamana) is excluded. Only the reaching of the place one wishes to reach is called 'upagamana' (arrival). The word 'upasaṅkamitvā', which is not expanded upon here, indicates the conclusion of the approach.

Alternatively, 'gato' (gone) is simply 'upagato' (approached). A word without a prefix (upasagga) can express a special meaning like a word with a prefix, and a word with a prefix can express the same meaning as one without. Therefore, the meaning of the word 'upasaṅkamitvā' should be understood as: having thus approached and reached the vicinity of the monks, reaching a place where one is able to speak a question or deliver a discourse. Alternatively, 'yena' is an instrumental case used in the sense of cause (hetu). For which reason the Blessed One...
212:
...should approach that assembly pavilion, for that reason he approached. The reason for approaching has already been stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) starting with "These monks," etc.

In the phrase "He sat on the prepared seat," if there is a question "Who prepared this seat?", the phrase "It happened in the Buddha's time, it is said," etc., is stated to show that "it was prepared by the monks." In that context, "in the Buddha's time" means during the time of the Blessed One while he was still living. "Special Dhamma" refers to the jhānas, paths, and fruits that are superior to the Dhamma already attained. The particle *atha* is used in the sense of doubt, meaning "if he sees." It should be connected as "to that monk who was thinking." Similarly, it should be connected as "having shown the reason for seeing thus and having admonished." *Anamatagga* refers to the beginningless Saṃsāra. "Having flown into the sky" means ascending into the sky. In such cases, only the locative sense (in) is appropriate, as stated in the Udāna Commentary. "Burden" refers to a heavy task because it was difficult to obtain a seat suitable for the Blessed One at that moment. *Phalaka* is a wooden plank made for sitting. *Kaṭṭhaka* is a log of wood other than a plank suitable for sitting. *Saṅkaḍḍhitvā* means having collected. In that context, regarding "on old leaves," it is said so because sitting on those old leaves alone was unsuitable; or it could mean "on those benches," etc. In this case, the case ending should be changed and connected according to the meaning as "having collected, they prepared." *Papphoṭetvā* means having shaken off to clean it because it was unsuitable, being covered with dust and dirt as it was. Knowing that "our talk like this is fit to be the cause for another discourse; the Blessed One will surely come," they said this referring to the manner of sitting. Here, a seat placed by the King with the thought "Let any ascetic or Brahmin who comes here take it and use it temporarily," and which is used by the King when he comes, should be known as "the King's sitting place." It is not proper for monks to use or prepare for the Blessed One a seat that has not been so designated. Therefore, to show that such a King's sitting place is mentioned in the Pāḷi, the phrase "referring to that," etc., is stated. "Knowledge of dispositions" (*adhimutti-ñāṇa*) means the Omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) and the Knowledge of Powers (*bala-ñāṇa*) which take the various dispositions of beings as their object; this intended meaning has already been stated.

"Nisajjā" indicates the conclusion of the act of sitting, as shown by "thus," etc. Since it is said, "Having known these words of those monks," the meaning that "he asked even though he already knew" is established; therefore, it says "even while knowing." It should be understood that the questioning is for the purpose of initiating a conversation because, without a subject of discussion (kathāvatthu), a special discourse to be delivered subsequently in accordance with that talk would not arise. The word *nu* is used in the sense of questioning. The word *asa* is said to be in the sense of occurrence, as in "With what talk... are you [engaged]?" In this...
213:
In this context, by the power of euphonic combination (sandhi), the letter 'u' is changed to 'o' only; it does not differ in meaning from the first Pali text. This is shown by the statement: "Tassāpi purimoyeva attho" (The meaning of that is also just the same as the previous one). "The meaning of that is also just the same as the previous one" refers to the meaning expressed as: "With what talk are you now gathered?"

In the phrase "Kā ca panā," the word "ca" is used in the sense of distinction (vyatireka), as in "Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato" and so on. What is called 'vyatireka' is a specific or superior meaning that looks back to the meaning previously stated. That word "ca" illuminates the distinct meaning, characterized as the unfinished state of the talk previously asked about, which will be spoken of later. The word "pana" is merely an ornament of speech (vacanālaṅkāra). Since such a meaning can be well understood only from the grammar books, he said: "Antarākathā means the talk on meditation subjects..." and so on, to show a meaning other than that. The practice of meditation, the recitation of Pali, and the questioning of the commentaries are the duties of a recluse (samaṇakaraṇīya). Although the specific duty looked for by the word "antarā" should be spoken of as the object of connection (sambandha-apādāna), because those duties themselves are of the nature to be spoken of, it is said: "kammaṭṭhānamanasikāra-uddesa-paripucchādīnaṃ" (of meditation, recitation, questioning, etc.). This is because the very talk with which those monks were sitting together, that unfinished talk, is specifically asked about again as "antarākathā," and not other things like meditation, recitation, or questioning.

Another meaning of the word "antarā" is stated as "aññā" (another) and "ekā" (one). These two words are synonyms. This is because this word "antarā" occurs in the sense of 'another,' as in "bhūmantaraṃ" (another plane) and "samayantaraṃ" (another belief). Therefore, in the phrase "kammaṭṭhānamanasikāra-uddesa-paripucchādīnaṃ," the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) should be seen in the sense of the ablative (nissakka). Alternatively, the word "antarā" occurs in the sense of 'middle' (vemajjha). Because that talk occurred in the middle of meditation practice and so on, it is 'another' (aññā); and because it is not mixed with those duties, it is 'one' (ekā) separately. To show this intention, it is said: "aññā" and "ekā."

Doing in a particular way is called "pakata." Because it is free from that, or because it is a talk where the particular doing is absent, it is called "vippakatā" (unfinished talk); it is also called "apariṇiṭṭhitā." "Sikha" means the end (pariyosāna). This question, however, is a question asked with the desire to speak further (kathetukamyatā-pucchā) in connection with their talk. Aiming at that meaning, he said: "Nāhaṃ" and so on. "Kathābhaṅgatthaṃ" means for the purpose of breaking the talk. Since it has arrived by way of meaning, he makes the invitation of the Omniscient One (sabbaññu-pavāraṇa). Because it does not lead out of saṃsāra and is athwart the path to heaven and liberation, it is called "tiracchānakathā" (lowly talk). "Athwart" means having the nature of concealing or obstructing. In this context, by the word "ādi," he includes many kinds of useless talk such as talk about thieves, great ministers, armies, and dangers. This is indeed the talk...
214:
This statement is made with the intention of including the meaning within or excluding other meanings. The word 'atha' occurs only at the time when that talk was not yet finished. By the phrase 'taṃ no' and so on, he speaks of what has arrived by way of meaning. In such places, it should be understood in this very way. If one asks, "Did those monks not conclude that talk as they wished with 'iti ha me' and so on?", the answer is: they did not conclude it because it was interrupted by the arrival of the Blessed One. If the Blessed One had not arrived at that moment, they would have continued to speak further in connection with that very topic. But because the Blessed One arrived, they did not continue. Therefore, it is said: 'ayaṃ no...pe... anuppatto.'

Now, wishing to show the completion of the introduction (nidāna) or the completion of the commentary on the introduction, and also to confirm the suitability of that introduction with the words of the Blessed One, he said 'ettāvatā' and so on. The meaning of 'ettāvatā' should be understood in two ways: either that the introduction which was spoken by the sequence of words 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so on is finished, or that the commentary on the meaning by the sequence of words 'tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ' and so on is completed. By the phrase 'kamala...pe... salilāya' and so on, he illustrates the suitability of that introduction with the words of the Blessed One.

In that description, 'kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādurasasalilāya' means having water that is bright, pure, and sweet-tasting, shining with the lotuses called kamala (paduma, puṇḍarīka, white and red lotuses) and the blue water-lilies called kuvalaya. 'Nimmalasilātalaracanavilāsasobhitaratanasopānaṃ' means having a jeweled staircase beautified by the elegance of the construction with pure stone slabs. Or, it means a jeweled staircase beautified by the elegance of the construction with pure stone slabs and by the beauty of well-executed work. By the words 'vilāsa' and 'sobhita,' the state of being extremely beautiful is expressed. 'Vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāgaṃ' means having a ground area that is white with sand-dust resembling a surface strewn with various pearls. 'Suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassa' means being adorned with well-portioned walls and surrounded by variegated railings (vedikā). It is connected with the word 'vijambhita' as if wishing to touch the sky, the path of the stars, because of its great height. 'Vijambhitasamussayassa' means having a mass that is displayed or expanded. 'Dantamayasaṇhamuduphalakakañcanalatāvinaddhamaṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhaṃ' means endowed with a brilliant splendor produced by the collection of radiance from gems entwined with golden creepers upon very smooth and soft planks made of ivory. 'Suvaṇṇavalayanūpurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitakathitahasitamadhurassaragehajanaviciritassa' means being a place frequented by the people of the house, whose sweet voices of talking and laughing are mixed with the sounds produced by the clashing of golden bracelets, anklets, and so on...
215:
A place frequented by groups of people living in houses, who are endowed with sweet voices consisting of what is called speech and laughter, mingled with the sounds produced by the clashing of golden anklets, bracelets, and so forth. It is a place adorned with the majesty, sovereignty, and wealth of noble people, or by the supreme sovereignty and enjoyments of the men and women residing there. It has well-established wide doorposts illuminated by the spreading radiance of gold, silver, various gems, pearls, coral, and so forth.

It is called 'Buddhaguṇānubhāvasaṃsūcaka' (Indicating the Power of the Buddha's Virtues) because it effectively indicates the power of the Buddha's virtues through the manifestation of the three types of virtue (sīla) and so forth. Likewise, it is adorned by the indication of the time, the place, the speaker, the subject matter, and the assembly.

Why is the introductory discourse (nidāna) spoken here during the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One be rehearsed? It is said: For the purpose of establishing the longevity, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching. For a teaching that is established by indicating the time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly lasts long, is not subject to confusion, and is credible, like a legal decision established by time, place, matter, and cause. Therefore, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked about the place and so forth, saying, "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken?" (Cūḷavagga 439), the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, spoke the introduction while answering those questions. Thus, it is also said here: "The introduction is adorned by the indication of the time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly."

Furthermore, the introductory discourse is spoken to reveal the perfection of the Teacher (satthusampatti). For the Blessed One, the status of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is established because of the absence of prior composition, inference, reliance on other traditions, or mere speculation. Because of his being a Perfectly Enlightened One, the absence of prior composition, the absence of inference such as "it might be thus," and the absence of speculation based on other traditions is due to the fact that his knowledge is unimpeded in all things and is the sole measure among all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma). Likewise, the status of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is established because of the absence of the "teacher's closed fist" (secrecy), stinginess regarding the Dhamma, or acting according to the wishes of others. Because his taints are destroyed, there is an absence of the teacher's closed fist and so forth, and there is the pure activity of helping others. Thus, regarding the ignorance and craving which are the defilements of a speaker and which spoil the perfection of view and virtue...
216:
Through the Buddha's pure states, which indicate the absence of ignorance and craving—the defilements of a speaker that spoil the perfection of view and virtue—and which manifest the perfection of knowledge (ñāṇasampadā) and the perfection of abandonment (pahānasampadā), the first two grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja) are established. From the establishment of those first two grounds of self-confidence, the latter two grounds of self-confidence are established through the establishment of the absence of confusion regarding obstructive things and the path to deliverance. Thus, the Blessed One's possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own benefit and the benefit of others are revealed by the introductory discourse, because he explains the Dhamma with immediate wit (paṭibhāna) according to the inclinations of the assembled audience, and because of such words as "knowing and seeing." Therefore, it is said: "The introductory discourse is for the purpose of revealing the perfection of the Teacher."

Furthermore, the introductory discourse is for the purpose of revealing the perfection of the Dispensation (sāsanasampatti). For the Blessed One, whose every action is embraced by wisdom and compassion, there is no activity that is useless or for his own benefit alone. Therefore, when all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Enlightened One, which occur only for the benefit of others, are spoken as they occurred, it is called the Dispensation (sāsana) because it instructs beings according to their welfare in this life, the next life, and the ultimate goal; it is not mere poetic composition. That conduct (carita) of the Teacher is revealed in various suttas through the introductory discourses along with the time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly as they occurred. Or else, the introductory discourse is spoken to reveal the authoritative nature (pamāṇabhāva) of the Dispensation by revealing the authoritative nature of the Teacher. That demonstration of authority is manifested by the word "Bhagavā," which indicates his being the supreme of all beings distinguished by virtues, and by showing his engagement with the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings (āsayānusayañāṇa) through such words as "knowing and seeing." This is just a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory discourse here. For who is able to fully manifest the purposes of the introduction spoken by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who followed the Buddha in knowledge?

In this regard, there are these verses:
"The famous one of Videha (Ānanda) spoke the introduction for the sake of the longevity of the teaching, for non-confusion, and for the sake of faith.
It was also spoken to show the perfection of the Teacher, the perfection of the Dispensation, and the authoritative nature of that Dispensation."

Thus, in this Sumangalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, which explains the extremely subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings, and which generates pure and vast wisdom and skill—[written by the one] who is endowed with qualities such as uprightness, gentleness, restraint, faith, mindfulness, wisdom, patience, and energy; who moves with intrepid knowledge that is unattached and unshakeable in the three Pitakas along with their commentaries; who has plunged into the thicket of his own and others' various doctrines; who is a great leader of a group, and a great grammarian...
217: The explanation of the meaning of the internal introduction (abbhantaranidāna-vaṇṇanā) in the Līnatthappakāsanī (sub-commentary) named Sādhuvilāsinī, composed by the Elder Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, who holds the title Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, is finished. ## The Explanation of the Introduction is finished. Having thus provided the opening for the internal introduction, he now wishes to provide the opening for the Sutta as it was delivered. He provides an opening that is consistent from beginning to end, does not deviate from the sequence, removes the fault of confusion, and delights the minds of the wise. The commentator shows that he does not deviate from the tradition of the wise by unfailingly carrying the burden that has come upon him. Therefore, to clarify that meaning, he says “Idāni” (Now), etc., wishing to investigate the delivery (nikkhepa) of the Sutta. 'Nikkhittassa' means “of that which was delivered.” The two terms 'desanā' (teaching) and 'nikkhepa' (delivery) differ in meaning but are identical in essence. Because the meanings such as virtue (sīla), which are to be taught, are placed (nikkhipana) within the continuities of those to be guided (veneyya), the teaching itself is called 'nikkhepa'. One might object, “Is it not the Sutta itself that is being commented upon?” To this, he says “Sā panesā,” etc. The meaning here is: the commentary stated after investigating the delivery (nikkhepa) of the Sutta becomes clear and easily understood because the introduction (nidāna) of the Sutta is well-known, as in “this teaching arose due to this cause.” Therefore, we shall first investigate that delivery of the Sutta (suttanikkhepa) in general. Any word that clarifies the meaning of the Sutta while commenting should be stated by the commentator. Because such words are the means to understand the meaning of the Sutta, they are figuratively (pariyāyena) the commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) itself. In this Brahmajāla Sutta, while investigating that delivery of the Sutta, the reason for which this Sutta was delivered is explained. By analyzing that matter, the commentary on the portions of the Sutta stated as “Whether it be of me, O monks,” etc., “This, O monks, is a trifle,” etc., and “There is, O monks,” etc., should be understood as easily comprehensible because it is easy to show the respective connections (anusandhi). In that regard, just as the Suttas, though they have many hundreds and thousands of divisions, do not exceed the sixteenfold categories according to the method of the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna such as the 'partaking of defilement' (saṃkilesabhāgiya), etc., so too they do not exceed the fourfold categories by way of the delivery of the Sutta (suttanikkhepa) such as 'by one's own inclination' (attajjhāsaya), etc. Thus he says, “There are four deliveries of Suttas.” One might ask, “Since mixed types (saṃsaggabheda) are also possible, why say there are only four?” It is because mixed types are not found in all Suttas. Indeed, 'by one's own inclination' (attajjhāsaya) and 'by the occurrence of an event' (atthuppatti) can have mixed types with 'by the inclination of others' (parajjhāsaya) and 'by the power of a question' (pucchāvasika).
218:
“One's own inclination and others' inclination; one's own inclination and the power of questioning; one's own inclination, others' inclination, and the power of questioning; causal origin and others' inclination; causal origin and the power of questioning; causal origin, others' inclination, and the power of questioning”—thus, combinations can exist due to the presence of inclination, questioning, and connection. However, there is no mutual combination between 'one's own inclination' and 'causal origin'. Therefore, because the division by combination cannot be obtained by the method of exhaustive expansion, it should be understood that it is said “four Sutta-nikkhepas”.

Alternatively, causal origin (atthuppatti) could also have a division by combination with one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya). However, because the remaining nikkhepas mentioned by way of combination are included within the primary nikkhepas, it is said “four Sutta-nikkhepas” with that intention. In this alternative interpretation, it should be understood that he shows only the method, stating that Sutta-nikkhepas should be spoken of according to the method of the Dispensation's foundations (sāsanapaṭṭhāna) by way of groups of one, two, three, and four as appropriate. In this context, this is the word-meaning (vacanattha): Nikkhepa means placing or speaking. Placing a Sutta is Sutta-nikkhepa; it means the teaching of a Sutta. Or, it is called nikkhepa because it is placed; the Sutta itself is the nikkhepa, hence Sutta-nikkhepa. One's own inclination is attajjhāsaya; it is called attajjhāsaya because that inclination exists by way of cause. Or, according to the aforementioned method, it is called attajjhāsaya because one's own inclination belongs to this person. The same method applies to parajjhāsaya (others' inclination). The power of questioning is pucchāvasa; it is called pucchāvasika because that power belongs to this person according to the aforementioned method. The subject matter (vatthu) of the Sutta teaching is called 'attha' because it should be known (araṇīya). The arising of that subject matter is atthuppatti. In that very word 'atthuppatti', by changing the letter 't' to 'ṭṭh', it becomes aṭṭhuppatti. It is called aṭṭhuppattika because that causal origin belongs to this person according to the aforementioned method. Furthermore, it is called nikkhepa because the Sutta is delivered by this means; it is simply the cause for the teaching of the Sutta, such as one's own inclination and so forth. In this alternative interpretation, one's own inclination is attajjhāsaya. Others' inclination is parajjhāsaya. That which is asked is pucchā, the meaning to be questioned. The speech of those receiving the Dhamma that proceeds by the power of that questioning is pucchāvasika. That very pucchāvasika is called “pucchāvasiko” in the masculine gender, in consideration of the word 'nikkhepa'. According to the aforementioned method, aṭṭhuppatti itself is aṭṭhuppattiko; thus the meaning should be understood.

And here, because the teaching proceeds for the purpose of establishing the Dhamma-tradition (dhammatanti) by one's own inclination alone, without regarding causes such as the maturity of others' faculties (indriya), it is appropriate to treat attajjhāsaya as a separate nikkhepa. Therefore, he will say later: “By one's own inclination”.
219:
"He teaches solely by His own inclination," it is stated (in the Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1, 5). It should not be objected: "Since the inclinations and questions of others are the causes for the arising of the teaching (atthuppatti), why are they not included in the atthuppatti-nikkhepa (presentation based on circumstances)?" or "Since pucchāvasika (based on questions) and atthuppattika (based on circumstances) are teachings given in accordance with the inclinations of others, why are they not included in the parajjhāsaya-nikkhepa (presentation based on others' inclination)?" Because only the arising of a Sutta teaching that is free from the aspirations or questions of others is taken as atthuppatti, parajjhāsaya and pucchāvasika are taken separately. For this reason, in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta and others, the cause of the teaching, such as the arising of material requisites (āmisa), is called "atthuppatti". A teaching given by making only the inclination the cause, without the questioning of others, is called parajjhāsaya. A teaching given based on a question is called pucchāvasika. This meaning is very clear.

"Anajjhiṭṭho" means not being urged or requested through questions and so forth, but teaching solely by His own inclination for the sake of the longevity of the Dhamma. "Hāro" is a sequence, like a pearl necklace (muttāhāra). That very sequence is called hāraka. The sequence of the Sammappadhāna Suttas is called "Sammappadhānasuttantahāraka". The sequence of Suttas related to the Right Efforts (sammappadhāna) as explained in order in the Saṃyutta Nikāya is called "Sammappadhānasuttantahāraka". Likewise, Iddhipādahāraka and so forth are the same. In the preceding terms like Iddhipāda, Indriya, Bala, Bojjhaṅga, and Maggaṅga Suttantahāraka, there is either the dropping of the subsequent term, or it is a dvandagabbhasamāsa (a compound containing a coordinate compound), or it is indicated by an ellipsis (peyyāla). "Tesaṃ" refers to the meaning of those aforementioned Suttas.

"Paripakkā" means matured. "Vimuttiparipācanīyā" refers to the factors such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and others that bring the fruit of Arahatship to maturity. "Khaye" means for the sake of exhaustion, or in the Dhamma teaching which is the cause of exhaustion. "Ajjhāsayaṃ" refers to adhimutti (inclination/resolution). "Khantiṃ" refers to diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti (acceptance through pondering views). "Manaṃ" refers to the mind. "Abhinīhāraṃ" refers to paṇidhāna (aspiration). "Bujjhanabhāvaṃ" refers to the nature of awakening or the manner of awakening. "Avekkhitvā" means having reflected or having considered.

"Cattāro vaṇṇā" refers to the four castes or the four types of beings measured by physical appearance (rūpa) and so forth. "Mahārājāno" refers to the four Great Kings of the devas. "Vuccanti": what is being said? It means "What are the five aggregates of clinging?"

Regarding the question "Why?", it is stated starting with "Atthuppattiyaṃ hi". In the term "vaṇṇāvaṇṇe", the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimitta). By this word "vaṇṇa", the praise uttered by the Saṅgha of monks such as "It is wonderful, friends!" is also included. Taking that very praise of the monks as the occasion (atthuppatti), He said, "Monks, there is..."
220:
The Buddha will begin the teaching further above with the words “Aññe dhammā,” etc. He explains that very meaning with the words “Ācariyo,” etc. In this teaching, “Monks, others might speak praise of me,” because it was taught based on the praise spoken by the youth Brahmadatta, it is said to be “the praise of a student.” Now, to show the connection in the Pali text, he says “Iti,” etc.

“Desanākusalo” means being skilled in teaching, in the sense of knowing, “By this occasion, this teaching is appropriate.” By this, he praises the Blessed One with qualities suitable for the treatise. This is the nature of commentators: to praise the Blessed One with qualities found within the respective treatises.

In this context, the word “vā” is found in many senses such as simile (upamā), conjunction (samuccaya), doubt (saṃsaya), relinquishing of speech (vacanavossagga), verse-filler (padapūraṇa), similarity (sadisa), and alternative/distinction (vikappa). Thus, in passages like “Paṇḍitovāpi tena so,” it is found in the sense of a simile, meaning a state of similarity. In passages like “Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muniṃ pavedayanti,” it is found in the sense of conjunction. In passages like “Ke vā ime kassa vā,” it is found in the sense of doubt. In passages like “Ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho,” it is found in the sense of relinquishing of speech (vacanavossagga). In passages like “Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī,” it is found in the sense of a verse-filler (padapūraṇa). In passages like “Madhūṃ vā maññati bālo, yāva pāpaṃ na paccati,” it is found in the sense of similarity (sadisa). In passages like “Ye hi keci bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā,” it is found in the sense of alternative/distinction (vikappa).

Here too, it is used in the sense of distinction (vikappa). Because it distinguishes various entities separately as “of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha,” he says, “The word ‘vā’ has the sense of distinction (vikappanattha).”

The word “para” also exists in the sense of “other” in passages like “Ahañceva kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyuṃ.” It exists in the sense of “superior/excessive” in passages like “Indriyaparopariyatta.” It exists in the sense of “latter part/after” in passages like “Parato āgamissati.” It exists in the sense of “adversary/opposition” in passages like “Uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā.” Here too, he shows the sense of opposition by the words “paṭiwiruddhā sattā” (opposing beings). It means the enemy beings who are opposed to the Dispensation (Sāsana). The word “ta” refers back to the meaning mentioned as “pare,” specifically those distinguished by the action of speaking dispraise; thus it is said, “Among those who speak dispraise.”
221: Since these monks are of great virtue, is it not true that malice (āghāta) cannot exist towards them? If so, why is it said 'one should not harbor malice'? To address and dispel this objection (codanā), the phrase beginning with 'kiñcāpi' is stated. The meaning is: even if [malice] does not exist, it is still so. In the phrase 'even in such cases' (īdisesu pi), the word 'pi' has the sense of possibility (sambhāvanattha). By this word, it is meant: if one should not produce unwholesome thoughts even based on the Triple Gem, what need is there to mention that they should not be produced based on material gain (vatthu-āmisa) or worldly gain (loka-āmisa)? Only the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-dhamma) is called 'dhammanetti' (the guide of Dhamma) because it leads to the Noble Dhamma (Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna). 'Āhanati' means it strikes hard, or it harms, oppresses, or causes distress. In some versions, the reading 'ettha' is found, but that reading should not be accepted because it was inserted later and contradicts the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) which follows the ancient versions, and because it lacks logical meaning. Although distress (domanassa) and so on also strike [the mind], the word 'āghāta' is specifically well-known for anger (kopa); to show this, it is said, 'This is a designation (adhivacana) for anger.' This is stated because [the author] wishes to show the meaning by way of figurative expression (pariyāya) after showing the literal meaning of the component. 'Adhivacana' means a word used with reference to something, or a well-known word, or a name. The same applies to the remaining terms. Here, to show that there is no other doer (kattā) besides the ultimate nature of phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma), the word 'āghāta' is shown in the sense of an agent (kattu) as 'āhanati' (it strikes). The senses of instrument (karaṇa) and state (bhāva) are also possible, such as 'one strikes by this' or 'the mere act of striking is āghāta.' The meaning of the word 'appatītā' is stated as 'displeased, unhappy.' This is the definition of the word 'appaccaya' by way of a well-known figurative expression. It should be defined as 'appaccaya' because one does not find satisfaction (na pacceti) through that distress. 'Abhirādhayati' means it accomplishes (satisfies). 'Ettha' refers to these three words. 'By two' refers to the words āghāta and anabhiraddhi. 'By one' refers to the word appaccaya. If only these words are taken, the mental factors associated (sampayutta) with them might be left out; however, since they have the nature of arising together and so on, they cannot be left out. To resolve this objection, the phrase beginning with 'tesaṃ' is stated. 'Tesaṃ' refers to a portion of the aforementioned formations aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha) and feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha). 'Sesānaṃ' refers to the perception aggregate (saññā), consciousness aggregate (viññāṇa), and the remaining portion of the formations aggregate. 'Karaṇa' means causing to arise. The gathering of conditions for the arising of malice and so on is called 'karaṇa' here; in meaning, it is indeed production (uppādana). With reference to the non-arising of those states, it is said in the Pāli text 'na karaṇīyā' (should not be done). They are simply to be abandoned as appropriate because they share the same arising, cessation, object, and base. Regarding that 'mental corruption' (mano-padosa), the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) in the sense of a container (ādhāra) is shown by the phrase 'tesu avaṇṇabhāsakesu' (towards those who speak dispraise). Alternatively, this locative case is in the sense of a cause (nimittattha) or a characteristic of a state (bhāva-lakkhaṇa), as stated 'tasmiṃ vā avaṇṇe' (or regarding that dispraise). This is because lack of virtue or dispraise cannot be the container (ādhāra) for anger and distress, as those states are connected only with the person who speaks the dispraise.
222:
## 
'Assatha' is shown by the word 'bhaveyyātha' as it is a form of the optative mood (sattamī-vibhatti) used in the context of a hypothesis in conjunction with the word 'ce'. Teachers say that by saying 'bhaveyyātha ce' and 'yadi bhaveyyātha', it is intended to show that these words 'ce' and 'yadi' are used respectively before and after. By the phrase 'angry due to anger, displeased due to distress', the previous statement 'thus by the first method' and so on is supported by showing that there is no difference in meaning. The single word 'tumha' has the same meaning as the word 'tumhākaṃ'. It is just as the word 'amha' has the same meaning as 'amhākaṃ'. Therefore, just as 'amhaṃ' is used in the Jātaka Pāli, 'tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare' (therefore our young ones do not die), it means 'only of you' (tumhākaṃyeva). By changing the gender (to feminine) according to the sense, it is said 'by that unhappiness' (tāya ca anattamantāya). When 'danger' (antarāya) is mentioned, since the meaning 'danger to the special qualities of a recluse' (samaṇadhamma-visesa) is understood from the context, and since one may use words as one pleases when the meaning is understood, it is said 'danger to the first jhāna and so on.' Here, the word 'antarāya' is the statement of the reason why mental corruption should not be committed. The intention is: because that anger and so on would be a danger to your first jhāna and so on, therefore malice and so on, which are included in that anger, should not be committed. By this, it is shown: 'I do not forbid you by the power of being the Omniscient Lord, but rather I forbid you for this very reason.' Since that statement of reason clarifies the disadvantage, it should be understood as previously stated, 'wishing to show the disadvantage.' That mental corruption not only causes danger to welfare and happiness that will occur in the future, but also causes danger to welfare and happiness that should occur at that very moment. Therefore, to show the disadvantage of mental corruption more firmly, the connection should be stated that the phrase beginning with 'api nu' is said. 'Paresaṃ' means of those other than oneself. It does not mean 'opposing enemies' as in 'others might speak dispraise'; thus it is said 'of any persons whatsoever.' That meaning is supported by the phrase 'one who is angry' and so on. In the Pāli, since knowing well-spoken and ill-spoken words is accomplished by knowing their meaning, it is said 'the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken words.' 'Andhatamaṃ' means darkness that causes blindness, or extreme darkness. It is connected as: 'to the person whom it overcomes, it is blinding darkness.' Alternatively, the word 'yaṃ' is the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) used in the sense of the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti). It means: 'at the time when it overcomes, then there is blinding darkness.'
223:
The meaning is either the explanation of the cause, or it is called 'blind darkness' (andhatama) because it oppresses through a certain cause. In this case, since the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' are always connected, the word 'yadā' (when) should be added. Alternatively, this word 'yaṃ' is a term that refers to the action. The dominance of anger, described as 'anger oppresses,' is what is meant by 'blind darkness.' Therefore, it should be understood by connecting it as: 'One who is angry does not know the benefit; one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.' 'Attha' and 'Dhamma' refer to the meaning of the Pali and the doctrine of the Pali text.

'Cittappakopana' refers to the nature that destroys by causing the mind to abandon its natural state. 'Antarato' means danger arising from within or from the mind through the power of anger. 'Taṃ' (nti) refers to anger of such a nature, or to the manner of causing harm, and so forth, by anger.

'Sabbatthāpi' means in all the first, second, and third methods as well. The phrase 'avaṇṇe paṭipajjitabbākāraṃ' (the manner to be practiced when dispraise is spoken) follows as a heading (adhikāra). Since it is not the domain of those who speak dispraise, the meaning of the word 'tatra' is shown only as 'in that dispraise.' 'Abhūtaṃ' is a word acting as the subject, meaning the speech is untrue. 'Abhūtato' is expressed by this word as 'only in an untrue manner,' because the action of being untrue is the primary state (bhāvapradhāna) and because the word 'bhāva' has been elided. The words 'iti petaṃ' and so forth are stated as 'kathaṃ' and so forth to show the manner of explanation. 'Tatra' means in that speech. 'Yojanā' is the application of the intended purpose. 'Tuṇhī' is an indeclinable (nipāta) in the sense of not speaking, and it is a bhāvana-neuter. Having said, 'Thus, this speech is untrue,' the meaning is explained with 'that which by you...' and so forth. In the word 'imināpi,' the word 'pi' includes various causes. The nature of the cause is stated as 'sabbaññuyeva' and so forth. The word 'eva' should be applied to all three terms. It means that the explanation should also be made by this reason: 'Because of being Omniscient, He is not non-omniscient; because of being well-expounded, it is not ill-expounded; because of being well-practiced, they are not ill-practiced.' Even in the case of further objections such as 'Why is He Omniscient?', the explanation must be made by showing that cause; thus it is said, 'In that matter, this and this is the cause.' 'Tatra' means in those matters of omniscience and so forth. By showing the causes and sub-causes in various ways as 'this and this is the cause,' the meaning is that the statement 'not Omniscient' and so forth should be refuted.

In that matter, this is the cause—our Teacher, the Buddha, is indeed Omniscient (Sabbaññū) because He teaches the Dhamma without error. The Dhamma is indeed well-expounded (Svākkhāta) because it definitely leads out of Saṃsāra. The Saṅgha is indeed well-practiced (Suppaṭipanna) because they are free from defilements. In this context, showing the sub-causes is also the refutation of the statement 'not Omniscient' and so forth, because such a demonstration is the cause for those qualities of omniscience and so forth. Indeed, the cause of a cause is also called a 'cause,' and the support of a support is also called a 'support,' just as 'with grass...'
224:
...as in the examples: 'The rice is sticky,' or 'He recites the Dhamma in the palace.' The second word is 'ataccha.' The first word is 'abhūta.' The fourth word is 'na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjati.' The third word is 'natthi cetaṃ amhesu.' Speech that occurs in various ways for a single meaning is called vivacana, and that same vivacana is called vevacana (synonym). Or it means speech (vacana) because the meaning is expressed by the sound, as in: 'The word Bhagavā is noble, the word Bhagavā is supreme,' and so forth. It is also understood as figurative language (pariyāyavacana) because it is speech free from diverse natures, or by the method mentioned above.

Here, an objector asks: Why is such figurative language (pariyāyavacana) taught? Is the intended meaning not achieved by each individual word alone? If it is so achieved, what is the use of that figurative language? Such teaching causes many faults, such as making the text too heavy. If that word should be spoken, only that word should have been spoken, and not any other, should it not? The answer is: Figurative language is taught so that during the time of preaching, or in the future, someone may penetrate and understand that meaning in some way. Among those who receive the teaching, one who has previously made a convention regarding those synonyms, thinking 'this word expresses this meaning,' will penetrate that meaning through that very word. Furthermore, figurative language is also taught to enable those whose minds are distracted at that moment, those who are occupied with other things, or those who have misunderstood, to understand that meaning through another synonym. For those who do not hear a certain word, they might not fully and correctly understand the stated meaning because of missing that word; however, when figurative language is spoken, they can fully understand the meaning through those other words. Alternatively, figurative language is taught for those of duller intellect so that they do not become confused by repeatedly identifying the characteristics of that meaning. For those of duller intellect, confusion may arise when identifying a single meaning with only one word, but when identifying a single meaning through many synonyms, they do not become confused because the intended meaning is determined by words occurring in a single sense through various origins of application.

Another method: It should be understood that figurative language is also taught to avoid the assumption of alternative meanings, such as 'many meanings may have the same syllables (consonants).' Since many meanings may have the same syllables through being expressed by a single word, a listener might wonder about a stated word: 'Is this meaning intended, or is that meaning intended?' Synonyms (vevacana) avoid such assumptions of alternative meanings by acting as mutual differentiators. And it is said—
225:
A word usually occurs in a single sense; it does not [by itself] make known a specific meaning. However, when associated with a synonym (pariyāya), that synonym acts as a differentiator and can make known the specific meaning.

Alternatively—even if it is not a different word, in speaking a synonymous expression, the synonym is used for the purpose of making known various meanings through those various name-designations (nāma-paññatti). Indeed, when a synonymous expression is spoken, it causes the listeners to understand various name-designations, thinking, "This meaning also has this name." From that understanding, proficiency in those various designations arises, just as proficiency arises through practice in the Nighaṇṭu (lexicon) texts.

Furthermore, synonymous expressions are used for the easy success of Dhamma preachers in firmly establishing the meaning of the scriptures (tanti) in their own minds and in making others understand easily. By speaking such synonyms, Dhamma preachers can firmly establish the meaning of the scriptures in their own minds, thereby making it easy to achieve the understanding of the listeners.

Alternatively, the Blessed One points out synonymous expressions to manifest his own attainment of the analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and to sow the seeds of such analytical knowledge in the continuities of those to be guided (veneyya). For one who has not attained such analytical knowledge, speaking such synonymous expressions is not possible. Through those synonymous expressions as heard, through practicing those synonymous expressions, and through the cultivation of other good conducts, the sowing of the seed of merit known as the attainment of the analytical knowledge of Dhamma and language becomes possible. If such an attainment is known, who would not desire those synonymous expressions? What is the use of many words?

Because the Blessed One has well-penetrated the Dhamma-dhātu, just as his knowledge ranges without obstruction in all meanings, so too does it range without obstruction in all linguistic usages. Therefore, he makes known even a single meaning through many synonyms.
