In making it known thus, there is no sluggishness of intellect nor excessive expansion of meaning, nor is there any deficiency in the Dhamma teaching. This is the unique quality (āveṇika-dhamma) of the Buddhas.

Because of the well-penetrated nature of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), just as he makes things known through the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), so too with that omniscience, because of his unobstructed activity in meaning (attha), doctrine (dhamma), and language (nirutti), he makes known even a single meaning through many synonyms with the Buddha's grace (Buddha-līḷā). There is no sluggishness of intellect in those linguistic usages or in making them known thus, because it is a means of perfect explanation. There is no expansion of meaning because of those synonyms, because they are the cause for the easy understanding of the single meaning to be taught. Nor is there any deficiency in the Dhamma teaching by speaking those words, because those synonyms constitute the perfection of the teaching.

Therefore, synonymous expressions are purposeful. One should not regard those synonyms as causing many faults such as making the text burdensome. As for the statement, "If that word were to be spoken, only that word should be spoken, not another," that too is improper because of the existence of other special benefits. By not speaking that original word but speaking another synonym, for those with concentrated minds during the time of the teaching and for those who receive it well...
226:
...the realization of the meaning of that word occurs based on the linguistic basis (sadda-pavatti-nimitta) included in those various words. Otherwise, if that same word were spoken repeatedly, those listeners might not realize the meaning. In this regard, there are summary verses:

"For the sake of making a certain meaning known through other words, synonymous discourse (pariyāya-kathā) was made even for those with distracted minds.

To prevent confusion for the dull-witted and to exclude other meanings, making the meaning clear in those various names, synonymous discourse was made.

For the sake of ease for the preachers in understanding the meaning of the scriptures (tanti), and for the sake of understanding the analytical knowledge of language (dhamma-nirutti), synonymous discourse was made.

For the sake of sowing the seed in those to be guided (veneyya) and for the sake of the Buddha's own display of power in the Dhamma-dhātu, synonymous discourse was made.

Without saying that same word, but making it known through other synonyms, it was done for the realization of the meaning for those who receive it well."

To show that this explanation applies only to such a context and should not be applied everywhere, he said "And this..." (Idañca) etc. Therein, "Only in dispraise" (avaṇṇeyevā) means only in the case of blame by way of attributing faults, whether there is a logical reason or not. "Not everywhere" (na sabbattha) means that a full explanation should not be made in all cases such as abuse, disparagement, or contempt. He makes that meaning clear with "If indeed..." (Yadi hi) etc. The word "Therefore" (tasmā) refers back to the reason for such an explanation being necessary, as stated in "He becomes suspicious" (sāsaṅkanīyo hoti). "You are a camel-lip" (oṭṭhosī) etc. is the explanation of "not everywhere." Patience (khanti) in the face of the ten grounds of abuse (akkosa-vatthu)—namely birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, disease, physical features, defilements, offenses, and abuse—is indeed called patience, because it is not the patience of reflecting on views (diṭṭhi-nijjhāna-khanti) etc.; thus it is called "patience of endurance" (adhivāsana-khanti).

Having thus explained the ground for dispraise (avaṇṇa-bhūmi), he now said "Thus" (evaṃ) etc. to explain the ground for praise (vaṇṇa-bhūmi). Therein, "in the ground for dispraise" (avaṇṇa-bhūmiyaṃ) means in the place where dispraise is manifested. Regarding "the characteristic of the Such One" (tādī-lakkhaṇaṃ), according to the method in the Mahāniddesa: "He is a Such One (tādī) in five ways: he is a Such One in the face of the desirable and undesirable; he is a Such One because he has crossed over; he is a Such One because he has transcended; he is a Such One because he is liberated; he is a Such One because of that description." Among these five meanings, the first meaning of tādī should be taken here. In that regard, there is this detailed explanation:

How is an Arahant a Such One in the face of the desirable and undesirable? An Arahant is a Such One in gain and in loss, in fame and in obscurity, in praise and in blame,
227:
He is such (tādī) in both happiness and suffering. If one arm were to be smeared with perfume, and if the other arm were to be carved with an adze, there would be no lust (rāga) for that smearing of perfume, and no anger (paṭigha) for that carving with an adze. Being free from attraction and anger, having transcended rise and fall (uggāṭinigggāṭi), and having well surpassed compliance and resistance (anurodha and virodha). Thus, it is said (in the Mahāniddesa) that the noble Arahant is such (tādī) regarding pleasant (iṭṭhāruṃ) and unpleasant (aniṭṭhāruṃ) objects.

As for the word-meaning (vacanattha)—he is called 'tādī' because he sees (unpleasant objects) just like those (pleasant objects). It means he sees unpleasant objects just as he sees pleasant objects. The characteristic of that 'tādī' is called 'tādi-lakkhaṇa'; it is the nature of looking with equal equanimity at pleasant and unpleasant objects. Alternatively, he is called 'tādī' because he is seen just like that (equanimous); that very nature is the nature of tādī, and that very characteristic is 'tādi-lakkhaṇa'. It should be connected as 'to show the characteristic of tādī in the context of dispraise (avaṇṇabhūmi)'. The word 'para' occurs in another sense, so he said 'ye keci' and so on. 'Ānandanti' means that beings endowed with that joy (pīti) rejoice greatly through this Dhamma; thus, he shows that the word 'ānanda' has the sense of instrument (karaṇattha).

A beautiful mind is called 'sumana', referring to the mind. Or, one who has a beautiful mind is called 'sumana', referring to the person endowed with that joy (somanassa). While it is appropriate for the meaning to be mental happiness (cetasika sukha) when referring to the mind, should not the mind itself be the meaning when referring to a person? It should not be mental happiness, because the word 'sumana' occurs with reference to a substance (person), like 'daṇḍittaṃ' (state of having a staff) or 'sikhittaṃ' (state of having a crest), etc.—this might be an objection. That statement is true if one considers the substance; however, here, without considering that personal substance, the word 'sumana' arises considering only the mental happiness which is the primary cause associated with that person. Therefore, here too, only mental happiness can be the meaning; thus he said, 'it is a designation (adhivacana) for mental happiness'. By this statement, the objection that other mental factors (cetasika), because they are connected to the mind and are activities of the mind, could also possibly become somanassa, is not possible, because that word is a conventional term (ruḷhī-sadda) like 'paṅkaja' (lotus)—thus he explains.

It is called 'ubbila' because it arises; it means breaking away from the previous state and reaching a special state. That very 'ubbila' is called 'ubbilāvita' due to the arrival of other causes. Or it is called 'ubbilāvita' because it floats upwards, formed by changing vowels to 'i' and 'ā'. Since the mind itself is called 'cetaso'. When the derivative (taddhita) word is formed, that word is general (sāmañña) because the meaning expressed in that word is of a general nature, or because that word is a noun. Therefore, to show that he said 'of the mind (cetaso)' when specifically investigating the connection 'of whom (is this ubbilāvita)?', he said 'kassā' and so on. In such cases, it should be understood in this way.

When that joy (pīti) arises, the body and mind reach a state of inflation like a leather bag filled with air; to show the nature that it is a designation for the worldly (gehasita) joy of elation, he said 'uddhaccāvahāyā' and so on. 'Uddhaccāvahāyā' means bringing about a state of agitation (uddhata).
228:
It is called 'ubbilāpanā' (mental excitement) because it causes the mind to float or be elated. That 'ubbilāpanā' is indeed joy (pīti); it refers to that joy. By the phrase 'in this dispensation also' (idha pi) and so on, he speaks of the distinction of the Dhamma by way of the five aggregates. As in places like 'this person also is a parajika' (ayampi parājiko), the word 'api' here is used with regard to something blameworthy. Although there is no mental excitement at all for those monks in this dispensation, he establishes the guide of the Dhamma (dhamma-netti) wishing to prevent the arising of unwholesome states in future sons of good family in such situations. In this context, where the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is mentioned by two words and the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) by one word, it is not mentioned further because it can be understood by the method stated in the Commentary: 'By way of those (formations and feelings), the inclusion of the remaining associated states is indeed excluded.' The meaning here should be understood as appropriate according to the method stated, such as 'the word api has the sense of commendation'.

In the phrase 'that very excitement of yours will be your danger (antarāya)', the word 'danger' should be understood according to the method we stated below in the section on dispraise, such as 'a word stating the reason why mental excitement should not be done'. Here too, taking the joy (pīti) described as 'one who is joyful and excited', in the statement 'because of that state of excitement', since there is no joy (pīti) devoid of mental happiness (somanassa), it is stated assuming that the mental happiness described as 'one with a happy mind (sumanā)' is also established by that very word. Alternatively, it should be understood that this is said because the fact that mental happiness causes danger is clear, whereas it is not so clear for joy (pīti). With the words 'Why is this so?', he questions by taking to heart the aforementioned meaning without analysis. The teacher, acknowledging that meaning by saying 'True', explains by way of analytical answering (vibhajja-vyākaraṇa) starting with 'But that...'.

In that context, 'this' refers to the statement that such things should not be done by the Venerable Ānanda and others. The connection is: 'Was it not praised by the Blessed One?' 'To one who praises as Buddha' means to a virtuous person who speaks the word 'Buddha' by way of recollecting the virtues. 'In its entirety (kasiṇena)' means in the sense of being whole or complete. The word 'Jambudīpassa' is a possessive connection as a part of that whole. Other teachers, however, say that 'Jambudīpassa' is a genitive case (chaṭṭhī) used in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇa); in their view, the words 'kasiṇa' and 'Jambudīpa' should be seen as being in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa). The instrumental case is also in the sense of the ablative (nissakkattha). In the phrase 'not to mention even a part', the word 'api' is in the sense of commendation (sambhāvana). Here, by the word 'ādi' (and so on):

'Udāyi, do not grieve; if Ānanda were to pass away without being free from lust, by that clarity of mind, he would rule as a king of devas for seven times, and he would rule as a king in this Jambudīpa for seven times...'
229:
“Udāyi, do not worry. If Ānanda were to pass away without being free from passion, with that clear mind, he would rule as a king of devas seven times, and as a great king in this Jambudīpa seven times. However, Udāyi, Ānanda will indeed attain Parinibbāna in this very life.” This sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.81) and others should be taken as the reference.

This refers to the joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) taught in another sutta. “Nekkhammassita” means based on wholesome states that are the means of renunciation from sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and defilements (kilesa-kāma). “Idha” means in this sutta. “Gehassita” means based on the cords of sensual pleasure, known as the household, due to the habitual practice of those living in a house.

Because the question may arise as to why only that household-based happiness (gehassita-somanassa) is intended here, the passage beginning with “Idañhi” is stated. To clarify or to establish the meaning stated as “similar to what arose for the Venerable Channa,” the passage beginning with “Teneva” is stated.

Because of the household-based affection (gehassita-pema) for the Buddha and the Dhamma, the monk Channa was unable to attain the higher distinction. “Parinibbānakāle” should be construed as being threatened and stirred by the training rule prescribed by the Blessed One near the time of his Parinibbāna. Alternatively, “Parinibbānakāle” should be construed as being stirred by the Saṅgha after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, thereby attaining the higher distinction.

“Brahmadaṇḍena” refers to the Brahma-punishment imposed as: “The monks should not speak to, should not admonish, and should not instruct the monk of such a name.” “Tajjito” means being stirred or made to fear. “Tasmā” means because household-based joy and happiness are obstacles to jhāna and so forth. For this reason, the Blessed One said in the Sakkapañha Sutta: “O Sakka, Lord of Devas, I speak of happiness (somanassa) as twofold: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”

With the passage beginning with “Ayañhi,” that same meaning is established by providing the reason. Because it is associated with lust (rāga), that joy is an obstacle. Here, although it should be said, “This is joy and happiness associated with lust,” by taking joy (pīti), happiness (somanassa) is also included. This is because there is no joy without happiness; thus, only joy is mentioned as per the method stated below.

Furthermore, because the division of happiness into what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated is mentioned in the sutta, the nature of happiness as an obstacle is clear; the nature of joy as an obstacle is not as clear. Therefore, that joy itself is specifically mentioned in the sense of being associated with lust. To make it clear in connection with the grounds for dispraise (avaṇṇabhūmi), the passage beginning with “Lobho ca” is stated. “Kodhasadiso va” means it is just like the anger mentioned in the grounds for dispraise. The meaning of the verses beginning with “Luddho” should be understood according to the method stated for the verses beginning with “Kuddho.”

“Bhikkhus, if others should speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, and if you were to be pleased, glad, and filled with joy therein, would you then be able to know whether what they said was well-spoken or ill-spoken?” the Blessed One asked. “No, Bhante,” they replied. This is called the third round (tatiya vāra). Therefore, because it is extracted at the occasion of the third round as per the method already stated in the grounds for praise (vaṇṇabhūmi), that round, at the time of teaching, because there was no person to be enlightened by that round, in the teaching...
230:
It is clear that joy (pīti) can cause an obstacle to [attaining] the higher Dhamma. Similarly, the fact that joy can be an obstacle is also not [always] obvious. Therefore, that joy is specifically spoken of as being grasped in the sense of being accompanied by lust (rāga). To clarify regarding the ground of dispraise (avaṇṇabhūmi), the words beginning with 'Yatheva' are spoken. 'Kōdhasadisō vā' means it is just like the anger already mentioned in the ground of dispraise. The meaning should be understood in the manner stated in the verses beginning with 'Kuddhō'.

"Monks, others might speak in praise of the Buddha, or in praise of the Dhamma, or in praise of the Saṅgha. If they speak such praise, and you are elated and overflowing with joy, [the Buddha asks,] 'Would you know whether what others have spoken is well-spoken or ill-spoken?' They reply, 'No, Bhante.'" This is called the Third Round (tatiya-vāra). Therefore, because it is extracted at the position of the Third Round according to the method stated in the ground of praise (vaṇṇabhūmi), although this round does not directly appear in the discourse at the time of preaching because there were no individuals to be enlightened by that round, it is included by way of meaning since that meaning is possible.

To show that this Third Round appears in detail, as shown in the Kathāvatthu treatise, the words beginning with 'Tatiya-vāro pana' are spoken. By this, the commentator shows that this round should be brought in and explained for the sake of beings who can understand it in that way at the time of the commentary. By the words beginning with 'Yatheva hi', the possibility of that meaning is illustrated with a simile. It should be connected with the statement: "An angry person does not know the meaning."

In the Fourth Round (catuttha-vāra), which is spoken of based on the aforementioned Third Round in the section showing the mode of practice, the construction (yojanā) is from the words 'Your teacher' (tumhākaṃ satthā) up to the words 'For this reason also it is true' (imināpi kāraṇena tacchaṃ). The words beginning with 'So hi Bhagavā' are the explanation of that statement. Therein, 'itipī' means 'for this reason also'. The detail should be seen in the Visuddhimagga. Although it is stated that 'there is no offense for an ordained monk to report what is true (regarding jhāna, magga, phala)', it is said that 'it should be acknowledged only to similar (sabhāga) monks' because it is appropriate. Only those similar monks desire his welfare and regard his words as trustworthy; because of that, the meaning stated as 'the non-emptiness of the Dispensation is illustrated' can be fulfilled. The words beginning with 'Evañhi' are a statement of reason. It should be connected as: evil desire (pāpicchatā) is avoided, or that evil desire is eliminated. 'Amoghatā' (non-emptiness) means not being empty because of its nature of leading out (niyyānika). 'Vuttanayena' (in the manner stated) means according to the method already stated, such as 'therein, by you' (tatra tumhehi) in that praise, and 'the second term is a synonym of the first, and the fourth of the third'.

## Cūḷasīla-vaṇṇanā

The question 'What is the connection (anusandhi)?' is asked because the inquiry might arise: 'Has the teaching not reached its climax with the praise and dispraise already mentioned?' It is expressed by the two terms 'by praise and by dispraise' (vaṇṇena ca avaṇṇena ca). Grammarians (akkharacintakā) say that just as the meaning is indicated, the sound is also indicated. Or else, because it is the cause of such speaking and because it is a portion, it is said 'by terms' (padehi). 'By dispraise and by praise' is the presentation of the actual nature by way of lack of quality and quality, and by way of blame and praise. 'Nivattō'...
